case_title: Tubos de Acero de Mexico, SA vs. Oil Country Tubular Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tubos de Acero de Mexico, SA (Appellant/Joint Shareholder/Original Petitioner, Mexican entity); Oil Country Tubular Limited (Respondent/Company); Tamtrade Ltd. (First Joint-Holder/Subsidiary of Appellant, dissolved Cayman Islands entity)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint shareholding in the Respondent Company under Folio No. OCT701946 (Certificate No. 1485) covering 14,97,000 equity shares (distinctive nos. 5483001-6980000), coupled with a Share Sale Agreement dated 29.09.1994 whereby Tamtrade Ltd. agreed to sell and transfer its rights in the shares to Appellant[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Refusal by the Respondent Company on 09.10.2012 and 17.04.2015 to rectify the Register of Members to record the Appellant as sole surviving shareholder, and transfer of the disputed shares to the IEPF on 06.12.2017[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Share sale agreement executed 29.09.1994; Tamtrade dissolved 30.09.1999; Appellant formally approached Respondent in 2012; RBI clarification issued 24.11.2014; final refusal letter dated 17.04.2015; CP No. 24/59/HDB/2017 filed on 20.01.2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original share certificates in joint names; Share Sale Agreement dated 29.09.1994; Dissolution Certificate of Tamtrade Ltd. dated 30.09.1999; RBI letter dated 24.11.2014 confirming FEMA non-applicability; Article 69 of Respondent's Articles of Association[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 24/59/HDB/2017 under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed the petition on 13.07.2017 on grounds of delay, laches, and Cayman Islands laws; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 21].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the surviving corporate joint shareholder is entitled under Regulation 25 of Table A and company Articles of Association to have the register of members rectified by transmission following the dissolution of the first joint holder[cite: 21]. 2. Whether an application for transmission and rectification of the register of members under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be defeated on grounds of limitation, delay, and laches where the right asserted is a continuing statutory right[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon the dissolution or death of a corporate or individual joint shareholder, title to the shares vests exclusively in the surviving joint holder by operation of transmission under statutory regulations and company articles, creating a continuing legal right to rectification of the register of members that cannot be defeated by mere delay[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 25 of Table A, Schedule I of the 1956 Act read with Article 69 of the company's Articles mandates that the surviving joint holder is the only entity recognized as possessing title; Section 59 rectification operates to enforce transmission rights, and Section 124(6) proviso enables the rightful owner to claim shares transferred to the IEPF[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented legal transmission standard; production of the official dissolution certificate of the first joint holder establishes the survivor's absolute title, subject to providing share certificates and an indemnity bond to protect the company[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant as the surviving joint entity was legally entitled to transmission and sole ownership of the 14,97,000 shares, rendering NCLT's dismissal erroneous[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; NCLT order dated 13.07.2017 is set aside; Appellant is declared sole shareholder entitled to 14,97,000 equity shares; Respondent is directed to rectify the Register of Members once Appellant obtains transfer orders from IEPF Authorities, upon Appellant furnishing original share certificates and an indemnity bond; no order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: Appellant, a Mexican company, appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's dismissal of its petition under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking rectification of the Register of Members of Oil Country Tubular Limited[cite: 21]. Appellant was a joint holder of 14,97,000 shares along with its subsidiary Tamtrade Ltd., which was dissolved in 1999[cite: 21]. Respondent refused transmission, prompting Appellant to approach NCLT, which dismissed the claim for delay[cite: 21]. The NCLAT held that under Regulation 25 of Table A and Article 69 of the Articles of Association, title to jointly held shares automatically vests in the survivor upon the other holder's dissolution[cite: 21]. Finding the right to transmission to be a continuing right not barred by delay, the NCLAT allowed the appeal[cite: 21].

case_title: M/s. Ind-Swift Limited vs. Registrar of Companies, Punjab & Chandigarh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Ind-Swift Limited (Appellant/Listed Defaulting Company); Registrar of Companies, Punjab & Chandigarh (Respondent); various small fixed deposit holders/objectors[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Acceptance of public fixed deposits by the Appellant company pursuant to the Companies Act, followed by default in repayments and subsequent restructuring schemes[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of public fixed deposits aggregating to Rs. 49.83 crores matured as of 31.05.2013, with additional unmatured deposits of Rs. 44.99 crores; outstanding default of Rs. 8.84 crores unpaid out of Rs. 11.66 crores due between 01.10.2016 and 31.12.2017[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CLB sanctioned 4-5 year repayment scheme on 30.09.2013; Form DPT-4 filed 28.08.2014; CA 08/2016 filed 27.09.2016; CA 39/2017 filed 28.03.2017; CA 144/2017 filed 12.09.2017; NCLT dismissed applications on 08.12.2017[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bounced repayment cheques issued to senior citizen depositors; RoC inspection reports noting continuous investor complaints and failure to provide compliance undertakings; speculative proposal to sell 20 flats of a sister entity[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After obtaining an initial restructuring order from CLB on 30.09.2013, Appellant defaulted and filed CA Nos. 8/2016, 39/2017, and 144/2017 in CP No. 27/2/2013 before NCLT New Delhi under Section 74(2) seeking further extensions and interest reduction to 4%; NCLT dismissed the applications on 08.12.2017; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a company that has already obtained a comprehensive extension scheme from the Company Law Board under Section 58AA of the 1956 Act can maintain successive applications under Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 for further rescheduling of public deposits and interest reduction[cite: 23]. 2. Whether Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 permits repeated extensions 'from time to time' to the prejudice of small fixed deposit holders[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 does not contemplate repeated or rolling extensions of time for deposit repayments, and courts cannot read the words 'from time to time' into the provision to allow serial defaults against public depositors[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 74(1)(b) imposes a strict mandate to repay pre-commencement deposits within one year or due dates; Section 74(2) provides a limited, one-time reasonable extension on financial considerations, and failure to abide attracts severe penal consequences under Section 74(3); the section cannot be abused to thwart debt recovery[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bona fide compliance test; bouncing repayment cheques, unilateral cessation of repayments, and speculative future asset disposal proposals negate genuine financial impossibility and demonstrate mala fides[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to adhere to the CLB scheme and was not entitled to second-tier extensions or interest reductions, justifying NCLT's dismissal[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 52 and 53 of 2018 are dismissed without any order as to costs, affirming the order of the NCLT New Delhi dated 08.12.2017[cite: 23].
summary: Appellant Ind-Swift Limited appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing its applications under Section 74(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking further extension of time and reduction of interest to 4% for repaying public deposits[cite: 23]. The Appellant had previously obtained an extensive 4-to-5-year repayment scheme from the CLB in September 2013 but defaulted and sought fresh extensions based on purported real estate sales of a sister entity[cite: 23]. The NCLAT held that Section 74(2) is a protective provision for depositors and cannot be interpreted as granting multiple extensions 'from time to time'[cite: 23]. Finding that the Appellant exhibited lack of bona fides and defaulted on cheques, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 23].

case_title: Mr. Ajith Kunimal Venugopal & Ors. vs. Oil Tools International Services Private Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ajith Kunimal Venugopal, Sajith Venugopal, Kunimal Parangattil Venugopal (Appellants/Original Respondents 2 to 4/Minority Directors); Oil Tools International Services Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Company); Ace Oil Fields Supply Inc. (Respondent No. 2/Original Petitioner No. 1/84.98% Majority Shareholder); Paul Waters (Respondent No. 3/Original Petitioner No. 2/Director); Gopalkumar Puthan Kattoor (Respondent No. 4/Third-Party Allottee)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture private company incorporated on 12.01.2005 for manufacturing oil and gas tools, wherein Respondent No. 2 acquired 84.98% controlling shareholding and provided unsecured loans, while Appellants managed Indian day-to-day operations[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unauthorized increase of authorized capital from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2.5 crores and preferential allotment of 18,16,158 shares at par to an outsider (Respondent No. 4) for Rs. 1.81 crores plus Rs. 9.86 crores loan, severely diluting Respondent No. 2 from 84.98% to minority, accompanied by illegal ouster of Respondent No. 3 as director[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting on 04.10.2013; EOGM notice issued 27.11.2013 for meeting on 28.11.2013; Board meeting allotting shares on 14.12.2013; Board meeting dated 30.01.2014 resolving vacation of office w.e.f. 14.12.2013; TCP No. 44/397-398/2015 filed before NCLT Mumbai[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Notice of EOGM sent by post from India to the USA only one day prior to the meeting (delivered 02.12.2013 after the meeting concluded); annual 'calendar of events' relied upon as substitute notice; contradictory dates in Form 32 versus board meeting notices[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 2 and 3 filed TCP No. 44/397-398/2015 under Sections 397-398; NCLT Mumbai on 18.09.2017/03.10.2017 allowed the petition, setting aside the capital increase, allotments, and removal of Respondent No. 3, ordering management handover, forensic audit, and exit; Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether circulating an annual 'calendar of events' dispenses with the mandatory statutory requirement under Section 172 of the Companies Act, 1956 to serve formal meeting notices with agendas 21 days in advance[cite: 24]. 2. Whether a private company whose articles mandate compliance with Section 81(1A) can validly allot unsubscribed rights shares to an outsider at par without passing a special resolution[cite: 24]. 3. Whether a director can be declared to have vacated office under Section 283(1)(g) for non-attendance where meeting notices were unserved or served post-facto[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An annual calendar of events is merely an administrative guide and cannot substitute for mandatory statutory notices with agendas under Section 172, and any general or board meeting convened without actual and timely service on directors or majority shareholders is void ab initio[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 172 requires 21 days' notice specifying agenda and venue; Section 81(1A), when adopted by articles of a private company, strictly requires a special resolution to allot shares to non-members; Section 283(1)(g) automatic vacation cannot be invoked when the director was denied notice[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict proof of dispatch and receipt; sending a postal notice to an overseas director 24 hours before a meeting constitutes intentional denial of notice, rendering the proceedings bogus[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The capital expansion, allotments to outsider, and directorship ouster were fraudulent and oppressive; NCLT's directions are maintained with minor modifications regarding refund timelines for funds infused by the outsider[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 338 of 2017 is partly allowed; Directions (i) to (iii) of NCLT Mumbai ordering management handover to Respondents 2 and 3, exit of Appellants on 31.03.2017 fair valuation, and quashing of shares to Respondent No. 4 are affirmed; Direction (iv) modified granting original petitioners option to verify and refund funds infused by Respondent No. 4 within two months, failing which refund shall be made with 10% interest within three months of the audit report[cite: 24].
summary: Appellants, minority shareholder-directors of Oil Tools International Services Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order allowing an oppression petition filed by Ace Oil Fields Supply Inc. (84.98% shareholder) and Paul Waters[cite: 24]. The Appellants had increased authorized share capital from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2.5 crores at an EOGM on 28.11.2013 and allotted 18,16,158 shares to an outsider (Gopalkumar Puthan Kattoor) at par, diluting the majority to a minority, while removing Paul Waters under Section 283(1)(g)[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that providing an annual calendar of events did not constitute legal notice under Section 172, postal notice sent to the US one day before the meeting was a sham, and allotment to an outsider violated Section 81(1A)[cite: 24]. Affirming the cancellation of allotments and management handover, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal with modified refund terms[cite: 24].

case_title: Gopalkumar Puthan Kattoor vs. Oil Tools International Services Private Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gopalkumar Puthan Kattoor (Appellant/Third-Party Investor/Allottee of 18,16,158 shares); Oil Tools International Services Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Company); Ace Oil Fields Supply Inc. & Paul Waters (Respondents 2 and 3/Original Petitioners/Majority Shareholders); Ajith Kunimal Venugopal & Ors. (Respondents 4 to 6/Promoter-Directors)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of 18,16,158 equity shares at par (Rs. 10 each) amounting to Rs. 1.81 crores to Appellant (an outsider) pursuant to a Board meeting on 14.12.2013, coupled with an unsecured loan of Rs. 9.86 crores advanced by Appellant to the company[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete quashing of Appellant's 18,16,158 shares and removal from directorship by NCLT Mumbai on grounds that the capital increase and allotment were executed behind the back of the 84.98% majority foreign shareholder[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EOGM convened 28.11.2013; Board meeting allotting shares held 14.12.2013; TCP No. 44/397-398/2015 filed in 2015; NCLT final order passed 03.10.2017; Appeal disposed 09.03.2018[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank receipts evidencing infusion of Rs. 1.81 crores towards share capital and Rs. 9.86 crores towards unsecured loan; absence of special resolution authorizing share allotment to non-members as mandated by Section 81(1A) and company articles[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 2 and 3 succeeded before NCLT Mumbai in having Appellant's share allotment and directorship declared invalid; Appellant preferred Company Appeal (AT) No. 373 of 2017 seeking refund of infused capital and loans with interest[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an outside investor whose share allotment is quashed due to procedural illegalities and lack of notice committed by managing directors is entitled to immediate refund of infused share application monies and loan amounts[cite: 24]. 2. Whether an unsubscribed rights issue in a private company can be allotted to a third party at par where the articles require a special resolution under Section 81(1A)[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where share allotments to an outsider are set aside due to lack of authority, failure of corporate notice, or breach of pre-emptive articles, the quashed allottee is entitled to restitution and restitutionary refund of all funds actually infused as share capital or loans, together with commercial interest[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 81(1A) safeguards equity structure; failure to pass a special resolution renders an outsider allotment invalid, but equity requires the returning company to refund verified infusions under equitable principles[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verifiable cash infusion standard; financial records, auditor review, and bank statements determine actual fund utilization for refund purposes[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant's share allotment remains quashed, but refund terms are modified to ensure ascertainment and prompt repayment of loan and equity funds[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 373 of 2017 is disposed of; the quashing of Appellant's shares is upheld; original petitioners permitted to ascertain infusion and refund funds within two months, failing which the company shall refund the funds within three months of forensic audit with 10% interest per annum from petition filing date[cite: 24].
summary: Appellant Gopalkumar Puthan Kattoor, a third-party investor who infused Rs. 1.81 crores for 18,16,158 shares and advanced Rs. 9.86 crores as loan to Oil Tools International Services Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order quashing his shares and directorship[cite: 24]. The NCLT found the allotment illegal as it bypassed the 84.98% foreign shareholder without notice or special resolution under Section 81(1A)[cite: 24]. The Appellant contended that as a bona fide investor, his capital and loans should be refunded with interest[cite: 24]. The NCLAT affirmed the quashing of the shares but modified the operative relief, directing the restored management to verify records and refund the infused loan and capital amounts, with 10% interest defaulting after the stipulated period[cite: 24].

case_title: K.J. Paul & Ors. vs. Seaqueen Builders Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K.J. Paul, Bindu Paul, K.A. Mathai (Appellants/Original Respondents 2 to 4); Seaqueen Builders Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Company); P.M. Johny (Respondent No. 2/Original Petitioner No. 1/62% Majority Shareholder); K.P. Augustine (Respondent No. 3/Original Petitioner No. 2/1% Shareholder and Director)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development private company incorporated on 02.01.1995, where base shareholding as of 30.09.2005 stood at 63% for Respondents 2 and 3 collectively (Johny 62%, Augustine 1%) and 37% for Appellants 1 and 2 (husband and wife), followed by clandestine allotments of 5,05,000 shares to Appellants[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Clandestine allotment of 55,000 shares on 25.04.2008 and 4,50,000 shares on 11.08.2010 to Appellants 1 and 2, inflating their stake from 37% to 90% and reducing Respondents 2 and 3 from 63% to 10%, accompanied by removal of Respondent No. 3 as director[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Base shareholding fixed 30.09.2005; allotment of 55,000 shares on 25.04.2008; Form 2 filed after 26 months on 25.06.2010; allotment of 4,50,000 shares on 11.08.2010; CP 24/2011 (TCP No. 67/2016) filed before CLB/NCLT Chennai; NCLT allowed petition on 07.12.2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificates of Posting dated 11.04.2008 bearing Satyajit Ray postal stamps which were only released by the Postal Department on 01.03.2009; Form 2 filed 26 months late violating Section 75(1); unapproved directorship continuation of Appellant No. 2 under Article 28(iii); bogus share application ledgers[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 2 and 3 filed TCP No. 67/2016; NCLT Chennai allowed the petition on 07.12.2017, quashing the 5,05,000 share allotment, invalidating meetings, appointing Respondent No. 2 as Managing Director, restoring 2005 shareholding, and granting Respondent No. 2 first option to purchase Appellants' shares; Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether share allotments and board meetings can be substantiated by Certificates of Posting bearing postage stamps released long after the purported date of posting[cite: 25]. 2. Whether an additional director who fails to retire by rotation and seek re-appointment at subsequent AGMs as required by company articles continues lawfully in office to participate in board decisions and share allotments[cite: 25]. 3. What is the appropriate cut-off date for share valuation when granting a purchase buyout option to an oppressed majority shareholder[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Production of fabricated postal certificates bearing stamps issued subsequent to the alleged date of dispatch vitiates proof of notice and demonstrates fraud; share allotments orchestrated without notice by an invalidly constituted board to convert a majority into a minority constitute gross oppression and mismanagement[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 75(1) requires return of allotment within 30 days, and inordinate delays reflect clandestine conduct; Article 28(iii) requires rotational retirement at AGMs failing which directorship ceases; Section 290 cannot validate fraudulent allotments made without quorum[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evidentiary fraud standard; documentary proof from the Postal Department establishing post-dated stamp issuance conclusively proves fabrication of notice records[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The share allotments and directorship changes were fraudulent, the 2005 base pattern must be restored, and valuation for buyout by the oppressed party must be fixed as of the date of the final order[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of; NCLT order dated 07.12.2017 is maintained with a modification to paragraph 34 substituting the share valuation period to 'determine the true and fair value of the shares of 1st respondent company, as on the date of this decision, i.e. 7.12.2017'; interim orders vacated; no order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Appellants appealed against the order of NCLT Chennai Bench allowing an oppression and mismanagement petition filed by P.M. Johny and K.P. Augustine against Seaqueen Builders Pvt. Ltd. and its managing directors[cite: 25]. Appellants 1 and 2, holding a 37% minority, issued 5,05,000 shares to themselves in 2008 and 2010 to raise their stake to 90%, reducing the 63% majority holding of Respondents 2 and 3 to 10%[cite: 25]. To prove notice of meetings, Appellants relied on Certificates of Posting from 2008 bearing a commemorative postal stamp released only in March 2009[cite: 25]. The NCLAT held that the notices were fraudulent, the board lacked quorum, and the allotments were illegal[cite: 25]. Affirming the quashing of allotments and directorship changes, the NCLAT maintained the order with share valuation fixed as of 07.12.2017[cite: 25].

case_title: Abdusalam Kurikkal Manjeri Puthusseri & Ors. vs. Ayoli Abdulla & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Abdusalam Kurikkal Manjeri Puthusseri, Mohamed Kutty Chelat, Pocker Ullattil (Appellants/Original Respondents 2, 3, and 4); Ayoli Abdulla (Respondent No. 1/Original Petitioner/50% Shareholder and Managing Director); M/s. Meezan Realtors Private Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Company)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Incorporation of private real estate company on 25.08.2003 with authorized capital of Rs. 1 lakh (1,000 shares of Rs. 100 each), where Respondent No. 1 subscribed to 500 shares (50%) and co-founder Salahuddin failed to subscribe[cite: 16]; followed by disputed transfer of 1,000 equity shares to Appellant No. 3 without consideration under pressure of a community meeting chaired by Panakkadu Hameed Ali Shihad Thangal[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete divestment and purported transfer of 1,000 equity shares (entire company capital) and unilateral removal of Respondent No. 1 from directorship without compensation[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated 25.08.2003; share transfer instruments stamped by prescribed authority on 15.11.2010; executed under coercion on 27.04.2011; approved in purported board meetings dated 27.04.2011 and 15.05.2011; Form 32 filings made on 12.09.2011; CP 100/2011 (TCP 234/2016) filed thereafter[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Expired share transfer forms presented beyond the statutory 2-month limit under Section 108(1A); board minutes written on an unnumbered 'Classmate' notebook in gross violation of Section 193; contradictory Form 32 filings by Appellant No. 2 altering Respondent No. 1's designation to Executive Director while asserting share divestment[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai allowed TCP No. 234 of 2016 on 07.08.2017 after remand from Kerala High Court, declaring share transfers to Appellants void, setting aside removal of Respondent No. 1, and invalidating ROC filings under Appellant No. 2's digital signature; Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: 1. Whether share transfer instruments presented to the prescribed authority under Section 108(1A) of the Companies Act, 1956 can be validly registered by a company after the statutory expiry of two months from presentation without revalidation[cite: 16]. 2. Whether share transfer deeds obtained under duress and physical intimidation during an informal assembly of an unincorporated entity can effectuate a valid transfer of shares and divestment of directorship in a registered company[cite: 16]. 3. Whether informal minutes scribbled on unnumbered school notebooks satisfy the mandatory evidentiary presumptions under Sections 193, 194, and 195 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Share transfer deeds that are not delivered and registered within the mandatory statutory period following government stamping under Section 108(1A) of the Companies Act, 1956 are statutorily invalid and incapable of conveying title to shares, and transfers procured through coercion and recorded by an illegally constituted board constitute actionable oppression and mismanagement[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 108(1A)(b)(ii) is mandatory; a private company cannot register an instrument of transfer delivered beyond two months from the date of presentation to the prescribed authority unless duly revalidated; Section 193 requires consecutively numbered, formally maintained minute books to attract the statutory presumptions under Sections 194 and 195[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict procedural compliance standard; unauthenticated notebooks with unnumbered pages and zero notices issued to the registered Managing Director cannot substantiate corporate resolutions or validate contested share transfers[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondent No. 1 was coerced into executing stale transfer instruments, no valid board sanctioned the transfer, and the subsequent inductions and designations were illegal and void[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with costs of Rs. 50,000/- to be paid by each of the Appellants (total Rs. 1,50,000/-) to Respondent No. 1; the order of NCLT Chennai restoring Respondent No. 1 as Managing Director and invalidating fraudulent ROC filings is affirmed; ROC Kerala is directed to inspect the company's statutory records[cite: 16].
summary: Appellants appealed against an order of NCLT Chennai Bench allowing the oppression and mismanagement petition of Respondent No. 1, Ayoli Abdulla[cite: 16]. Respondent No. 1, holding 50% equity and serving as Managing Director of Meezan Realtors Pvt. Ltd., was coerced during a community gathering on 27.04.2011 into executing share transfer forms in favour of Appellant No. 3[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that the share transfer forms were stale and invalid under Section 108(1A) of the 1956 Act having been stamped in November 2010[cite: 16]. Further, the purported board meetings were held without notice and recorded on informal notebooks violating Section 193[cite: 16]. Affirming the cancellation of transfers and restoration of the Managing Director, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal with costs[cite: 16].

case_title: Nasik Diocesan Trust Assn. Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Uday Daniel Khare & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Nasik Diocesan Trust Assn. Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant No. 1/Section 8 Company); Ajay P. Shrivastava and 5 others (Appellants 2 to 7/Directors); Uday Daniel Khare and Arvind Gangadhar More (Respondents 1 and 2/Original Petitioners/Members); Rt. Rev. Pradip Lamuel Kamble & Ors. (Respondents 3 to 9)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management and governance of a guarantee-based Section 8 charitable company holding and administering Christian ecclesiastical properties, churches, and schools across Nashik, Aurangabad, and Ahmednagar districts[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Purported vacation of office and mass removal of 19 directors/members on 30.09.2015, reduction of company membership from 46 members to 8 members, and shifting of the registered office from Nashik to Mumbai[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AGM held on 28.11.2014 attended by 46 members; disputed EGM convened on 30.09.2015; Board meetings held on 18.12.2015 and 19.12.2015; CP No. 28/2016 filed before NCLT Mumbai; MA No. 99/2017 for waiver filed during pendency; waiver allowed on 12.06.2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Attendance sheet of AGM dated 28.11.2014 establishing Respondents 1 and 2 participated as members (Sl. Nos. 4 and 5); conflicting self-serving register of members produced by Appellants reflecting only 8 members; lack of proof demonstrating lawful cessation of membership[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 1 and 2 filed CP No. 28/2016 under Section 241-242; finding their numbers fell short of the one-fifth statutory requirement under Section 244(1)(b), they filed MA No. 99/2017 for waiver; NCLT Mumbai granted waiver on 12.06.2017, against which Appellants appealed[cite: 18].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the jurisdiction to grant waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 where a serious, bona fide dispute exists as to whether the applicants are continuing members of a Section 8 company[cite: 18]. 2. Whether arbitrary exclusion of historical members, shifting of registered office outside territorial charter limits, and sudden reduction of membership from 46 to 8 constitute exceptional circumstances justifying waiver under Section 244(1)[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In a Section 8 charitable company, where historical records reflect that applicants were members and their sudden exclusion or reduction in total membership is disputed without statutory proof of lawful cessation, such exceptional circumstances justify granting waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) to enable adjudication of oppression and mismanagement claims on merits[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 confers judicial discretion on the Tribunal to waive numerical thresholds upon being objectively satisfied on the pleadings that a bona fide cause merits consideration, departing from the executive permission model under Section 399(4) of the 1956 Act[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie membership test; AGM attendance sheets containing verified signatures demonstrate membership status sufficient to seek waiver, placing the burden on the company to strictly prove lawful removal of members[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT Mumbai properly exercised sound judicial discretion in granting waiver under Section 244(1) given the drastic reduction of members and shifting of church properties[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the waiver order dated 12.06.2017 in MA No. 99/2017; NCLT Mumbai is directed to expeditiously dispose of CP No. 28/2016 in terms of Section 422 of the Act[cite: 18].
summary: Appellants challenged the order of NCLT Mumbai Bench granting waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to Respondents 1 and 2 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition against Nasik Diocesan Trust Assn. Pvt. Ltd., a Section 8 company[cite: 18]. Appellants contended that Respondents 1 and 2 were not members and the company had only 8 members[cite: 18]. The NCLAT observed that AGM attendance sheets proved Respondents were among 46 attendees in 2014, and Appellants failed to establish how membership plummeted to 8[cite: 18]. Finding that the mass removal of directors and illegal shifting of the registered office from Nashik to Mumbai constituted exceptional circumstances, the NCLAT affirmed the waiver and dismissed the appeal[cite: 18].

case_title: Proddaturi Malathi vs. M/s. SRP Logistics Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mrs. Proddaturi Malathi (Appellant/Original Petitioner/Founding 49.95% Shareholder); M/s. SRP Logistics Private Limited (Respondent No. 1/Company); Sekhar Pendam and Salalitha Parsha (Respondents 2 and 3/Managing Director and Director); Mallesham Mekala (Respondent No. 4/Third-party Allottee); Proddaturi Rama Krishna (Respondent No. 5)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Private logistics company incorporated in 2003 with 10,000 equity shares (Rs. 10 each) equally held between Appellant and Respondent No. 2 (49.95% each) and Respondent No. 5 (0.10%), which later witnessed sequential capital expansions and preferential share allotments[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unauthorized increase of authorized capital from Rs. 15 lakhs to Rs. 40 lakhs and preferential allotment of 1,50,000 shares at par (Rs. 15,00,000) to Respondent No. 2 and 100 shares at par (Rs. 1,000) to Respondent No. 4, diluting Appellant's equity from 28.58% down to 14.29%[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Incorporation in 2003; AGM on 30.09.2015 increasing capital to Rs. 15 lakhs; Board meeting on 31.10.2016; EOGM on 25.11.2016; Board meeting on 26.11.2016 allotting shares; CP No. 36/241/HDB/2017 filed on 19.03.2017; dismissed by NCLT on 19.12.2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of registered valuer report required under Section 62(1)(c); absence of explanatory statements under Section 102 and Rule 13(2) of Share Capital Rules, 2014; non-compliance with private placement offer forms (PAS-4) and banking channel rules under Section 42; unserved notices of corporate meetings[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 36/241/HDB/2017 before NCLT Hyderabad alleging oppression and illegal dilution; NCLT dismissed the petition on 19.12.2017 citing Appellant's attendance; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 19].
legal_issues: 1. Whether preferential allotment of shares and private placement to insiders and outsiders under Section 62(1)(c) and Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be legally sustained without obtaining a registered valuer's report and issuing mandatory explanatory disclosures under Rule 13 of the Share Capital and Debentures Rules, 2014[cite: 19]. 2. Whether allotting substantial shares at par to a controlling director to dilute a co-founder's equity from 49.95% to 14.29% followed by steps to oust her from directorship constitutes oppressive conduct under Section 241-242[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Any increase in subscribed capital via preferential allotment or private placement under Section 62(1)(c) read with Section 42 and Rule 13 of the Companies (Share Capital and Debentures) Rules, 2014 is mandatory, and failure to obtain a valuation report from a registered valuer and provide prescribed explanatory disclosures renders the allotment null, void, and oppressive[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 62(1)(c) mandates price determination by a registered valuer; Rule 13 requires comprehensive disclosures in the explanatory statement regarding justification, pre/post shareholding patterns, and allottee identities; Section 42 requires private placement offer letters in Form PAS-4 and strict proof of receipt through prescribed banking channels[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance standard; mere presence or signatures of a shareholder on minutes do not cure substantive statutory non-compliance or validate the absence of mandatory valuation reports and explanatory statements[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The capital expansion from Rs. 15 lakhs to Rs. 40 lakhs and the allotments to Respondents 2 and 4 violated corporate law and served solely to oppress the Appellant, warranting quashing[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed; Board resolutions dated 31.10.2016 and 26.11.2016, and EOGM resolution dated 25.11.2016 increasing share capital from Rs. 15 lakhs to Rs. 40 lakhs and allotting shares to Respondents 2 and 4 are quashed and set aside; the induction of Respondent No. 4 and removal of Appellant as Director are set aside; Respondents 2 and 3 are directed to pay costs of Rs. 1 lakh each to the Appellant[cite: 19].
summary: Appellant Proddaturi Malathi, a 49.95% founding shareholder and director of SRP Logistics Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's dismissal of her oppression petition[cite: 19]. Respondents 2 and 3 (husband and wife) conducted board and general meetings on 25.11.2016 and 26.11.2016 increasing authorized capital from Rs. 15 lakhs to Rs. 40 lakhs, allotting 1,50,000 shares to Respondent No. 2 and 100 shares to an outsider (Respondent No. 4) at par, diluting Appellant's holding to 14.29% and attempting to remove her as director[cite: 19]. The NCLAT held that the allotments violated Section 62(1)(c), Section 42, and Rule 13 due to absence of a registered valuer's report and explanatory disclosures[cite: 19]. Partly allowing the appeal, the Appellate Tribunal quashed the capital increase, restored directorship, and awarded costs[cite: 19].

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Synergies Dooray Automotive Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Appellant/Dissenting Financial Creditor with 8.94% debt); Synergies Dooray Automotive Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor); Synergies Castings Limited (Respondent No. 2/Resolution Applicant/Related Party of Debtor); Millennium Finance Limited (Respondent No. 3/Assignee Financial Creditor with 69.32% debt); Mamta Binani (Resolution Professional)[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Restructuring and insolvency resolution under IBC where Synergies Castings assigned its acquired financial debts (originating from ICICI, SBI, IDBI under 2007 MRA) amounting to Rs. 749.63 crores to Millennium Finance Limited via three assignment agreements dated 24.11.2016, followed by approval of a resolution plan proposing merger of SCL with the corporate debtor[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Multi-crore financial debts defaulted under Master Restructuring Agreement of 2007; admitted claims: MFL (Rs. 673.91 cr / 76.33% vote), AARC (Rs. 122.06 cr / 13.83% vote), EARC (Rs. 86.92 cr / 9.84% vote), SCL (Rs. 89.26 cr / 0% vote)[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SICA Repeal Act notified to take effect 01.12.2016; assignment agreements executed on 24.11.2016; Form CHG-1 charge registered 24.11.2016; agreements registered with Sub-Registrar on 25.04.2017; CoC approved resolution plan with 91.06% majority on 24.06.2017; NCLT approved plan on 02.08.2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three registered assignment agreements dated 24.11.2016 accompanied by payment penalty and registration endorsements; Form CHG-1 charge registration certificates on MCA portal; Payment Schedule Agreement dated 24.11.2016 confirming consideration arrangements between SCL and MFL[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA Nos. 43, 56, 57, 123, and 124 of 2017 before NCLT Hyderabad challenging debt assignment to MFL, CoC constitution, and plan approval; NCLT dismissed all applications and approved the plan on 02.08.2017; Appellant preferred appeals (Company Appeals No. 169-173 of 2017) to NCLAT[cite: 20].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the assignment of financial debt by a related party of the corporate debtor to a third-party NBFC prior to the enforcement of the IBC is valid, entitling the assignee to sit and vote in the Committee of Creditors as an independent financial creditor[cite: 20]. 2. Whether subsequent registration of an assignment agreement under Section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908 relates back to the date of execution for establishing admissible debt under the IBC[cite: 20]. 3. Whether a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC can provide for amalgamation or merger without conducting separate proceedings under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assignment of debt validly executed between corporate entities and contemporaneously evidenced by the registration of charges creates an enforceable legal right in the assignee, and under the relation-back doctrine of Section 47 of the Registration Act, subsequent registration operates from the date of execution; furthermore, by virtue of Section 238 of the IBC, a resolution plan can legitimately provide for corporate amalgamation without separate company court approvals[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(24) and Section 21 disqualifications apply strictly to the entity holding the debt at the relevant time; an independent assignee is not tainted as a related party merely because its assignor was one; Section 238 of the IBC overrides Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013 during corporate insolvency resolution[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Legal admissibility and public register standard; registration of charges on Form CHG-1 with the RoC and registered instruments stamped under law defeat allegations of sham or fraudulent assignments in summary insolvency proceedings[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Millennium Finance Limited was legally competent to vote in the CoC, and the resolution plan approved by 91.06% majority containing an amalgamation scheme was entirely legal[cite: 20].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 169, 170, 171, 172, and 173 of 2017 are dismissed with no order as to costs; the approval of the resolution plan dated 02.08.2017 is affirmed[cite: 20].
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's approval of the resolution plan submitted by Synergies Castings Limited (SCL) for Synergies Dooray Automotive Ltd.[cite: 20] Edelweiss contended that SCL, a related party, fraudulently assigned Rs. 749.63 crores of debt to Millennium Finance Limited (MFL) on 24.11.2016 to dilute appellant's voting share from 41.59% to 9.85% and circumvent Section 21 of the IBC[cite: 20]. It also argued that the plan's merger scheme violated Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 20]. The NCLAT held that the assignment was evidenced by contemporaneous charge filings (Form CHG-1) and subsequent registration related back to execution under Section 47 of the Registration Act[cite: 20]. MFL was not a related party, and Section 238 of the IBC overrides the Companies Act regarding merger schemes[cite: 20]. The appeals were dismissed[cite: 20].

case_title: M/s. Priyaranjani Fibres Limited & Ors. vs. D. Srinivasa Rao & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Priyaranjani Fibres Limited (Appellant No. 1/Company); Kandula Sivananda Reddy, Kandula Uttam Reddy, Kora Siva Sudershan Reddy (Appellants 2 to 4/contesting Respondents); D. Srinivasa Rao (Respondent No. 1/original Respondent No. 2/Promoter); Tej Kumar and 49 others (Respondents 2 to 51/original Petitioners/Shareholders)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A private share purchase and management transfer agreement dated 09.10.2003 executed between Respondent No. 2 and Appellant No. 2 to sell 80 lakh shares (amounting to 51% equity) for Rs. 1 crore (Rs. 8 lakhs paid upfront) and transfer management control during reference before BIFR, followed by contested allotments of 1,13,00,000 equity shares to outsiders[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Severe erosion of net worth and financial distress resulting in term loan defaults of Rs. 16 crores to IDBI and working capital defaults to State Bank of India and Allahabad Bank, leading to BIFR registration as Case No. 366/2001 on 17.09.2002[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR reference registered on 17.09.2002; impugned agreement executed on 09.10.2003; purported board/general meetings dated 29.09.2003, 30.04.2004, 31.05.2004, and 02.06.2004; termination letter issued by Respondent No. 2 on 14.10.2006; EOGMs convened on 26.12.2006 and 02.01.2008; CLB interim restraint passed on 16.07.2008[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forged AGM/Board minutes dated 29.09.2003 signed by non-shareholder attendees; back-dated Form 23, 29, and 32 filings made on 05.08.2008 after CLB injunction; disciplinary reprimand of CA K. Ranganathan by ICAI; civil court decree in OS 86/2008 permanently restraining Appellants 2 to 4 from acting as directors; power of attorneys executed by Petitioners 2 to 50[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP No. 87/2007 (T.P. No. 15/HDB/2016) was filed before CLB/NCLT alleging oppression and mismanagement; NCLT Hyderabad Bench allowed the petition on 15.05.2017, declaring the agreement terminated, setting aside share allotments and appointments of Appellants 2 to 4, and imposing Rs. 3 lakhs costs, which was appealed before NCLAT[cite: 11].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an agreement between individual promoters to transfer majority shareholding and management control during the pendency of SICA proceedings before BIFR without statutory approvals or general body sanction is valid and binding on the company and its shareholders[cite: 11]. 2. Whether the appointment of directors and allotment of 1,13,00,000 equity shares executed without notice to existing directors/shareholders and in breach of CLB injunction orders can be sustained[cite: 11]. 3. Whether powers of attorney granting broad authorization to an authorized petitioner satisfy the requirement of intelligent consent under Section 399(3) of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An agreement executed by an individual director to transfer company management and pledged shares during the pendency of statutory rehabilitation proceedings without shareholder approval or regulatory sanction is void and unenforceable against the company and non-signatory shareholders, and back-dated share allotments made without statutory notices or compliance with pre-emption rights constitute oppression and mismanagement[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Pending reference under Section 15 and 16 of SICA strips individual directors of the capacity to execute private management transfers; Section 32 of SICA overrides inconsistent private agreements; Section 260 of the Companies Act, 1956 requires additional directors to be approved by shareholders at the ensuing AGM failing which their office ceases automatically; Section 399(3) requires valid written authorization, which is satisfied by comprehensive power of attorney referring to share folio details[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict scrutiny of corporate meeting records; minutes showing presence of non-shareholders, unserved notices of EGMs/BMs, and back-dated statutory filings made subsequent to judicial injunctions are fraudulent and cannot confer directorship or title to shares[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellants 2 to 4 never legally acquired shares or directorship, rendering their acts oppressive, while the agreement dated 09.10.2003 is non-binding on the company and its shareholders[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with modification of direction 'A' of NCLT's order to declare the agreement dated 09.10.2003 non-binding on the Company and the Petitioners-shareholders, rather than deemed terminated; Appellants 2 to 4 are directed to pay costs of Rs. 1 lakh each into the bank account of the Company[cite: 11].
summary: Respondents 2 to 51 holding 10.33% equity in Priyaranjani Fibres Limited filed a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against Appellants 2 to 4 and Respondent No. 2[cite: 11]. Respondent No. 2 had privately agreed to transfer 80 lakh shares and company management to Appellant No. 2 during pending BIFR reference[cite: 11]. Appellants 2 to 4 took over the factory, purported to act as directors, and fabricated board resolutions allotting 1,13,00,000 equity shares to outsiders[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that the management transfer lacked BIFR and general body approval, minutes were fabricated, and share allotments were void[cite: 11]. Confirming the NCLT's order with slight modification, the NCLAT declared the agreement non-binding and dismissed the appeal with costs[cite: 11].

case_title: Belfin Spa & Ors. vs. Cima Shyam Springs Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Belfin Spa, Sergio Bellazzi, and Rita Bellazzi (Appellants/Original Petitioners/Majority Shareholders); Cima Shyam Springs Private Limited (Respondent No. 1/Company); Jaimin Girish Patel and Hemal Patel (Respondents 2 and 3/Directors); Shyam Management Services, Shyam Marketing, Shyam Industries, Pinakin Raman Amin (Respondents 4 to 7/Allottees)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture private company incorporated on 26.09.2008 with authorized capital of 45 lakh shares (Rs. 10 each), where Appellant No. 1 held a 51.36% controlling majority and Respondents 2 and 3 managed Indian operations, followed by successive share and debenture issuances to dilute Appellants[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants invested Rs. 1.82 crore initial equity; company incurred operational losses and credit limits of Rs. 9 crores from Bank of Baroda were secured against personal guarantees of Respondents 2 and 3[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting on 28.02.2011 allotting 95,500 shares and convertible debentures; meeting on 19.04.2011 converting 35% debentures; meeting on 18.05.2011 filing Form 32 ousting Appellants; EOGM on 18.06.2011; meeting on 02.07.2011 allotting 3,83,334 shares on 07.07.2011; meeting on 18.09.2011 allotting 3,87,066 shares; meeting on 25.07.2012 allotting 80,010 shares[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Incomplete email notices without valid email addresses; protest letters dated 15.06.2011 and 04.07.2011 proving Appellants travelled from Italy but were wrongfully kept waiting outside and blocked from attending the 02.07.2011 board meeting; ROC search dated 03.03.2014 revealing covert allotments[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CP No. 3/397-398/CLB/MB/2013 (T.P. No. 31/397-398/NCLT/AHM/2016) was partly allowed by NCLT Ahmedabad on 05.05.2017 by setting aside allotments of 19.04.2011 and 25.07.2012; Appellants appealed against the refusal to set aside the other allotments and directorship removals[cite: 12].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the issuance of shares and convertible debentures to sister entities on short, defective, or unserved notices resulting in the dilution of a foreign majority shareholder constitutes oppressive conduct and abuse of fiduciary power[cite: 12]. 2. Whether directors can declare foreign directors to have vacated office under Section 283(1)(g) of the Companies Act, 1956 when notices of meetings were unserved or when the directors were physically prevented from participating[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In closely held companies, directors occupy a fiduciary position and cannot exercise the power to issue additional share capital or convertible instruments for the improper motive of converting a majority shareholder into a minority, nor can they oust directors for non-attendance under Section 283(1)(g) when meetings suffer from defective notice or deliberate exclusion[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Principles of Section 81 of the Companies Act, 1956 govern closely held companies; shares must be offered pro-rata to existing shareholders; Section 283(1)(g) requires three consecutive absences pursuant to legally valid and duly served notices; Section 424 of the 2013 Act bars unpermitted additional documents in appeal[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden is on the company/directors to prove actual dispatch and valid receipt of notices with clear agendas; sending vague agendas to truncated email addresses within 3 working days to overseas directors fails the test of service[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Allotments dated 28.02.2011, 07.07.2011, and 18.09.2011, together with the capital increase and director vacations, were fraudulent and oppressive, warranting cancellation and restoration of status quo ante[cite: 12].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; allotments of 95,500 shares and convertible debentures on 28.02.2011, capital increase on 18.06.2011, allotments of 3,83,334 shares on 07.07.2011, and 3,87,066 shares on 18.09.2011, as well as the removal of Appellants 2 and 3 as directors, are set aside; shareholding is restored ante 28.02.2011; forensic audit and valuation ordered with buyout mechanism; Respondents 2 and 3 ordered to pay personal costs of Rs. 1 lakh each[cite: 12].
summary: Appellants, holding 51.36% in Cima Shyam Springs Private Limited, challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order which failed to set aside various allotments and board removals orchestrated by Indian directors (Respondents 2 and 3) that reduced Appellants' equity to 39.87%[cite: 12]. The Appellants were served with defective notices, provided short notice periods, and physically prevented from entering the board meeting on 02.07.2011 after travelling from Italy[cite: 12]. The NCLAT held that the fiduciary power to issue capital was abused to wrest control and that the removal under Section 283(1)(g) was illegal[cite: 12]. Allowing the appeal, the Appellate Tribunal quashed the allotments, restored the Appellants' directorship and majority shareholding, ordered forensic audit and independent valuation, and imposed personal costs on Respondents 2 and 3[cite: 12].

case_title: M/s. Power Finance Corporation Limited vs. M/s. Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Power Finance Corporation Limited (Appellant/Original Petitioner/Lead Lender); M/s. Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation Limited (Respondent No. 1/Company); Kasliwal Promoters (Respondents 2 to 6); M/s. Entegra Limited (Respondent No. 8/Holding Company/Pledgor); MW Infra and S. Kumar entities (Respondents 7 & 9/Guarantors); Ramkrishnan N (Respondent No. 10/Ex-Company Secretary)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation and financing of 400 MW Maheshwar Hydel Dam Project involving term loans of Rs. 100 crores and foreign currency loans of USD 34 million by PFC, supported by pledge deeds dated 30.11.2006, 16.11.2010, and 14.01.2011 covering 29,17,20,330 shares, and subordinate loan agreement dated 29.09.2006 of Rs. 375 crores[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Persistent default in loan repayments and inability to infuse promoter equity leading to classification as NPA on 31.03.2012; loan recall notice issued on 05.01.2016 for aggregate defaults including subordinate debt of Rs. 375 crores plus interest[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Level Committee Report dated 02.05.2015; subordinate debt partial conversion notices dated 18.12.2015 and 27.05.2016; pledge invocation notice dated 19.05.2016 giving 30 days; transfer of shares executed in 15 days on 01.06.2016; Company Petition filed in early 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Certificate No. 47 lacking valid transfer endorsement under Section 56; board minutes of 01.06.2016 passed solely by lender nominees over promoter dissent; valuation report by SBI Capital Markets fixing equity share value at Nil and transferring shares for token Re. 1/-; ROC complaint and management dispute status flagged on 29.04.2016[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP No. 15/241-242/NCLT/AHM/2017 alleging past mismanagement and siphoning, while seeking statutory immunities; NCLT Ahmedabad dismissed the petition on 15.06.2017 on grounds of defective title, limitation, delay, lack of bona fides, and lenders' prior control, which was appealed before NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a lender that assumes management control since 2005 through altered articles can maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 based on concluded historical defaults[cite: 13]. 2. Whether the unilateral appropriation of pledged shares for token consideration of Re. 1/- within 15 days of a 30-day notice is permissible under Section 176 of the Contract Act, 1872 and Section 56 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 13]. 3. Whether conversion of debt to equity under Section 62(3) of the Act is valid when the special resolution authorizing it was passed four years after entering into the loan agreement[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party whose acquired shareholding title is tainted by illegal pledge invocation and invalid debt conversion lacks clean title and bona fides to invoke Section 241, and an entity exercising de facto and de jure management control cannot maintain oppression proceedings against ousted promoters for historical defaults[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 phrase 'have been' signifies continuous affairs extending to the present, not past, concluded acts; Section 176 of the Contract Act is mandatory and pawnors cannot acquire ownership of pledged goods unilaterally; Section 62(3) requires general meeting approval 'before' raising the loan; Section 106 prohibits denying voting rights on pledged shares[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance standard for corporate acquisitions and bona fide intent; premature transfer before notice expiry, non-compliance with transfer form requirements, and self-serving resolutions passed by interested nominee directors vitiate acquisition[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petition was mala fide and aimed at evading regulatory prosecution; dismissal was justified, and public interest required a statutory investigation under Section 210[cite: 13].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the dismissal of the Company Petition is maintained; affairs of the Company are referred to the Central Government for investigation under Section 210 with forensic audit under CAG supervision; Contempt Case 10/2017 and pending IAs disposed[cite: 13].
summary: Power Finance Corporation appealed against NCLT Ahmedabad's dismissal of its oppression and mismanagement petition against Shree Maheshwar Hydel Power Corporation and its promoters[cite: 13]. PFC claimed a 23.32% shareholding acquired by converting subordinate debt and invoking pledged shares, alleging promoter siphoning and seeking immunity from prosecution by statutory authorities[cite: 13]. The NCLAT held that PFC had exercised complete management control since 2005 through altered articles and could not blame promoters[cite: 13]. The share transfer violated Section 176 of the Contract Act and Section 56 and 62(3) of the Companies Act[cite: 13]. Dismissing the appeal for lack of bona fides and maintainability, the NCLAT directed an investigation under Section 210[cite: 13].

case_title: M/s. Sanchar Tele Systems Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar Of Companies, NCT Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Sanchar Tele Systems Limited (Appellant No. 1/Company); Chandra Kant Bhardwaj (Appellant No. 2/Whole-time Director); Sanjay Gupta, Suresh Chandra Gupta, Priyanka Gupta (Appellants 3 to 5/Directors); Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana (Respondent)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate statutory compliances concerning the mandatory appointment of a whole-time Company Secretary under the paid-up capital threshold requirements[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to appoint a whole-time Company Secretary spanning a continuous period of 2,190 days from 01.04.2011 to 31.03.2017 (comprising 1,095 days under the 1956 Act and 1,095 days under the 2013 Act)[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Period of default: 01.04.2011 to 31.03.2014 under Section 383A(1A) of the Old Act; 01.04.2014 to 31.03.2017 under Section 203(5) of the New Act; Compounding application filed under Section 441 in 2017 after making good the default[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC statutory records; Form 23AC and digital signature records of Appellants 4 and 5 establishing active involvement in management; absence of any board resolution or statutory return filed under Section 5 allocating compliance exclusively to Appellant No. 2[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 16/110/2017 under Section 441 of the 2013 Act; NCLT New Delhi on 18.08.2017 compounded the offence by taking a lenient view and imposing one-fifth of the maximum fine (Rs. 2,10,000 on Company and Rs. 3,35,000 on each Director), which was appealed to NCLAT seeking exemption for Appellants 3 to 5[cite: 14].
legal_issues: 1. Whether ordinary non-executive directors can be exempted from compounding penalties under Section 383A(1A) of the Companies Act, 1956 and Section 203(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 in the absence of a board resolution and statutory return designating a specific officer in default[cite: 14]. 2. Whether the penal liability under Section 203(5) is restricted to 'officers who are in default' or applies strictly to 'every director' by virtue of the plain statutory language[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of a board resolution assigning compliance responsibilities to a specified director and a corresponding return filed with the RoC, all directors who actively participate in the company's affairs remain liable as officers in default under Section 383A(1A) of the 1956 Act, and under Section 203(5) of the 2013 Act, statutory liability is explicitly fastened on every director[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5 of the 1956 Act requires a board resolution and a timely filed return under clauses (f) and (g) to shield other directors; Section 203(5) of the 2013 Act intentionally uses the phrase 'every director and key managerial personnel who is in default', which directly attaches liability to all directors rather than borrowing the general definition of officer in default[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory compliance standard; bald assertions that a company had a managing director cannot discharge penal liability without certified board resolutions and statutory returns proving exclusive delegation of compliance duties[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The compounding order properly imposed proportionate fines across all appellant directors, warranting no interference[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs, upholding the compounding order dated 18.08.2017 passed by the NCLT New Delhi[cite: 14].
summary: Appellants, comprising Sanchar Tele Systems Limited and its directors, appealed against the compounding order of NCLT New Delhi in CP No. 16/110/2017[cite: 14]. The company had defaulted in appointing a whole-time Company Secretary from 01.04.2011 to 31.03.2017[cite: 14]. NCLT imposed a compounded fine of one-fifth of the maximum penalty on the company and each of the four individual directors[cite: 14]. Appellants 3 to 5 argued that only the whole-time director was an officer in default[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that under Section 5 of the 1956 Act, directors cannot escape liability without showing a filed return specifying an officer in default[cite: 14]. Furthermore, Section 203(5) of the 2013 Act explicitly penalizes every director[cite: 14]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 14].

case_title: M/s. Sanchar Tele Systems Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar Of Companies, NCT Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Sanchar Tele Systems Limited (Appellant No. 1/Company); Chandra Kant Bhardwaj (Appellant No. 2/Whole-time Director); Sanjay Gupta, Suresh Chandra Gupta, Priyanka Gupta (Appellants 3 to 5/Directors); Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana (Respondent)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate statutory compliances regarding timely filing of Annual Returns and Balance Sheets/Financial Statements with the RoC[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Complete failure to file Financial Statements and Annual Returns for the financial years 2013-2014 within the prescribed statutory period, attracting per-day continuing default fines[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Defaults occurred for FY 2013-2014; defaults were belatedly rectified and documents filed with RoC on 31.03.2017 and 11.04.2017, after which compounding was sought in 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC complaint before ACMM Tis Hazari; statutory forms digitally signed by Appellants 4 and 5; absence of any board resolutions or filed returns proving designated responsibility upon a particular director[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 16/94/2017 under Section 441 of the 2013 Act read with Section 621A of the 1956 Act; NCLT New Delhi on 18.08.2017 compounded the default by imposing one-fifth of the maximum fine (Rs. 1,93,500 on Company and Rs. 1,89,500 on each Director), which Appellants appealed to absolve Appellants 3 to 5[cite: 14].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the directors of a company can avoid liability under Section 162 of the Companies Act, 1956 and Section 137(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 on the ground that the RoC originally prosecuted only the company and the managing director before the criminal court[cite: 14]. 2. Whether individual directors are liable under Section 137(3) of the 2013 Act in the absence of a designated Managing Director, CFO, or director specifically charged with filing duties[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A complaint filed by the RoC against select officers in a magistrate court does not estop the RoC or the tribunal from enforcing compounding liabilities against all directors who joined in the compounding application and took part in company management without producing statutory delegation returns[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 137(3) of the 2013 Act mandates that in the absence of a Managing Director, CFO, or specifically charged director, all the directors of the company shall be punishable; Section 5 of the 1956 Act similarly fastens liability on all directors if no specific officer is designated via a registered return[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented participation in corporate filings; digital signing of financial records and notices by directors refutes the defense of being mere non-executive directors with no operational liability[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all directors actively participated in affairs and failed to prove any statutory resolution charging a single director, all applicants were legally liable and the compounded penalty was justified[cite: 14].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs, affirming the order of the NCLT New Delhi dated 18.08.2017[cite: 14].
summary: Appellants, Sanchar Tele Systems Limited and its directors, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order in CP No. 16/94/2017 compounding the default of non-filing of Financial Statements and Annual Returns for FY 2013-2014 under Section 162 of the 1956 Act and Section 137(3) of the 2013 Act[cite: 14]. Fines amounting to one-fifth of the statutory maximum were imposed on the company and all four directors[cite: 14]. Appellants 3 to 5 argued they were ordinary directors and pointed out that the RoC only prosecuted the company and managing director in criminal court[cite: 14]. The NCLAT rejected the plea, holding that Section 137(3) holds all directors liable in the absence of a formal statutory designation, and affirmed the order[cite: 14].

case_title: Synthite Industries Limited vs. Plant Lipids (P) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Synthite Industries Limited (Appellant/Company); Plant Lipids (P) Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Transferee/Original Petitioner); Beena George (Respondent No. 10/Transferor); C.V. Jacob & other directors (Respondents 2 to 9)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lodgment of share transfer deed for 25 equity shares (Rs. 10 each) of Synthite Industries Limited by Respondent No. 10 in favour of Respondent No. 1 for a total consideration of Rs. 12,50,000/-[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Refusal by the Board of Directors of the Appellant Company on 26.10.2016 to register the transfer of 25 equity shares[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Unanimous shareholder resolution to convert to private company passed on 25.09.2015 adopting Articles 3A and 23A; share transfer form executed on 31.08.2016 and lodged on 01.09.2016; application for conversion filed before NCLT on 20.09.2016; Board refusal communicated on 27.10.2016; Section 58 petition filed thereafter[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolution of Plant Lipids dated 31.08.2016 authorizing purchase of up to 15,000 shares of Synthite from the open/off-market; concurrent identical resolution by sister company Aromatic Ingredients; existing Article 24 empowering directors to decline undesirable transferees; admissions in pleadings of direct commercial rivalry and employee poaching[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 9 of 2016 under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Chennai Bench allowed the petition on 27.03.2018 declaring the board refusal null and void and directing share transfer registration; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 15].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Board of Directors of an unlisted public company undergoing reconversion to a private company has 'sufficient cause' under Section 58(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to refuse registration of a share transfer to an admitted commercial competitor[cite: 15]. 2. Whether an existing Article in the Articles of Association empowering directors to reject undesirable transferees operates as a valid contract and justifiable basis to refuse transfer under Section 58(2) and 58(4)[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory free transferability of shares in a public company under Section 58(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is subject to the board's fiduciary power under Section 58(4) to refuse registration for 'sufficient cause' where an acquisition by a hostile competitor threatens the stability and business interests of a closely held entity[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58(4) acts as a limited restriction on Section 58(2); whether sufficient cause exists is a mixed question of law and fact; articles of association constitute a binding statutory contract between the company and members, and pre-existing discretionary rejection articles remain fully enforceable[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bona fide exercise of board discretion; a board decision will not be second-guessed judicially when backed by evidence of rival commercial interest, admitted corporate hostility, and formal corporate resolutions demonstrating an intent to orchestrate a hostile creep-in or takeover[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Synthite possessed bona fide, sufficient cause to refuse registration to protect company interests, rendering the NCLT order unsustainable[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench is quashed and set aside; CP No. 9 of 2016 is rejected with no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Synthite Industries Limited appealed against the NCLT Chennai Bench order directing it to register the transfer of 25 shares transferred by shareholder Beena George to Plant Lipids (P) Ltd. under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15]. Synthite, an unlisted company in the process of converting into a private entity, refused registration citing Article 24 and its fiduciary duty to prevent entry of a fierce commercial competitor aiming for a hostile creep-in via a board resolution to acquire 15,000 shares[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that Section 58(4) permits refusal for sufficient cause and that protecting the company from destabilization by an admitted competitor is a bona fide exercise of power[cite: 15]. Setting aside the NCLT order, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and rejected the transfer petition[cite: 15].

case_title: Synthite Industries Limited vs. M/s Aromatic Ingredients (P) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Synthite Industries Limited (Appellant/Company); M/s Aromatic Ingredients (P) Ltd. (Respondent No. 1/Transferee/Original Petitioner); C.J. George (Respondent No. 10/Transferor/Managing Director of Transferee); C.V. Jacob & other directors (Respondents 2 to 9)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lodgment of share transfer instrument for 10 equity shares (Rs. 10 each) of Synthite Industries Limited executed by Respondent No. 10 in favour of Respondent No. 1[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Rejection by the Board of Directors of Synthite Industries Limited on 26.10.2016 refusing registration of the 10 equity shares[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Unanimous special resolution for conversion into private company passed on 25.09.2015 adopting Articles 3A and 23A; board resolution of Aromatic Ingredients passed on 31.08.2016; transfer instrument executed on 31.08.2016 and lodged on 01.09.2016; conversion application filed on 20.09.2016; refusal notice issued on 27.10.2016[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolution of Aromatic Ingredients dated 31.08.2016 authorizing acquisition of up to 15,000 shares of Synthite from open/off-market; identical resolution by sister company Plant Lipids; Article 24 authorizing directors to reject undesirable members; common control of transferee by transferor C.J. George[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 10 of 2016 under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Chennai Bench allowed the petition on 27.03.2018 setting aside the refusal and directing registration; Appellant appealed before NCLAT[cite: 15].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Board of Directors has 'sufficient cause' under Section 58(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to decline registration of share transfers where a common promoter of competitor companies seeks to introduce corporate entities under his control into a closely held company[cite: 15]. 2. Whether an apprehension of destabilization and hostile takeover based on formal resolutions to acquire up to 15,000 shares constitutes a legitimate legal ground to refuse registration of a miniscule tranche of 10 shares[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The right of free transferability under Section 58(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 is restricted by the company's statutory power under Section 58(4) to refuse registration upon sufficient cause where a transfer is part of a concerted design by rival management to gain an obstructive foothold[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 58(4) recognizes sufficient cause as a legitimate protection for corporate autonomy; Articles of Association allowing rejection of transferees remain binding and operative alongside statutory standards[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Holistic intent test; miniscule share transfers cannot be evaluated in isolation from contemporaneous board resolutions of the transferee evidencing a broader strategy to purchase substantial share blocks from open or off-market channels[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Synthite's Board acted in good faith within its fiduciary powers in concluding that the transferee's entry was prejudicial, warranting dismissal of the petition[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai Bench is quashed and set aside; CP No. 10 of 2016 is rejected with no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Synthite Industries Limited appealed against the order of NCLT Chennai Bench directing registration of 10 equity shares transferred by C.J. George to M/s Aromatic Ingredients (P) Ltd. under Section 58 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15]. Synthite, an unlisted company converting to a private company, refused the transfer relying on Article 24 and citing the transferee's concerted move with sister competitor Plant Lipids (both led by C.J. George) to acquire 15,000 shares to destabilize management[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that the Board exercised its fiduciary powers in good faith for sufficient cause under Section 58(4)[cite: 15]. Setting aside the NCLT's decision, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and dismissed the company petition[cite: 15].

case_title: S.N. Plumbing Pvt Ltd vs. IL&FS Engg & Construction Company Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S.N. Plumbing Pvt Ltd (Appellant); IL&FS Engg & Construction Company Ltd (Respondent)[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An insolvency appeal arising from commercial transactions and contractual dealings between the operational entity and the construction company[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact quantified default metrics, dates of default, and specific amounts are not set out in the appellate record[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The matter was scheduled for hearing before the Appellate Tribunal on 04.06.2018[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The order sheet record reflecting that the case was called twice (morning session and second call) with no appearance entered by the Appellant or their counsel[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal was preferred before the NCLAT, which came up for determination on 04.06.2018[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency appeal is liable to be dismissed for non-prosecution when the appellant fails to appear upon multiple calls and demonstrates no interest in pursuing the proceedings[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal before an appellate forum is liable to be dismissed for non-prosecution where the appellant, after repeated calls, remains unrepresented and evinces no interest in proceeding with the matter[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural provisions governing appellate adjudication permit termination of proceedings without adjudication on the merits if default of appearance is total and unpursued[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Record of successive calls and passes-over demonstrating repeated non-appearance of the appellant and its counsel[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The complete absence of representation on behalf of the appellant upon two successive calls confirms lack of interest in pursuing the appeal, warranting dismissal for non-prosecution[cite: 6].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for non-prosecution[cite: 6].
summary: The Appellant, S.N. Plumbing Pvt Ltd, filed an appeal against the Respondent, IL&FS Engg & Construction Company Ltd, before the NCLAT[cite: 6].
