On 04.06.2018, when the matter was called in the morning session, no one appeared on behalf of the Appellant, prompting the matter to be passed over[cite: 6]. Upon being called a second time, the Appellant and its counsel remained absent[cite: 6]. The Appellate Tribunal observed that the Appellant was not interested in pursuing the matter[cite: 6]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal for non-prosecution without going into the merits of the dispute[cite: 6].

case_title: Sohan Singh Aujla & Anr. vs. Haveli Restaurant & Resorts Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sohan Singh Aujla & Anr. (Appellants); Haveli Restaurant & Resorts Ltd. & Ors. (Respondents)[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rectification of register of members arising from an alleged illegal transfer of company shares that took place in the year 2011[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The alleged illegal transfer occurred in 2011; no specific monetary default figures are applicable to this share transfer dispute[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed transfer was executed in 2011, and the Company Petition under Section 59 was filed in the year 2018[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lack of documentary evidence, specific dates, or concrete details on record to substantiate the Appellants' bare assertion that they obtained knowledge of the transfer in September 2015[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The National Company Law Tribunal, Chandigarh Bench dismissed the Company Petition under Section 59 on the ground of limitation; the Appellants challenged this dismissal before the NCLAT[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for rectification of the register of members under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 filed in 2018 for a transfer of shares that occurred in 2011 is barred by limitation in the absence of substantiated evidence showing delayed discovery or source of knowledge[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An action for rectification of a share register must be initiated within the prescribed limitation period from the date of the impugned transfer, and an assertion of delayed discovery cannot defeat limitation without demonstrable proof of the date and source of knowledge[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be invoked after an inordinate delay of several years unless a legally valid, factually substantiated basis for condoning delay or computing limitation from discovery is established[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Self-serving verbal assertions of delayed discovery through third parties are legally insufficient unless supported by concrete record evidence indicating the specific date and authentic source of knowledge[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the transfer occurred in 2011 and the petition was initiated in 2018 without any evidential backing for the claimed late discovery in 2015, the petition was hopelessly time-barred, and the appeal was devoid of merit[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and I.A. No. 1877 of 2018 is disposed of[cite: 7].
summary: The Appellants, Sohan Singh Aujla and another, challenged the order of the NCLT Chandigarh Bench dismissing their petition filed under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 on limitation grounds[cite: 7]. The impugned share transfer occurred in 2011, whereas the petition was initiated in 2018[cite: 7]. The Appellants claimed they only learned of the illegal transfer from a third party in September 2015[cite: 7]. The NCLAT rejected this submission, holding that there was no evidence on record proving the exact date or source of knowledge to substantiate delayed discovery[cite: 7]. Upholding the NCLT's finding that the claim was barred by limitation, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 7].

case_title: Thothappa Nainar Mohamed Sirajdheen vs. Intex Technologies (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Thothappa Nainar Mohamed Sirajdheen (Appellant), Managing Director/shareholder of the Corporate Debtor; Intex Technologies (India) Ltd. (Respondent/Operational Creditor)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods/materials by Intex Technologies (India) Ltd. to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from unpaid supplies and dishonoured cheques issued by the Corporate Debtor's Managing Director; specific debt metrics are not quantified in the order[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC was issued by the Operational Creditor; on 22 June 2018, the Adjudicating Authority admitted the Section 9 petition[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter dated 11 June 2017 regarding a pending criminal proceeding against the Managing Director concerning cheque bounce and alleged unauthorized purchases, and the absence of any contemporaneous communication disputing the quality or supply of goods[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Division Bench, Chennai admitted the Section 9 application on 22 June 2018 finding no pre-existing dispute, which order was appealed before the NCLAT[cite: 9].
legal_issues: 1. Whether pending criminal proceedings against a Managing Director regarding cheque dishonour and unauthorized procurement constitute a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 9]. 2. Whether an operational debt under Section 9 can be resisted without raising a prior dispute regarding the supply or quality of goods before receipt of the Section 8(1) demand notice[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pre-existing dispute under the IBC must directly concern the quality, supply, or contractual liability of the operational goods/services raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice, and unrelated criminal proceedings against a director do not constitute a statutory dispute against the debt[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(1) read with Section 9 requires a demonstrable dispute regarding the commercial transaction itself prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice; pending criminal liability before another court does not negate the existence of an operational default[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous evidence standard; the debtor must produce proof that a grievance touching upon the supply or quality of goods was communicated to the creditor prior to the Section 8(1) notice[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: As no dispute regarding the goods was raised prior to the demand notice, the NCLT correctly admitted the application under Section 9, rendering the appeal without merit[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without cost[cite: 9].
summary: The Appellant, Thothappa Nainar Mohamed Sirajdheen, appealed an order of NCLT Chennai admitting a Section 9 application filed by Intex Technologies (India) Ltd.[cite: 9] The Appellant contended that a pre-existing dispute existed, citing an 11 June 2017 letter concerning criminal proceedings against the Managing Director for bounced cheques and unauthorized purchases[cite: 9]. The NCLAT held that pending criminal proceedings do not decide operational debt admissibility under the IBC[cite: 9]. Because the Corporate Debtor failed to produce any evidence demonstrating a dispute regarding the quality or supply of goods raised prior to the Section 8(1) demand notice, the Appellate Tribunal affirmed the admission of the insolvency petition and dismissed the appeal[cite: 9].

case_title: Arise India Limited vs. TCI Freight
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arise India Limited (Appellant/Corporate Debtor); TCI Freight, a division of Transport Corporation of India Ltd. (Respondent/Operational Creditor)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Freight and transport logistics services provided by TCI Freight to Arise India Limited giving rise to operational dues[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose out of unpaid freight operational invoices; exact default amount and default date are not specified in the appellate order[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority was passed prior to the appellate determination on 03.05.2018[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Company court/tribunal records establishing that a Provisional Liquidator had already been appointed for the Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An application under Section 9 of the IBC was initiated against Arise India Limited, culminating in an order that was carried in appeal by Arise India Limited before the NCLAT[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 can be initiated against a Corporate Debtor for whom a Provisional Liquidator has already been appointed[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a Provisional Liquidator has already been appointed to take custody of a company's estate, parallel or subsequent initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC against the same company is legally impermissible[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC cannot be invoked against an entity whose liquidation process has already been set in motion via the appointment of a Provisional Liquidator[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial record test; proof of a preexisting order appointing a Provisional Liquidator acts as a threshold jurisdictional bar against initiating CIRP[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appointment of a Provisional Liquidator precludes the commencement of CIRP under Section 9, requiring dismissal of the appeal[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without cost, declining interference with the impugned order[cite: 10].
summary: The Appellant, Arise India Limited, challenged an order passed in an insolvency proceeding involving operational creditor TCI Freight (a division of Transport Corporation of India Ltd.)[cite: 10]. The core question before the NCLAT was whether insolvency resolution proceedings could proceed against a company where liquidation had already commenced[cite: 10]. The Appellate Tribunal held that where a Provisional Liquidator has already been appointed, the question of initiating a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 against the same Corporate Debtor does not arise[cite: 10]. Finding no reason to interfere with the lower authority's decision, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 10].

case_title: Suresh Chand Garg vs. Aditya Birla Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Suresh Chand Garg (Appellant), Director of Garg Inox Limited (Corporate Debtor); Aditya Birla Finance Limited (Respondent/Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/lending facilities extended by Aditya Birla Finance Limited to Garg Inox Limited, against which personal/individual properties of the Appellant-Director were encumbered/mortgaged. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under the credit facilities triggering enforcement measures under the SARFAESI Act, 2002; specific quantified amounts and precise default dates are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Financial Creditor initiated enforcement by issuing a notice under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 against the director's individual properties. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Notices issued under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 by Aditya Birla Finance Limited concerning properties owned personally and individually by Suresh Chand Garg. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant moved an application before NCLT New Delhi seeking directions against Aditya Birla Finance Limited to withdraw its SARFAESI notice; the NCLT dismissed the application on 27 February 2018 holding that the moratorium does not extend to personal assets of a director, against which the Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 extends to protect the personal and individual assets of a Director of the Corporate Debtor, thereby restraining a financial creditor from enforcing SARFAESI proceedings against such personal properties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium declared under the corporate insolvency resolution process strictly protects only the assets of the Corporate Debtor and does not extend immunity or protection to the personal or individual properties of its Directors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC applies solely to the assets, operations, and proceedings against the Corporate Debtor itself; the scope of the moratorium cannot be expanded to encompass personal and individual assets of a corporate guarantor or director. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determination of asset ownership; if the asset subject to enforcement under the SARFAESI Act is owned individually by a director and does not form part of the corporate debtor's estate, it lies outside the jurisdictional bar of the moratorium. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that the personal assets of the Director are not the subject matter of the corporate insolvency resolution process, rendering the appeal devoid of merits.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without cost, upholding the order dated 27th February 2018 passed by the Adjudicating Authority.
summary: The Appellant, Suresh Chand Garg, a Director of the Corporate Debtor Garg Inox Limited, appealed against the NCLT New Delhi's order dismissing his application to direct Aditya Birla Finance Limited to withdraw a notice issued under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 against his personal properties. The Appellant contended that enforcement against his personal assets should be restricted during the corporate insolvency resolution process. The NCLAT held that the moratorium under the IBC is exclusively confined to the assets of the Corporate Debtor and does not cover the personal or individual assets of its Directors. Consequently, finding no grounds to interfere with the NCLT's order, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Haravtar Singh Arora vs. Punjab National Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Haravtar Singh Arora (Appellant), Director of the Corporate Debtor James Hotels Limited; Punjab National Bank & Ors. (Respondents/Financial Creditors) and the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of James Hotels Limited involving the appointment of valuation/accounting professionals and the management of pending judicial proceedings against the corporate debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics and specific debt figures are not recorded in the appellate text; the company was placed under CIRP leading to statutory moratorium. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chandigarh Bench) passed an order on 8 August 2018, which was appealed before the NCLAT after a delay of two days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appointment orders/records of valuers and accountants engaged by the Resolution Professional, and pending court proceedings against the Corporate Debtor claimed to have been omitted from stay actions by the Resolution Professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Chandigarh Bench's order dated 8 August 2018 on grounds that the engagement of a valuer/accountant was illegal and that the Resolution Professional failed to stay court proceedings against the corporate debtor.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional is legally empowered under Section 25(2)(d) of the IBC to appoint an accountant, valuer, or other professionals without rendering the appointment invalid. 2. Whether Section 14 of the IBC operates automatically to halt all pending court proceedings against the Corporate Debtor, thereby relieving the Resolution Professional from taking independent affirmative steps to stay such cases.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional has express statutory authority to appoint professionals to carry out resolution functions, and by operation of law, the statutory moratorium automatically stays all judicial proceedings against the corporate debtor without requiring affirmative procedural intervention by the Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(2)(d) explicitly vests power in the Resolution Professional to engage accountants, legal or other professionals; Section 14 is self-executing in nature, causing all pending suits and proceedings against the Corporate Debtor to automatically come to a halt before all courts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory competence test; actions falling within explicit statutory delegations require no further justification, and statutory automaticity negates allegations of procedural default by the resolution professional. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenges raised against the appointment of the valuer/accountant and the conduct of the Resolution Professional regarding pending proceedings lack merit, justifying dismissal of the appeal.
operative_order: The delay of two days in filing the appeal was condoned. The appeal was dismissed on merits with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, Haravtar Singh Arora, a Director of Corporate Debtor James Hotels Limited, challenged an order of NCLT Chandigarh Bench regarding the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. The Appellant alleged that the Resolution Professional illegally appointed valuers/accountants and failed to stop pending court cases against the Corporate Debtor during the moratorium. The NCLAT rejected both contentions, holding that Section 25(2)(d) of the IBC explicitly empowers the Resolution Professional to engage accountants and legal professionals. Furthermore, under Section 14 of the IBC, all pending proceedings against the Corporate Debtor automatically halt by operation of law, requiring no further action by the Resolution Professional. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Chandra Kalian Parkash vs. Rajeev Mannadiar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Chandra Kalian Parkash, promoter of Corporate Debtor Esskay Motors Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant), and Rajeev Mannadiar & Ors. along with the Liquidator (Respondents)[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Esskay Motors Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Underlying default metrics initiating CIRP are not stated in the order[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial 180-day statutory CIRP period was scheduled to end on 21.01.2018; the CoC met on 31.08.2017 and subsequently voted to liquidate on 03.10.2017; the NCLT liquidation order was passed on 08.01.2018; the appeal was decided on 24.07.2018[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the CoC meeting dated 31.08.2017 directing the RP to present a concrete revival plan or face liquidation; absence of any resolution applicant coming forward with a plan; disqualification of the promoter from proposing a plan under Section 29A[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order on 08.01.2018 under Section 33(2) ordering liquidation and appointing a Liquidator upon the recommendation of the CoC; the promoter appealed on grounds that 180 days had not expired and CIRP was prematurely concluded without inviting further plans[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the jurisdiction under Section 33(2) to resolve to liquidate the Corporate Debtor prior to the completion of the 180-day CIRP period when no resolution applicant has submitted a resolution plan, and whether an ineligible promoter under Section 29A can challenge such a decision[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors possesses statutory authority to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor prior to the expiration of the statutory 180-day period if no viable resolution plan has been received, and an ineligible person under Section 29A cannot challenge such liquidation on the premise of offering a resolution plan[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) empowers the CoC to decide to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time before the confirmation of a resolution plan; it is not mandatory to wait for the entire 180-day window to lapse if no resolution applicant comes forward and no viable revival proposal exists[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Record showing absence of any submitted resolution plans and statutory disqualification of the appellant under Section 29A[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no resolution applicant came forward and the promoter was ineligible under Section 29A to submit a plan, the CoC's decision to liquidate under Section 33(2) was fully lawful and required no judicial interference[cite: 11].

1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors possesses statutory authority to resolve to liquidate a corporate debtor prior to the expiration of the statutory 180-day period if no viable resolution plan has been received, and an ineligible person under Section 29A cannot challenge such liquidation on the premise of offering a resolution plan[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) empowers the CoC to decide to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time before the confirmation of a resolution plan; it is not mandatory to wait for the entire 180-day window to lapse if no resolution applicant comes forward and no viable revival proposal exists[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Record showing absence of any submitted resolution plans and statutory disqualification of the appellant under Section 29A[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no resolution applicant came forward and the promoter was ineligible under Section 29A to submit a plan, the CoC's decision to liquidate under Section 33(2) was fully lawful and required no judicial interference[cite: 11].
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Mumbai Bench liquidation order dated 8th January 2018[cite: 11].
summary: Chandra Kalian Parkash, promoter of Esskay Motors Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order under Section 33(2) ordering liquidation, contending that the CIRP was prematurely ended prior to the expiry of 180 days on 21.01.2018[cite: 11]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that where no resolution applicants submit a plan and the CoC finds no concrete revival proposal, the CoC is legally empowered under Section 33(2) to resolve to liquidate before 180 days expire[cite: 11]. Furthermore, because the promoter was statutorily disqualified under Section 29A from submitting a plan, no relief could be granted[cite: 11].

case_title: M/s. Laina Power Engineering vs. Sokeo Power Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Laina Power Engineering as Operational Creditor (Appellant) and Sokeo Power Private Limited as Corporate Debtor (Respondent)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contract for engineering, execution of works, piping, and handling of scrap/tonnage materials[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics and claimed amounts are not specified in the order[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Pre-notice dispute emails exchanged on 03.05.2017, 05.05.2017, and 18.05.2017; Section 8(1) demand notice issued on 07.07.2017; subsequent email relied on by appellant dated 12.07.2017; NCLT order passed on 03.07.2018; appellate order passed on 16.08.2018[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced emails dated 3rd, 5th, and 18th May 2017 demonstrating complaints regarding non-submission of work completion certificates, incomplete work, deductions for lead piping, non-removal of scrap material charges, and exorbitant tonnage claims contrary to industry practice; Appellant relied on an email dated 12.07.2017 alleging admission of dues[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application before NCLT Hyderabad Bench; NCLT dismissed it on 03.07.2018 holding that pre-existing disputes existed; Operational Creditor appealed[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable when contemporaneous emails sent prior to the Section 8 demand notice reveal disputed questions of fact regarding non-completion of works, deductions, and inflated tonnage claims[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be dismissed if there are documented pre-existing disputes regarding the performance, deductions, and completion of work raised prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice, as summary proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority cannot resolve disputed questions of fact[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The existence of a dispute under Section 8 and Section 9 requires only a plausible, pre-existing contestation regarding the debt or performance of service; disputed factual questions regarding work rectification, scrap removal, or deduction amounts cannot be adjudicated under summary Section 9 proceedings[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous pre-notice email correspondence showing specific operational and accounting objections raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The presence of unresolved pre-notice disputes regarding work completion certificates, deductions, and tonnage claims rendered the Section 9 application non-maintainable[cite: 12].
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissal order dated 3rd July 2018[cite: 12].
summary: M/s Laina Power Engineering challenged the NCLT Hyderabad Bench's dismissal of its Section 9 petition against Sokeo Power Pvt. Ltd., relying on an email dated 12.07.2017 to claim an admission of dues[cite: 12]. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, finding that prior to the Section 8 demand notice issued on 07.07.2017, the parties had exchanged emails in May 2017 raising substantive disputes regarding incomplete works, lack of completion certificates, deductions for lead piping, scrap removal, and exorbitant tonnage claims[cite: 12]. As these disputed questions of fact cannot be resolved under Section 9, the existence of a pre-existing dispute barred admission[cite: 12].

case_title: Raj Builders vs. Raj Oil Mills Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Raj Builders as Landlord of the registered office (Appellant) and Raj Oil Mills Ltd. as Corporate Debtor along with Resolution Applicant (Respondents)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenancy/lease agreement for premises occupied as the registered office of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Tenancy period had expired, requiring technical surrender and possession of the premises; financial default amounts not detailed[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC-approved resolution plan approved by NCLT under Section 31 on 19.04.2018, bringing moratorium to an end; NCLAT order passed on 08.08.2018[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tenancy agreement had ended; premises remained in occupation of the Corporate Debtor during and after CIRP; Appellant sought eviction/possession[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plan on 19.04.2018 without passing orders for eviction or handing over of possession of the premises to the landlord; landlord appealed against the plan approval order seeking possession[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction during or upon conclusion of CIRP to pass eviction orders against a Corporate Debtor whose tenancy has expired, and what remedy is available to a landlord following the cessation of moratorium upon Section 31 approval[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to order eviction of a corporate debtor from leased premises, and while Section 14 bars eviction during the moratorium, the landlord is entitled to seek eviction before a competent civil forum once the moratorium ceases upon approval of the resolution plan under Section 31[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 14, an owner or lessor cannot evict a corporate debtor from premises occupied by it during the moratorium; upon approval of a resolution plan under Section 31, the moratorium ceases, allowing the landlord to pursue eviction under ordinary property and tenancy laws[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Jurisdictional threshold test—the NCLT is not a civil court empowered to adjudicate landlord-tenant relationships or grant decrees of eviction[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly refrained from passing eviction orders, but because the moratorium expired on 19.04.2018, the landlord was fully entitled to institute eviction proceedings before a court of competent jurisdiction[cite: 13].
operative_order: Appeal disposed of without costs, clarifying that the moratorium ceased on 19.04.2018 and the Appellant is free to seek eviction of the Corporate Debtor in accordance with law before a court of competent jurisdiction[cite: 13].
summary: Raj Builders, landlord of the registered office of Raj Oil Mills Ltd., challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 19.04.2018 approving a resolution plan under Section 31, aggrieved that possession of the premises was not handed over despite expiry of the tenancy[cite: 13]. The NCLAT held that while Section 14 prohibited eviction during the moratorium, the moratorium expired upon approval of the plan on 19.04.2018[cite: 13]. Because the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to pass eviction orders or determine landlord-tenant disputes, the appeal was disposed of granting liberty to the landlord to initiate eviction proceedings before a competent civil court[cite: 13].

case_title: Alok Kaushik vs. ASREC (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Alok Kaushik, former Interim Resolution Professional (Appellant), and ASREC (India) Ltd., Financial Creditor/Respondent[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution proceedings wherein the Appellant was appointed as IRP and replaced after 30 days by the CoC appointing another individual as RP[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics initiating CIRP not stated; dispute pertained to unpaid professional fees and expenses incurred by the IRP[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: IRP served 30 days before replacement; certified copy of NCLT order delivered on 19.11.2018; appeal filed on 01.12.2018 (held within limitation in IA No. 1986/2018); decided on 07.12.2018[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC approval of IRP professional fees and expenses; NCLT directed reimbursement of incurred expenses but ordered payment of IRP fees to be deferred until liquidation[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application before NCLT Chandigarh Bench for payment of fees and costs; NCLT approved reimbursement of expenses but directed that professional fees be paid at the stage of liquidation; IRP appealed[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether an Interim Resolution Professional whose tenure concludes upon replacement by a Resolution Professional can be made to wait until the liquidation stage to receive professional fees duly approved by the Committee of Creditors[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional is legally entitled to timely payment of professional fees as approved by the Committee of Creditors and cannot be compelled to defer recovery until the uncertain occurrence of liquidation[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: IRP fees approved by the CoC form part of the insolvency resolution process costs; deferring approved fees until liquidation under Section 33 is improper since it remains indeterminate during CIRP whether a corporate debtor will be revived via resolution or liquidated[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Approval of the professional fees by the Committee of Creditors in accordance with the Code and regulations[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Deferral of approved IRP fees to the liquidation stage was legally erroneous; the Adjudicating Authority must determine and direct payment of CoC-approved fees within a fixed timeframe[cite: 14].
operative_order: Matter remitted to NCLT Chandigarh Bench to determine the fees in terms of CoC approval and direct the concerned person to pay the admitted fees to the Appellant preferably within 30 days. No costs[cite: 14].
summary: Mr. Alok Kaushik, outgoing Interim Resolution Professional replaced after 30 days by the CoC, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh Bench order which directed payment of his incurred expenses but deferred payment of his professional fees until the liquidation stage[cite: 14]. The NCLAT held that an IRP cannot be forced to wait for liquidation to receive professional fees that have been approved by the CoC, especially when the outcome of CIRP (resolution or liquidation) remains undecided[cite: 14]. The Tribunal remitted the matter to the NCLT to determine and enforce payment of the approved fees within 30 days[cite: 14].

case_title: M/s. Daya Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. UIC Udyog Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Daya Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd. as applicant/buyer (Appellant) and M/s UIC Udyog Ltd. as Corporate Debtor/supplier (Respondent)[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advance payment/investment for the supply of materials[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Materials worth Rs. 4,02,33,473/- were supplied; default claimed for unsupplied balance advance of Rs. 12,09,443/- along with interest @ 24% per month[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 application dismissed by NCLT on 16.05.2018; appellate order passed on 26.07.2018[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Purchase and supply documentation showing full payment made for supply, receipt of partial goods worth Rs. 4.02 Crore, and retention of balance advance of Rs. 12,09,443/- without supply of corresponding material[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an application under Section 9 of the IBC before NCLT Kolkata Bench; on 16.05.2018, NCLT rejected the petition holding that the applicant does not qualify as an Operational Creditor; Appellant appealed, additionally arguing it should be treated as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7)/(8)[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether an advance paid by a purchaser for the procurement of materials constitutes an operational debt enabling the purchaser to initiate CIRP under Section 9, and whether a petition filed under Section 9 can be converted or treated as a Section 7 financial debt application in appeal[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity seeking refund of an unadjusted advance paid for goods that were not supplied does not qualify as an operational creditor under Section 9 of the IBC, nor can an appellate tribunal convert a Section 9 application into a Section 7 petition[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: An operational debt arises out of the provision of goods or rendering of services by the creditor to the corporate debtor; a purchaser who advances money for goods has not provided goods or services under Section 9[cite: 15]. If an applicant claims financial creditor status under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8), remedy must be sought independently under Section 7[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Characterization of the transaction establishing that the claimant was a customer/buyer seeking refund rather than a supplier of goods/services[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT correctly held that the Appellant was not an Operational Creditor under Section 9; the Appellant remains at liberty to pursue appropriate remedies under Section 7 if legally advised[cite: 15].
operative_order: Appeal disposed of without costs, upholding the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated 16th May 2018, with liberty to the Appellant to initiate proceedings under Section 7 before the Adjudicating Authority in accordance with law[cite: 15].
summary: M/s Daya Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd. advanced funds to M/s UIC Udyog Ltd. for supply of materials[cite: 15]. While materials worth Rs. 4.02 Crore were delivered, materials worth Rs. 12,09,443/- were not supplied[cite: 15]. The buyer filed a Section 9 application seeking refund of the balance with 24% interest, which was dismissed by NCLT Kolkata Bench on the ground that the buyer was not an Operational Creditor[cite: 15]. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that Section 9 cannot be invoked for refund of advance purchase money, while granting liberty to the Appellant to independently approach the NCLT under Section 7 if it claimed status as a Financial Creditor[cite: 15].

case_title: Gaurav Bhargava & Ors. vs. Noble Cooperative Bank Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gaurav Bhargava and other shareholders of the Corporate Debtor (Appellants); Noble Cooperative Bank Ltd. as Financial Creditor (Respondent); M/s Shivalika Developers Pvt. Ltd. as Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of a plot in Sector 63 NOIDA on 09.06.2016 for development; Corporate Debtor sought a loan on 31.03.2009 with an overdraft (OD) limit of Rs. 30 Lakhs and executed a General Term Loan Agreement; Corporate Debtor and guarantors purchased bank shares pursuant to the sanction order; management changed on 16.10.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under the credit facility of Rs. 30 Lakhs; exact claimed default amount and specific date of default are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed a petition under Section 7 of the IBC; NCLT admitted the petition on 12.02.2018; appellate order passed on 17.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement executed on behalf of the Corporate Debtor; loan account maintained in the name of the Corporate Debtor where proceeds were credited; Appellants alleged erstwhile directors Mr. Asit Mittal and Mr. Mahim Mittal took the loan personally and operated accounts post-resignation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Section 7 petition, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP on 12.02.2018; shareholders appealed contending no prior notice was served and the loan was a personal transaction of erstwhile directors.
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 is maintainable against a Corporate Debtor when the credit facility was sanctioned and disbursed in its name, notwithstanding allegations that erstwhile directors utilized the funds personally, and whether lack of pre-admission notice mandates remand.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor remains liable under Section 7 for financial debt availed in its corporate name and credited into its bank account, irrespective of internal management changes or allegations that former directors appropriated the funds personally. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 requires establishing default of a financial debt owed by the corporate debtor; internal mismanagement or unauthorized operations by directors after availing loan facilities in the corporate entity's name does not extinguish corporate liability. Remand for lack of pre-admission notice will not be granted where it is a mere formality because admission is otherwise legally inevitable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented existence of a corporate loan agreement and bank records demonstrating that loan accounts were held and disbursed in the name of the corporate entity. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the loan was availed on behalf of the Corporate Debtor and disbursed into its account, the Section 7 application was maintainable, and the lack of notice did not warrant interference as remand would be a mere formality.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT admission order dated 12th February 2018.
summary: Shareholders of Shivalika Developers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the admission of a Section 7 petition filed by Noble Cooperative Bank Ltd., contending that the Rs. 30 Lakh credit facility was misappropriated by erstwhile directors for personal use and that no pre-admission notice was served. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the loan agreement was executed on behalf of the Corporate Debtor and funds were credited into its account, establishing valid corporate liability. The Tribunal also held that remanding the case for lack of notice would be an empty formality since the debt and default were indisputable.

case_title: State Bank of India & Anr. vs. Ajay Agarwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India and another Financial Creditor (Appellants); Ajay Agarwal & Ors. and Mr. Venakataramanarao Nagarajan, Resolution Professional/Liquidator (Respondents). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Lending/credit facilities extended by Financial Creditors to a Corporate Debtor undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics initiating CIRP are not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The statutory CIRP period of 270 days lapsed on 05.09.2018; impugned order passed by NCLT on 09.11.2018; appeal decided on 13.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Committee of Creditors passed a resolution with 100% majority voting share to remove the RP; however, no resolution plan was approved by the CoC prior to the expiry of 270 days. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditors filed an application to remove the RP, while the RP filed an application under Section 33(1)(a)/34(1) for liquidation; on 09.11.2018, NCLT Chennai Single Bench rejected the CoC's removal application and ordered liquidation; Financial Creditors appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an order of liquidation passed under Section 33(1)(a) upon the expiry of 270 days without an approved resolution plan can be challenged on the ground that the Adjudicating Authority rejected the CoC's 100% resolution to remove the Resolution Professional.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon expiry of the statutory maximum CIRP period without approval of a resolution plan, liquidation is mandatory under Section 33, rendering the Committee of Creditors functus officio and precluding appellate invalidation of the liquidation order based on an unapproved RP removal application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(1)(a) requires the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation where no resolution plan is received or approved within the prescribed CIRP timeline (including extensions up to 270 days); on issuance of such an order, the CoC ceases to exist and has no standing to challenge the liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Passage of the statutory 270-day maximum period without an approved resolution plan on the record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order of liquidation cannot be declared illegal because the statutory period of 270 days had expired, making the dismissal of the CoC's removal application irrelevant to the mandatory requirement of liquidation.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed without costs. Clarified that the dismissal does not constitute a finding on the performance or activity of Mr. V. Nagarajan as RP/Liquidator, which remains for the IBBI to adjudicate based on complaints.
summary: State Bank of India and another Financial Creditor appealed against the NCLT Chennai Bench order dated 09.11.2018, which rejected their application to remove Resolution Professional Mr. V. Nagarajan (approved by 100% CoC voting share) and ordered liquidation under Section 33(1)(a)/34(1). The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that no resolution plan was approved within the statutory 270-day CIRP period, which expired on 05.09.2018. Consequently, the CoC became functus officio, and the liquidation order could not be declared illegal, leaving complaints regarding the RP's conduct to be determined independently by the IBBI.

case_title: M/s. Drulum India Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Sharma Kalypso Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Drulum India Pvt. Ltd. as Operational Creditor (Appellant) and M/s Sharma Kalypso Pvt. Ltd. as Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of false ceiling goods/materials pursuant to a Purchase Order dated 01.06.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under invoice No. IN1718TDS-046 dated 26.06.2017; exact monetary default amount not stated; terms required 50% payment within 20 days upon complete delivery and remainder within 30 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued (no reply sent by Corporate Debtor); Section 9 petition rejected by NCLT on 22.05.2018; appellate order passed on 09.07.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Endorsements on packing list dated 28.06.2017 and logistics receipt dated 27.06.2017 showing delivery of only 588 boxes instead of the invoiced 650 boxes (8 bundles); operational creditor emails dated 16.06.2017 acknowledging delay where time was of the essence; dishonoured cheques; altered invoice omitting short-delivery endorsements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 petition before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III; NCLT rejected the petition on 22.05.2018 due to a pre-existing dispute concerning short delivery, delay, and contract non-performance; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Corporate Debtor is precluded from raising a pre-existing dispute before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 9 if it failed to reply to the statutory Section 8 demand notice, and whether contemporaneous evidence of short delivery and delayed supply constitutes a genuine pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate debtor's failure to respond to a Section 8 demand notice does not forfeit its legal right to establish the existence of a genuine pre-existing dispute at the time of admission under Section 9. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 requires the Adjudicating Authority to reject the petition if notice of dispute or an existing dispute is shown; the absence of a reply under Section 8(2) does not create an irrebuttable presumption of default or preclude the debtor from placing contemporaneous dispute evidence before the NCLT. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous documentary evidence—consisting of endorsements on packing slips, logistics receipts demonstrating delivery shortages, and party emails showing delayed performance—establishing a plausible, non-spurious dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because verified contemporaneous records showed short delivery and delayed supply where time was of the essence, a pre-existing dispute existed, justifying the rejection of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, upholding the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejection order dated 22nd May 2018.
summary: Operational Creditor Drulum India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the dismissal of its Section 9 application by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III, arguing that Corporate Debtor Sharma Kalypso Pvt. Ltd. failed to reply to the Section 8 demand notice and had issued cheques that bounced. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, ruling that failure to reply to a Section 8 notice does not deprive the Corporate Debtor of raising a pre-existing dispute before the NCLT. Documentary evidence showed short delivery (588 boxes received against 650 invoiced) and delayed supply violating contractual terms, establishing a genuine pre-existing dispute.

case_title: KLA Construction Technologies Pvt. Ltd. vs. CKG Realty Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: KLA Construction Technologies Pvt. Ltd. as Operational Creditor (Appellant) and CKG Realty Pvt. Ltd. as Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement for civil construction and structural concrete works at CKG Expresswalk, Rudrapur, valued at Rs. 74,135,813.32 (excluding taxes). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed for non-payment of Rs. 11 Lakh mobilization advance, subsequently claimed as Rs. 21 Lakh based on minutes of meeting; final bill dated 04.09.2017 claimed Rs. 2,880,837.30. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 12.09.2017 (no notice of dispute sent by debtor); NCLT order passed on 02.02.2018; appellate order passed on 26.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor withheld advance due to site waterlogging and non-mobilization of machinery/equipment, alleging demobilization by Appellant and resulting losses; variance between Section 8 demand notice (Rs. 11/21 Lakhs) and final bill (Rs. 2,880,837.30); no actual construction or supply commenced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application before NCLT New Delhi Bench-III; NCLT dismissed it on 02.02.2018 holding that an unpaid mobilization advance under a composite contract where no work or goods were supplied does not constitute an operational debt, and variance in claim amounts existed; Operational Creditor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a claim solely for an unpaid mobilization advance under a composite civil works contract—prior to the commencement of any work or supply of materials, and subject to mutual allegations of non-performance—constitutes an operational debt under Section 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unpaid advance payment under an executory composite contract where neither goods have been supplied nor services rendered does not constitute an operational debt default justifying the initiation of CIRP under Section 9, especially when genuine contractual disputes exist. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with the definition of operational debt requires an undisputed liability arising directly from the provision of goods or rendering of services; non-payment of a mobilization advance prior to actual mobilization and commencement of works does not qualify as an operational debt default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether consideration had moved via supply of goods or rendering of services, alongside inconsistencies in claim figures between the Section 8 notice and final billing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no works or supplies were initiated, a plausible dispute existed over contractual breach, and variance existed between the statutory notice and bills, the claim was not maintainable under Section 9.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs. Liberty granted to the Appellant to seek appropriate remedies before a competent civil forum for alleged breach of contract.
summary: KLA Construction Technologies appealed the NCLT New Delhi Bench-III order dismissing its Section 9 petition against CKG Realty Pvt. Ltd. The claim arose from non-payment of an Rs. 11 Lakh mobilization advance under a composite construction contract worth Rs. 7.41 Crore. The Corporate Debtor resisted on grounds of site waterlogging, non-mobilization of equipment, and demobilization by the creditor. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that an advance payment claim where no works were performed or goods supplied does not constitute an operational debt under the IBC, and substantial variances in claimed amounts indicated a contractual dispute proper for civil adjudication.

case_title: Vandana Garg, RP of Jyoti Structures Ltd. vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ms. Vandana Garg, Resolution Professional of Jyoti Structures Ltd. (Appellant); State Bank of India (Respondent Financial Creditor); DBS Bank (Respondent Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Jyoti Structures Ltd. under CP (IB) 1137(MB)/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP default metrics not specified; dispute centered on CoC voting share calculations for a proposed resolution plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC voting held on 26/27 March 2018; additional votes received on 28.03.2018; maximum 270-day CIRP period was completing on 31.03.2018; impugned NCLT order passed on 25.07.2018; appeal decided on 26.10.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC initially voted 62.66% in favour and 23.12% against the plan; RP subsequently accepted post-voting affirmative votes of IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (0.42%) and Indian Bank (6.31%) to save the Corporate Debtor from liquidation; NCLT passed adverse observations and imposed costs on the RP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an order on 25.07.2018 in multiple M.A.s/I.A.s making adverse personal observations and imposing costs on the RP for accepting late votes; RP appealed specifically against the adverse remarks and cost imposition.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can make adverse observations and impose costs against a Resolution Professional for acts done in bona fide discharge of duties without serving prior individual show-cause notice and providing a hearing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Adverse remarks cannot be recorded nor costs imposed against a Resolution Professional acting in bona fide discharge of functions without adhering to principles of natural justice through the issuance of a prior show-cause notice and providing an opportunity to be heard. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Resolution Professional acts under statutory duties to make every endeavor to facilitate resolution rather than liquidation; where an RP accepts belated votes of CoC members acting in bona fide belief without deliberate inaction or mala fide intent, penal observations impacting professional reputation cannot be sustained. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of bona fides and adherence to procedural fairness (Audi Alteram Partem standard) prior to recording adverse judicial remarks or penalising court officers/RPs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted bona fide to avoid liquidation on the specific request of voting CoC members, and no show-cause notice was served prior to the remarks, warranting the expunging of remarks and setting aside of costs.
operative_order: Appeal allowed to the extent of expunging all adverse remarks against the Resolution Professional and setting aside the imposition of costs in the order dated 25th July 2018. Clarified that substantive merits of the order will be determined in connected appeals without prejudice. No costs.
summary: Ms. Vandana Garg, Resolution Professional of Jyoti Structures Ltd., appealed against adverse remarks and costs imposed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in its order dated 25.07.2018. The NCLT criticized her for accepting belated affirmative votes from CoC members (IDBI Trusteeship and Indian Bank) after formal voting concluded, just prior to the 270-day expiry. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and expunged the remarks and costs, holding that the RP acted in bona fide interest to prevent liquidation and that principles of natural justice were breached because no individual show-cause notice or hearing was afforded before censuring her.

case_title: Krishna Enterprises vs. Gammon India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Krishna Enterprises, Om Industrial Corporation, Swastik Enterprises, Orissa Sales, and Pavan Enterprises) acted as Operational Creditors, and M/s Gammon India Ltd. was the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions involving unpaid claims for which the Operational Creditors sought initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The principal debt amounts were paid; the exact original default metrics and dates are not specified in the order, but the remaining claim comprised solely interest for delayed payment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Applications were initiated under Section 9 of the IBC; the Appellants contested that the NCLT failed to dispose of the matter within the 14-day statutory timeline under Section 9. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The record evidenced that the principal debt amount had already been paid by the Corporate Debtor and no underlying agreement existed between the parties providing for the payment of interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditors filed Section 9 petitions before NCLT Mumbai Bench; upon appearance, the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the petitions after noting that the principal amount of the debt due had already been fully discharged.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application under the IBC is maintainable solely for the recovery of interest on delayed payments when the principal operational debt has already been paid and there is no agreement providing for interest.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application for the initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is not maintainable solely for claims of interest on delayed payment in the absence of a contractual stipulation providing for such interest once the principal operational debt has been discharged. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(6) ('claim') and Section 3(11) ('debt') include interest within the meaning of 'debt' only if interest is payable in terms of an agreement between the parties; in the absence of an agreement, the principal amount alone constitutes the debt. Further, the 14-day timeline prescribed under Section 9 for disposal of an application by the Adjudicating Authority is directory and not mandatory. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of an express contractual agreement or covenant stipulating the payment of interest between the creditor and corporate debtor. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the principal debt had been fully satisfied and no contractual agreement for interest existed, the Section 9 applications seeking only interest were non-maintainable, leaving the creditors to pursue any remedy for delayed payment before a competent civil court.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed on merits without costs. Liberty granted to the Appellants to move before a court of competent jurisdiction for delayed payment interest.
summary: Operational Creditors, including Krishna Enterprises, filed Section 9 applications against Gammon India Ltd. Before admission, the Corporate Debtor paid the principal debt, leaving only claims for interest. The NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the applications. On appeal, the NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, holding that under Sections 3(6) and 3(11) of the IBC, 'debt' includes interest only when an agreement expressly provides for it. Absent a contractual provision for interest, an insolvency application cannot be maintained solely to recover interest on delayed payments after the principal amount is satisfied, and CIRP cannot be used as a recovery mechanism.

case_title: Kannan Tiruvengandam vs. M. K. Shah Exports Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kannan Tiruvengandam acted as the Resolution Professional (Appellant) for the Corporate Debtor, Assam Company India Ltd.; M/s M. K. Shah Exports Ltd. was a prospective Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated under Section 7 of the IBC against Assam Company India Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under Section 7 initiating CIRP are not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Advertisement inviting Resolution Plans published on 11.04.2018; eligibility criteria reaffirmed in the 7th CoC meeting on 02.05.2018; impugned NCLT order passed on 26.04.2018; NCLAT granted stay on 10.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Professional followed Section 25(2)(h) read with Regulation 36A and CoC-approved criteria prescribing a minimum tangible net worth of Rs. 400 crore for Category-A prospective applicants; four resolution plans were received post-stay; Respondent withdrew its candidature. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed IA No. 24/2018 in CP(IB)/20/GB/2017 before NCLT Guwahati Bench seeking relaxation or recasting of the Rs. 400 crore net worth criterion; NCLT directed reconsideration on 26.04.2018 observing avenues were left for modification; RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to modify, relax, or sit in appeal over the commercial eligibility criteria (such as minimum tangible net worth) framed by the Resolution Professional and approved by the Committee of Creditors under Section 25(2)(h).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to sit in appeal over or interfere with the commercial wisdom and decisions of the Committee of Creditors regarding eligibility criteria for prospective resolution applicants, provided the criteria are not perverse or contrary to law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(2)(h) empowers the Resolution Professional, with the approval of the Committee of Creditors, to determine eligibility criteria having regard to the complexity and scale of operations of the corporate debtor; such determinations fall squarely within the domain of expert bodies and not the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standard of commercial perversity or patent illegality under the provisions of the IBC and existing law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction by directing the modification/relaxation of the eligibility criteria approved by the CoC; the order was liable to be set aside to allow the CoC to evaluate received compliant plans under Section 30(2) and Section 29A.
operative_order: Impugned order dated 26th April 2018 set aside. RP and CoC directed to complete the CIRP immediately, evaluate compliant plans under Section 30(2) read with Section 29A, and submit any CoC-approved plan before the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31. No costs.
summary: During the CIRP of Assam Company India Ltd., prospective applicant M.K. Shah Exports Ltd. challenged the eligibility condition requiring a minimum tangible net worth of Rs. 400 crore approved by the CoC under Section 25(2)(h). The NCLT Guwahati Bench directed the RP and CoC to consider relaxing the criterion. Setting aside the NCLT order, the NCLAT held that setting eligibility criteria is within the exclusive commercial domain of the CoC as an expert body. The Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to interfere or sit in appeal over such criteria unless shown to be perverse or contrary to the IBC or existing law.

case_title: ICICI Bank Ltd. & State Bank of India vs. Venakataramanarao Nagarajan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Ltd. and State Bank of India acted as Financial Creditors/Appellants; Mr. Venakataramanarao Nagarajan was the Resolution Professional/Liquidator (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit/lending facilities provided by the Financial Creditors to the Corporate Debtor undergoing Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and initiation dates are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The statutory CIRP period of 270 days expired on 05.09.2018; impugned NCLT order passed on 31.10.2018; appeal disposed of on 13.12.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC passed a resolution with 100% majority voting share to remove the Resolution Professional; however, no resolution plan was approved by the CoC prior to the expiry of the maximum statutory 270-day period. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC filed a miscellaneous application before NCLT Chennai Single Bench to remove the RP, while the RP filed an application under Section 33(1)(a)/34(1) for liquidation; on 31.10.2018, the NCLT rejected the CoC's removal application and ordered liquidation; Financial Creditors appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the decision of the Adjudicating Authority ordering liquidation and refusing to replace the Resolution Professional can be interfered with when the statutory maximum period of 270 days for CIRP has expired without the approval of any resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon the expiry of the statutory maximum CIRP period without an approved resolution plan, liquidation is mandatory under Section 33, rendering the Committee of Creditors functus officio and precluding appellate interference with the liquidation order or replacement of the Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(1)(a) mandates that if no resolution plan is received or approved before the expiry of the insolvency resolution process period (including extensions up to 270 days), the Adjudicating Authority must order liquidation; upon passing such an order, the CoC ceases to exist. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective determination of the passage of the statutory time limit (270 days) without an approved resolution plan on record. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Even if the CoC had voted to replace the RP, the order of liquidation is legally unassailable because the 270-day timeline expired without an approved plan, rendering the CoC functus officio; any complaints against the conduct of the RP fall under the separate purview of the IBBI.
operative_order: Appeals dismissed without costs. Clarified that the order shall not prejudice or influence any proceedings or inquiry by the IBBI regarding complaints against the conduct/performance of the RP/Liquidator.
summary: The CoC of the Corporate Debtor voted with 100% majority to remove Resolution Professional Mr. V. Nagarajan. However, no resolution plan was approved, and the maximum statutory CIRP period of 270 days expired on 05.09.2018. The NCLT Chennai Bench rejected the CoC's removal application and passed a liquidation order under Section 33(1)(a)/34(1). The NCLAT dismissed the Financial Creditors' appeals, ruling that once the 270-day deadline lapses without an approved resolution plan, liquidation is mandatory and the CoC becomes functus officio, rendering the liquidation order valid irrespective of the pending removal application.

case_title: J.P. Engineers Private Limited vs. Murti Udyog Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: J.P. Engineers Private Limited was the Operational Creditor (Appellant) and Murti Udyog Limited was the Corporate Debtor (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of goods by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Exact monetary default value not stated; Corporate Debtor contended that the debt was zero as full payment had been made. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) issued on 13.06.2017; Section 9 petition filed on 13.09.2017; subsequent civil suit filed by Corporate Debtor on 12.12.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced evidence of payment of the claimed debt via bank cheques; Operational Creditor relied on a Chartered Accountant certificate claiming non-payment; no dispute was raised regarding the quality or supply of goods. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed a Section 9 application before NCLT New Delhi Bench; on 08.11.2017, NCLT rejected the petition holding that the Respondent had raised a dispute with sufficient particulars and established that the debt was satisfied.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable where the Corporate Debtor demonstrates that the claimed debt has been fully satisfied and paid through cheques, thereby establishing that no default occurred.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application under Section 9 cannot be admitted if the Corporate Debtor proves that the claimed debt has been discharged and satisfied, establishing the absence of default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court doctrine in Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank, a Corporate Debtor in Section 9 proceedings is fully entitled to demonstrate that default has not occurred because the debt is not due, having been previously discharged. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of verified payment particulars (bank cheque payments) rebutting the allegation of default, prevailing over a general Chartered Accountant certificate of non-payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor proved that the debt was paid and satisfied via cheques, no default existed under the IBC, justifying the rejection of the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT New Delhi Bench order dated 8th November 2017.
summary: J.P. Engineers Pvt. Ltd. filed a Section 9 petition against Murti Udyog Ltd. following an unpaid Section 8 demand notice. The Corporate Debtor resisted admission by demonstrating that the claimed operational debt had been fully satisfied and paid via cheques, whereas the creditor submitted a CA certificate alleging unpaid sums. The NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the petition. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Innoventive Industries, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a Corporate Debtor is entitled to prove that no default occurred because the debt was satisfied, making Section 9 initiation unsustainable.

case_title: Mahesh Kumar Panwar vs. Abhishek Anand
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mahesh Kumar Panwar, Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Mega Soft Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant), and Abhishek Anand, Resolution Professional (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of M/s Mega Soft Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Metrics of the underlying default initiating CIRP are not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 23.08.2017; initial statutory period of 180 days expired on 19.02.2018; liquidation order passed by NCLT on 28.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board of Directors failed to cooperate with the RP and failed to provide records and title deeds of the Corporate Debtor's properties; Appellant's defense that emails were sent was rejected as insufficient statutory cooperation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Upon recommendation of the CoC after the expiry of 180 days without resolution plans, NCLT New Delhi Bench ordered liquidation on 28.02.2018; suspended Director appealed alleging RP failed to follow statutory procedure for inviting resolution applications.
legal_issues: Whether an order for liquidation passed upon the recommendation of the CoC after the expiry of 180 days of CIRP is valid where the Resolution Professional was unable to invite resolution plans due to non-cooperation and non-production of property records by the Corporate Debtor's directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the statutory CIRP period expires without the possibility of resolution due to the suspended management's refusal to supply essential asset title deeds and records, the Adjudicating Authority must order liquidation upon the recommendation of the Committee of Creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33 mandates liquidation where the CIRP period expires without an approved resolution plan; the statutory obligation of the suspended board of directors to cooperate and surrender assets/records to the RP is mandatory and cannot be substituted by informal emails. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical non-production of title deeds, statutory books, and company records preventing the preparation of an Information Memorandum and evaluation of resolution plans within the statutory timeline. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The expiry of the 180-day period coupled with proven non-cooperation by the directors left the Adjudicating Authority with no statutory alternative other than ordering liquidation.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed without costs, upholding the liquidation order dated 28th February 2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench.
summary: Mahesh Kumar Panwar, Director of Mega Soft Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., appealed a liquidation order passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench under Section 33 on the CoC's recommendation, arguing the RP failed to invite resolution plans. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, noting that the suspended directors failed to discharge their statutory duty to cooperate and hand over property title deeds and records to the RP. With the 180-day CIRP period having expired on 19.02.2018 without records to formulate a resolution, the Adjudicating Authority had no option but to order liquidation.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Ram Dev International Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor and Committee of Creditors member) as Appellant; Ram Dev International Ltd. (Corporate Debtor represented through outgoing Resolution Professional Rakesh Kumar Jain) as Respondent; Mr. K. G. Somani as the proposed replacement Resolution Professional[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process initiated against the Corporate Debtor, during which Mr. Rakesh Kumar Jain functioned as IRP and subsequently continued as RP under Section 22(2)[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural dispute regarding replacement of Resolution Professional; no specific financial default amounts adjudicated in the appeal[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC passed a resolution by majority voting share to replace Mr. Rakesh Kumar Jain with Mr. K. G. Somani under Section 27; NCLT Principal Bench rejected the appointment on 15 May 2018[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The CoC approved the replacement without recording adverse misconduct findings; NCLT disqualified the proposed RP solely because he was an empaneled professional/advocate with the erstwhile State Bank of Hyderabad (merged with SBI)[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi in CP No. (IB)178(PB)/2017 rejected the proposal to appoint Mr. K. G. Somani on grounds of conflict of interest due to panel membership; SBI appealed under Section 61[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to reject a Resolution Professional proposed by the Committee of Creditors under Section 27 solely on the ground that the candidate is on the general panel of advocates/professionals of a member bank of the CoC[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere presence on an institution's general panel of advocates or professionals does not render a proposed Resolution Professional an employee or interested person in the pay of a financial creditor, and does not constitute a legal disqualification under the IBC in the absence of pending disciplinary proceedings[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 27 read with Section 22 gives the CoC full discretion to replace an RP by the requisite majority without needing to formally record adverse findings or allegations; the only statutory disqualification is the pendency of disciplinary proceedings[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of employment records and disciplinary status to determine if the candidate is on the direct payroll of a creditor or subject to IBBI disciplinary action[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The proposed RP was neither an employee nor on the payroll of SBI and had no disciplinary proceedings pending, making the rejection of his appointment erroneous[cite: 28].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 15 May 2018 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi is set aside; Mr. Rakesh Kumar Jain is replaced and Mr. K. G. Somani is appointed as Resolution Professional; outgoing RP permitted to submit fee and cost claims before the CoC for inclusion under Regulations 31 and 32; appeal allowed with no order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: State Bank of India appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order rejecting the CoC's proposal under Section 27 of the IBC to replace Resolution Professional Rakesh Kumar Jain with K. G. Somani[cite: 28]. The NCLT had disqualified Somani because he was empaneled with the erstwhile State Bank of Hyderabad[cite: 28]. The NCLAT held that being on an institutional panel of professionals does not constitute employment, payroll engagement, or conflict of interest under the Code[cite: 28]. As no disciplinary proceedings were pending and the CoC exercised its statutory discretion by requisite majority, the disqualification was invalid[cite: 28]. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the order and appointed K. G. Somani as RP[cite: 28].

case_title: Tarini Steel Company Pvt. Ltd. vs. Trinity Auto Components Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Tarini Steel Company Pvt. Ltd. (Resolution Applicant/Promoter Entity) as Appellant; Trinity Auto Components Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) & Anr. as Respondents[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of a resolution plan by the sole Resolution Applicant proposing infusion of fresh promoter unsecured loans of Rs. 350 lakhs and interest-bearing deposits of Rs. 349.51 lakhs at 12% repayable by 2023, along with settling past contingent/statutory liabilities prior to 31 March 2011 at 15%[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Debt resolution involving corporate turnaround where NCLT modified the plan terms to convert fresh promoter loans into equity and disallowed the 15% ceiling cap on Government dues[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan approved with modifications by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 22 January 2018 in MA 544/2017 in CP No. 1032/I&BC/MB/MAH/2017[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution plan text revealing three internally contradictory propositions regarding promoter contributions (conversion of Rs. 2 crores into equity, unsecured loan repayment of Rs. 350 lakhs during 2021-23, and interest-bearing deposits of Rs. 349.51 lakhs @ 12%), alongside Section 29A eligibility declaration[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench approved the resolution plan subject to modifications requiring unsecured promoter loans to be converted into equity and excluding government dues from the 15% settlement cap; Appellant appealed challenging the tribunal's authority to modify a plan[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Applicant can challenge modifications imposed on its resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority to prevent liquidation, and whether the applicant retains the right to withdraw the plan if unsatisfied with such modifications[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: If a Resolution Applicant is dissatisfied with modifications directed by the Adjudicating Authority upon approving a resolution plan, its remedy is to seek withdrawal of the plan, which will result in the initiation of liquidation proceedings against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Adjudicating Authority must ensure that a plan is viable and satisfies statutory requirements; if the modifications ensuring debt feasibility and protection of statutory dues are not accepted by the applicant, the plan cannot stand approved and liquidation must follow[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of conflicting promoter financing clauses within the plan text to determine commercial soundness and assess whether statutory dues were impermissibly compromised[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal's modifications did not suffer from illegality; the applicant must either accept the approved modified plan or withdraw it and face liquidation[cite: 29].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of without interference with the approval order, granting liberty to the Appellant to withdraw the resolution plan before the Adjudicating Authority if dissatisfied with the modifications, whereupon the Adjudicating Authority shall proceed with liquidation; no costs[cite: 29].
summary: Tarini Steel Company Pvt. Ltd., the sole resolution applicant for Trinity Auto Components Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving its resolution plan with modifications[cite: 29]. The NCLT had resolved internal inconsistencies regarding promoter financing by directing that fresh promoter unsecured loans be converted into equity and removing a 15% settlement cap on government dues[cite: 29]. The Appellant contended that the tribunal lacked jurisdiction to modify a plan[cite: 29]. The NCLAT held that the modifications suffered from no illegality and observed that if the applicant refused to accept the modifications, its only option was to withdraw the plan, leaving the tribunal to order liquidation[cite: 29]. The appeal was dismissed with liberty to withdraw[cite: 29].
