case_title: State Bank of India vs. SKC Retails Ltd. Through IRP & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Financial Creditor and CoC member) as Appellant; SKC Retails Ltd. and Tech Magacorp International Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtors represented through IRPs), and IFFCO TOKIO General Insurance Co. Ltd. (CoC member) as Respondents[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes initiated under Section 7 and Section 9 of the IBC against the respective Corporate Debtors[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute concerned the liability to bear Interim Resolution Professional fees and process costs, where the applicant operational creditors paid public announcement costs but CoC refused to ratify remaining fees/expenses[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against SKC Retails on 12 July 2017 with first CoC meeting on 5 October 2017; CIRP initiated against Tech Magacorp on 28 September 2017 with first CoC meeting on 12 October 2017; NCLT Chennai issued cost directions on 26 October 2017 and 14 November 2017[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC minutes dated 5 October 2017 and 12 October 2017 evidencing the CoC's refusal to ratify the IRP's additional expenses and remuneration; applications/memos filed by the IRP for fixing fee liability[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Chennai Bench) directed the CoC to bear the IRP's expenses and remuneration in proportion to their claimed amounts within two weeks; SBI appealed contending CoC is not directly liable to fund unratified IRP expenses[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors can be directly compelled by the Adjudicating Authority to pay the fees and expenses of an Interim Resolution Professional that have not been ratified by the CoC under Regulation 33 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 33 of the CIRP Regulations, the initial burden to fix and bear the expenses and remuneration of the Interim Resolution Professional falls exclusively on the applicant who initiated the insolvency application, subject to reimbursement by the CoC solely to the extent ratified[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 33(1) and 33(3) mandate that the applicant shall bear the IRP expenses; the CoC is obligated to reimburse such costs only to the extent it formally ratifies them, whereupon they qualify as insolvency resolution process costs under Regulation 33(4)[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of CIRP initiation petitions to identify the applicant under Section 7 or Section 9 who proposed the IRP, cross-referenced with CoC minutes recording the extent of expense ratification[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing the CoC to directly pay unratified IRP remuneration; the initiating applicant must bear the expenses and seek reimbursement strictly to the extent ratified by the CoC[cite: 22].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 26 October 2017 and 14 November 2017 are modified to direct that the initiating applicant shall bear the IRP expenses and obtain reimbursement from the CoC only to the extent ratified; appeals disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: State Bank of India appealed orders of NCLT Chennai directing the Committee of Creditors to bear the outstanding remuneration and expenses of the Interim Resolution Professional in proportion to their claims after the CoC refused ratification[cite: 22]. The NCLAT examined Regulation 33 of the IBBI CIRP Regulations, 2016, holding that the applicant who triggers the CIRP under Section 7 or 9 is legally obligated to fix and bear the IRP expenses[cite: 22]. The Committee of Creditors is liable to reimburse such expenses only to the extent it ratifies them[cite: 22]. Modifying the NCLT orders, the Appellate Tribunal held the initiating applicants responsible for payment, subject to CoC ratification[cite: 22].

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank & Ors. vs. Kamineni Steel & Power India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 45, 23 & 335 of 2018 and 15 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kamineni Steel & Power India Pvt. Ltd. and Innoventive Industries Ltd. as Corporate Debtors/Applicants; Indian Overseas Bank, Indian Bank, Central Bank of India & Ors. as Financial Creditors/CoC members; Chandu Laxman Chavan (promoter) and United Seamless Tubular Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) as Appellants/Respondents[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency proceedings under Section 10 against Kamineni Steel and CIRP against Innoventive Industries involving corporate loan restructurings and resolution plans[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: In Kamineni Steel, an OTS/Resolution Plan of Rs. 600 Crores was proposed; in Innoventive Industries, a plan totaling Rs. 284.3 Crores was proposed against residual debt of Rs. 1,191.9 Crores[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in Kamineni Steel on 10 February 2017; CoC voted on OTS on 27 October 2017 reaching 66.67% approval by 30 October 2017; NCLT Hyderabad approved plan on 27 November 2017; Innoventive 270 days ended 14 October 2017 where plan received 66.57% vote, and NCLT Mumbai ordered liquidation on 23 November 2017[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting records demonstrating that the resolution plan in Kamineni Steel achieved only 66.67% affirmative voting share (with 26.97% dissenting and 6.36% abstaining) and in Innoventive Industries achieved only 66.57% voting share, both falling short of the statutory 75% threshold[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved Kamineni Steel's plan despite achieving only 66.67% CoC approval; conversely, NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected Innoventive's plan for obtaining only 66.57% and ordered liquidation under Section 33[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether the voting threshold of 75% under unamended Section 21(8) of the IBC for approval of a resolution plan by the Committee of Creditors is mandatory, rendering any approval by a lesser voting percentage invalid under Section 30(2)(e)[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory voting threshold prescribed under Section 21(8) of the IBC is strictly mandatory, and the Adjudicating Authority has no jurisdiction to approve a resolution plan that fails to obtain the requisite statutory majority of CoC voting shares[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 21(8) (prior to amendment) unambiguously required that all decisions of the CoC be taken by a vote of not less than 75% of the voting share; approval by a lower threshold violates Section 30(2)(e) as a contravention of law[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict arithmetic calculation of verified voting shares of consenting financial creditors against the total voting share of the CoC[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Resolution plans securing only 66.67% and 66.57% failed to meet the mandatory 75% threshold; approval of Kamineni Steel's plan was illegal, while liquidation of Innoventive Industries was lawful[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeal No. 15 of 2018 is dismissed, upholding the liquidation order of Innoventive Industries; Company Appeals Nos. 45, 23, and 335 of 2017 are allowed, setting aside the approval order dated 27 November 2017; Kamineni Steel & Power is remitted to NCLT Hyderabad for immediate passage of a liquidation order under Section 33 read with Section 34; no order as to costs[cite: 23].
summary: These consolidated appeals addressed whether the 75% voting threshold under unamended Section 21(8) of the IBC was mandatory for approving resolution plans[cite: 23]. In Kamineni Steel & Power, NCLT Hyderabad approved an OTS resolution plan that secured only 66.67% CoC approval, whereas in Innoventive Industries, NCLT Mumbai rejected a plan securing 66.57% and ordered liquidation[cite: 23]. The NCLAT held that Section 21(8) is strictly mandatory[cite: 23]. Approving a plan with less than 75% voting share directly contravenes Section 30(2)(e)[cite: 23]. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the liquidation of Innoventive Industries, set aside the approval in Kamineni Steel, and remitted Kamineni Steel for liquidation[cite: 23].

case_title: Mr. Devendra Padamchand Jain vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devendra Padamchand Jain, Resolution Professional of VNR Infrastructures Limited (Corporate Debtor), as Appellant; State Bank of India (sole voting financial creditor), other lending banks, and IBBI as Respondents; T.S.N. Raja appointed as Liquidator[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor filed an application under Section 10 initiating CIRP; resolution plan was rejected by the CoC, leading to an application for liquidation under Section 33[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor entered liquidation following failure to secure an approved resolution plan within the statutory 180-day window[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 180-day period expired on 9 August 2017; final CoC meeting held on 25 July 2017; liquidation application filed on 1 August 2017; NCLT liquidation and replacement order passed on 24 August 2017[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT record demonstrating that the RP delayed proceedings, failed to assist the Adjudicating Authority satisfactorily during hearings, and failed to certify compliance with Section 30(2)[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed an order under Section 33(1) and Section 34(1) ordering liquidation of the Corporate Debtor, but removed the Appellant RP due to unsatisfactory performance and appointed T.S.N. Raja as Liquidator; RP appealed alleging replacement exceeded tribunal jurisdiction[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 34(4) of the IBC to remove an incumbent Resolution Professional and appoint an independent Liquidator upon ordering liquidation when dissatisfied with the RP's performance and compliance under Section 30(2)[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority is vested with the jurisdiction under Section 34 to decline appointing an incumbent Resolution Professional as Liquidator and appoint an alternative professional where the RP fails to assist the tribunal satisfactorily or demonstrate compliance with statutory obligations under Section 30(2)[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 34(1) read with Section 34(4) does not give the RP an indefeasible right to continue as liquidator; an RP's failure to satisfy the tribunal regarding compliance with Section 30(2) requirements empowers the tribunal to replace the RP upon entering liquidation[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of tribunal hearing records demonstrating unsatisfactory assistance, lack of proactive management within statutory deadlines, and concurrence of 100% voting financial creditors supporting replacement[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted within its statutory powers in replacing the RP with an independent liquidator[cite: 24].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24 August 2017 replacing the Appellant as Liquidator is affirmed; the appeal is dismissed; I.A. No. 784 of 2017 stands disposed of with no costs[cite: 24].
summary: Resolution Professional Devendra Padamchand Jain appealed an order of NCLT Hyderabad Bench passed under Sections 33 and 34 of the IBC, which ordered the liquidation of VNR Infrastructures Ltd. but removed him and appointed T.S.N. Raja as Liquidator[cite: 24]. The Appellant argued that an RP can only be replaced under the strict grounds of Section 34(4)[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to replace the RP where it is dissatisfied with his assistance and performance, amounting to failure in fulfilling Section 30(2) responsibilities[cite: 24]. Given that the sole voting creditor (SBI) expressed full faith in the newly appointed liquidator, the Appellate Tribunal affirmed the replacement and dismissed the appeal[cite: 24].

case_title: J.B. Tiwari vs. Biostadt India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: J.B. Tiwari, Managing Director of Sonachi Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 2), as Appellant; Biostadt India Limited (Operational Creditor) as Respondent No. 1; Syamal Baran Bhattacharya as Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Agreement and purchase orders placed by the Corporate Debtor for the supply of agricultural/chemical materials by the Operational Creditor against issued invoices[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Undisputed outstanding operational debt of Rs. 1,14,41,776.61[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Legal notices issued on 22 June 2016, 19 September 2016, and 6 June 2017; statutory demand notice under Section 8 issued on 13 July 2017 via email and speed post; Corporate Debtor booked a purported reply on 20 July 2017 (predated 8 July 2017); notice of hearing served by counsel on 13 and 15 November 2017; NCLT admission order passed on 2 May 2018[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced emails dated 22 July 2016 admitting liabilities without raising quality disputes; Corporate Debtor's postal receipt confirmed Section 8 notice was received before any dispute reply was dispatched; emails confirmed counsel served notice of NCLT hearing[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Operational Creditor's Section 9 petition in C.P. No. 1479/I&BC/2017 on 2 May 2018; Appellant appealed alleging violation of natural justice due to lack of direct notice from the NCLT Registry[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the admission of a Section 9 application is vitiated for breach of natural justice when notice was served by the creditor's advocate under tribunal directions rather than by the tribunal registry itself, and whether an uncommunicated or post-demand quality dispute constitutes a pre-existing dispute under the IBC[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Service of notice of an insolvency petition by an authorized advocate under judicial direction satisfies natural justice, preventing a debtor with actual knowledge from setting aside an admission order on purely procedural registry-service technicalities where debt and default are undisputed[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and Section 9 mandate that an operational dispute must be genuinely pre-existing prior to the delivery of the Section 8 demand notice; post-dated replies or dispatched objections booked subsequent to the demand notice fail to bar admission[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of postal booking receipts and email chains demonstrating that written dispute notices were booked after receipt of the statutory demand notice, alongside unequivocal admissions of debt in contemporary communications[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had actual notice of the proceedings and failed to establish any pre-existing dispute prior to the Section 8 notice, rendering the Section 9 admission order sound[cite: 16].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 2 May 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting the Section 9 application is affirmed; the appeal is rejected with no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Appellant J.B. Tiwari, Managing Director of Sonachi Industries Limited, appealed an NCLT Mumbai Bench order admitting Biostadt India Limited's Section 9 application for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 1,14,41,776.61[cite: 16]. The Appellant contended that the order was ex parte without formal notice issued by the NCLT Registry and that goods were defective[cite: 16]. The NCLAT held that advocate-served notice under tribunal directions satisfied natural justice where the debtor had actual knowledge[cite: 16]. Furthermore, contemporary records showed unequivocal admissions of liability, and the alleged dispute reply was booked after the Section 8 demand notice was dispatched[cite: 16]. Finding no pre-existing dispute, the Appellate Tribunal rejected the appeal[cite: 16].

case_title: Rajesh Gupta vs. Mr. Dinesh Chand Jain & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajesh Gupta, Ex-Director of Fantastic Buildcon Private Limited (Corporate Debtor), as Appellant; Dinesh Chand Jain, Lata Jain (erstwhile promoter-directors holding 75% shares), and DJ Tradelink Pvt. Ltd. as Respondents/Financial Creditors; Om Prakash Vijay as Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondents advanced unsecured loans carrying 18% interest per annum to the Corporate Debtor for a hotel project; on 2 February 2015, a Share Purchase Agreement was executed where outgoing shareholders transferred 7,500 shares to Lalit Modi, and Lalit Modi and the Corporate Debtor jointly undertook to refund the outstanding loan[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding principal unsecured debt of Rs. 18,67,11,000 (after adjusting partial repayments) which was due for refund on or before 31 March 2015[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: SPA executed on 2 February 2015; repayment deadline was 31 March 2015; petition filed under Section 7 admitted on 11 June 2018[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's audited balance sheet for the year ending 31 March 2014 showing the loan as long-term borrowing; Clause 2 of the SPA dated 2 February 2015 wherein the Corporate Debtor expressly undertook to refund the unsecured loan[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitted the Section 7 petition on 11 June 2018, imposed moratorium under Section 14, and appointed an IRP; Appellant appealed challenging the creditors' status as Financial Creditors[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an unsecured loan originally advanced to a corporate debtor at interest, the repayment of which is subsequently undertaken by the corporate debtor in a Share Purchase Agreement upon the lenders exiting as shareholders, constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(a) of the IBC[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsecured loan advanced to a company with an interest stipulation constitutes money borrowed against the payment of interest under Section 5(8)(a), and it retains its character as a financial debt disbursed for time value of money even if consolidated for refund under a subsequent settlement or share transfer agreement[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(a) explicitly includes money borrowed against the payment of interest; the temporary omission of interest in an exit agreement due to an imminent repayment deadline does not alter the underlying commercial borrowing nature of the transaction[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Audited balance sheets acknowledging long-term borrowings coupled with contractual refund undertakings executed by the corporate debtor demonstrate debt disbursement for the time value of money[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 18,67,11,000 possessed all the trappings of a financial debt, making the Respondents Financial Creditors entitled to trigger Section 7[cite: 17].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 11 June 2018 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi is affirmed; the appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: Appellant Rajesh Gupta, ex-director of Fantastic Buildcon Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order admitting a Section 7 insolvency petition filed by Dinesh Chand Jain and others[cite: 17]. The Respondents had advanced loans carrying 18% interest per annum for a hotel project, leaving an outstanding balance of Rs. 18,67,11,000[cite: 17]. Under a subsequent Share Purchase Agreement dated 2 February 2015, the Corporate Debtor and an incoming promoter jointly undertook to refund the loan by 31 March 2015 upon the transfer of Respondents' shareholding[cite: 17]. The NCLAT held that the transaction originated as a borrowing against interest under Section 5(8)(a) and constituted a financial debt disbursed for time value of money[cite: 17]. The admission order was affirmed and the appeal dismissed[cite: 17].

case_title: Sandeep Kumar Gupta vs. Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sandeep Kumar Gupta, Resolution Professional, as Appellant; Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation) and IBBI as Respondents; Ms. Mamta Binani appointed as Liquidator[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated under the IBC against Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd. wherein the Resolution Professional failed to make substantive progress or obtain an approved resolution plan[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural dispute regarding replacement of RP upon liquidation; no monetary default quantum adjudicated in the appeal[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Only one CoC meeting was conducted on 12 June 2017; progress report filed 15 July 2017; public announcement issued 15 September 2017 with plan submission deadline 25 September 2017; 180-day CIRP expired without resolution; NCLT passed liquidation orders on 26 October 2017 and appointed Liquidator on 15 November 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC minutes establishing that only a single CoC meeting was convened throughout the statutory 180-day CIRP period, showing total lack of progress[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench in CP(IB) No. 213/KB/2017 declined to appoint the Appellant RP as Liquidator under Section 34 due to unsatisfactory performance, instead appointing Ms. Mamta Binani from the IBBI panel; Appellant appealed seeking expunction of observations and reinstatement as Liquidator[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction to replace a Resolution Professional and appoint an independent Liquidator from the IBBI panel under Section 34 of the IBC when dissatisfied with the RP's performance during CIRP, despite no formal rejection of a resolution plan under Section 34(4)[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction under Section 34 to decline the appointment of an incumbent Resolution Professional as Liquidator and appoint another professional from the regulatory board's panel if dissatisfied with the professional's performance during the resolution process[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 34(1) read with Section 34(4) does not create an absolute vested right for an RP to become Liquidator; appointment from the panel of insolvency professionals furnished by the IBBI operates as an appointment upon the recommendation of the Board[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Factual assessment of CIRP administration showing that only one CoC meeting was held within 180 days with no substantive steps taken until the eve of CIRP expiry[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted within its statutory powers in replacing the RP, while clarifying that performance dissatisfaction did not constitute a finding of professional misconduct[cite: 18].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 26 October 2017 and 15 November 2017 are sustained; observations are clarified as not amounting to professional misconduct; appeals are dismissed with no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: Resolution Professional Sandeep Kumar Gupta appealed against orders of NCLT Kolkata Bench passed in the liquidation of Stewarts & Lloyds of India Ltd., whereby the tribunal refused to appoint him as Liquidator and instead appointed Mamta Binani from the IBBI panel[cite: 18]. The Appellant contended that an RP can only be replaced under the specific contingencies enumerated in Section 34(4) of the IBC[cite: 18]. The NCLAT held that the tribunal acted well within its jurisdiction to replace the RP due to unsatisfactory performance, noting that only one CoC meeting was convened throughout the 180-day CIRP[cite: 18]. Clarifying that the remarks did not imply misconduct, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 18].

case_title: Bhavik Bhimjyani vs. Uday Vinodchandra Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhavik Bhimjyani, shareholder/ex-director of Neelkanth Township & Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation), as Appellant; Uday Vinodchandra Shah, RP/Liquidator, as Respondent No. 1[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor raised Rs. 51 crores from a Financial Creditor, out of which advances exceeding Rs. 30 crores were disbursed to wholly owned subsidiaries (Urban Rupi Infrastructure and Neelkanth Palm Realty) and Rs. 5.27 crores to Lighthouse Developers under an MoU dated 6 January 2015[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Information disclosure dispute; advances exceeded Rs. 30 crores to subsidiaries and Rs. 5.27 crores to a related developer, alongside Rs. 61 lakhs to individual third parties[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 6 January 2015; bank statements provided from 10 August 2015; RP requisition email sent on 2 April 2018; NCLT disclosure order passed on 26 April 2018; liquidation ordered subsequently[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Requisition chart itemizing missing signed MoUs, balance confirmation letters, title records, and financial statements of wholly owned subsidiary companies holding approximately 50 acres of project land[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 26 April 2018 passed adverse observations accusing promoter-directors of concealing records and directed disclosure of all requisitioned documents; Appellant appealed challenging the adverse remarks and the RP's attempt to take over subsidiary assets[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional or Liquidator of a Corporate Debtor has jurisdiction under the IBC to take over the assets and original statutory documents of distinct, wholly owned subsidiary companies[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional or Liquidator of a holding Corporate Debtor has no statutory jurisdiction or legal authority to seize or take over the physical assets or original documents of separate subsidiary corporate entities, although entitled to inspect and obtain authenticated photocopies[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Corporate personhood separates a corporate debtor from its incorporated subsidiaries; CIRP and liquidation powers extend only to the property, receivables, and shareholding of the debtor itself, not direct asset control of subsidiary entities[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented ownership showing land parcels held under distinct subsidiary legal entities rather than direct title resting with the parent Corporate Debtor[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator may only inspect records and retain authenticated photocopies; adverse observations accusing the director of hiding records were set aside[cite: 19].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 26 April 2018 is modified; adverse observations against the Appellant are set aside; Appellant directed to permit the Liquidator to inspect records and provide authenticated photocopies of relevant subsidiary documents, but Liquidator is barred from seizing original documents or taking over subsidiary assets; appeal disposed of with no costs[cite: 19].
summary: Appellant Bhavik Bhimjyani, an ex-director of Neelkanth Township & Construction Pvt. Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order directing disclosure of documents regarding over Rs. 30 crores advanced to wholly owned subsidiaries and related entities, which included adverse findings of concealment[cite: 19]. The NCLAT modified the order and expunged the adverse remarks, clarifying that while the Appellant must permit inspection and furnish authenticated photocopies of relevant corporate records, a Resolution Professional or Liquidator has no legal authority or jurisdiction to take over the assets or seize the original records of separate subsidiary companies[cite: 19].

case_title: Somesh Bagchi & Ors. vs. Nicco Corporation Ltd., through Liquidator
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Somesh Bagchi and 20 other retired employees of Nicco Corporation Ltd. as Appellants; Vinod Kumar Kothari, Liquidator of Nicco Corporation Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation), as Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment relationship and statutory gratuity entitlements accrued under the Payment of Gratuity Act during service with the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants alleged that Rs. 16 Crore out of Rs. 27 Crore pre-liquidation assets was disbursed to secured creditors, diverting gratuity funds; liquidator verified that Rs. 2,26,34,566 lay in the Gratuity Trust Fund (Rs. 2,05,51,304 in HDFC and Rs. 20,83,262 in LIC) with a fund shortage of Rs. 5.70 Crore. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution process failed and liquidation order was passed under Section 33; interim distribution made on 22 December 2018; Gratuity Fund balance verified as on 30 June 2018 and 6 July 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's reply affidavit and email dated 6 July 2018 from ex-HR head confirming that Rs. 27,94,19,639 in the no-lien account at Allahabad Bank excluded gratuity funds and that no gratuity trust monies were used for creditor distribution. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation under Section 33; NCLT passed order dated 8 March 2018 regarding distribution; Appellants appealed to NCLAT alleging impermissible diversion of employee gratuity under Section 53.
legal_issues: Whether monies held in an employee Gratuity Trust Fund constitute assets of the Corporate Debtor available for liquidation distribution to creditors under Section 53 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory Gratuity Trust Funds maintained for employees do not form part of the estate or liquidation assets of the Corporate Debtor and cannot be attached, diverted, or disbursed to satisfy general creditor claims under Section 53 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53 liquidation waterfall distribution applies strictly to assets of the corporate debtor; employee gratuity maintained under a dedicated trust falls outside the liquidation estate. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation via bank records and liquidator affidavit establishing that the liquidation no-lien account balances did not commingle or disburse funds from the separate Gratuity Trust Fund accounts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator did not divert gratuity trust assets to creditors, and questions regarding make-up of historical trust deficits fall outside IBC summary jurisdiction, lying before competent civil/labor authorities.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of confirming that the Gratuity Trust Fund is not an asset of the Corporate Debtor; observations in the NCLT order dated 8 March 2018 are declared non-binding on competent authorities; liberty granted to Appellants to approach competent civil or labor authorities regarding fund shortages; I.A. Nos. 880 and 881 disposed of with no costs.
summary: Retired employees of Nicco Corporation Ltd. appealed against an NCLT liquidation order, contending that the Liquidator was impermissibly diverting statutory employee gratuity funds to satisfy secured creditor debts under Section 53 of the IBC. The Liquidator submitted affidavit evidence demonstrating that Rs. 2.26 Crores held in dedicated Gratuity Trust Fund accounts was strictly segregated and not used for creditor distributions. The NCLAT affirmed that employee Gratuity Trust Funds do not form part of the Corporate Debtor's liquidation assets under Section 53. Leaving questions regarding a Rs. 5.70 Crore trust shortage to competent labor forums, the Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal without costs.

case_title: Rajeev K. Aggarwal vs. Panipat Texo Fabs Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajeev K. Aggarwal, shareholder of Exclusive Overseas Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 2), as Appellant; M/s Panipat Texo Fabs Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor) as Respondent No. 1. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale and supply of polyester staple fibre by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor in the first half of the year 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding operational debt of Rs. 6,56,788 as on 31 March 2018; Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 1,50,000 and Rs. 1,06,788, defaulting on the remaining balance of Rs. 4,00,000 plus interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Outstanding balance crystallized on 31 March 2018; Operational Creditor sent demand notice under Section 8(1) demanding Rs. 4,00,000; petition under Section 9 admitted on 26 October 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced emails dated 26 April 2018, 1 May 2018, 5 May 2018, 7 June 2018, and 14 June 2018; Corporate Debtor failed to produce any contemporaneous letter, email, or communication evidencing complaints of defective or substandard goods prior to the demand notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 9 petition in Company Petition No. (IB)1106(ND)/2018 on 26 October 2018, imposing moratorium and appointing an IRP.
legal_issues: Whether an uncommunicated defense of substandard and defective goods raised for the first time in response to a Section 8 demand notice or Section 9 petition qualifies as a pre-existing dispute under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A dispute regarding the quality or standard of goods supplied must be substantiated by contemporaneous record demonstrating communication to the creditor prior to the service of the statutory demand notice, failing which it is a sham defense. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 read with Section 8 requires an objective pre-existing dispute; raising objections to quality for the first time in reply to a Section 8(1) demand notice or before the Adjudicating Authority does not satisfy the test laid down in Innoventive Industries. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of contemporary commercial records, delivery receipts, and communications; total absence of prior written objection by the buyer defeats a claim of pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor failed to establish any pre-existing dispute regarding goods quality prior to the demand notice, rendering the Section 9 admission valid.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 26 October 2018 admitting the Section 9 petition is affirmed; the appeal is dismissed with no order as to costs.
summary: Shareholder Rajeev K. Aggarwal appealed an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Panipat Texo Fabs Pvt. Ltd. against Exclusive Overseas Pvt. Ltd. for default on an unpaid balance of Rs. 4,00,000 for the supply of polyester staple fibre. The Appellant contended that the goods were defective and substandard. The NCLAT found that multiple demand emails from the creditor went uncontroverted and the corporate debtor failed to produce a single contemporaneous communication disputing quality prior to the Section 8 demand notice. Holding the defense to be a sham and lacking a pre-existing dispute, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Nayan Shah vs. Viral Rajarashi Mehta & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Nayan Shah, Shareholder and Director of M/s Neptune Ventures and Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor), as Appellant; Mr. Viral Rajarashi Mehta (Operational Creditor) as Respondent No. 1; Interim Resolution Professional as Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Brokerage/advisory services provided by Respondent No. 1 in connection with the commercial transaction designated as the 'TATA-Neptune deal'. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 1 Crore towards brokerage fee; during prolonged negotiations Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 11 Lakhs against a requested Rs. 25 Lakhs, and the dispute was ultimately settled for Rs. 75 Lakhs plus GST with part-payment made and post-dated cheques handed over. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8(1) issued on 16 September 2017; Corporate Debtor delivered reply notice disputing the liability on 6 November 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email communications exchanged between the parties from 7 October 2015 to 2017 showing ongoing active negotiations, disputes over the actual fee payable, and partial settlement adjustments. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 9 petition in CP No. 1640/IBC/NCLT/MB/MAH/2017 on 24 May 2018, imposing moratorium and appointing an IRP.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-existing dispute regarding the debt quantum and fee liability under Section 8(2) bars the admission of an operational creditor's Section 9 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In an application under Section 9 of the IBC, a pre-existing dispute encompasses not only the quality of goods or services but also bona fide disputes regarding the debt itself or the quantum of payment, precluding the occurrence of default. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpreting Section 8(2) and Section 9 in terms of the Supreme Court's mandate in Innoventive Industries, the moment a genuine pre-existing dispute exists prior to the statutory demand notice, the operational creditor falls outside the purview of the Code. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contemporaneous email exchanges proving protracted negotiations on the exact amount payable prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice establish an existing bona fide dispute on quantum. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: A pre-existing dispute as to the quantum of payable debt existed prior to the Section 8 notice, rendering the Section 9 petition inadmissible.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24 May 2018 is set aside; the Section 9 application is dismissed; moratorium, appointment of IRP, and consequential actions are vacated; the Corporate Debtor is released to its Board of Directors; Corporate Debtor directed to pay Rs. 1.5 Lakh towards IRP fees and costs within a fortnight; liberty granted to Respondent No. 1 to move the Appellate Tribunal if handed settlement cheques bounce; appeal allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Nayan Shah, director of Neptune Ventures and Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Viral Rajarashi Mehta for alleged unpaid brokerage of Rs. 1 Crore. The Appellant proved that emails exchanged since October 2015 demonstrated ongoing negotiations and a dispute over the quantum payable, which was subsequently settled for Rs. 75 Lakhs plus GST. The NCLAT held that under Section 9, a pre-existing dispute encompasses genuine disagreements over the quantum of debt. Consequently, no statutory default could be established, and the Appellate Tribunal set aside the CIRP admission order.

case_title: Vijay Kumar Jain vs. Standard Chartered Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vijay Kumar Jain, Director of suspended Board of Ruchi Soya Industries Limited (Corporate Debtor), as Appellant; Standard Chartered Bank Ltd. & Ors. (Financial Creditors/CoC) as Respondents; Resolution Professional as Respondent No. 4. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Ongoing CIRP of Ruchi Soya Industries Limited wherein prospective resolution applicants submitted competing resolution plans under Section 30 of the Code. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute arose over procedural rights during resolution plan deliberation; no specific monetary default metrics at issue in the appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC meetings convened under Regulation 19 and 21 of the CIRP Regulations, 2016 to negotiate and vote upon compliant resolution plans. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agendas and notices issued under Regulation 21(3) by the Resolution Professional for CoC meetings, which withheld confidential copies of competing resolution plans from the suspended directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Suspended director preferred an appeal before NCLAT seeking mandatory supply of copies of all submitted resolution plans to the suspended Board of Directors based on attendance rights under Section 24(3)(b) and binding effect under Section 31.
legal_issues: Whether members of the suspended Board of Directors and non-voting participants attending CoC meetings under Section 24 of the IBC are entitled to receive confidential copies of competing resolution plans.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The right of suspended directors to attend Committee of Creditors meetings without voting power does not confer an entitlement to receive confidential resolution plans submitted by competing resolution applicants. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 24(3) and (4) read with Section 30(2) and Regulation 21 requires notice and agenda to be given to suspended directors, but resolution plans remain confidential proprietary documents that cannot be shared with non-voting participants or competing applicants. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of statutory role distinctions established that commercial feasibility and viability analysis rests exclusively within the domain and expert judgment of the voting financial creditors in the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While the suspended Board may offer suggestions during debt contract negotiations, they have no statutory right to demand copies of confidential resolution plans.
operative_order: The prayer for directions to provide copies of the resolution plans to the suspended Board of Directors is declined; the appeal is disposed of with observations; no order as to costs.
summary: Vijay Kumar Jain, a suspended director of Ruchi Soya Industries Ltd., appealed to the NCLAT seeking directions to compel the Committee of Creditors and Resolution Professional to supply the suspended Board with copies of all submitted resolution plans under Section 24 of the IBC. The NCLAT held that resolution plans are confidential commercial documents under Section 30(2) and cannot be distributed to non-voting participants, including suspended directors or competitor applicants. Although suspended directors are entitled to attend CoC meetings and provide suggestions regarding debt contract modifications, determining the feasibility and viability of plans remains the exclusive preserve of the voting CoC. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India vs. Wig Associates Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI, statutory regulatory body) as Appellant; Wig Associates Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) & Ors., including Mr. Mahendra Wig (Resolution Applicant), as Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Wig Associates Pvt. Ltd., where Expression of Interest was published on 4 April 2018, and Mr. Mahendra Wig submitted a resolution plan approved by 100% voting share of the CoC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Challenge confined to statutory eligibility and locus standi; no monetary loan default quantum adjudicated in the appeal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EOI published on 4 April 2018; Section 29A promulgated via Ordinance on 23 November 2017 and enacted via Amendment Act on 18 January 2018; NCLT approval order passed on 4 June 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution applicant was a connected person/relative of the promoter-directors and guarantor under Section 29A(h), but the Adjudicating Authority held the amendment to be prospective and approved the plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench by order dated 4 June 2018 approved the resolution plan, holding Section 29A to be prospective; IBBI filed an appeal under Section 61 challenging paras 7 and 8 of the NCLT order.
legal_issues: Whether the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) has locus standi as an 'aggrieved person' under Section 61 of the IBC to appeal against judicial orders interpreting statutory provisions such as Section 29A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A regulatory body established to monitor and make regulations does not qualify as an 'aggrieved person' under statutory appellate provisions to challenge judicial interpretations rendered by an Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 196 empowers the IBBI to perform regulatory and monitoring functions over insolvency professionals and utilities; it does not confer standing under Section 61, which is reserved for parties directly affected by CIRP orders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold jurisdictional examination of whether the appellant is an aggrieved entity with a direct legal interest or claim in the CIRP proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The IBBI lacks locus standi to prefer an appeal under Section 61; the duty to challenge erroneous interpretations of Section 29A rests with the Resolution Professional who represents the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: The appeal preferred by the IBBI is declined/not entertained for lack of locus standi; liberty is granted to IBBI to advise the Resolution Professional to prefer an appeal under Section 61 if statutory provisions were violated; appeal disposed of with observations; no order as to costs.
summary: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) appealed under Section 61 against an NCLT Mumbai Bench order approving a resolution plan submitted by Mahendra Wig for Wig Associates Pvt. Ltd., challenging the tribunal's finding that Section 29A applied only prospectively. The NCLAT held that IBBI, as a regulatory body exercising functions under Section 196 and Section 240, does not constitute an 'aggrieved person' entitled to appeal judicial orders under Section 61. The Appellate Tribunal observed that the duty to appeal legally erroneous interpretations rests with the Resolution Professional who represents the Corporate Debtor, and accordingly disposed of the appeal without costs.

case_title: Sri Pravir Kumar Roy vs. M/s. Bogidhola Tea & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Pravir Kumar Roy, Executive Director of M/s Bogidhola Tea & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Original Respondent No. 2); M/s Bogidhola Tea & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1); Sri Abhay Kumar Singh (Respondent No. 2/Substituted party); Sri Sajay Kumar Singh (Respondent No. 3/Original Petitioner); Smt. Prem Kumari Roy (Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Longstanding corporate dispute regarding oppression and mismanagement concerning the management, directorship, and tea estate operations of M/s Bogidhola Tea & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural and interim adjudication dispute; no monetary debt or default calculation involved. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Company Petition No. 80 of 2000 pending since 2000; substitution order passed by CLB on 8 February 2016; unnumbered recall application filed on 9 March 2016; IA No. 17 of 2018 dismissed/reserved on 15 May 2018 with order dated 1 June 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annexures A-3, A-4, and A-5 comprising the recall application dated 9 March 2016 and corresponding replies, which were retained in CLB New Delhi records and omitted during transfer of physical files to NCLT Guwahati. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 17 of 2018 before NCLT Guwahati to call for unnumbered CLB application records; NCLT passed the impugned order dated 1 June 2018 without hearing the pending recall application on merits.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can proceed to determine a company petition without calling for or adjudicating pending, untransferred interlocutory recall applications filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When judicial forums are reorganized, an untransferred application duly entertained by a predecessor forum must be formally adjudicated, and tribunals possess inherent powers to reconstruct records using parties' verified copies to avoid delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013 mandates expeditious disposal of company petitions within three months, requiring tribunals to balance procedural completeness with non-protraction of legacy litigation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that undisputed copies of the application and responsive pleadings are already in the physical possession of the parties and part of the appellate paper book. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: To prevent further delay in an eighteen-year-old petition, the NCLT must hear the recall application using reconstructed records without staying proceedings for physical retrieval from the CLB registry.
operative_order: Final order in para 51 of the impugned order dated 1 June 2018 is modified; NCLT Guwahati is directed to request NCLT Delhi for original records, while simultaneously proceeding to hear the recall application (Annexure A-3 to A-5) on the basis of reconstructed copies; NCLT granted discretion to dispose of the application along with final disposal of the company petition at the earliest; appeal disposed with no costs.
summary: Executive Director Pravir Kumar Roy appealed an order of NCLT Guwahati in IA No. 17 of 2018 arising from an eighteen-year-old oppression and mismanagement petition concerning Bogidhola Tea & Trading Co. Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant challenged the non-retrieval and non-adjudication of a 2016 recall application filed before the erstwhile CLB New Delhi that went missing during file transfer to Guwahati. Exercising inherent powers and emphasizing Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013, the NCLAT directed NCLT Guwahati to hear the application immediately using reconstructed copies without waiting for original files from Delhi, disposing of the appeal without costs.

case_title: R.B. Synthetics & Anr. vs. Bee Ceelene Textile Mills Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s R.B. Synthetics & HUF of Radhakishan Bhagwandas Ruchandani as Appellants/Financial Creditors; Bee Ceelene Textile Mills Pvt. Ltd. as Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unsecured loans and financial advances provided by the Appellants to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor's audited financial statements as on 31 March 2012 showed unsecured loans and advances from related parties totaling Rs. 8,35,944, which remained unpaid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Audited financial accounts covered the period 2006 to 2011; default reflected in financial statements as on 31 March 2012. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Annexure 'E' to the petition containing audited balance sheets and financial accounts of the Corporate Debtor reflecting related-party loans, though missing a formal authorization letter and itemized creditor ledger linkages in Parts IV and V of Form 1. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP(IB) No. 158/7/NCLT/AHM/2017 rejected the Section 7 petition on 31 January 2018 on grounds that the authorization letter was omitted and individual petitioner receivables were not specified in the balance sheet.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Section 7 insolvency petition for curable procedural defects, such as an omitted authorization letter or incomplete particulars in Form 1, without issuing mandatory statutory cure notice under the proviso to Section 7(5)(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the proviso to Section 7(5)(b) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority has a mandatory statutory obligation to issue notice granting the applicant seven days to rectify defects before rejecting an incomplete Section 7 application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(b) read with its proviso establishes that technical omissions, including missing letters of authorization or incomplete Part-IV/V details in Form 1, constitute procedural defects rather than substantive grounds for summary rejection. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the petition form against the statutory requirements of Rule 4 and Form 1 to distinguish between incurable absence of debt/default and curable procedural document omissions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rejection of the Section 7 petition without providing the mandatory opportunity to rectify defects was contrary to statutory mandate and unsustainable.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 31 January 2018 is set aside; Appellants granted three weeks to rectify all defects, file authorization letters, and complete Form 1 particulars, with copies furnished to the Corporate Debtor; Corporate Debtor granted liberty to settle, failing which NCLT Ahmedabad shall hear the matter within three weeks; appeal allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants R.B. Synthetics and Radhakishan Bhagwandas Ruchandani HUF appealed an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench rejecting their Section 7 application against Bee Ceelene Textile Mills Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT had summarily rejected the petition on grounds that no authorization letter was filed and the corporate debtor's balance sheet did not expressly link the Rs. 8,35,944 related-party loan to the petitioners. The NCLAT held that under the proviso to Section 7(5)(b), the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily required to grant an applicant seven days to rectify technical or procedural defects before rejecting a petition. Setting aside the rejection, the Appellate Tribunal allowed the Appellants three weeks to cure the record.

case_title: Anil Mahindroo & Anr. vs. Earth Iconic Infrastructure (P) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anil Mahindroo & Anr. were allottees/investors claiming as Financial Creditors; Earth Iconic Infrastructure (P) Ltd. was the real estate developer Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An MoU and allotment letter dated 14 May 2014 were executed for Flat No. ETTS 1959 on the first floor in the project 'Earth Titanium Studios' at Greater Noida, UP, under an assured return/committed return plan for a total sale consideration of Rs. 20,80,000 plus taxes, where possession was due in September 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was obligated to make commitment payments of Rs. 20,000 per month (varying based on PDCs) and defaulted by stopping payments from February 2016 onwards, despite the applicants having paid the full sale consideration. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The final instalment of sale consideration was paid by May 2015; commitment charges ceased after February 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU dated 14 May 2014 promising monthly commitment amounts, and the Corporate Debtor's Balance Sheet as of 31 March 2015 categorizing amounts under 'other current liabilities' (advance from customer) including commitment charges payable, establishing commercial borrowing. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 application (C.P. No. (IB)-16(PB)/2017) filed before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi was dismissed on 8 March 2017 relying on the lower tribunal's ruling in Nikhil Mehta & Sons, holding that assured return allottees are not Financial Creditors.
legal_issues: Whether real estate purchasers who opt for an assured/committed return plan qualify as Financial Creditors having disbursed debt against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(7) and 5(8)(f) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An investor-purchaser under a committed return scheme who disburses consideration to a developer having the commercial effect of a borrowing constitutes a Financial Creditor holding a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) encompasses transactions where money is raised with commercial effect of borrowing; commitment charges treated in financial statements as financial costs represent compensation for time value of money under Section 5(8). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance sheet entries reflecting advances from customers with commitment charges treated akin to loans and financial costs, paired with the absence of force majeure delays or purchaser default, establish debt and default. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants proved that the disbursement was for time value of money, establishing their status as Financial Creditors and rendering the Section 7 petition maintainable.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 8 March 2017 is set aside; the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority to admit the Section 7 application if complete, or provide seven days' cure notice under the proviso to Section 7 if incomplete. No order as to costs.
summary: Financial Creditors Anil Mahindroo and another appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their Section 7 application under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code against Earth Iconic Infrastructure. The applicants had fully paid the sale consideration of Rs. 20,80,000 for a studio apartment under an assured monthly return plan, which the Corporate Debtor stopped servicing after February 2016. Following the appellate precedent in Nikhil Mehta, the NCLAT held that committed return investments constitute financial debt under Section 5(8)(f) disbursed for the time value of money. Allowing the appeal, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the rejection and remitted the petition for admission.

case_title: Sh. Neeraj Bhatia vs. Davinder Ahluwalia & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Neeraj Bhatia, shareholder/director of M/s Summit Aviation Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, Respondent No. 3), as Appellant; Davinder Ahluwalia and Mrs. Mamta Ahluwalia (Respondents No. 1 & 2) as alleged Financial Creditors/Guarantors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed credit/loan facilities from PNB and Bank of Maharashtra (composite Rs. 12.05 crores); respondents mortgaged property and subsequently paid Rs. 1.05 crores to lenders to release mortgaged property, while also asserting payments of Rs. 29,97,000 made towards Corporate Debtor's liabilities (including employee salaries and bank deposits) in or before 2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Alleged default of Rs. 29,97,000 plus interest, alongside an outstanding guarantee refund claim of Rs. 78 lakhs (after Rs. 27 lakhs repayment by Corporate Debtor). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Claimed operational/miscellaneous payments were made in or prior to 2012; guarantee deposits of Rs. 80 lakhs initially and up to Rs. 1.05 crores were disbursed to banks prior to initiation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's liability entries were recorded in the name of the respondents' daughter; payments were routed directly to lender banks as personal guarantors or paid to third-party individuals/employees rather than disbursed to the Corporate Debtor against time value of money. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the Section 7 petition filed by respondents in IB No. (IB)-229(ND)/2017 on 1 August 2017, imposing moratorium and appointing an IRP.
legal_issues: Whether a personal guarantor who deposits amounts directly with a lender bank to discharge a guarantee or pay company expenses qualifies as a Financial Creditor having disbursed a Financial Debt against consideration for time value of money under Section 5(7) and 5(8) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A personal guarantor who pays money to a lender bank or pays operational expenses of a company without legal debt assignment or direct disbursement for the time value of money does not become a Financial Creditor against the Corporate Debtor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) mandates that a financial debt must be disbursed against consideration for the time value of money; payments made under guarantee to release mortgaged property do not convert the guarantor into a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) without commercial borrowing elements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To establish Section 7 maintainability, the applicant must produce evidence of direct disbursement or borrowing having commercial effect of borrowing with time value compensation rather than unilateral discharge of guarantee obligations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondents failed to establish disbursement for time value of money, rendering their Section 7 application unmaintainable.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 1 August 2017 admitting Section 7 is set aside; all consequential actions, moratorium, appointments of IRP, and bank freezes are declared illegal and vacated; Corporate Debtor is released to function independently via its Board; NCLT to fix IRP fees to be paid by Corporate Debtor; appeal allowed with no costs.
summary: Appellant Neeraj Bhatia, director of Summit Aviation Pvt. Ltd., challenged an NCLT New Delhi order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Davinder Ahluwalia and Mamta Ahluwalia. The respondents claimed financial creditor status after paying Rs. 1.05 crores to lenders to discharge guarantee obligations and paying Rs. 29,97,000 towards corporate expenses. The NCLAT held that discharging a guarantee to a lending bank does not constitute disbursement of a debt for the time value of money under Section 5(8). The respondents were not financial creditors, making the Section 7 petition unmaintainable. The appeal was allowed and the CIRP proceedings were terminated.

case_title: Pravinbhai Raninga vs. The Kotak Resources & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pravinbhai Raninga (Appellant/Shareholder); The Kotak Resources (Respondent No. 1/Alleged Financial Creditor Assignee); M/s Raninga Ispat Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Corporate Debtor); Navis Multitrade Pvt. Ltd. (Assignor/Third party). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alleged tripartite arrangement under an MoU dated 5 July 2012 and Pledge Agreement dated 5 September 2012 where Kotak Resources allegedly lent Rs. 50 lakhs to Navis to trade in pig iron, who in turn lent to Corporate Debtor, followed by a purported Deed of Assignment of Debt dated 25 October 2017 assigning Rs. 1 crore debt to Kotak Resources. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Rs. 1 crore principal plus interest; however, Corporate Debtor demonstrated that the initial Rs. 50 lakhs advance had been fully repaid via bank channels, leaving a credit of Rs. 4,27,000 due from the creditor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MoU executed on 5 July 2012; pledge agreement executed on 5 September 2012; notice issued on 16 September 2017; assignment deed executed on 25 October 2017 referring inconsistently to dues calculated up to future date 5 November 2017 and prior letter dated 24 October 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor produced ledger accounts (1 April 2011 to 31 March 2014) and bank statements proving complete refund of Rs. 50 lakhs; assignment deed contained unexplained discrepancies including referencing future dates and unverified second tranche of Rs. 50 lakhs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Ahmedabad Bench) admitted Respondent No. 1's Section 7 petition in C.P. (IB) No. 200/7/NCLT/AHM/2017 on 21 February 2017.
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can admit a Section 7 application where the underlying debt assignment documents are contradictory and dubious, and the debtor establishes that the disbursed amount has been fully repaid such that no debt is due or payable in law and fact.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7(5) of the IBC, an application cannot be admitted if the Corporate Debtor successfully proves that default has not occurred because the debt is not payable in law or in fact. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Supreme Court's mandate in Innoventive Industries, the Adjudicating Authority must be satisfied that a default has occurred; a debt is not due if it is not legally or factually payable. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where assignment deeds contain irreconcilable internal date contradictions (referring to subsequent dates) and lack evidence of actual secondary disbursals, while audited ledgers show full repayment of initial disbursements, existence of debt and default cannot be sustained. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The documents relied upon by the financial creditor were fabricated and doubtful, and the initial loan stood discharged, meaning no default occurred.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 21 February 2017 is set aside; the Section 7 application is dismissed; all moratorium orders, appointment of IRP, and subsequent actions are quashed; Corporate Debtor is released to its Board of Directors; appeal allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant challenged an order of NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitting a Section 7 application filed by The Kotak Resources against Raninga Ispat Pvt. Ltd. The applicant alleged default on a Rs. 1 crore debt assigned from Navis Multitrade under a 2017 assignment deed. The NCLAT examined the record and found serious inconsistencies, including the assignment deed referring to calculations of future dates and pre-dating letters. Furthermore, bank statements and ledgers confirmed that the initial disbursal of Rs. 50 lakhs was completely repaid, and no further disbursement occurred. Concluding that no debt was due or payable in fact or law, the NCLAT set aside the admission order.

case_title: Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. vs. Binani Industries Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Binani Cement Limited (Corporate Debtor); Binani Industries Limited (Holding company/Promoter); Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Resolution Applicant 1); UltraTech Cement Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant 2); Vijay Kumar Iyer (Resolution Professional); Committee of Creditors (Financed by SBI, Edelweiss, Exim Bank, etc.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Binani Cement Limited; resolution plans were invited by RP under a Process Document issued on 20 December 2017 for corporate turnaround. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Verified financial creditor claims totaled Rs. 7,289.05 crores, alongside operational debt and guarantee exposure claims. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Process document issued 20 December 2017; UltraTech submitted plan on 12 February 2018; Rajputana revised offer on 7 March 2018; UltraTech submitted revised offer on 8 March 2018; CoC voted for Rajputana on 14 March 2018; NCLT rejected Rajputana's plan on 2 May 2018; CoC subsequently approved UltraTech's plan unanimously with 100% vote on 28 May 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rajputana's plan paid 100% to certain direct lenders but discriminated against Exim Bank (72.59%), SBI HK (10%), and large operational creditors, threatening liquidation value; UltraTech's revised plan offered Rs. 7,950.34 crores including interest and working capital infusion, paying 100% to all financial and unrelated operational creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected Rajputana's plan for being discriminatory and directed CoC to reconsider offers including UltraTech; Binani Industries separately sought CIRP termination through private settlement.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan can discriminate between similarly situated financial creditors or operational creditors, and whether the CoC is obligated to consider higher revised bids that ensure asset value maximization and balanced treatment of all stakeholders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The primary objective of the IBC is resolution and asset value maximization for all stakeholders; resolution plans cannot discriminate between similarly situated classes of creditors or reduce operational creditors to mere liquidation value. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25(2)(h) read with Section 30(2) empowers the CoC to negotiate and accept compliant revised offers to maximize asset value prior to final approval; Regulation 38 cannot be used to impose discriminatory liquidation value treatment. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of resolution plan terms demonstrating unequal percentage distributions among similarly situated corporate guarantee beneficiaries and operational creditor bands proves facial discrimination contrary to the Code's objectives. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rajputana's plan was discriminatory, while UltraTech's revised plan satisfied all statutory requirements under Section 30(2) and achieved value maximization.
operative_order: Company Appeals Nos. 123/2018, 188/2018, 82/2018, and 216/2018 are dismissed; Company Appeal No. 234/2018 is allowed, expunging adverse remarks against the Resolution Professional; the revised Resolution Plan of UltraTech Cement Ltd. is approved under Section 31; matter remitted to NCLT for constitution of a monitoring committee.
summary: Multiple appeals were consolidated arising from the CIRP of Binani Cement Ltd. The Committee of Creditors initially approved Rajputana Properties' resolution plan, which provided 100% payouts to direct financial creditors but heavily discounted similarly placed guarantee beneficiaries and operational creditors, while ignoring a superior revised offer from UltraTech Cement. The NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected Rajputana's plan as discriminatory. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection, holding that the IBC mandates maximization of value and non-discriminatory, balanced treatment of all creditors. Upon considering the 100% CoC-approved revised plan of UltraTech Cement amounting to Rs. 7,950.34 crores, the Appellate Tribunal approved UltraTech's plan under Section 31.

case_title: Registrar of Companies-Cum-Official Liquidator, Rajasthan, Jaipur vs. Gyan Chand Agarwal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Registrar of Companies-Cum-Official Liquidator, Rajasthan, Jaipur as Appellant; Gyan Chand Agarwal, Director in default, as Respondent. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The respondent held directorships in contravention of the statutory directorship limits specified under Section 165(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Continuous statutory contravention lasting 849 days from 1 April 2015 to 18 July 2017, where the statute prescribes a mandatory minimum fine of Rs. 5,000 per day up to Rs. 25,000 per day. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Period of default ran from 1 April 2015 to 18 July 2017 (849 days). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Admitted continuation of excess directorships across 849 days without dispute regarding the duration of default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed a compounding application under Section 441 before NCLT New Delhi; by order dated 28 March 2018, NCLT compounded the offence and reduced the compounding fee to a lump sum of Rs. 10,00,000, which fell below the statutory minimum.
legal_issues: Whether the National Company Law Tribunal possesses jurisdiction while compounding an offence under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 to impose a fine lower than the minimum statutory quantum prescribed under Section 165(6).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a statute stipulates a mandatory minimum penalty for a continuous contravention, a tribunal compounding the offence has no legal discretion or jurisdiction to impose a compounding fee below the prescribed statutory minimum floor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 165(6) uses unambiguous mandatory language ('shall not be less than five thousand rupees... for every day'), fixing an irreducible statutory minimum fine. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Quantification of penalty requires multiplying the established, undisputed number of days of continuous default (849 days) by the statutory minimum daily rate (Rs. 5,000). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted without jurisdiction in reducing the fine below the minimum prescribed floor; the mandatory penalty for 849 days at Rs. 5,000 per day totals Rs. 42,45,000.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 28 March 2018 is set aside; the compounding fee is quantified to the statutory minimum of Rs. 42,45,000 (calculated at Rs. 5,000 per day for 849 days), directed to be paid by the Respondent within 45 days; appeal allowed with no order as to costs.
summary: The Registrar of Companies, Jaipur appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order compounding Gyan Chand Agarwal's contravention of directorship limits under Section 165(1) of the Companies Act, 2013. The NCLT had imposed a reduced compounding fee of Rs. 10,00,000 for a continuous violation spanning 849 days. The NCLAT held that Section 165(6) prescribes a mandatory minimum fine of Rs. 5,000 per day, leaving the Tribunal with no statutory discretion or jurisdiction to reduce the penalty below this floor. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the NCLT order and enhanced the fine to the statutory minimum of Rs. 42,45,000 payable within 45 days.

case_title: Dinesh Gupta vs. Hajura Singh Bhim Singh & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Dinesh Gupta, Director of Corporate Debtor M/s. Best Foods Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is M/s. Hajura Singh Bhim Singh (Operational Creditor)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial sale and supply of agricultural produce (paddy) by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor through authorized agents[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default are not specified in the appellate order; default arose from non-payment of invoices for supplied paddy[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial demand notice under Section 8(1) issued via advocate was received by Corporate Debtor on 25.08.2017; reply under Section 8(2) sent on 30.08.2017; initial Section 9 petition withdrawn on technical grounds regarding advocate notices; fresh Section 8(1) notice issued; Section 9 petition admitted by NCLT on 02.02.2018[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's reply dated 30.08.2017 under Section 8(2) disputing claim for the first time on grounds of inferior paddy quality and pending Section 138 NI Act proceedings, with no evidence of pre-existing dispute raised prior to receipt of the initial demand notice[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted the Operational Creditor's Section 9 petition on 02.02.2018, declared a moratorium under Section 14, and initiated IRP appointment; Appellant director appealed contending a pre-existing dispute existed[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether a dispute raised for the first time in reply to a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) qualifies as a pre-existing dispute to bar the admission of a Section 9 application under the IBC, and whether re-filing Section 9 after technical withdrawal of an earlier notice affects maintainability[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To bar an operational debt application under Section 9 of the IBC, the dispute regarding the quality or provision of goods must demonstrably exist prior to the issuance and receipt of the initial statutory demand notice under Section 8(1); a defense raised for the first time in response to the statutory demand notice does not constitute a pre-existing dispute[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) read with Section 9 requires proof of a dispute pre-dating the statutory demand; withdrawing an application purely to cure technical defects in the notice does not legitimize belated disputes raised after receipt of the first notice[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict temporal verification of communications showing that quality grievances were raised only subsequent to receipt of the demand notice on 25.08.2017[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no dispute existed prior to the first Section 8(1) demand notice, the Section 9 petition was maintainable and rightly admitted[cite: 26].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned admission order dated 2nd February, 2018 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 26].
summary: Appellant Dinesh Gupta, Director of Corporate Debtor Best Foods Ltd., appealed against the NCLT's order dated 2 February 2018 admitting an insolvency application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 filed by Operational Creditor Hajura Singh Bhim Singh for unpaid paddy supplies[cite: 26]. Appellant contended that a pre-existing dispute existed regarding paddy quality and pending Section 138 NI Act proceedings[cite: 26]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, holding that no dispute was raised prior to the receipt of the initial Section 8(1) demand notice on 25 August 2017, and disputes concocted only in reply to statutory notices cannot constitute a valid pre-existing dispute under the Code[cite: 26].

case_title: Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. (Resolution Professional) vs. Government of India, Ministry of Coal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd.; Respondent is the Government of India, Ministry of Coal[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement dated 02.03.2015 executed between the President of India and the Corporate Debtor, followed by Vesting Order No. 104/18/2015/NA dated 23.03.2015 in respect of Gare Palma IV/7 Coal Mine in Raigad, Chhattisgarh[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default of CIRP not detailed; termination of the coal mine agreement was prompted by an estimated annual revenue loss of Rs. 314.3 Crores to the State Exchequer[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated under Section 7 on 18.07.2017; show cause notice for termination issued by Ministry of Coal on 13.04.2017; formal termination order issued on 30.12.2017; NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the challenge in MA 17/2018 on 16.01.2018[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Terms of the Coal Mine Agreement requiring execution of a formal mining lease with the State Government pursuant to Section 8(4)(b) and 8(8) of the Ordinance, which was never executed, and pre-CIRP show cause notice dated 13.04.2017[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed MA 17/2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench challenging the termination order dated 30.12.2017 as violative of the Section 14 moratorium; NCLT held on 16.01.2018 that the termination was valid and not hit by Section 14(1)(d), which was appealed to NCLAT[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether the termination of a Coal Mine Development and Production Agreement by the Ministry of Coal during the CIRP moratorium violates Section 14(1)(d) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 where the mining lease was never formally granted by the State Government[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC protecting properties occupied by or in possession of the corporate debtor does not bar a statutory authority from terminating a development agreement where vesting remained incomplete and no formal statutory lease was executed to grant legal possession or occupation to the debtor[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(d) prohibits recovery of property occupied by or in the possession of the corporate debtor; where vesting conditions are unfulfilled and no mining lease is granted by the State Government under mining laws, the corporate debtor lacks legal possession, removing the termination from the purview of Section 14(1)(d)[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented verification of the execution of the statutory mining lease and the timing of cause of action, noting show cause notices were issued well prior to the insolvency commencement date[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The coal mine was not legally occupied or possessed by the Corporate Debtor, and the pre-insolvency cancellation proceeding was valid and unhindered by Section 14[cite: 27].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 16th January, 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is affirmed; the interim order dated 8th February, 2018 is vacated; Government of India is at liberty to accept bids and create third-party interests in the mines; no order as to costs[cite: 27].
