summary: The Resolution Professional of Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 16 January 2018 upholding the Ministry of Coal's termination order dated 30 December 2017 regarding the Gare Palma IV/7 Coal Mine[cite: 27]. The RP contended that the termination violated the Section 14 moratorium under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 27]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, holding that because the Corporate Debtor had not entered into a formal mining lease with the State Government, the vesting was incomplete and the debtor had no legal possession or occupation under Section 14(1)(d)[cite: 27]. The termination, initiated prior to CIRP, was therefore valid[cite: 27].

case_title: M/s. J.R. Agro Industries (P) Ltd. vs. Resolution Professional, Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. J.R. Agro Industries (P) Ltd. (Resolution Applicant); Respondent is Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd.; connected entities are promoter Y.K. Jhunjhunwala and associate company J.R. Organics Limited[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd., wherein the Appellant submitted a resolution plan that was rejected at threshold by the Resolution Professional[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not applicable; J.R. Organics Ltd., an associate of the applicant, had defaulted on credit facilities of Rs. 6.94 Crores with Punjab National Bank, classified as NPA/doubtful[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 29A enforced on 23.11.2017; Appellant filed manipulated annual returns on 25.12.2017; PNB NPA letter issued on 05.03.2018; NCLT Allahabad rejected Appellant's application on 31.05.2018[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC Annual Returns (MGT-7) for FY 2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17 proving Y.K. Jhunjhunwala and HUF held 15% shares and were promoters of Appellant, with Y.K. Jhunjhunwala disqualified as director (01.11.2016 to 31.10.2021); Balance sheet showing Appellant held 43% equity in J.R. Organics Ltd., an NPA account holder with PNB[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench upheld the RP's decision on 31.05.2018 disqualifying Appellant under Section 29A(c), (e), and (j); Appellant appealed contending it was merely an operational creditor without connection to the debtor[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution applicant is rendered ineligible under Section 29A(e) and 29A(c) read with Section 29A(j) of the IBC if its promoter/connected person is disqualified as a director under the Companies Act, 2013, or if its associate company holds an unresolved Non-Performing Asset (NPA) account[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 29A read with its Explanation, a resolution applicant is strictly barred from submitting a resolution plan if its promoter or connected person is disqualified to act as a director under the Companies Act, 2013, or if an associate company under its significant influence has an account classified as an NPA for more than one year without clearing overdue debts[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(j) extends the disqualifications under clauses (a) to (i) to connected persons, which includes promoters under Explanation (i) and associate companies (holding 20% or more voting power under Section 2(6) of the Companies Act, 2013) under Explanation (iii); retroactive manipulations in annual returns cannot evade statutory ineligibility[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of statutory MGT-7 filings, RoC disqualified director registries, and bank credit classification reports confirming promoter standing and NPA classification[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant was disqualified under Section 29A(e) due to a disqualified promoter and under Section 29A(c) through its NPA associate entity J.R. Organics Ltd., fully justifying rejection of its plan[cite: 28].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned judgment dated 31st May, 2018 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: Appellant J.R. Agro Industries (P) Ltd. challenged NCLT Allahabad's order dated 31 May 2018 upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of its resolution plan for Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 28]. The NCLT found that Appellant's promoter, Y.K. Jhunjhunwala (holding 15%), was disqualified to act as a director under Section 164(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, triggering Section 29A(e) read with Section 29A(j)[cite: 28]. Additionally, Appellant held a 43% stake in J.R. Organics Ltd., whose bank account was an unregularized NPA, attracting Section 29A(c)[cite: 28]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, affirming that the applicant was disqualified under Section 29A(c), (e), and (j)[cite: 28].

case_title: Randhiraj Thakur vs. M/s. Jindal Saxena Financial Services Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Randhiraj Thakur, Director of Corporate Debtor Mayfair Capital Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is M/s. Jindal Saxena Financial Services Private Limited (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Mayfair Capital Private Limited[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-Corporate Deposit Agreement executed between Jindal Saxena Financial Services and Mayfair Capital Private Limited[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default not specified in the appellate order; default arose from non-repayment of the inter-corporate deposit[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Certificate of registration granted by RBI on 16.03.2012; Section 7 petition CP (IB)-84(PB)/2017 admitted ex-parte on 27.06.2017; recall application CA No. 233(PB)/2017 rejected by NCLT on 08.01.2018[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificate of Registration issued by RBI under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934 registering Mayfair Capital as a non-banking financial institution, and its Memorandum of Association establishing investment and financial service operations[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 27.06.2017 and rejected the debtor's recall application on 08.01.2018; director appealed challenging jurisdiction on grounds that the company was a financial service provider excluded from the Code[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether an entity registered as a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) with the Reserve Bank of India qualifies as a 'corporate person' or 'corporate debtor' amenable to CIRP under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An entity carrying on the business of a non-banking financial institution under a license granted by a financial regulator is a financial service provider, expressly excluded from the definition of a corporate person under the IBC, and cannot be subjected to corporate insolvency resolution proceedings under Section 7[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(7) of the IBC defines 'corporate person' but explicitly carves out an exception stating that it 'shall not include any financial service provider'; under Section 3(8), a corporate debtor must be a corporate person. Consequently, NBFCs registered under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act are excluded from the ambit of Part II of the Code[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production of a valid Certificate of Registration issued by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 45-IA confirming the company's status as a regulated non-banking financial institution[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Mayfair Capital is a financial service provider excluded from the IBC; the Section 7 application was non-maintainable ab initio and the admission order lacked jurisdiction[cite: 30].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned orders dated 27th June, 2017 and 8th January, 2018 passed by the Adjudicating Authority are set aside; CIRP, moratorium, and account freezes are quashed; Corporate Debtor is released to function through its Board; NCLT to determine IRP fees payable by Mayfair Capital; no costs[cite: 30].
summary: Appellant Randhiraj Thakur, Director of Mayfair Capital Private Limited, appealed against NCLT New Delhi's orders dated 27 June 2017 and 8 January 2018 initiating CIRP under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 on an application by Jindal Saxena Financial Services[cite: 30]. The Appellant contended that the company was an NBFC registered with the Reserve Bank of India under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act[cite: 30]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and quashed the insolvency proceedings, holding that financial service providers are expressly excluded from the definition of 'corporate person' under Section 3(7) of the Code, rendering Section 7 applications against registered NBFCs legally non-maintainable[cite: 30].

case_title: Engin Nasiroglu & Anr. vs. RVR Projects Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Engin Nasiroglu (Ex-Director/shareholder) and Fernas Insaat AS (holding company) of Corporate Debtor Fernas Construction India Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is RVR Projects Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Work orders dated 04.08.2011 (contract value Rs. 10,25,10,275/-) and a second order (Rs. 2,05,02,500/-) for piling works for integrated utilities at Dahej, Gujarat, both foreclosed midway by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted liability of Rs. 1,45,28,508/- on 17.06.2013; after part payment of Rs. 42,35,000/-, unpaid balance stood at Rs. 1,02,93,508/- with default occurring in August 2013[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8(1) demand notice issued on 01.12.2017 (served on 04.12.2017 and 05.12.2017); Section 9 petition CP-IB-158/ND/2018 admitted on 09.07.2018 by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance confirmation letter dated 17.06.2013, two job completion certificates dated 07.08.2013 certifying works of Rs. 1.48 Crores and Rs. 4.21 Crores, and letter dated 13.12.2013 stating bills were undergoing reconciliation[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III admitted the Section 9 petition on 09.07.2018, holding debt and default established; Appellants appealed arguing the operational claim was barred by limitation[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor's claim is barred by limitation when the corporate debtor issued job completion certificates and sought reconciliation of pending bills without finalizing the reconciliation, thereby constituting an acknowledgement of subsisting liability and continuous cause of action under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgement in writing that admits a subsisting jural relationship and affirms an intention to settle accounts upon completion of joint reconciliation constitutes a valid acknowledgement of liability, preserving a continuing cause of action that prevents a debt from becoming time-barred[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 alongside Section 9 of the IBC, a debtor's written communication keeping accounts open for verification and reconciliation amounts to an admission of subsisting liability to pay rather than a stale claim[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of completion certificates and corporate correspondence acknowledging executed works and inviting joint reconciliation meetings without disputing the underlying liability[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor consciously acknowledged its subsisting debt via certificates and letters, keeping reconciliation pending, which established a continuous cause of action validating the Section 9 admission[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned admission order dated 09.07.2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: Appellants Engin Nasiroglu and Fernas Insaat AS, representing Corporate Debtor Fernas Construction India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 9 July 2018 admitting an insolvency application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 filed by Operational Creditor RVR Projects Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid balance of Rs. 1,02,93,508/-[cite: 21]. The Appellants argued that the debt was time-barred since default occurred in August 2013[cite: 21]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, holding that job completion certificates and a December 2013 letter requesting reconciliation created a valid acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, establishing a continuous cause of action[cite: 21].

case_title: S. Ahamed Meeran vs. Ronny George & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S. Ahamed Meeran (shareholder holding 8.45%); Respondent No. 1 is Ronny George (minority shareholder holding 7.79%); remaining respondents are other individual shareholders and public shareholders in Professional Couriers Network Limited ('PCNL')[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate shareholding structure and operation of courier logistics services under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; proceedings arose from an application under the Proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking waiver of qualification thresholds to initiate an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai initially allowed waiver; NCLAT remanded the matter for reasoned consideration; upon reconsideration, NCLT Single Bench Chennai granted waiver in CA/121/2017 on 14 March 2018[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Undisputed shareholding pattern of PCNL as on 31.03.2018 showing 9 shareholder blocks where every single individual member held under 10% equity (ranging from 7.72% to 8.45%), relatives held 13.84%, and public shareholders held 30.84%[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai granted waiver to Ronny George on 14 March 2018; Appellant challenged the order before NCLAT contending that no exceptional circumstances were demonstrated[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT correctly exercised its judicial discretion under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant waiver of minimum qualifying criteria where all individual shareholders in the company held less than 10% equity, making it impossible for any single member to file an application under Section 241[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a company's shareholding is structured such that no individual member holds the statutory 10% threshold, requiring a minority shareholder to solicit and form alliances with other members would defeat statutory protection; such widespread fragmentation constitutes an exceptional circumstance warranting waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1)[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In considering an application for waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1), the Tribunal cannot adjudicate the substantive merits, limitation, or directorial nature of the proposed Section 241 petition, but must confine itself to examining whether allegations prima facie pertain to oppression and whether compelling circumstances exist[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the shareholding register to determine whether numerical barriers deprive all individual members of the right to independently initiate oppression proceedings[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because every shareholder held less than 10% of the share capital, the case fell squarely within the exceptional circumstances rule articulated in Cyrus Investments, justifying the grant of waiver[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 14th March, 2018 passed by NCLT Single Bench Chennai in CA/121/2017 granting waiver under Section 244(1) is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 22].
summary: Appellant S. Ahamed Meeran challenged the NCLT Chennai's order dated 14 March 2018 granting Respondent No. 1 Ronny George a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242[cite: 22]. The Appellant argued that no exceptional circumstances existed to dispense with the statutory shareholding threshold[cite: 22]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal, holding that where shareholding is so widely distributed that every individual member holds under 10% of the company's capital, exceptional circumstances exist under the Cyrus Investments rule, as no single member could otherwise independently seek redress against oppression[cite: 22].

case_title: Mrs. Mamatha vs. AMB Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mrs. Mamatha (real estate allottee/financial creditor); Respondent No. 1 is AMB Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. (Land Owner); Respondent No. 2 is Earth Galleria Pvt. Ltd. / Earth Infrastructure Ltd. (Developer)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Collaboration Agreement dated 03.05.2013 executed between Land Owner and Developer to construct a commercial complex on 10.4375 acres in Hayatpur, Gurgaon, sharing saleable space as a joint venture; followed by an MoU dated 20.06.2014 allotting a cineplex screen to Appellant for Rs. 3,00,00,000/-[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Advance payment of Rs. 5,00,000/- paid by the allottee towards the Rs. 3 Crore purchase consideration; default arose from failure to deliver possession or refund advances[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Collaboration Agreement executed on 03.05.2013; building plans approved on 03.04.2014; MoU with allottee executed on 20.06.2014; supplementary tripartite MoU signed on 06.02.2016; NCLT New Delhi dismissed CP (IB)-608(ND)/2017 on 12.03.2018[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Collaboration Agreement with irrevocable Power of Attorney under Section 202 Contract Act, Clause 55 specifying joint venture branding, and tripartite MoU dated 06.02.2016 designating both respondents jointly as the 'Company'[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the Section 7 application on 12.03.2018, holding that a single insolvency petition cannot be filed jointly against two corporate debtors collaborating in a joint venture; allottee appealed[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 can be maintained jointly against two distinct corporate entities acting together as land owner and developer in a joint venture project[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When two corporate entities collaborate and form an integrated commercial unit or joint venture to develop real estate and allot premises to buyers, an application for corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 is maintainable against both corporate debtors jointly as a single economic unit[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The scheme of Section 7 permits allottees to initiate CIRP against joint venture corporate entities where contractual agreements and powers of attorney establish joint representation and shared commercial allocation for project development[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of underlying collaboration agreements, project marketing mandates, and subsequent memoranda of understanding demonstrating that the entities held themselves out jointly as the composite 'Company' to allottees[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Land owner and developer operated as a single corporate unit regarding the project, rendering the joint Section 7 petition maintainable and the NCLT rejection erroneous[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 12th March, 2018 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench is set aside; the matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority for admission after notice if records are complete, with liberty to parties to settle prior to admission; no costs[cite: 23].
summary: Appellant real estate allottee Mrs. Mamatha appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 12 March 2018 rejecting her Section 7 IBC application filed jointly against AMB Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. (Land Owner) and Earth Galleria Pvt. Ltd. (Developer)[cite: 23]. The Adjudicating Authority had held that Section 7 does not permit initiating CIRP jointly against two corporate debtors involved in a collaboration[cite: 23]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal set aside the order and remitted the matter, ruling that where two corporate entities enter into a collaboration agreement and project themselves jointly as a single developer entity to allottees, a joint Section 7 application is fully maintainable[cite: 23].

case_title: Dr. (Mrs.) Manjeet Kaur Monga vs. Mr. K.L. Suneja & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Complainant is Dr. (Mrs.) Manjeet Kaur Monga (represented by legal heir Karanvir Singh Monga); Respondents 1 and 2 are K.L. Suneja and M/s. Suneja Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Builder); Respondent No. 3 is Citibank N.A. (Drawee Bank)[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and allotment of Flat No. D-301 (1,375 sq. ft.) in 'Siddharth Shila Apartments', Vaishali, Ghaziabad, under allotment letter dated 21.05.1992[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal deposited sum was Rs. 4,53,750/- across seven installments between 1989 and 1993; project remained unfinished for over a decade, culminating in unlawful allotment cancellation on 30.04.2005[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Allotment issued on 21.05.1992; cancellation letter with pay order issued on 30.04.2005; pay order expired uncashed on 30.10.2005; complaint UTPE No. 90/2005 filed before MRTP Commission; COMPAT awarded 15% compound interest up to 30.04.2005 on 03.08.2015; Supreme Court remanded post-2005 interest questions on 18.07.2017[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder's brochure promising delivery within 36 months; Citibank pay order No. 885894 dated 30.04.2005 for Rs. 4,53,750/- debited from builder's current account and transferred to DEAF; replacement cheque issued to complainant only on 07.05.2016[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Post-remand from the Supreme Court, NCLAT determined whether compensation was payable beyond 30.04.2005 and whether Citibank bore interest liability[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a flat purchaser subjected to unfair trade practices is entitled to compensation under Section 12B of the MRTP Act in the form of compound interest beyond the cancellation date up to the actual date of principal refund; and whether a drawee bank is liable to pay interest on unencashed funds drawn from a non-interest-bearing current account[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Compensation awarded to a consumer under trade protection statutes in the form of interest on withheld deposits cannot be cut off on the date of unilateral contract cancellation if the actual refund of principal has not been realized by the aggrieved party[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12B of the MRTP Act authorizes restitutionary compensation for loss suffered from unfair trade practices; restricting interest to the cancellation date when money remained unrefunded constitutes an error of law[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of actual monetary receipt and banking records; an unencashed stale pay order lying in court does not constitute repayment, and a bank holding unencashed demand drafts drawn from a current account cannot be burdened with interest where delay lies entirely with the account holder[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Builder remained liable to pay 15% compound interest until the actual refund date of 07.05.2016, plus pendente lite and future interest; Citibank bore no liability[cite: 24].
operative_order: The petition is disposed of; Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are directed to pay further compensation as compound interest @ 15% per annum on Rs. 4,53,750/- from 1st May, 2005 to 7th May, 2016, plus pendente lite and future interest till realization within one month, failing which execution may ensue; Citibank is exonerated; no costs[cite: 24].
summary: Transferred proceedings from the erstwhile MRTP Commission were heard on remand from the Supreme Court to decide whether complainant Dr. (Mrs.) Manjeet Kaur Monga was entitled to interest compensation beyond 30 April 2005 against builder Suneja Towers Pvt. Ltd., and whether Citibank N.A. was liable for interest on an unencashed pay order[cite: 24]. The builder had delayed apartment construction for over a decade and sent a refund pay order in 2005 which was never encashed, only refunding the principal in May 2016[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that the builder must pay 15% compound interest up to 7 May 2016 alongside future interest, while exonerating Citibank[cite: 24].

case_title: Mr. Vijay Kumar Jain vs. Standard Chartered Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Standard Chartered Bank Ltd. and DBS Bank Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Ruchi Soya Industries Limited; Appellant is Vijay Kumar Jain (Director and Shareholder of Corporate Debtor)[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-currency corporate banking lending, credit accommodation, and external commercial borrowing ('ECB') debt facilities extended to Ruchi Soya Industries Limited[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date not itemized in the appellate judgment; default arose from failure to service credit facilities leading to separate Section 7 petitions[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Standard Chartered Bank and DBS Bank filed petitions CP Nos. 1371 & 1372/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017; NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the applications by common order on 15 December 2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 filed by Pallav Sangal under a Power of Attorney executed by CEO Zarin Daruwala (authorized by the Bank's deed of 01.04.2016), and Form 1 filed by Pankaj Jain under DBS Bank's Power of Attorney dated 26.06.2013 under corporate seal[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 applications on 15.12.2017, imposed a moratorium, and appointed an IRP; Appellant director appealed challenging the competence of the signatory bank officers[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 filed by an officer of a banking financial creditor holding a Power of Attorney / letter of authority from its governing board or Chief Executive Officer is maintainable as an authorized representative under the Code[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a mere general power of attorney holder cannot institute an insolvency application, an officer of a financial institution who has been specifically empowered through corporate authorization or delegated board authority acts as an authorized representative of the juristic person, satisfying statutory filing mandates[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7 of the IBC read with Form 1 of the Adjudicating Authority Rules, the financial creditor acts through an authorized person; the nomenclature 'Power of Attorney' does not strip an officer of authority if the instrument constitutes a valid delegation of corporate power to initiate legal and insolvency proceedings[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the chain of delegation from the corporate board/charter to the executing official and down to the specific branch officer instituting the petition[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Both bank officers were properly authorized representatives holding valid powers to initiate Section 7 proceedings, rendering the admission orders lawful[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed; the impugned common order dated 15th December, 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP Nos. 1371 & 1372/I&BP/NCLT/MAH/2017 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Appellant Vijay Kumar Jain, Director and shareholder of Corporate Debtor Ruchi Soya Industries Limited, appealed against NCLT Mumbai's common order dated 15 December 2017 admitting Section 7 IBC applications filed by Standard Chartered Bank Ltd. and DBS Bank Ltd.[cite: 25]. The Appellant contended that the bank officers who signed Form 1 held powers of attorney and were incompetent to trigger CIRP under the Palogix Infrastructure rule[cite: 25]. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals, holding that where bank officers are delegated authority to represent the bank in legal and insolvency proceedings, they act as authorized representatives rather than mere attorney holders, fully satisfying Section 7 requirements[cite: 25].

case_title: Shyam Manglunia & Ors. vs. Ravi Shankar Srivastava & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are investor group shareholders/directors Shyam Manglunia (Appellant No. 1) and associates; Respondents 1 and 2 are original promoters Ravi Shankar Srivastava (Managing Director) and Nivedita Srivastava (Director); Respondent No. 3 is Invent Bio-Med Private Limited (Company)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Share Purchase Agreement and Memorandum of Understanding entered on 24 April 2017 between original promoters and the investor group to inject funds after the company became NPA in January 2015, resulting in allotment of 2,83,342 equity shares and induction of three investor directors regularized on 28 September 2017[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not applicable; the underlying dispute concerned alleged bad debt write-offs of Rs. 4,19,75,606/- and siphoning of corporate funds[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice not applicable; investor group issued notice dated 30 January 2018 convening an EOGM on 24 February 2018 to remove the promoter directors; promoters filed CP No. 272/241-244/NCLT/MB/MAH/2018 on 17 February 2018; interim orders passed on 23 February 2018 and 26 February 2018[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolutions dated 22.12.2017 and 27.01.2018 altering bank signatories and directing secretarial/financial audits; EOGM Notice dated 30.01.2018 with explanatory statement; emails sent on 24.02.2018 informing investors of sub judice proceedings; Form DIR-12 filed on MCA website on 25.02.2018 following the meeting and subsequently withdrawn[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai passed an ad-interim order on 23 February 2018 staying the EOGM and constituting a three-member Committee of Directors, and on 26 February 2018 ordered status quo ante after the meeting was held in defiance[cite: 16]. Investors appealed both orders before NCLAT[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT properly exercised its equitable jurisdiction under Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 by issuing ad-interim orders to stay an EOGM convened to remove founder-promoters and appointing an independent management committee; and whether an order directing status quo ante could be issued following an EOGM conducted while orders were pending communication[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory tribunal possesses broad statutory discretion under company law to issue interim protective orders regulating corporate management and maintaining equilibrium between warring factions during the pendency of oppression and mismanagement proceedings to prevent irreversible prejudice to the enterprise[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal to make any interim order it deems fit on terms that are just and equitable to regulate corporate affairs; such power is not constrained by preliminary observations regarding winding-up prospects and encompasses restoring status quo ante when an extraordinary meeting is conducted under a cloud of communication lapses[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of balance of convenience and preservation of corporate substratum; the court evaluates whether managerial alterations disrupt operations and whether appointing an independent shareholder-director strikes an equitable balance without deciding substantive merits[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT exercised sound judicial discretion in restraining the removal of directors, forming a balanced tripartite management committee, and ordering status quo ante[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed; the interim orders dated 23rd February, 2018 and 26th February, 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench are affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary: Appellants Shyam Manglunia and the investor group appealed against interim orders dated 23 and 26 February 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai in an oppression and mismanagement petition filed by promoter-directors Ravi Shankar Srivastava and Nivedita Srivastava under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 16]. The NCLT stayed an EOGM called to remove the promoters, appointed an independent shareholder-director, and formed a three-member management committee to oversee expenditure over Rs. 1 Lakh, subsequently ordering status quo ante after appellants conducted the meeting[cite: 16]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, affirming that Section 242(4) grants wide discretion to pass just and equitable interim orders to protect company operations pendente lite[cite: 16].

case_title: Kanti Commercials Pvt. Ltd. vs. Belthangady Taluk Rubber Growers Marketing & Processing Co-operative Society Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Kanti Commercials Pvt. Ltd. (shareholder of Corporate Debtor Falcon Tyres Limited); Respondent No. 1 is Belthangady Taluk Rubber Growers Marketing & Processing Co-operative Society Ltd. (Operational Creditor)[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial sale and supply of natural rubber goods to Corporate Debtor Falcon Tyres Limited[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default amount of Rs. 1,18,34,618.66/-[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Operational Creditor issued a winding-up notice under Section 434(1)(a) of the 1956 Act; filed civil suit OS No. 83 of 2017 before Addl. Senior Civil Judge and CJM, Mysuru on 20 January 2017; issued Section 8(1) demand notice on 24 January 2017; filed Section 9 application on 23 February 2017; admitted by NCLT Bengaluru on 30 August 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Institution of Original Suit OS No. 83 of 2017 on 20.01.2017 four days prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice dated 24.01.2017, proving pendency of pre-existing litigation at the time of demand and subsequent admission[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench admitted the Section 9 petition in CP (IB) No. 01/BB/2017 on 30 August 2017, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP[cite: 17]. The shareholder appealed to NCLAT contending that pre-existing litigation barred admission under Section 9(5)(ii)(d)[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is maintainable when a recovery suit concerning the operational debt had been instituted prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) and remained pending at the time of admission[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The initiation of an operational debt insolvency resolution process under Section 9 of the IBC is strictly barred if a civil suit or arbitral proceeding concerning the disputed claim was instituted and pending prior to the receipt of the statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) of the Code[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court's mandate in Mobilox Innovations, Section 8(2)(a) read with Section 9(5)(ii)(d) requires the Adjudicating Authority to reject an application if notice of an existing dispute or record of a pending suit/arbitration filed prior to the demand notice is demonstrated; subsequent withdrawal of the civil suit post-admission cannot cure the statutory bar existing at the time of demand[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Date of institution of the civil suit vis-à-vis the date of issuance and receipt of the Section 8 statutory demand notice; where a suit predates the demand notice, existence of a pre-existing dispute is established as a matter of law[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because OS No. 83 of 2017 was instituted on 20 January 2017 prior to the demand notice of 24 January 2017, the Section 9 petition was non-maintainable and liable to be rejected[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned admission order dated 30th August, 2017 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench in CP (IB) No. 01/BB/2017 is set aside; the appointment of IRP, moratorium, and account freezing orders are declared illegal and vacated; Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP to function independently; NCLT to determine IRP fees payable by Corporate Debtor; no costs[cite: 17].
summary: Appellant Kanti Commercials Pvt. Ltd., a shareholder of Corporate Debtor Falcon Tyres Limited, challenged the NCLT Bengaluru's order dated 30 August 2017 admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by Belthangady Taluk Rubber Growers Co-operative Society for an operational debt of Rs. 1.18 Crores[cite: 17]. The Operational Creditor had instituted a civil suit (OS No. 83 of 2017) on 20 January 2017 before issuing its Section 8 demand notice on 24 January 2017, later withdrawing the suit post-admission[cite: 17]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the admission, holding under the Mobilox rule that pendency of a pre-existing suit prior to the demand notice creates an absolute statutory bar under Section 9(5)(ii)(d)[cite: 17].

case_title: Anil Haldipur vs. Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are individual former officers/employees Nazura Yash Ajaney and Anil Umesh Haldipur; Respondents include Union of India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) and Gitanjali Gems Ltd. group entities[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Massive banking fraud investigation involving Punjab National Bank credit facilities, Letters of Undertaking, and siphoning of public funds by Gitanjali Gems Ltd. and allied entities[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Multi-billion rupee banking fraud exposure to Punjab National Bank currently under investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office ('SFIO')[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: MCA filed an application under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013; NCLT Mumbai passed an ex-parte asset freezing order on 23 February 2018; modified on 2 April 2018; NCLAT disposed of analogous appeals on 12 July 2018 and the instant appeals on 13 July 2018[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Investigation references from SFIO indicating extensive banking exposure and prima facie beneficiary standing; banking freezes imposed across accounts of key personnel and entities[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench passed an ad-interim order freezing assets on 23.02.2018, and by order dated 02.04.2018 permitted monthly withdrawals for living expenses (Rs. 2 Lakhs for Haldipur, Rs. 1 Lakh for Ajaney) while maintaining the freeze, and exonerated certain other respondents[cite: 18]. Appellants challenged the continuation of asset freeze orders[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 241(2), and 339-340 of the Companies Act, 2013 has the jurisdiction to freeze assets of individuals during an SFIO investigation, and whether permitting fixed monthly living withdrawals without exoneration pending investigation was legally justified[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings initiated by the Central Government under Section 241(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 regarding corporate fraud, the Tribunal possesses statutory and inherent powers to freeze properties and assets of companies and connected individuals during the pendency of an SFIO investigation, subject to providing reasonable monthly allowances for personal subsistence[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 246, 339, 340, 341, and Section 420 allows the Tribunal to issue comprehensive interim preservation and asset-freezing orders against any beneficiary or officer; the Tribunal cannot pass orders definitively exonerating implicated persons prior to the submission of the final SFIO investigative report[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie nexus to the banking fraud and corporate exposure pending SFIO investigation justifies asset freezing, balanced against basic humanitarian needs for personal subsistence[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Modification allowing monthly living expense withdrawals of Rs. 2 Lakhs for Haldipur and Rs. 1 Lakh for Ajaney while keeping asset freezes operational was valid and aligned with the coordinate appellate ruling in Gitanjali Gems[cite: 18].
operative_order: Both appeals are disposed of in terms of the NCLAT coordinate judgment dated 12th July, 2018 in Gitanjali Gems Ltd.; the order permitting monthly subsistence withdrawals while sustaining asset freezes is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: Appellants Anil Haldipur and Nazura Ajaney appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 2 April 2018 in proceedings initiated by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs under Section 241(2) arising from the Punjab National Bank fraud involving Gitanjali Gems Ltd.[cite: 18]. The NCLT had maintained an asset freeze under Section 242(4) while permitting monthly withdrawals of Rs. 2 Lakhs and Rs. 1 Lakh for personal subsistence[cite: 18]. Following its precedent in the Gitanjali Gems appeals, the NCLAT disposed of the appeals, affirming that the Tribunal has full statutory jurisdiction under Sections 221, 242(4), and 339 to freeze individual assets during ongoing SFIO investigations while permitting necessary living expenses[cite: 18].

case_title: Pr. Commissioner of Income-Tax-7 vs. M/s. Modern Terry Towels Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Principal Commissioner of Income-Tax-7 (statutory tax authority); Respondents are M/s. Modern Terry Towels Ltd. and Cimmco Birla Ltd. (industrial enterprises under rehabilitation)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rehabilitation schemes sanctioned under the erstwhile Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 ('SICA') regarding debt restructuring and tax concessions[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not applicable; the appeal concerned tax claims and revenue waivers granted under rehabilitation schemes sanctioned under BIFR Case No. 372 of 2000[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BIFR passed rehabilitation orders on 11 March 2010 and 28 July 2016; Central Government issued Notification No. S.O. 1683(E) on 24 May 2017 amending the Eighth Schedule to provide a 90-day appeal window to NCLAT; appeals filed beyond 45 days[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BIFR rehabilitation schemes dated 11.03.2010 and 28.07.2016 framed without prior notice to the revenue department/unsecured creditors and containing directions impacting Income-tax Act liabilities[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Income Tax Department filed appeals before NCLAT under Section 61(1) of the IBC relying on Central Government Notification No. S.O. 1683(E) dated 24.05.2017 treating BIFR orders as Section 31(1) approval orders[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is maintainable against BIFR schemes sanctioned years prior to the enactment of the Code pursuant to Central Government Notification No. S.O. 1683(E); and whether the Central Government can expand the statutory limitation period under Section 61(2) from 45 days to 90 days[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Central Government cannot, by executive notification under statutory removal-of-difficulties provisions, alter or enlarge mandatory limitation periods fixed by substantive parliamentary enactment, nor can it confer appellate jurisdiction on a tribunal over historical rehabilitation schemes beyond the strict 45-day outer limit of the Code[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a strict limitation period of 30 days extendable by a maximum of 15 days upon sufficient cause; the Appellate Tribunal has no statutory power to condone delay beyond 45 days. Executive instructions issued under Section 242 of the IBC cannot override substantive limitation provisions, rendering Notification S.O. 1683(E) ultra vires and ineffective to create a 90-day window[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Date of notification and computing of statutory limitation; appeals presented after the outer 45-day limit from knowledge are barred by limitation as a matter of jurisdictional law[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals are barred by limitation and non-maintainable under Section 61, leaving NCLAT without jurisdiction to formally set aside the BIFR schemes despite their substantive legal infirmities[cite: 19].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 151 of 2018 and 192 of 2018 are dismissed as non-maintainable and barred by limitation; parties left to raise objections if implementation of the schemes is sought; no order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: The Principal Commissioner of Income-Tax-7 appealed under Section 61(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 against BIFR rehabilitation schemes dated 11 March 2010 and 28 July 2016 sanctioned in favor of Modern Terry Towels Ltd.[cite: 19]. The appellant relied on Central Government Notification S.O. 1683(E) dated 24 May 2017, which sought to deem BIFR schemes as Section 31 resolution plans appealable within 90 days[cite: 19]. Following its Spartek Ceramics ruling, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals as non-maintainable and time-barred, holding that executive notifications cannot expand the maximum 45-day statutory limitation period under Section 61(2) of the Code[cite: 19].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Shakti Bhog Foods Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Financial Creditor is State Bank of India; Respondent/Corporate Debtor is M/s. Shakti Bhog Foods Limited[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Banking and commercial credit facilities extended by State Bank of India to Corporate Debtor Shakti Bhog Foods Limited[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific default date not specified in the order; application filed due to commercial non-payment of banking credit[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice not applicable; winding-up proceedings initiated under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 1956 were admitted and pending before the High Court; NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed the Section 7 petition on 8 February 2018[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Judicial record demonstrating that winding-up proceedings against the Corporate Debtor had already been admitted and ordered by the High Court prior to the Section 7 petition[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed SBI's Section 7 petition on 8 February 2018 due to the pendency of pre-existing admitted winding-up proceedings[cite: 20]. SBI appealed to NCLAT contending that Section 238 overrides winding-up proceedings[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 can be admitted to initiate CIRP against a Corporate Debtor when winding-up proceedings have already been ordered and admitted against the company by a High Court under the Companies Act[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a High Court has formally admitted a winding-up petition and ordered winding-up against a company, the second-stage liquidation/winding-up process has commenced, and a financial creditor cannot thereafter initiate corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC against the same corporate debtor[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11(d) bars initiation of CIRP against a corporate debtor in respect of whom a liquidation order has been made; under Section 2(94A) of the Companies Act, 2013 as amended by Section 255 of the IBC, 'winding up' is synonymous with 'liquidation'. Consequently, saved High Court winding-up proceedings where orders have been made bar reverting the company back to the stage of resolution under Section 7[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the High Court passed an admission and winding-up order; proof of an admitted winding-up proceeding conclusively precludes the initiation of CIRP[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The case was squarely covered by the precedent in Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. Kumar Motors Pvt. Ltd., affirming that initiation of CIRP against a company ordered to be wound up does not arise[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 8th February, 2018 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissing the Section 7 petition is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 20].
summary: Appellant State Bank of India appealed against NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi's order dated 8 February 2018 dismissing its Section 7 IBC application filed against Shakti Bhog Foods Limited[cite: 20]. The NCLT dismissed the petition on the ground that winding-up proceedings against the Corporate Debtor had already been admitted and were pending before the High Court[cite: 20]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, following its established precedent in Innoventive Industries v. Kumar Motors, holding that where a High Court has already admitted winding-up proceedings against a company, fresh CIRP cannot be triggered under Section 7 as the company is already undergoing liquidation[cite: 20].

case_title: S. Ahamed Meeran vs. Ronny George & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S. Ahamed Meeran (Managing Director holding 13.08% shares); Respondent No. 1 is Ronny George (minority shareholder holding 8.99% shares); Respondent No. 2 is Professional International Couriers Private Limited; Respondents 3 to 7 and relatives hold the remaining equity capital[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate shareholding distribution and management of courier logistics business operations under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; proceedings arose from an application seeking waiver of the minimum shareholding threshold under Section 244(1) to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notices not applicable; NCLT Single Bench Chennai initially granted waiver on 14 July 2017; NCLAT set aside that order and remanded the matter on 5 October 2017; on remand, NCLT Chennai granted waiver in CA/122/2017 on 14 March 2018[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Official shareholding pattern of the Company as on 31 March 2018 establishing that out of 8 shareholder groups/members, 6 individual members held more than 10% each (including Ahamed Meeran at 13.08%, PM Abraham at 11.17%, Oomen Chackalayil Chacko at 11.17%, Thomas John at 11.17%, Vadesseri Srinath at 13.62%, and relatives collectively at 26.16%), leaving only two shareholders holding below 10% (Ronny George at 8.99% and Suresh Bharatan at 4.63%)[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai allowed Ronny George's waiver application CA/122/2017 on 14 March 2018; Appellant Ahamed Meeran challenged the waiver order before NCLAT arguing non-fulfillment of the exceptional circumstances standard established in the Cyrus Investments precedent[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT properly exercised its discretion under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant a waiver of qualification thresholds to an 8.99% shareholder where a substantial majority of the company's shareholders individually held more than 10% shareholding[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 cannot be granted as a matter of routine or merely because an applicant holds marginally less than 10% shareholding; exceptional circumstances justifying waiver do not exist where the capital structure is such that a majority of the shareholders individually possess the requisite 10% threshold to initiate proceedings independently without needing to act collectively[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 244(1) enables the Tribunal to waive statutory numerical thresholds on exceptional grounds; however, unlike cases where shareholding is highly fragmented such that virtually no single shareholder holds 10%, the presence of multiple shareholders holding above 10% negates the rationale of minority disenfranchisement[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the shareholding distribution table; where individual shareholdings demonstrate that eligibility under Section 244(1) is concentrated in the hands of multiple independent members rather than restricted to a dominant minority or majority block, no compelling necessity for waiver is demonstrated[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because six out of eight shareholders individually held more than 10% equity, the applicant failed to demonstrate any exceptional circumstance, rendering the grant of waiver unsustainable and the main company petition non-maintainable[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order of the NCLT Chennai dated 14th March, 2018 passed in CA/122/2017 is set aside; the petition under Section 241-242 preferred by the 1st Respondent against Respondent No. 2 company is held non-maintainable and dismissed; no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary: Appellant S. Ahamed Meeran, Managing Director of Professional International Couriers Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chennai's order dated 14 March 2018 which granted a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to Respondent No. 1 Ronny George (an 8.99% shareholder) to file an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 11]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the waiver, holding that mere sub-10% shareholding does not constitute an exceptional circumstance[cite: 11]. In contrast to cases where extensive fragmentation precludes any shareholder from meeting statutory thresholds, here the majority of members individually held over 10% equity, disqualifying the applicant from claiming exceptional grounds for waiver[cite: 11].

case_title: Jagmohan Bajaj vs. Shivam Fragrances Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jagmohan Bajaj (shareholder of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Shivam Fragrances Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Amiga Informatics Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 2 extended financial assistance in the form of a loan amounting to Rs. 1.02 Crores in 2016 to enable the Corporate Debtor to construct a commercial building on Plot No. A-184, Sector 63, Noida, carrying interest at 1.5% per month w.e.f. December 2016[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed was the principal financial debt of Rs. 1.02 Crores plus accrued interest at 1.5% per month; default occurred upon failure to adhere to the repayment schedule in late 2016 and subsequent non-compliance with the arbitral award dated 14 August 2017[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice not applicable; loan recalled in late 2016; arbitration agreement invoked on 24.09.2016; arbitral award passed on 14.08.2017 directing transfer of immovable assets; CP No. (IB) 553 (ND)/2017 admitted by NCLT New Delhi on 11 June 2018[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement, demand recall notices, arbitral award dated 14.08.2017 confirming liability, subsequent undertaking by Corporate Debtor to convey immovable property, and Form 1 Section 7 petition records establishing occurrence of default[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench admitted the Section 7 petition on 11 June 2018, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP; Appellant shareholder appealed contending that a pre-existing dispute and an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 pending before NCLT barred CIRP admission[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the pendency of internal disputes among directors/shareholders and a pending petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 constitutes a valid defense to bar the admission of a Section 7 CIRP application filed by a Financial Creditor under the IBC[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory right of a Financial Creditor to initiate corporate insolvency resolution under Section 7 of the IBC upon establishing the existence of a financial debt and an undisputed default cannot be defeated or stayed on account of internal shareholder-director disputes or the pendency of oppression and mismanagement proceedings under company law[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates admission once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that default occurred and the petition is complete; the concept of a 'pre-existing dispute' applies exclusively to operational debts under Section 9 and has no statutory applicability to Section 7 financial debt admissions. By virtue of Section 238, the IBC overrides ordinary remedies and internal corporate disputes under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective ascertainment of debt and default under Section 7(4) and (5); unfulfilled arbitral awards and admitted loan defaults conclusively establish default[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 1.02 Crores and default were undisputed; internal managerial friction under Sections 241-242 cannot eclipse the IBC, rendering the appeal a frivolous ploy to avoid an arbitral award[cite: 12].
operative_order: Admission of the appeal is refused and the appeal is dismissed; the impugned NCLT admission order dated 11th June, 2018 is affirmed; Appellant is saddled with costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- to be deposited with the Registrar, NCLAT within 15 days[cite: 12].
summary: Appellant Jagmohan Bajaj, a shareholder of Corporate Debtor Shivam Fragrances Pvt. Ltd., appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 11 June 2018 admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Financial Creditor Amiga Informatics Pvt. Ltd. for default on a Rs. 1.02 Crore loan[cite: 12]. The Corporate Debtor had failed to satisfy an arbitral award dated 14 August 2017 directing asset transfers to satisfy the debt[cite: 12]. Appellant argued that pending oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 barred CIRP[cite: 12]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal with Rs. 1 Lakh costs, holding that Section 7 does not recognize pre-existing disputes and that the IBC overrides company law disputes under Section 238[cite: 12].

case_title: Aditya Kumar Jajodia vs. Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors are Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd. and consortium members including Allahabad Bank; Corporate Debtor is Assam Company India Limited; Appellants are Aditya Kumar Jajodia (Shareholder and Director) and Allahabad Bank[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium infrastructure and project debt financing facilities disbursed to Assam Company India Limited[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaulting amount recorded by the Adjudicating Authority in paragraph 84 was Rs. 59,56,06,55,355/- (approx. Rs. 5,956 Crores); specific date of default identified as 11 August 2017[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notice not applicable; recovery actions under Section 19 DRT Act and Section 13(4) SARFAESI Act initiated prior to Section 7 filing; NCLT Guwahati admitted CP (IB) No. 20/GB/2017 on 26 October 2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 application filed by authorized representatives of the Financial Creditor accompanied by loan agreements, records of debt, and proof of non-payment as on 11.08.2017[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Guwahati Bench admitted Srei's Section 7 petition on 26 October 2017, declared a moratorium, appointed a Resolution Professional, and recorded in Para 84 that CD owed Rs. 5,956 Crores to Srei[cite: 13]. Aditya Kumar Jajodia appealed challenging maintainability due to pending SARFAESI/DRT actions, while Allahabad Bank appealed the Para 84 quantification[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the initiation of recovery proceedings under Section 19 of the DRT Act, 1993 or enforcement under Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act, 2002 bars a Financial Creditor from filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC; and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to adjudicate and fix the definitive claim amounts owed to individual creditors at the threshold admission stage[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pendency of parallel debt recovery proceedings before a Debt Recovery Tribunal or enforcement actions under the SARFAESI Act does not bar the initiation of CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC, nor does the Adjudicating Authority possess statutory jurisdiction to conclusively quantify the claims of respective creditors at the Section 7 admission stage[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of the non-obstante clause in Section 238, the provisions of the IBC override the RDDBFI Act, 1993, and the SARFAESI Act, 2002. At the Section 7 stage, the Adjudicating Authority is solely tasked under Section 7(5) with ascertaining whether default exceeding the statutory threshold occurred; the determination, verification, and collation of specific claim amounts fall within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Resolution Professional and the Committee of Creditors[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict threshold determination of the existence of a debt and default; detailed claim calculations and allocations are matters of evidence reserved for the insolvency professional during CIRP[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Srei validly triggered CIRP as default occurred, but the Adjudicating Authority erred in conclusively quantifying the debt owed to Srei in paragraph 84 of the admission order[cite: 13].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 292 & 293 of 2017 are dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) No. 324 of 2017 is allowed to the extent that Paragraph No. 84 of the impugned order dated 26th October, 2017 is set aside while affirming the remainder of the order; no order as to costs[cite: 13].
summary: Director Aditya Kumar Jajodia and Allahabad Bank appealed against NCLT Guwahati's order dated 26 October 2017 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd. against Assam Company India Limited[cite: 13]. Jajodia argued that pending proceedings under Section 19 of the DRT Act and Section 13(4) of the SARFAESI Act barred the petition[cite: 13]. Allahabad Bank challenged paragraph 84 of the order, which judicially quantified the debt owed to Srei[cite: 13]. The NCLAT dismissed Jajodia's appeals, confirming that Section 238 of the IBC overrides recovery laws, but allowed Allahabad Bank's appeal by expunging paragraph 84, ruling that claim collation and determination are functions of the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors[cite: 13].

case_title: VLS Finance Limited vs. Southend Infrastructure Private Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is VLS Finance Limited (third-party decree holder/creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Southend Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Dinesh Kumar Gupta (promoter); Respondent Nos. 6 to 11 and 13 to 21 are shareholders/creditors; Respondent No. 22 is Vikrant Puri (Original Petitioner)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Investment agreements dated 12.07.2007 and 24.09.2007 between VLS Finance and BMS IT Institute (promoted by Dinesh Gupta) to co-develop a 34,275 sq. meter IT park in Sector-62, NOIDA[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount under project agreements culminated in an arbitral award dated 02.03.2015 in favor of VLS Finance; high-stake execution claims pending before Delhi High Court and Supreme Court[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: High Court interim injunctions restraining alienation of properties/shares issued on 27.04.2012, 04.09.2012, and 30.09.2014; arbitral award passed on 02.03.2015; CP 24/2016 filed before NCLT; NCLT allowed withdrawal via CA 459/2017 on 19 December 2017[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered conveyance deed dated 10.06.2013 executed by Southend in favour of Wonder Space Properties transferring development rights over Okhla land in alleged contempt of High Court orders; transfer of shares to Vikrant Puri; application CA 459/2017 recording amicable settlement between warring shareholders[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi allowed VLS Finance to intervene on 04.09.2017 but denied impleadment[cite: 14]. On 19.12.2017, NCLT permitted Vikrant Puri to withdraw CP 24/2016 following amicable settlement[cite: 14]. VLS Finance appealed the withdrawal order under CA 57/2018[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT abused its discretion under Rule 82 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 by allowing an oppression and mismanagement petition to be withdrawn following settlement between shareholder factions over the objection of an intervenor non-member claiming fraud and violation of High Court orders[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory jurisdiction of the NCLT under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 is intended exclusively for the redressing of member-driven grievances regarding oppression and mismanagement; the Tribunal cannot be compelled to maintain a company petition or conduct roving inquiries at the instance of a third-party non-member once the actual petitioner and company members have amicably settled and sought leave to withdraw[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 82 of the NCLT Rules, 2016, leave of the Tribunal is required to withdraw a Section 241 petition, vesting broad judicial discretion in the Tribunal. Technical non-compliance in Form NCLT-9 does not vitiate leave where parties appear and confirm settlement. Section 397/398 petitions cannot be commandeered or prosecuted by non-members lacking locus under Section 399/244[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of proprietary locus standi and legitimate forum remedies; non-members possessing external injunctions from the High Court or Supreme Court must pursue contempt or execution remedies before those civil forums rather than hijacking company law proceedings[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT acted within its discretion in permitting the unconditional withdrawal of the petition, leaving the third-party intervenor free to pursue its enforcement remedies before the High Court and Supreme Court[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 57 of 2018 is dismissed; the impugned NCLT withdrawal order dated 19th December, 2017 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) No. 370 of 2017 is disposed of as infructuous; no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: Appellant VLS Finance Limited appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 19 December 2017 allowing Vikrant Puri to withdraw Company Petition No. 24/2016 (filed under Sections 397-398/241-242) following an amicable settlement between shareholder groups[cite: 14]. VLS Finance, an external creditor holding an arbitral award against associated promoters, objected to the withdrawal, asserting that the petition was collusive and used to evade High Court and Supreme Court asset injunctions[cite: 14]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that company petitions cannot be kept alive at the behest of non-members who lack locus standi under Section 244, and that the appellant remained free to enforce its claims and contempt applications before the High Court and Supreme Court[cite: 14].

case_title: P. Ram Bhopal & Ors. vs. Pragnya Riverbridge Developers Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Petitioners are P. Ram Bhoopal (10.20%), Vishnu Bhoopal (16.40%), and family associates holding an aggregate 26.60% shareholding; Respondent No. 1 is Pragnya Riverbridge Developers Ltd. (formerly Vision Heights Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Pragnya Capital I Pvt. Ltd. (Mauritius PE fund holding 73.40%); Respondent No. 7 is Educomp Infrastructure and School Management Ltd.[cite: 15] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Residential and commercial real estate development project at Rajahmundry; Respondent No. 2 invested US$ 5 million in September 2011; Appellants acquired 26.60% equity in February 2012 from erstwhile promoters under an unamended Share Purchase Agreement[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; petition concerned allegations of oppression and mismanagement regarding refusal to demerge commercial land and leasing school space to Educomp[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Pragnya Capital invested via SHA on 28.09.2011; Appellants acquired shares in February 2012; Board Meeting approving Educomp lease held on 05.11.2012; NCLT Hyderabad dismissed CP No. 109/2012 on 13.03.2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of Interest dated 14.07.2011, SHA dated 28.09.2011, Letter dated 28.02.2012 written by Appellant No. 1 admitting that the SHA had become defunct due to non-incorporation in Articles of Association, and Minutes of Board Meeting dated 05.11.2012 approving the master lease to Educomp without recorded objections to the school lease[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 109/2012 before NCLT Hyderabad alleging that Respondent No. 2 failed to demerge the commercial land parcel in their favor and acted oppressively; NCLT dismissed the petition on 13.03.2017 holding the affairs were run legally; Appellants appealed under Section 421[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether shareholders subscribing to shares can claim proprietary rights over specific segmented assets of a company or demand asset demerger based on an unincorporated SHA; whether non-re-election of a director upon retirement constitutes oppression; and whether bona fide commercial leasing decisions approved by the Board amount to mismanagement under Section 397/398[cite: 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Subscribing to or purchasing shares in an incorporated company vests rights in the company's capital and management, but confers no direct proprietary interest or title over specific physical assets; commercial disputes seeking specific enforcement of an extrinsic, unincorporated agreement cannot form the basis of an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956, oppression requires demonstrating that corporate affairs are conducted in a manner prejudicial to public interest or oppressive to members; normal commercial decisions taken in the interest of the company, and the non-re-election of a retiring director in accordance with corporate procedures, do not constitute actionable oppression[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict burden of proof requiring demonstrable legal entitlement; letters acknowledging that an SHA is defunct preclude relying on legitimate expectation, and failure to object to corporate resolutions in contemporaneous correction requests refutes allegations of oppressive board conduct[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellants held no proprietary right to force a demerger of company land, the commercial lease to Educomp was validly approved in the corporate interest, and the petition was properly dismissed[cite: 15].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned NCLT order dated 13th March, 2017 dismissing Company Petition No. 109/2012 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: Appellants P. Ram Bhoopal and others, holding 26.60% shares in Pragnya Riverbridge Developers Ltd., appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 13 March 2017 dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 15]. Appellants claimed that majority shareholder Pragnya Capital breached an understanding to demerge the commercial portion of a development project in their favor, improperly leased school premises to Educomp, and removed Appellant No. 1 as director[cite: 15]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that shareholding does not confer proprietary ownership over specific corporate assets and that unincorporated agreements cannot be specifically enforced under Section 397/398[cite: 15]. The Board's leasing decision and director retirement adhered to corporate law, disproving oppression[cite: 15].

case_title: Gangadhar Madupu vs. Katta Corp Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Petitioner/Appellant Gangadhar Madupu held 9.33% share capital in Respondent No. 1 Katta Corp Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 Katta Jagadeesh acted as MD; Respondent No. 3 Katta Srinivasa Rao is his brother; Respondent No. 4 Katta Lalitha is Respondent No. 3's son; Respondent No. 7 Gade Saraswathi Devi is mother-in-law of Respondent No. 3; Respondent No. 8 Vara Boomi Homes is a partnership firm[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Katta Corp owned 3 acres of prime land in Nadergul Village, RR District[cite: 6]. Respondent No. 2 executed a registered sale deed on 03.11.2015 alienating this property to Respondent No. 7 for Rs. 1.20 Crores, who subsequently transferred it on 04.11.2016 to Respondent No. 8[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; underlying dispute involved unlawful asset siphoning and diversion of company funds[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 2 was convicted of an offence on 04.06.2015 (sentenced to 6 months imprisonment); an EOGM was called on 26.08.2015 to remove him for misappropriation but cancelled on 25.08.2015 claiming his resignation on 24.08.2015; sale deeds were executed on 03.11.2015 and 04.11.2016[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered sale deed dated 03.11.2015 reciting payment of Rs. 1.20 Crores which contradicted pleadings before NCLT asserting a land exchange for 2.75 acres in Guntur; lack of any board resolution or notice authorizing the sale; evidence of disqualification under Section 164(2)/167; subsequent encumbrance certificate dated 22.11.2016 and mutation proceedings dated 10.12.2016 demonstrating post-transaction attempts to establish bona fides[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No. 06/241/HDB/2017 filed under Sections 241-242 before NCLT Hyderabad, which on 05.10.2017 found oppression and mismanagement and set aside both sale deeds dated 03.11.2015 and 04.11.2016 while rejecting other reliefs[cite: 6]. Both the Petitioner and Respondent No. 8 appealed[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the alienation of company property by a director who had resigned and incurred statutory disqualification can be protected under Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013; whether the subsequent purchaser could claim bona fide purchaser status; and whether such unauthorized transfers constitute oppression and mismanagement under Section 241[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An individual who has resigned and suffered statutory disqualification cannot execute conveyances of company assets under the cloak of a de facto director, and acts done by usurping managerial authority without board approval are void ab initio and cannot be legitimized under validating provisions intended for technical appointment defects[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 176 of the Companies Act, 2013 protects acts done by a director where a defect is subsequently discovered in their appointment, but does not extend to insulate blatant, unauthorized transfers executed by an individual who knowingly suffered disqualification under Section 164(2) read with Section 167 and had already resigned[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict scrutiny of the chain of title, authority to convey, and bona fides of purchasers; where a conveyance contradicts contemporaneous pleadings regarding consideration and lacks board authorization, and where due diligence documents are obtained post-execution, the purchaser fails the test of a bona fide purchaser for value without notice[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The sale deeds executed by the disqualified director and the subsequent conveyance in favour of the partnership firm were fraudulent, unauthorized acts of oppression and mismanagement correctly set aside by the NCLT[cite: 6].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) No. 3 of 2018 and Company Appeal (AT) No. 409 of 2017 are dismissed; the NCLT order setting aside the sale deeds dated 3rd November, 2015 and 4th November, 2016 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: Petitioner Gangadhar Madupu and purchaser Vara Boomi Homes cross-appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 5 October 2017 in a petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 6]. The NCLT had set aside a sale deed dated 3 November 2015 executed by Katta Jagadeesh alienating Katta Corp's prime land to a relative, and a subsequent sale deed dated 4 November 2016 to Vara Boomi Homes[cite: 6]. NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that Jagadeesh was already disqualified and resigned when executing the deed, precluding protection under Section 176[cite: 6]. Furthermore, Vara Boomi Homes failed to establish bona fide purchaser status, justifying the invalidation of both transfers as acts of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 6].

case_title: Logvis AG vs. Quinn Logistics India Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd.; Corporate Debtor is Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd.; Appellants include Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. and shareholder entities Logvis AG and Mecon FZE[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Quinn Logistics acquired majority shareholding in Mack Soft Tech on 23 October 2007 for Rs. 126.73 Crores[cite: 7]. Between 2007 and 2010, Quinn Logistics disbursed interest-free unsecured loans amounting to Rs. 62.90 Crores to Mack Soft Tech to develop an office complex named 'Q-City' in Hyderabad, which included direct payments made to Indu Projects on the debtor's behalf[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed was Rs. 62,90,45,905/-, with the date of default identified as 15 June 2017 following failure to repay upon demand[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Quinn Logistics issued a demand notice on 15 June 2017 calling for repayment on or before 30 June 2017; Corporate Debtor sought time on 29 June 2017; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2017 was subsequently filed and admitted by NCLT Hyderabad on 11 August 2017[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form 1 Part IV and V submissions containing computation tables, HSBC bank statements showing disbursements, and audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor as on 31 December 2008, 31 December 2009, 31 December 2010, 31 March 2012, and 2015-16 filed with the RoC acknowledging the debt[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad admitted the Section 7 petition on 11 August 2017, imposed a moratorium, and appointed an IRP[cite: 7]. The Corporate Debtor and shareholder Logvis AG appealed arguing that the debt was interest-free without time value of money, the claim was barred by limitation, and Form 1 was defective[cite: 7].
