legal_issues: Whether an interest-free unsecured loan advanced by a parent/holding entity for project development constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC; whether continuous acknowledgment in audited balance sheets prevents a debt from being barred by limitation; and whether the Section 7 petition satisfied the statutory requirements of Form 1[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interest-free loan advanced by an investor/holding entity into an enterprise for commercial project development satisfies the requirement of disbursement against consideration for the time value of money, as the commercial benefit and appreciation anticipated from the development serve as consideration, thereby qualifying the advance as a financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) does not mandate the payment of interest for an advance to constitute financial debt so long as it is disbursed against the time value of money, which includes economic gains from capital development; further, continuous entries in audited balance sheets constitute an acknowledgment of debt establishing a continuous cause of action[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of Section 7(5) requires clear proof of debt and default through statutory forms, bank records, and audited corporate balance sheets submitted to the Registrar of Companies acknowledging outstanding liabilities[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Quinn Logistics was a valid Financial Creditor owed an admitted debt that fell into default upon non-compliance with the demand notice, rendering the Section 7 admission unassailable[cite: 7].
operative_order: All connected Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 143, 175, and 176 of 2017 are dismissed; the NCLT admission order dated 11th August, 2017 is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: Appellants Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and shareholders Logvis AG and Mecon FZE appealed against the NCLT Hyderabad's order dated 11 August 2017 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 62.90 Crores[cite: 7]. Appellants contended that the interest-free unsecured loan was not a financial debt under Section 5(8) and was time-barred[cite: 7]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that interest-free loans granted to develop a real estate project carry the time value of money through expected developmental benefits, audited balance sheets provided continuous debt acknowledgment defeating limitation, and the default was fully established[cite: 7].

case_title: Montreaux Resorts (P) Ltd. & Ors. vs. Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Petitioners are Montreaux Resorts (P) Ltd. (Petitioner No. 1 company) and individual shareholders Vir Jai Khosla, Shiv Khosla, and Neel Khosla; Respondents include Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd. (alleged vehicle entity), Vikram Bakshi (former director), and family members/nominees[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint venture business arrangement dated 31 March 2006 to develop a holiday resort at Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh, on land belonging to the Khosla family, under which Respondent No. 2 infused capital and assumed directorial control[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; proceedings concerned oppression and mismanagement allegations under Sections 241-242 regarding diversion of company land parcels to Respondent No. 1 and competing business activities[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Montreaux Resorts incorporated on 13.04.2005; agreement entered into on 31.03.2006; Delhi High Court passed restraining orders on 29.02.2008; Company Petition No. 144(ND)/2016 was dismissed at the preliminary stage by NCLT New Delhi on 13 January 2017[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share transmission claims following the demise of Mrs. Sonia Khosla, share transfers from Vini Ahuja, absence of an explicit company board resolution authorizing the institution of the petition by the individual petitioners, and evidence showing the petitioners held shares in Montreaux Resorts but not in respondent Ascot Hotels[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed CP No. 144(ND)/2016 at the preliminary stage prior to notice, holding that the petition lacked a supporting board resolution from Petitioner No. 1, petitioners were not shareholders of Respondent No. 1, and shareholding proof was disputed, prompting an appeal under Section 421[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement can be dismissed at the threshold on grounds that petitioners are not shareholders of an arrayed respondent entity; whether the lack of an initial board resolution by the aggrieved company justifies dismissal without allowing rectification or individual prosecution; and whether disputed title to shares should be adjudicated during hearings rather than by summary dismissal[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241-242 cannot be summarily dismissed at the threshold on preliminary objections where the petitioners are members of the victimized company whose affairs are mismanaged; external entities arrayed as corporate vehicles may be deleted if misjoined, and individual members retain an independent right to sue irrespective of a formal board resolution[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241 read with Section 244 mandates that applicants must hold the requisite threshold shareholding in the company whose affairs are being conducted oppressively, not in external third-party respondents[cite: 8]. Procedural defects like the lack of a board resolution by the company itself do not extinguish individual members' derivative rights or statutory rights to challenge oppression[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Threshold maintainability cannot depend on resolving contentious, disputed share transmission facts at a pre-notice stage without affording petitioners an opportunity to produce substantiating shareholding evidence[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in summarily dismissing the company petition; at highest, the non-shareholder respondent could have been struck from the memo of parties and an opportunity provided to cure resolution defects[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 13th January, 2017 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench in CP No. 144(ND)/2016 is set aside; the matter is remitted to the NCLT for re-hearing with directions for parties to appear on 26th November, 2018; no order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Appellants Montreaux Resorts (P) Ltd. and its individual shareholders appealed an order of NCLT New Delhi dated 13 January 2017 dismissing their oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 at the pre-notice stage[cite: 8]. The NCLT dismissed the petition because appellants were not shareholders of respondent Ascot Hotels & Resorts Ltd., lacked a board resolution authorizing the company to sue, and lacked documented share transmission records[cite: 8]. The NCLAT set aside the dismissal and remitted the petition, holding that petitioners need only be shareholders of the oppressed company, third-party entities can merely be struck off if misjoined, and procedural defects regarding board authorizations do not extinguish individual shareholders' statutory rights[cite: 8].

case_title: Innoventive Industries Limited vs. Kumar Motors Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Financial Creditor is Innoventive Industries Limited; Respondent/Corporate Debtor is Kumar Motors Private Limited[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial lending/credit transactions between the parties resulting in outstanding unpaid claims[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed by the Appellant was Rs. 24,06,52,849.50/- along with interest[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellant filed Company Petition No. 468 of 2013 for winding up before the Bombay High Court; the Bombay High Court admitted the winding-up petition on 4 August 2015 and directed newspaper publication; Appellant subsequently filed a Section 7 petition under IBC, which NCLT Mumbai rejected on 27 July 2017[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: High Court order dated 04.08.2015 recording deemed inability to pay under the 1956 Act, admitting the petition, and directing advertisements in the Free Press Journal, Navshakti, and Maharashtra Government Gazette alongside a Rs. 10,000/- publication deposit[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the Appellant's Section 7 petition in CP No. 1201/I&BP/NCLT/MB/MAH/2017 on 27 July 2017, holding that the petition could not be entertained due to the pre-existing, admitted winding-up proceeding pending before the Bombay High Court[cite: 9]. Innoventive Industries appealed to NCLAT[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 for initiation of CIRP is maintainable against a Corporate Debtor when a winding-up petition against the same company has already been admitted and ordered to be advertised by a High Court under the Companies Act[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When a High Court has already admitted a company winding-up petition under the Companies Act and ordered winding-up proceedings, such proceedings are saved under statutory transfer rules, and an application under Section 7 or Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code to trigger corporate insolvency resolution against the same corporate debtor is not maintainable[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 255 and the 11th Schedule of the IBC alongside Section 434 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016, winding-up proceedings pending before the High Court where notice has been served are saved; Section 238 of the Code does not override saved High Court winding-up proceedings where an order has already been passed, and Section 11(d) bars reverting a company already undergoing winding-up/liquidation back to CIRP[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the stage of the winding-up proceedings; where an admission order with advertisement directions has already been passed, liquidation/winding-up has commenced, extinguishing the scope for CIRP[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Bombay High Court had already admitted the winding-up petition against the Corporate Debtor and ordered advertisement, the corporate debtor was already subject to liquidation proceedings, precluding initiation of CIRP under Section 7[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed; the impugned order dated 27th July, 2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench rejecting the Section 7 application is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: Innoventive Industries Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated 27 July 2017 rejecting its application under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 to initiate CIRP against Kumar Motors Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 24.06 Crores[cite: 9]. The NCLT rejected the application because a winding-up petition filed by the appellant was already admitted by the Bombay High Court on 4 August 2015[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that once a High Court has formally admitted a winding-up petition and initiated liquidation proceedings, such proceedings are saved and Section 238 of the IBC cannot override them to initiate fresh CIRP against the debtor[cite: 9].

case_title: Photon Infotech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Medici Holdings Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Original Applicant/Respondent No. 1 is Medici Holdings Ltd. (holding 6.62% paid-up capital); Appellants/Original Respondents include Photon Infotech Pvt. Ltd. (Company), promoters Srinivas Balasubramanian and Mukund Balasubramanian (holding ~46.43% each), Latha Balasubramanian (holding 0.03%), and transferee entity Photon Interactive Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Medici acquired 19,69,000 equity shares (6.62%) in Photon Infotech; the promoters subsequently transferred the entire software business—the company's sole business substratum—to affiliate Photon Interactive on a slump sale basis under a Business Transfer Agreement dated 27 March 2013[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics not applicable; proceedings concerned an application seeking waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to initiate oppression and mismanagement proceedings under Section 241[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Slump sale agreement executed on 27.03.2013; Central Government granted permissions under Section 399(4) of the 1956 Act on 06.05.2015 and 03.07.2015 (challenged in Madras High Court writ petitions); CA No. 90/2017 for waiver under the 2013 Act filed before NCLT Chennai, which granted waiver on 17 October 2017[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share register showing promoters held over 92% while transferring 15 shares each to employees on 15.11.2011 to artificially inflate member count and dilute Medici's percentage under Section 399/244; issuance and instant buy-back of 8,50,000 ESOP shares enriching the CFO by Rs. 1.08 Crores; and Business Transfer Agreement dated 27.03.2013 disposing of the entire software business[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Single Bench allowed CA No. 90/2017 on 17 October 2017 granting Medici waiver of Section 244(1) criteria to pursue its Section 241 petition[cite: 10]. Promoters and affiliate entities appealed under Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 375, 395, and 396 of 2017[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT correctly exercised its judicial discretion under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant waiver of the minimum shareholding criteria to a 6.62% minority shareholder; whether transfer of the entire business substratum and artificial multiplication of shareholders constitute exceptional circumstances for waiver; and whether a pending derivative civil suit bars a waiver application[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory power to grant a waiver of minimum qualifying criteria under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 is an equitable judicial discretion designed to ensure substantial justice; exceptional circumstances exist where a minority shareholder is rendered incapable of meeting the numerical threshold due to deliberate share dilution or distribution among employee nominees, particularly where the entire commercial substratum of the company has been alienated[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While the Tribunal cannot determine the final merits of an oppression/mismanagement claim under Section 241 when deciding a waiver application under Section 244(1), it must objectively evaluate whether the petition is non-frivolous and presents exceptional circumstances; the proviso to Section 244(1) is open-ended and broad, not restricted by narrower phrases of predecessor enactments[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of prima facie shareholding distribution, absence of alternative remedies in civil court (which lacks jurisdiction over internal oppression matters), and demonstrated alienation of core assets to an affiliate without minority consent[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transfer of the company's entire software substratum on a slump sale basis coupled with artificial dilution constituted exceptional circumstances justifying waiver under Section 244(1)[cite: 10].
operative_order: All three Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 375, 395, and 396 of 2017 are dismissed; the impugned NCLT order dated 17th October, 2017 granting waiver under Section 244(1) is affirmed; no order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary: Appellants Photon Infotech Pvt. Ltd. and its majority shareholders appealed against NCLT Chennai's order dated 17 October 2017 granting Medici Holdings Ltd. (a 6.62% shareholder) a waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241[cite: 10]. Appellants argued that no exceptional circumstances existed and that a pending civil suit barred relief[cite: 10]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the slump sale transfer of the company's entire software business substratum to an affiliate, combined with deliberate employee share allocations preventing the minority from meeting threshold requirements, constituted exceptional circumstances warranting waiver[cite: 10].

case_title: Hyundai Motor India Ltd. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Hyundai Motor India Limited ('HMIL') is an automobile manufacturer/distributor. Informant No. 1 is Fx Enterprise Solutions India Pvt. Ltd. (dealer from May 2006 to May 2014) and Informant No. 2 is St. Antony's Cars Pvt. Ltd. (dealer in Kollam/Trivandrum), both acting as dealers/complainants against HMIL before the Competition Commission of India ('CCI'). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying dealership agreements governing the sales, distribution, and service of Hyundai passenger cars and spare parts, containing clauses restricting business investment (Clause 5(iii)), mandating designated oils/lubricants, and imposing discount control schemes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary default amount not applicable; the allegations concerned anti-competitive vertical restraints resulting in Resale Price Maintenance ('RPM') and tie-in arrangements leading to an administrative penalty of Rs. 87 Crores (0.3% of HMIL's average turnover) imposed by the CCI. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 notices not applicable; Informant No. 1 submitted a termination notice on 25 April 2014; CCI formed a prima facie view under Section 26(1) on 12 September 2014 (Case No. 36 of 2014) and 20 November 2014 (Case No. 82 of 2014), clubbing both matters; CCI passed its final Section 27 order on 14 June 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Evidence comprised Director General ('DG') reports alleging ex-showroom price-fixing, mystery shopping agencies for monitoring discounts, dealer agreements, and recommendations on lubricants, though the CCI cited no independent supporting evidence demonstrating actual dealer penalties or market foreclosure. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI passed an order under Section 27 on 14 June 2017 finding HMIL in contravention of Sections 3(4)(e) and 3(4)(a) read with Section 3(1), directing HMIL to cease and desist and imposing an Rs. 87 Crore penalty, which HMIL challenged before NCLAT under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether the CCI could establish contraventions of Section 3(4)(a) and Section 3(4)(e) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002 purely by relying on the DG report without conducting an independent inquiry or assessing evidence; and whether the CCI failed to determine the 'relevant geographic market' and 'relevant product market' under Section 19(6) & (7) and assess the factors in Section 19(3) prior to finding an appreciable adverse effect on competition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An administrative or quasi-judicial competition authority cannot base its findings of anti-competitive practices solely on the opinions or findings of an investigative report without undertaking an independent appreciation and analysis of concrete evidence on record, nor can it find anti-competitive vertical agreements without delineating the relevant product and geographic markets and assessing statutory adverse competitive impact factors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 26(3) establishes that a DG report is merely an investigative opinion to assist the Commission and is not binding; Section 27 requires an independent inquiry into contraventions. Furthermore, 'market' under Section 3 and Section 19(3) refers to 'relevant market', which mandates explicit determination of both 'relevant geographic market' and 'relevant product market' pursuant to the statutory criteria of Sections 19(6) and 19(7). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The evidentiary test mandates independent evaluation of primary documents and substantiating evidence; mere reference to statutory provisions or blanket adoption of DG conclusions without citing specific evidentiary proof (such as actual penalisation of dealers) fails the required legal standard of inquiry. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CCI failed to independently examine and appreciate evidence, failed to properly delineate the relevant product and geographic markets under Section 19(6) and (7), and drew contradictory conclusions regarding oil recommendations without evidence of penalties, the impugned Section 27 order was unsustainable in law.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 14th June, 2017 passed by the Competition Commission of India is set aside in its entirety; the Appellant is entitled to a refund of any amounts deposited pursuant to the interim order dated 18th July, 2017; no order as to costs.
summary: Hyundai Motor India Limited appealed against the Competition Commission of India's order dated 14 June 2017, which found HMIL guilty of anti-competitive vertical arrangements involving resale price maintenance and tie-in arrangements for engine oils/lubricants under Section 3(4) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, imposing an Rs. 87 Crore penalty. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal set aside the CCI order, holding that the Commission mechanically relied upon the Director General's investigative report without independently assessing evidence, failed to delineate the relevant product and geographic markets under Section 19(6) and (7), and failed to evaluate appreciable adverse effects under Section 19(3). The appeal was accordingly allowed without costs.

case_title: Jaiprakash Associates Ltd. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Informant is the Builders Association of India ('BAI'); Appellants are 11 cement manufacturing companies (including Ambuja Cements, ACC, Jaiprakash Associates, UltraTech, Century, Ramco, JK Cement, India Cements, Nuvoco Vistas, Binani) and the Cement Manufacturers' Association ('CMA') acting as the trade association platform; Respondent No. 1 is the Competition Commission of India ('CCI'). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Manufacture, wholesale, retail supply, and nationwide distribution of cement to construction players and distributors across India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The dispute involves statutory cartel contraventions rather than a debt default; CCI imposed monetary penalties under Section 27(b) calculated on turnover percentages against the manufacturers and a fine on CMA, alongside cease-and-desist directions. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information filed under Section 19(1)(a); CCI issued initial order on 20 June 2012; COMPAT remanded the matter on 11 December 2015; fresh hearings ensued culminating in CCI's final order on 31 August 2016. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CMA meetings on 15 March 2007, 18 December 2008, 26 March 2009, 30 November 2009, and High Powered Committee meetings in early 2011; systematic collection and circulation of weekly retail/wholesale prices, production, and dispatches among competitors; sudden coordinated price spikes (up to ~30%) in late 2010/early 2011 despite fall in capacity utilization and drop in dispatches amidst surging construction demand. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Post-remand by COMPAT, the CCI passed a fresh order dated 31 August 2016 holding the cement companies and CMA guilty of cartelization and price/supply coordination under Section 3(1) read with Section 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, which was appealed by the manufacturers and CMA before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether the Cement Manufacturers' Association and the 11 cement manufacturers acted in concert as a cartel under Section 2(c) in violation of Section 3(1) read with Sections 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002 by coordinating prices and limiting production/supplies; whether the standard of proof for establishing an anti-competitive agreement was satisfied; and whether the CCI properly defined the relevant market under Section 19.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In establishing the existence of a cartel or an anti-competitive horizontal agreement, the applicable legal standard is the balance of probabilities rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt; direct evidence of explicit agreement is not required where parallel behavior, exchange of commercially sensitive non-public data, and meeting of minds can be inferred through strong circumstantial evidence and plus factors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 2(b) ('agreement') and Section 2(c) ('cartel') encompass informal understandings, tacit concert, or actions based on 'a nod or a wink'. Under Section 3(3), once horizontal price determination or supply limitation is established, a statutory presumption arises that such agreement causes an appreciable adverse effect on competition, shifting the evidentiary burden to the enterprises to justify the trend. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strong probability test based on cumulative circumstantial evidence: exchange of forward-looking and sensitive pricing and dispatch data via a common trade association platform coupled with inexplicable price parallelism, uniform reduction in production/supply during peak demand periods, and low capacity utilization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CCI validly established a coordinated meeting of minds to manipulate prices and throttle supply in contravention of Sections 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(b), and properly evaluated state-wise and region-wise relevant geographic and product markets under Section 19(6) and (7).
operative_order: All appeals filed by the cement manufacturing companies and the Cement Manufacturers' Association are dismissed; the impugned CCI order dated 31st August, 2016 imposing cease-and-desist orders and penalties is upheld; all interlocutory applications stand disposed of; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, comprising 11 leading cement manufacturing companies and the Cement Manufacturers' Association (CMA), challenged the Competition Commission of India's order dated 31 August 2016 finding them guilty of cartelization under Section 3(1) read with Sections 3(3)(a) and 3(3)(b) of the Competition Act, 2002. The CCI found that the manufacturers utilized the CMA platform to exchange commercially sensitive data, coordinate price increases, and deliberately restrict supply and capacity utilization. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeals, holding that cartels may be established on a balance of probabilities via strong circumstantial evidence and plus factors, and confirmed the statutory presumption of appreciable adverse effects on competition and the penalties imposed.

case_title: M/s Shekhar Resorts Ltd. & Ors. vs. The Registrar of Companies, NCT of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are corporate entities including Pahuja Takii Seed Ltd., Shekhar Resorts Ltd., Magnon Interactive Pvt. Ltd., Magnon Solutions Pvt. Ltd., and their respective defaulting officers; Respondent is the Registrar of Companies ('RoC'), NCT of Delhi & Haryana. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate statutory compliance petitions seeking compounding of technical corporate governance defaults under the Companies Act, 2013, relating to delayed filing of annual returns, financial statements, and failure to convene annual general meetings or board meetings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount not applicable; involves non-compliance with statutory disclosure filings across multiple financial years carrying various prescribed daily and maximum fines under the Act. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Petitions filed under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 following the issuance of RoC reports calculating imposable maximum fines; NCLT New Delhi Bench-III passed the impugned order disposing/dismissing the applications on 16 February 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consolidated applications filed jointly by the companies alongside their officers-in-default covering repeated non-compliances over several years, accompanied by RoC reports detailing delay metrics, corrective filings undertaken, and maximum imposable fines. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed or returned multiple company petitions on 16 February 2018 holding that joint compounding petitions for successive years or joint parties were impermissible, that fines below Rs. 5 lakh fell outside NCLT's pecuniary jurisdiction, and that Section 451 made repeated defaults within 3 years mandatorily punishable with imprisonment and non-compoundable.
legal_issues: Whether the Companies Act, 2013 bars the filing of a joint application for compounding of an offence by a defaulting company along with its officers in default; whether a single composite application can cover identical offences committed across successive financial years; whether an offence punishable with fine or imprisonment becomes mandatorily punishable with imprisonment under Section 451 upon repetition within three years thereby barring compounding; and whether NCLT lacks jurisdiction to compound offences where the prescribed fine is below Rs. 5,00,000.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural rules are handmaids of justice and every procedure is permitted unless expressly prohibited; joint compounding petitions covering a company and its officers across successive financial years are maintainable, and repeat offences under general provisions do not automatically mandate imprisonment so as to strip tribunals of compounding jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 441 grants NCLT plenary jurisdiction to compound offences punishable with fine only, without any minimum pecuniary floor (the Rs. 5,00,000 threshold only restricts the Regional Director). Under Section 451, the phrase 'in addition to any imprisonment provided for that offence' does not mandate imprisonment where none is prescribed, nor does it eliminate judicial discretion of the competent court to impose fine instead of imprisonment. Section 451's repeat default mechanism contemplates prior compounding within three years before triggering harsher penalties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Literal interpretation of penal statutes strictly preserving judicial discretion, rejecting statutory construction that implies non-compoundability where the primary statute permits fines. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT committed an error in holding it lacked jurisdiction over fines under Rs. 5,00,000, in rejecting joint petitions, and in declaring repeat defaults under Section 451 automatically non-compoundable.
operative_order: The appeals are allowed; the impugned common order dated 16th February, 2018 passed by the NCLT New Delhi is set aside; all respective Company Petitions are remitted back to the Tribunal for determination on the merits in accordance with law; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants challenged the NCLT New Delhi's order dated 16 February 2018, which dismissed their compounding applications filed under Section 441 of the Companies Act, 2013 for defaults such as delayed filing of annual returns and financial statements. The NCLT had held that joint applications by a company and its officers across multiple financial years were impermissible, that it lacked pecuniary jurisdiction where maximum fines were below Rs. 5 lakh, and that repeated defaults under Section 451 attracted mandatory imprisonment making them non-compoundable. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, setting aside the order and clarifying that joint applications are maintainable, NCLT has unlimited pecuniary jurisdiction under Section 441, and Section 451 does not make imprisonment mandatory.

case_title: Renaissance Steel India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Electrosteels Steel India Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditor is State Bank of India; Corporate Debtors are Electrosteel Steels Limited and Bhushan Steel Ltd.; Resolution Applicants include Vedanta Limited and Tata Steel Limited; Objectors/Appellants include rival resolution applicant Renaissance Steel India Pvt. Ltd., shareholder Neeraj Singal, and operational creditor Larsen & Toubro Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes initiated under Section 7 of the IBC against large corporate steel manufacturers; resolution plans submitted by Vedanta Limited (for Electrosteel) and Tata Steel Limited (for Bhushan Steel). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bhushan Steel had outstanding financial debts of approximately Rs. 56,051 Crores with an assessed liquidation value of Rs. 14,541 Crores; operational debts admitted were approximately Rs. 1,422 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 applications admitted in 2017; NCLT Kolkata approved Vedanta's plan for Electrosteel on 17 April 2018; NCLT Principal Bench approved Tata Steel's plan for Bhushan Steel on 15 May 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Renaissance Steel challenged Vedanta's eligibility citing its connected Zambian subsidiary Konkola Copper Mines ('KCM'), which had been convicted and fined under the Zambian Environmental Protection and Pollution Control Act in 2010; Renaissance and Neeraj Singal challenged Tata Steel citing Tata Steel UK's fine under the UK Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata (17 April 2018) held Vedanta eligible and approved its plan; NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi (15 May 2018) held Tata Steel eligible and approved its plan; these orders were challenged in separate appeals before the NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution applicant becomes ineligible under Section 29A(d) read with Section 29A(j) of the IBC where its connected juristic entity (subsidiary) has been convicted abroad for an offence providing for fine or imprisonment; whether corporate entities can be disqualified under Section 29A(d) which stipulates punishment 'with imprisonment for two years or more'; and whether the allocation of Rs. 1,200 Crores to operational creditors in the approved resolution plan was discriminatory or violated property rights.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Disqualification of a resolution applicant under Section 29A(d) on account of conviction requires that the underlying offence be specifically punishable with mandatory imprisonment for two years or more; offences carrying alternative sentences of fines, or convictions solely of juristic entities incapable of being incarcerated without individual natural persons/officers being convicted, do not trigger ineligibility under Section 29A(d). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(d) requires an offence 'punishable with imprisonment for two years or more' without alternative lighter options. Foreign statutory provisions (such as Zambian or UK safety/environmental laws) providing for fines or imprisonment up to a term are less severe than the threshold of Section 29A(d). Section 29A(d) directly contemplates imprisonment, which applies primarily to natural persons, unless a natural person acting on behalf of the company is convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of statutory penalty severity and strict evaluation of whether any natural person (director/officer) acting in concert was convicted with custodial imprisonment for the requisite duration. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Neither Vedanta Limited nor Tata Steel Limited incurred disqualification under Section 29A(d) as their overseas subsidiaries were juristic bodies merely fined without any individual director being sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more; the resolution plans were fair, equitable, and properly approved.
operative_order: All Company Appeals challenging the NCLT orders dated 17th April, 2018 (regarding Electrosteel Steels Ltd.) and 15th May, 2018 (regarding Bhushan Steel Ltd.) are dismissed; approved resolution plans of Vedanta Limited and Tata Steel Limited are upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants, including rival resolution applicant Renaissance Steel and former promoter Neeraj Singal, challenged NCLT orders approving the resolution plans of Vedanta Limited (for Electrosteel Steels Ltd.) and Tata Steel Limited (for Bhushan Steel Ltd.). Appellants contended that the successful applicants were ineligible under Section 29A(d) read with Section 29A(j) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 because connected overseas subsidiaries had suffered environmental and workplace safety convictions in Zambia and the UK. The NCLAT dismissed all appeals, ruling that Section 29A(d) is not triggered where juristic corporate entities are merely fined under foreign statutes prescribing alternative penalties and no natural person or officer was sentenced to imprisonment for two years or more.

case_title: Jharkhand Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. vs. IVRCL Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jharkhand Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. (counter-claimant in arbitration); Respondent No. 1 is IVRCL Ltd. (Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP represented by Resolution Professional Sutanu Sinha). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying contractual and infrastructure execution disputes referred to an Arbitral Tribunal where the Corporate Debtor raised claims and the Appellant raised counterclaims. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount and specific date of default under the Code not specified in the order; the issue pertains to unadjudicated claims and counterclaims pending before an Arbitral Tribunal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arbitral proceedings were underway when CIRP commenced and the Section 14 moratorium took effect; NCLAT passed an interim order on 11 July 2018 and final order on 3 August 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Arbitral claim filed by the Corporate Debtor and counterclaims raised by the Appellant in the same arbitration proceeding arising out of the same contract; Resolution Professional consented to having the counterclaims determined. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Adjudicating Authority permitted the Corporate Debtor to pursue its arbitral claims but left the question of the counter-claim open or pending, leading the Appellant to appeal before the NCLAT arguing that counterclaims cannot be excluded while claims are pursued.
legal_issues: Whether an Arbitral Tribunal can proceed with and determine a counter-claim against a Corporate Debtor during the subsistence of a moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 when the Corporate Debtor is permitted to pursue its own claim in the same arbitration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The determination and adjudication of claims and counterclaims arising from the same transaction in an arbitral proceeding can proceed simultaneously during a corporate insolvency resolution process moratorium, provided that any resulting monetary award against the corporate debtor is not executed or recovered during the moratorium period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC, which stays the continuation of suits or proceedings against the corporate debtor, does not bar the mere quantification or adjudication of counterclaims where the corporate debtor itself is asserting claims in the same proceeding and set-off may be required. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Interdependence of claims and counter-claims in contractual arbitration; determination of the net liability of the corporate debtor is necessary to establish the validity and extent of the debtor's own claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Claims and counterclaims should be heard and decided together by the Arbitral Tribunal in the absence of an express statutory bar, subject to the strict prohibition that no recovery or execution can be enforced against the corporate debtor while the moratorium remains operative.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of with the direction that both the claim of the Corporate Debtor and the counter-claim of the Appellant shall be heard and determined together by the Arbitral Tribunal; if the Corporate Debtor is found liable to pay any amount upon determination, no recovery can be made during the period of moratorium; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellant Jharkhand Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. appealed against an order of the Adjudicating Authority regarding whether its counter-claim could proceed before an Arbitral Tribunal during the CIRP moratorium of IVRCL Ltd., while the Corporate Debtor was allowed to pursue its claim. The Resolution Professional consented to the determination of the counter-claim. The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal disposed of the appeal, directing the Arbitral Tribunal to determine both the claim and counter-claim together in the same proceeding, while clarifying that if any amount is determined to be payable by the Corporate Debtor, no recovery can be executed during the moratorium under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.

case_title: V. Navaneetha Krishnan vs. Central Bank of India, Coimbatore & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: V. Navaneetha Krishnan (Director/Resolution Applicant) is the Appellant; Central Bank of India (Coimbatore Branch) is Respondent No. 1/Financial Creditor; C. Ramasubramaniam is Respondent No. 2/Resolution Professional/Liquidator[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying credit facilities extended by Central Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor resulting in Section 7 insolvency proceedings[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under commercial credit facilities leading to Section 7 admission; specific monetary default figures are not detailed in the appellate order[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Information Memorandum prepared during CIRP[cite: 27]. The Appellant submitted a Resolution Plan on the 178th day of CIRP (two days prior to the completion of the 180-day timeline)[cite: 27]. On the 179th day, the Committee of Creditors resolved to request liquidation[cite: 27]. The 180-day statutory period was completed immediately thereafter[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing submission of the Resolution Plan on the 178th day and the CoC resolution passed on the 179th day deciding against extension and opting for liquidation due to absence of timely plans[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC applied to the Adjudicating Authority for liquidation of the Corporate Debtor under Section 33[cite: 27]. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT alleging that the CoC acted arbitrarily without affording him an opportunity to negotiate or have his plan considered[cite: 27].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Committee of Creditors is bound to consider a resolution plan submitted on the 178th day of CIRP without seeking an extension of time under Section 12[cite: 27]. 2. Whether an applicant can seek withdrawal of the insolvency application under Section 12A during the liquidation stage[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors is under no statutory obligation to entertain a belated resolution plan submitted at the eleventh hour (on the 178th day) where no extension of the 180-day period is sought or justified, and may legitimately resolve to proceed with liquidation[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 strictly governs CIRP timelines[cite: 27]. However, pursuant to Section 12A, even during the liquidation period, if an eligible person under Section 29A satisfies the claims of the Committee of Creditors and receives approval from a 90% voting share of the CoC, the Adjudicating Authority may permit withdrawal of the Section 7 petition unhindered by a liquidation order[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the submission date of the plan against the expiration date of the 180-day timeline and whether the CoC exercised commercial discretion against seeking an extension[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the plan was submitted on the 178th day without any valid justification for extending time, the CoC's liquidation decision was lawful, subject to potential post-liquidation settlement under Section 12A[cite: 27].
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed without costs, with the observation that under Section 12A, the appellant may submit an offer during liquidation which the CoC may approve with a 90% voting share for withdrawal of the Section 7 application[cite: 27].
summary: The Appellant challenged the CoC's decision to seek liquidation of the Corporate Debtor instead of evaluating his resolution plan submitted on the 178th day of CIRP[cite: 27]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the CoC was justified in voting for liquidation on the 179th day in the absence of good reasons to extend the 180-day deadline[cite: 27]. The Tribunal clarified that under Section 12A, an eligible person may still offer to satisfy creditors' claims during liquidation, and if approved by a 90% voting share of the CoC, the Adjudicating Authority may allow withdrawal of the Section 7 application[cite: 27].

case_title: Central Bank of India vs. Resolution Professional of the Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Central Bank of India is the Appellant/Dissenting Financial Creditor; Resolution Professional of the Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. is Respondent No. 1; Successful Resolution Applicant is Respondent No. 2; Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd. resulting in an approved Resolution Plan providing upfront cash payments and 20-year redeemable preference shares to creditors[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default owed to consortium lenders, including Central Bank of India; specific default amounts are not detailed in the appellate order[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated; CoC approved resolution plan; NCLT Hyderabad Bench approved the plan under Section 31 on 19.07.2018; Central Bank of India appealed on grounds of plan illegality[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan treating dissenting and consenting financial creditors equally on the same level, without restricting dissenting creditors to liquidation value as contemplated under Regulation 38(1)(c)[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Central Bank of India, having dissented and voted against the plan, appealed the NCLT Hyderabad Bench approval order dated 19.07.2018 before NCLAT, arguing that the plan violated Regulation 38(1)(c) by not granting it differential liquidation-value priority[cite: 28].
legal_issues: 1. Whether clauses (b) and (c) of Regulation 38(1) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations, which mandate payment of mere liquidation value to operational and dissenting financial creditors, are ultra vires the IBC and invalid[cite: 28]. 2. Whether a resolution plan can be challenged for treating dissenting and consenting financial creditors equally rather than relegating dissenting creditors to liquidation value[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulations framed by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India cannot override or introduce discriminatory mandates inconsistent with the IBC; a resolution plan cannot discriminate among financial creditors solely on the ground of whether they voted in favor of or dissented from the resolution plan[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 240(1), IBBI's regulation-making power is strictly restricted to provisions consistent with the Code[cite: 28]. Regulation 38(1)(b) and (c), which mandate paying liquidation value to operational and dissenting financial creditors, are inconsistent with the IBC and ultra vires Section 240(1)[cite: 28]. Section 53 waterfall priorities apply only at liquidation, not during CIRP under Section 30(2)(b)[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the resolution plan enforces an arbitrary classification between consenting and dissenting financial creditors or ensures parity among equals[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Equal treatment of dissenting financial creditors alongside consenting financial creditors is lawful, and non-compliance with the invalid provisions of Regulation 38(1)(c) does not vitiate the approved plan[cite: 28].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 28]. The order of approval dated 19.07.2018 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench is sustained[cite: 28].
summary: Central Bank of India appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order approving the resolution plan for Sirpur Paper Mills Ltd., contending the plan violated Regulation 38(1)(c) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations by treating dissenting and consenting financial creditors equally instead of paying dissenting creditors their liquidation value[cite: 28]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Regulation 38(1)(b) and (c) are inconsistent with the IBC and ultra vires Section 240(1), as the Board lacks delegated authority to compel discrimination between similarly situated creditors[cite: 28]. The Tribunal ruled that Section 53 applies only during liquidation and that equal treatment of all financial creditors in a resolution plan is valid[cite: 28].

case_title: Darshak Enterprise Pvt. Ltd. vs. Chhaparia Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 327 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 328 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Darshak Enterprise Pvt. Ltd. and Symphony Ltd. are Appellants/Operational Creditors; Chhaparia Industries Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor; Resolution Professional is Respondent No. 2[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying trade transactions involving supply of goods/services; Symphony Ltd. had earlier instituted winding-up proceedings before the Bombay High Court[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Darshak Enterprise claimed principal operational dues of Rs. 26,57,271/-, and Symphony Ltd. claimed contingent operational dues of Rs. 67,76,000/- subject to litigation[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor filed voluntary insolvency under Section 10 (CP No. 23/I&BP/NCLT/MB/MAH/2017)[cite: 29]. Neither appellant filed its claim within the time stipulated under Regulation 12 of the IBBI CIRP Regulations[cite: 29]. The resolution plan was approved by NCLT Mumbai Bench on 29.09.2017 in MA No. 349/2017[cite: 29]. On 28.10.2017, a settlement cheque for Rs. 1,32,864/- (5% of dues) was issued to Darshak Enterprise and encashed[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Books of accounts of the Corporate Debtor reflecting operational liabilities; extracts of the approved resolution plan providing 5% settlement for non-current operational dues within 30 days, and classifying disputed claims as contingent operational dues payable upon final legal adjudication[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 29.09.2017 based on independent valuation and vacated the moratorium[cite: 29]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT contending that paying only 5% of dues or treating claims as contingent was unlawful[cite: 29].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an approved resolution plan is liable to be interfered with because it allocates only a small percentage (e.g., 5%) to operational creditors whose claims were not submitted within the statutory time limit[cite: 29]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can modify the commercial percentage allocation approved by the Committee of Creditors in the absence of discrimination or perversity[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial determination of the percentage of debt payable to various classes of creditors (financial, operational, secured, or unsecured) falls within the exclusive commercial domain of the Committee of Creditors; in the absence of unlawful discrimination or perversity, adjudicatory bodies cannot interfere with or modify an approved resolution plan[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where operational creditors fail to submit claims within the statutory window under Regulation 12 of the CIRP Regulations, the inclusion of their dues based on the corporate debtor's books (at a discounted payout or classified as contingent pending litigation) satisfies the requirements of Section 30 and Section 31 of the IBC[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the plan arbitrary discriminates against a creditor class or reflects a reasoned commercial determination by the CoC based on enterprise valuation and timely claim collation[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan adequately accounted for the appellants' belated claims based on company records, and the 5% allocation was within the CoC's commercial discretion[cite: 29].
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed without costs[cite: 29]. The Tribunal refrains from expressing any opinion on pending winding-up or other litigations before competent courts[cite: 29].
summary: Operational creditors Darshak Enterprise and Symphony Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order approving the resolution plan of Chhaparia Industries Pvt. Ltd., contending that the plan provided only 5% of principal dues to Darshak and classified Symphony's claim as contingent dues subject to litigation[cite: 29]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the percentage of payout to different classes of creditors is a commercial decision of the Committee of Creditors based on the facts of each case[cite: 29]. As the appellants failed to submit claims within the Regulation 12 deadline and their claims were nonetheless accommodated from company books without arbitrariness, no grounds existed to modify the approved plan[cite: 29].

case_title: Sanjay Kewalramani vs. Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjay Kewalramani is the Appellant/Director of the Corporate Debtor; Sunil Parmanand Kewalramani is Respondent No. 1 (signatory to the petition); Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 are family relatives (father and sister of Respondent No. 1); Medilux Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Family-sourced, interest-free unsecured advances granted by the father and sister to the Corporate Debtor at the instance of Respondent No. 1, who was a Director of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default was alleged to exceed Rs. 1 Lakh, but Form-1 failed to specify the precise date of default, loan tenure, or default records concerning Respondent Nos. 2 & 3[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-1 Section 7 petition was signed exclusively by Respondent No. 1 without authorization letters from Respondent Nos. 2 & 3. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the petition on 02.02.2018[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form No. 1 showing unsecured loans without written agreements, lacking repayment terms, and devoid of interest covenants, notwithstanding occasional past ad-hoc payments of 12% interest; absence of power of attorney or authorization letters executed by Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 in favor of Respondent No. 1[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents 1 to 3 filed a joint Section 7 petition (CP No. (IB) 130/7/NCLT/AHM/2017)[cite: 30]. NCLT Ahmedabad Bench held Respondent No. 1 was not a financial creditor, but nonetheless admitted the application on behalf of Respondent Nos. 2 & 3[cite: 30]. Director Sanjay Kewalramani appealed to NCLAT[cite: 30].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an interest-free unsecured advance provided by relatives without terms stipulating the time value of money constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) to qualify the lenders as 'Financial Creditors' under Section 5(7) of the IBC[cite: 30]. 2. Whether a joint Section 7 application can be maintained by an unauthorized co-applicant after the sole signing applicant is determined not to be a financial creditor[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Mere grant of an unsecured advance and its admission by a corporate debtor does not automatically constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC unless it is established that the disbursement was made against consideration for the time value of money; furthermore, a joint Section 7 application cannot proceed where the sole signatory is ineligible and holds no written authorization from the other co-applicants[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8), disbursement against consideration for the time value of money is an indispensable prerequisite for financial debt[cite: 30]. Intermittent or gratuitous payments of interest cannot transform an informal family advance lacking loan agreements or repayment terms into a financial debt[cite: 30]. Under Section 7, while co-creditors may join, the petition must be executed under valid legal authorization; when the primary applicant is not a financial creditor, unauthorized co-applicants cannot sustain the petition[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of loan documents in Form-1 to verify presence of commercial loan agreements, interest stipulations, defined default metrics, and formal letters of authorization[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 failed to prove financial debt or default metrics, and Respondent No. 1 lacked authority to sign on their behalf, rendering the petition non-maintainable[cite: 30].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 02.02.2018 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is set aside[cite: 30]. The appointment of the IRP, order of moratorium, account freezing, and all consequential actions are declared illegal and quashed[cite: 30]. The Section 7 application is dismissed, the Corporate Debtor is released from IBC rigors to function independently through its Board of Directors, and NCLT is directed to determine IRP fees payable by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 30]. Appeal allowed without costs[cite: 30].
summary: An appeal was filed by a director of Medilux Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. challenging an NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed jointly by three family members[cite: 30]. The NCLT found the sole signing applicant (Respondent No. 1) was not a financial creditor, but admitted the application on behalf of his father and sister (Respondent Nos. 2 & 3)[cite: 30]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that informal, interest-free unsecured advances lacking loan terms do not meet the criteria of disbursement for the time value of money under Section 5(8) to qualify as financial debt[cite: 30]. Since the sole signatory lacked legal authorization to represent the co-applicants and default metrics were missing, the Section 7 petition was declared non-maintainable[cite: 30].

case_title: Quantum Limited (Corporate Debtor) vs. Indus Finance Corporation Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Quantum Limited (acting through Resolution Professional) is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; Indus Finance Corporation Limited and JM Financial Assets Reconstruction Co. Ltd. are Respondents/Creditors/CoC members[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 12 of the IBC arising from defaulted credit facilities[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under commercial finance facilities leading to CIRP in C.P. No. 1043/(MAH)/2017; specific quantified sums of default are not stated in the order[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial 180-day CIRP period expired on 25.11.2017[cite: 31]. The Committee of Creditors passed a resolution on 24.11.2017 (on the 179th day) approving an extension[cite: 31]. The Resolution Professional filed the extension application before NCLT on 30.11.2017 (5 days after the 180-day period ended)[cite: 31]. NCLT dismissed the application on 18.12.2017[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the CoC meeting dated 24.11.2017 recording a resolution passed by a 75% majority of voting shares instructing the RP to seek a 90-day extension from the Adjudicating Authority under Section 12(2)[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the application on 18.12.2017, holding that there is no provision to revive or condone the expiry of 180 days and that it lacked jurisdiction to entertain an extension application filed after the 180th day[cite: 31]. The Corporate Debtor through the RP appealed to NCLAT[cite: 31].
legal_issues: 1. Whether Section 12(2) of the IBC mandates that the application for extension of the CIRP period must be filed before the Adjudicating Authority prior to the expiry of the initial 180 days[cite: 31]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to extend the CIRP period by up to 90 days where the CoC passed its resolution within 180 days but the court application was filed after the 180th day[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 12(2) of the IBC requires that the resolution of the Committee of Creditors instructing the resolution professional to apply for an extension be passed within the 180-day period, but does not prescribe that the formal application must be filed before or heard by the Adjudicating Authority prior to the expiry of the 180 days[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(2) and (3) aim to ensure resolution over liquidation[cite: 31]. If a resolution is passed by a 75% majority of the CoC within the 180-day period (including on the 180th day), the Adjudicating Authority is empowered to grant an extension of up to 90 days; liquidation is the last recourse and should not be ordered purely due to post-180th-day court filing[cite: 31]. The intervening days between the 181st day and the appellate order must be excluded from computation[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the CoC passed the resolution instructing the RP with a 75% voting share within the statutory 180 days[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC resolved on 24.11.2017 (before 25.11.2017) to seek an extension, the NCLT had full jurisdiction to grant the extension, and its refusal was erroneous[cite: 31].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 18.12.2017 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside[cite: 31]. The CIRP duration is extended for another 90 days counted from the date of this order (20.02.2018), and the period between the 181st day and 20.02.2018 is excluded for all purposes[cite: 31]. Appeal allowed without costs[cite: 31].
summary: The Corporate Debtor appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting a Section 12(2) application for a 90-day CIRP extension[cite: 31]. The NCLT had held that it lacked jurisdiction to extend CIRP because the formal application was filed on 30.11.2017, five days after the initial 180 days expired on 25.11.2017[cite: 31]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT established the rule that Section 12(2) does not mandate filing the court application prior to the 180th day, provided the CoC passed the resolution within the 180 days[cite: 31]. Because the CoC approved the extension on 24.11.2017 with the requisite 75% majority, the NCLAT set aside the rejection, granted a 90-day extension from the date of the order, and excluded the intervening period[cite: 31].

case_title: ANG Industries Ltd. vs. Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ANG Industries Ltd. (acting through Resolution Professional Ilam Chand Kamboj) is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; M/s Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. and M/s Ashok Leyland Limited are Respondents/Operational Creditors[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial operational transactions involving the supply of goods and services giving rise to admitted operational debts against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. claimed an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 26,44,17,155/- (inclusive of interest) and Ashok Leyland Limited claimed an operational debt of Rs. 15.50 Crores, together aggregating to more than 10% of the total debt of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ongoing CIRP under CP (IB)-292 (ND)2017 before NCLT New Delhi Bench; the Resolution Professional convened Committee of Creditors (CoC) meetings without giving notice to the operational creditors[cite: 22]; NCLT passed the impugned direction on 16.02.2018[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Verified operational debt claims demonstrating that the respondents collectively held more than 10% of the aggregate debt of the Corporate Debtor, triggering statutory representation thresholds[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents filed applications before NCLT New Delhi Bench seeking directions to the Resolution Professional to allow them to attend CoC meetings pursuant to Section 24(3)(c) of the IBC[cite: 22]. On 16.02.2018, NCLT allowed their plea and directed the RP to pass a speaking order on their claim and attendance[cite: 22]. The Resolution Professional appealed before NCLAT[cite: 22].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated under Section 24(3)(c) of the IBC to serve notice of CoC meetings to operational creditors or their representatives when their aggregate dues equal or exceed 10% of the total debt[cite: 22]. 2. What is the scope of participation for non-voting attendees (suspended directors, operational creditors, and resolution applicants) in CoC meetings under Sections 24 and 30(5) of the IBC[cite: 22]?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Notice of each meeting of the Committee of Creditors must be mandatorily issued to operational creditors or their appointed representatives if their aggregate dues constitute not less than ten percent of the corporate debtor's total debt; such participants, though lacking voting rights, possess the statutory right to attend, observe, voice concerns, and submit views, which the CoC must consider and record with brief reasons[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 24(3)(c) read with Section 24(4) and Section 30(5) of the IBC ensures transparency in the resolution process; the exclusion of voting rights for operational creditors does not permit their complete exclusion from CoC proceedings if the statutory 10% threshold is met[cite: 22]. The CoC is required to deliberate on their views and record short reasons when accepting or rejecting resolution plans[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether the operational debts claimed and admitted meet the threshold of ten percent of the aggregate corporate debt[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The respondents met the statutory threshold under Section 24(3)(c) and were entitled to receive notice and attend CoC meetings; NCLT's direction was fully justified and warrants no interference[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs[cite: 22]. The Resolution Professional is directed to act in accordance with law and comply with the guidelines governing notice, attendance, and transparency established in the Rajputana Properties precedent[cite: 22].
summary: The Resolution Professional of ANG Industries Ltd. appealed against an NCLT New Delhi order directing him to permit two operational creditors (Shah Brothers Ispat and Ashok Leyland) to attend Committee of Creditors meetings, as their claims collectively exceeded 10% of the total debt[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT affirmed that Section 24(3)(c) mandates issuance of notice to operational creditors holding 10% or more of the aggregate debt[cite: 22]. The Tribunal ruled that while such creditors do not possess voting rights, they have a statutory right to attend and voice concerns, which the CoC must consider and record reasons for when evaluating resolution plans[cite: 22].

case_title: M/s. Shilpi Cable Technologies Ltd. vs. Macquarie Bank Ltd.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 101 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 102 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Shilpi Cable Technologies Ltd. (acting through its suspended Board of Directors) is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; Macquarie Bank Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial contracts for the purchase and supply of goods involving commercial invoices[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of operational debt under unpaid commercial invoices raised by Macquarie Bank Ltd.; the Corporate Debtor claimed debts fell within an ongoing 180-day credit cycle[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 9 petitions CP (IB)-64(PB)/2017 and CP (IB)-65(PB)/2017 admitted by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi on 24.05.2017[cite: 23]. NCLAT initially set aside the orders on 01.08.2017[cite: 23]. Supreme Court reversed NCLAT and remitted the matter on 15.12.2017[cite: 23]. NCLAT restored CIRP continuation on 15.01.2018 and finalized the appeals on 08.08.2018[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unpaid invoices establishing default; commercial agreements containing an English governing law clause and an arbitration clause[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After the Supreme Court remitted the appeals, the suspended directors repeatedly sought adjournments on new grounds (English governing law and credit cycle) without arguing on merits[cite: 23]. NCLAT took up the appeals on merits on 08.08.2018[cite: 23].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal challenging the admission of a Section 9 CIRP petition can be maintained by the Corporate Debtor through its suspended Board of Directors[cite: 23]. 2. Whether an arbitration clause or an agreement to be governed by foreign law (English law) bars the initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging the admission of an insolvency petition is not maintainable if filed by the corporate debtor through its suspended board of directors; furthermore, contractual stipulations designating foreign law or providing for arbitration do not oust the statutory insolvency jurisdiction under Section 9 where debt and default are established[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the Supreme Court mandate in *Innoventive Industries*, once insolvency commences and the board is suspended, the corporate debtor cannot maintain an appeal through its erstwhile directors[cite: 23]. Moreover, the existence of an arbitration clause or foreign governing law does not ipso facto constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 9 in the presence of admitted and defaulted operational invoices[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of corporate authorization locus standi and examining invoice admissions against unsupported credit-cycle assertions[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals are non-maintainable and devoid of merit; CIRP stands restored, with litigation delays excluded from the statutory 180/270-day limit[cite: 23].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 101 and 102 of 2017 are dismissed on grounds of non-maintainability and on merits without costs[cite: 23]. The Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is restored, the time spent during the pendency of appeals before the NCLAT and Supreme Court is excluded from the 180/270-day timeline, and the Resolution Professional is directed to resume proceedings from the stage they were interrupted[cite: 23].
summary: The suspended Board of Directors of Shilpi Cable Technologies Ltd. challenged NCLT New Delhi orders admitting Section 9 insolvency applications filed by Macquarie Bank Ltd.[cite: 23] Following remand from the Supreme Court, the Appellant argued that the dispute was governed by English law and that transactions fell within a 180-day credit cycle[cite: 23]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the appeal was not maintainable at the behest of the suspended Board under the *Innoventive* doctrine[cite: 23]. On merits, the Tribunal ruled that arbitration and foreign law clauses do not oust IBC jurisdiction over defaulted operational debts, ordering CIRP restored with exclusion of appellate litigation time[cite: 23].

case_title: Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals Limited vs. K.P.R. Industries (India) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Crompton Greaves Consumer Electricals Limited is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; M/s K.P.R. Industries (India) Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale, supply, and delivery of materials for designing, engineering, manufacturing, testing, erection, and commissioning spares of industrial light fixtures pursuant to a purchase order dated 25.07.2014[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of unpaid operational debt amounting to Rs. 34,42,005.57[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised; demand notices issued on 07.07.2016, 07.04.2017, and 25.04.2017[cite: 24]. The 25.04.2017 notice was returned on 04.05.2017 marked 'Refused'[cite: 24]. Application under Section 9 filed in CP (IB) No. 177/9/HDB/2017 and dismissed by NCLT on 15.11.2017[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank confirmation letter dated 11.09.2017 from ICICI Bank certifying no receipt of funds from the Corporate Debtor between 07.07.2016 and 11.09.2017; returned postal endorsement 'Refused hence returned to sender'[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 177/9/HDB/2017 under Section 9. NCLT Hyderabad Bench rejected the application on 15.11.2017, relying on NCLAT's overturned decision in *Uttam Galva*, holding that the Section 8 demand notice was invalid because it was issued by an advocate without Board authorization[cite: 24]. Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT[cite: 24].
legal_issues: 1. Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 8(1) of the IBC issued by an advocate on behalf of an operational creditor is legally valid[cite: 24]. 2. Whether an Adjudicating Authority can reject a Section 9 application without providing the mandatory statutory opportunity to cure defects in the demand notice or application[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A demand notice issued under Section 8(1) of the IBC by an advocate or authorized legal counsel on behalf of an operational creditor is valid and legally enforceable; where default and debt are established without a pre-existing dispute, an adjudicating authority must provide an opportunity to rectify curable procedural defects before rejecting a petition[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in *Macquarie Bank Ltd. v. Shilpi Cable Technologies Ltd.* (reversing *Uttam Galva*), the term 'operational creditor' in Section 8 encompasses its authorized lawyers and agents[cite: 24]. Under Section 9(5)(i), upon satisfaction of debt and default without pre-existing dispute, the petition must be admitted, and any technical discrepancy requires a statutory cure notice[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation of unpaid debt via bank certifications and postal records demonstrating service or deemed service ('refusal') of statutory demand notices[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The rejection based solely on the notice being issued by an advocate was erroneous; the operational debt and default stood proved without any pre-existing dispute[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed and the impugned order dated 15.11.2017 is set aside[cite: 24]. The matter is remitted back to NCLT Hyderabad Bench to admit the Section 9 application under Section 9(5)(i), while providing an opportunity to cure any remaining defects[cite: 24].
summary: Crompton Greaves appealed an NCLT Hyderabad Bench order rejecting its Section 9 CIRP application against K.P.R. Industries for an unpaid operational debt of Rs. 34,42,005.57[cite: 24]. The NCLT had rejected the petition on the ground that the Section 8 demand notice was issued by an advocate without express Board authorization, relying on the NCLAT decision in *Uttam Galva*[cite: 24]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that *Uttam Galva* was overruled by the Supreme Court in *Macquarie Bank*, confirming that demand notices issued by lawyers are legally valid[cite: 24]. As debt and default were evidenced without a pre-existing dispute, the matter was remitted for admission[cite: 24].

case_title: Amar Remedies Ltd. vs. IDBI Bank Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amar Remedies Ltd. (acting through Resolution Professional) is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; IDBI Bank Ltd. and other consortium lenders are Respondents/Financial Creditors/CoC members[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying consortium bank lending facilities and corporate insolvency resolution proceedings under the IBC[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under corporate insolvency proceedings; specific monetary default amount is not specified in the appellate order[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The initial 180-day CIRP period expired on 13.12.2017[cite: 25]. The Committee of Creditors passed a resolution on 06.12.2017 (within the 180 days) instructing the RP to seek an extension[cite: 25]. The RP filed the extension application on 15.12.2017 (2 days after the 180th day)[cite: 25]. NCLT dismissed the application on 09.01.2018[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC meeting minutes dated 06.12.2017 showing a resolution passed by more than 75% voting shares instructing the RP to apply for a 90-day extension under Section 12(2)[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The RP filed an application under Section 12(2) before NCLT Mumbai Bench for a 90-day extension[cite: 25]. NCLT dismissed the application on 09.01.2018, ruling that it was devoid of jurisdiction to revive a CIRP period that had already expired by the time the application came up for hearing[cite: 25]. The RP appealed to NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application for extension of the CIRP period beyond 180 days under Section 12(2) of the IBC must be filed before the Adjudicating Authority prior to the expiry of the 180-day timeline, provided the CoC resolution was passed within the 180 days[cite: 25]. 2. Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to grant a 90-day extension after the 180th day has elapsed[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 12(2) of the IBC requires the Committee of Creditors to pass a resolution instructing the resolution professional to seek an extension within the 180-day period, but does not mandate that the application itself must be filed before or decided by the Adjudicating Authority prior to the 180th day[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12(2) and 12(3) empower the Adjudicating Authority to extend the CIRP duration up to 90 days if the CoC passed a resolution with the requisite majority within 180 days[cite: 25]. Liquidation is a measure of last resort; where the CoC and RP acted diligently, the tribunal has jurisdiction to grant the extension to enable resolution[cite: 25]. The intervening period between the 181st day and the extension order must be excluded from computation[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of CoC meeting minutes to confirm whether the 75% majority vote was passed within the initial 180 days[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the CoC resolved on 06.12.2017 to seek an extension, the filing of the application two days after the 180th day was not fatal, and NCLT erred in holding it lacked jurisdiction[cite: 25].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 09.01.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside[cite: 25]. The CIRP period is extended for another 90 days counted from the date of this order (05.03.2018), and the period between the 181st day and 05.03.2018 is excluded for all purposes[cite: 25].
