Appeal allowed without costs[cite: 25].
summary: The Resolution Professional of Amar Remedies Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing a Section 12(2) application for a 90-day CIRP extension on the ground that the initial 180 days had expired before the application was heard[cite: 25]. The Committee of Creditors had approved the extension with over 75% majority on the 173rd day, but the RP filed the application two days after the 180th day[cite: 25]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 12 does not require the court application to be filed within 180 days so long as the CoC passed the resolution within that timeframe[cite: 25]. Setting aside the order, NCLAT granted a 90-day extension from the date of the order, excluding the intervening delay[cite: 25].

case_title: GAIL (India) Limited vs. Rajeev Manaadiar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: GAIL (India) Limited is the Appellant/Beneficiary of the Performance Bank Guarantee; Rajeev Manaadiar is Respondent No. 1/Resolution Professional; M/s Petron Engineering Construction Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying engineering and construction infrastructure contract executed between GAIL and the Corporate Debtor, secured by a Performance Bank Guarantee issued by a financial institution on behalf of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Contractual non-performance and breach of execution obligations under the turnkey project leading to GAIL's decision to invoke the Performance Bank Guarantee[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ongoing CIRP in CP 1374/I&BC/MNCLT/MB/MAH/2017; Resolution Professional filed MA No. 521/2018 seeking an injunction against PBG encashment; NCLT Mumbai Bench issued the stay order on 12.06.2018 (erroneously referenced in part as 15.09.2016)[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Performance Bank Guarantee documentation furnished by the Corporate Debtor to secure performance of contractual works[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: During the moratorium period, the Resolution Professional applied to NCLT Mumbai to stay GAIL from encashing the Performance Bank Guarantee[cite: 26]. NCLT prohibited GAIL from invoking the guarantee, holding that it was barred by the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 26]. GAIL appealed to NCLAT[cite: 26].
legal_issues: 1. Whether the invocation of a Performance Bank Guarantee is prohibited by the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC[cite: 26]. 2. Whether a Performance Bank Guarantee falls within the statutory definition of 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Performance Bank Guarantee is expressly excluded from the definition of 'security interest' under the IBC; consequently, the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(c) does not prohibit a beneficiary from invoking or encashing a performance guarantee during the CIRP period[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(c) bars enforcement of any security interest created by the corporate debtor in respect of its property[cite: 26]. However, the proviso to Section 3(31) explicitly mandates that 'security interest shall not include a performance guarantee'[cite: 26]. Therefore, performance bank guarantees stand outside the ambit of Section 14 moratoriums[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the bank guarantee instrument to determine whether it constitutes a performance guarantee or an ordinary financial security interest over corporate debtor assets[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT erred in prohibiting GAIL from invoking the Performance Bank Guarantee; GAIL is entitled to invoke the guarantee in full or in part, subject to informing the Resolution Professional[cite: 26].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 12.06.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in MA No. 521/2018 is set aside[cite: 26]. GAIL is permitted to invoke the Performance Bank Guarantee in full or in part and extend its validity for six months, with directions to inform the IRP/RP to update records and notify resolution applicants[cite: 26]. Appeal allowed without costs[cite: 26].
summary: GAIL (India) Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order restraining it from invoking a Performance Bank Guarantee issued on behalf of the Corporate Debtor, Petron Engineering Construction Ltd., during the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 26]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 14(1)(c) prohibits the enforcement of a 'security interest', but the proviso to Section 3(31) of the IBC explicitly excludes performance guarantees from that definition[cite: 26]. Consequently, performance bank guarantees are not covered by the moratorium, and beneficiaries are legally entitled to invoke them in whole or in part during the CIRP[cite: 26].

case_title: Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. vs. P. Mohanraj & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Complainant/Creditor; P. Mohanraj & Ors. are the Respondents/Directors of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying commercial supply transactions leading to the issuance of negotiable cheques that were subsequently dishonored upon presentation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from dishonor of cheques, prompting penal complaints under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act; exact cheque amounts are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint CC No. 552/SS/2017 was filed prior to 06.06.2017; CIRP was initiated and moratorium was declared on 06.06.2017 in CP/507/IB/2017; subsequent complaint CC No. 690/SS/2017 was filed after 06.06.2017; NCLT Chennai passed the impugned order in MA/102/IB/2018 on 24.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Complaints CC No. 552/SS/2017 and CC No. 690/SS/2017 filed under Section 138 of the NI Act before the Metropolitan Magistrate 59th Court, Kurla, Mumbai, against the company and its directors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor's directors filed MA/102/IB/2018 before NCLT Single Bench, Chennai, contending that Section 138 proceedings are barred by the Section 14 moratorium. By order dated 24.05.2018, NCLT Chennai directed the Appellant to withdraw the Section 138 complaints as misuse of legal process during moratorium. The Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the statutory moratorium declared under Section 14 of the IBC prohibits the institution or continuation of criminal proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 against the Corporate Debtor and its Directors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory moratorium prohibiting civil suits, recovery proceedings, and execution of money decrees against a corporate debtor does not encompass penal proceedings under criminal law; prosecution and penal sanctions against a corporate debtor's directors are not money claims and can proceed despite moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(a) of the IBC prohibits institution/continuation of suits, proceedings, or execution of judgments/decrees of money claims; Section 138 of the NI Act is a penal provision providing for imprisonment or punitive fine, which does not constitute a proceeding or decree for a debt recovery or money claim. No criminal proceeding falls within the purview of Section 14. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determining whether the statutory proceeding sought to be stayed is civil/recovery in nature or a penal/punitive prosecution for an offense. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Criminal complaints under Section 138 of the NI Act are not barred by Section 14 of the IBC and may proceed before the competent criminal court during the moratorium period.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24.05.2018 passed by NCLT Single Bench, Chennai in MA/102/IB/2018 in CP/507/IB/2017 is set aside[cite: 17]. The court of competent jurisdiction may proceed with the Section 138 NI Act complaints even during the moratorium period[cite: 17]. Appeal allowed; connected I.A. Nos. 820/2018, 821/2018, 822/2018, and 823/2018 stand disposed of with no costs[cite: 17].
summary: Shah Brothers Ispat Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Chennai order directing it to withdraw Section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act complaints filed against the directors of a corporate debtor on the ground that the proceedings were barred by the Section 14 moratorium under the IBC[cite: 17]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 14 of the IBC does not encompass criminal or penal proceedings, as Section 138 of the NI Act involves criminal liability and potential imprisonment or punitive fines rather than civil debt recovery[cite: 17]. The Tribunal ruled that criminal prosecutions under the NI Act can proceed during the moratorium period[cite: 17].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Debashish Nanda
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Debashish Nanda is the Respondent/Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium banking credit facilities and cash-credit/overdraft accounts maintained by the Corporate Debtor with State Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under Section 7 insolvency proceedings; as on the date of moratorium (01.06.2017), the Corporate Debtor had overdrawn its bank account by Rs. 8,04,81,486.35/- beyond the sanctioned Rs. 8 Crore limit. Subsequent refund deposits of approximately Rs. 2 Crores were made by the Sales Tax Department. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Moratorium declared by the Adjudicating Authority on 01.06.2017; bank account adjustments and bank guarantee encashments occurred on or after 01.06.2017; NCLT Principal Bench passed the impugned order on 25.01.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements of the Corporate Debtor for the period from 01.06.2017 to 31.07.2017 establishing an overdrawn balance of Rs. 8,04,81,486.35/- as on 01.06.2017; records of debit entries, bank guarantee encashment, and post-moratorium tax refunds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional filed an application before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi alleging that SBI violated Section 14(1)(c) by debiting sums and encashing bank guarantees post-moratorium. By order dated 25.01.2018, NCLT allowed the application, directed SBI to roll back all post-01.06.2017 debits, restore the account, defreeze it for the RP's operations, and imposed a cost of Rs. 25,000/- on SBI payable to the Prime Minister Welfare Fund. SBI appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a financial creditor bank is prohibited under Section 14 of the IBC from adjusting or debiting amounts deposited into a corporate debtor's bank account after the declaration of a moratorium. 2. Whether a financial creditor bank can debit interest or must maintain it separately in accordance with RBI guidelines during a moratorium. 3. Whether the imposition of costs of Rs. 25,000/- on SBI was justified.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon declaration of a moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, a creditor bank is strictly prohibited from recovering, adjusting, or appropriating any funds or deposits credited into the corporate debtor's account towards its pre-CIRP dues, and cannot freeze bank accounts necessary for day-to-day operations managed by the Resolution Professional. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 creates an absolute statutory bar against any recovery, foreclosure, or enforcement of security interests during the CIRP period; any post-moratorium deposit (including statutory tax refunds) belongs to the corporate debtor's operations and cannot be set off by the bank. However, the bank is permitted to account for accruing interest under a separate ledger head in line with RBI guidelines, provided it is not debited as an adjustment against the debtor's operational funds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of bank statements demonstrating whether post-moratorium credits were appropriated towards loan recovery and whether account balances were available for operations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT's substantive direction ordering the rollback of post-moratorium debit adjustments and unfreezing the account was correct; however, the cost of Rs. 25,000/- imposed on the bank was uncalled for and set aside.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 25.01.2018 is modified; the cost of Rs. 25,000/- imposed on the Appellant is set aside, while the interim directions dated 21.03.2018 (prohibiting debit adjustments/account freezes and permitting interest entries under a separate head per RBI norms) are made absolute for the moratorium period[cite: 18]. Appeal disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 18].
summary: State Bank of India appealed against an NCLT Principal Bench order directing it to roll back post-moratorium debit adjustments, defreeze the bank account of the corporate debtor, and pay Rs. 25,000/- as costs for violating Section 14(1)(c) of the IBC[cite: 18]. The NCLAT affirmed the core finding that banks cannot appropriate post-moratorium deposits or freeze bank accounts required by the Resolution Professional for day-to-day operations[cite: 18]. However, the Tribunal clarified that the bank may record interest under a separate ledger head in compliance with RBI guidelines and set aside the cost of Rs. 25,000/- imposed on the bank[cite: 18].

case_title: ICICI Bank Ltd. vs. Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Ltd. is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Guarantor-Corporate Debtor; an unnamed borrower entity is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial lending facilities extended to the Principal Borrower, secured by a corporate guarantee executed by Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on underlying financial debt facilities guaranteed by the Corporate Guarantor; exact default figures are not specified in the appellate order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed a Section 7 application against the Guarantor in 2017; NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the petition on 15.12.2017; subsequent resolution plan in the Principal Borrower's CIRP (CP (IB) No. 37/KB/2017) was approved later on 12.02.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate guarantee agreement executed by Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd.; resolution plan approved in the Principal Borrower's proceedings containing a clause restraining legal actions during implementation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: ICICI Bank filed a Section 7 application against the Guarantor, Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd. NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed the petition on 15.12.2017 on the ground that no CIRP can be triggered against a guarantor during the pendency of insolvency proceedings against the principal borrower. ICICI Bank appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the pendency of insolvency proceedings or a moratorium against a principal borrower bars a financial creditor from initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC against the corporate guarantor. 2. Whether a resolution plan approved in the principal borrower's CIRP subsequent to the dismissal of the Section 7 petition affects the maintainability of the creditor's application against the corporate guarantor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory moratorium declared under Section 14 in respect of a corporate debtor does not bar the institution or triggering of a Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 or Section 9 against a guarantor or personal guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 prohibits suits, execution, and security enforcement against the specific debtor under moratorium; Section 60(2) explicitly contemplates concurrent or separate insolvency resolution proceedings against both the corporate debtor and its guarantor. An order of moratorium in a principal borrower's proceeding does not bar a Section 7 application against the corporate guarantor, nor can a subsequently approved resolution plan extinguish pre-existing filings initiated prior to such approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the timeline of filing to confirm whether the Section 7 petition against the guarantor was filed prior to plan approval, and assessing the scope of Section 14 prohibitions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT Kolkata erred in dismissing the Section 7 petition on the erroneous premise that proceedings against a guarantor cannot co-exist with those against the principal borrower.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 15.12.2017 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench is set aside[cite: 19]. The matter is remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench for admission of the Section 7 application if complete, with liberty to the Appellant to cure defects within a reasonable time[cite: 19]. Appeal allowed with no costs[cite: 19].
summary: ICICI Bank appealed against an order of the NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissing its Section 7 application against Vista Steel Pvt. Ltd. (corporate guarantor) on the premise that CIRP cannot be initiated against a guarantor during the pendency of proceedings against the principal borrower[cite: 19]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that Section 14 moratorium in the principal borrower's case does not bar triggering insolvency resolution under Section 7 or Section 60(2) against a guarantor[cite: 19]. The Appellate Tribunal further held that subsequent approval of a resolution plan in the borrower's CIRP does not nullify a pre-existing Section 7 filing against the guarantor, remitting the matter to NCLT for admission[cite: 19].

case_title: Jaya Patel vs. Gas Jeans Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jaya Patel (Director of Corporate Debtor) is the Appellant; Gas Jeans Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Operational Creditor; Vama Apparels India Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial supply of apparel and merchandise giving rise to unpaid operational invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt default claimed at Rs. 21,63,359/-, with the Corporate Debtor admitting liability to the extent of approximately Rs. 6 Lakhs in its response. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up petition filed under Sections 433-434 of the Companies Act, 1956 before the Bombay High Court was transferred to NCLT Mumbai under Rule 5 of the Companies (Transfer of Pending Proceedings) Rules, 2016. On the very same day the Section 8(1) demand notice was issued, the Operational Creditor simultaneously filed Form-5 under Rule 6 to convert the petition under Section 9 of the IBC. NCLT admitted the petition on 17.05.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record showing identical filing dates for the Section 8(1) demand notice and the Form-5 application under Section 9. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the transferred petition under Section 9 on 17.05.2018, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP. The Director of the Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT on the ground that the mandatory ten-day statutory waiting period between demand notice and petition filing was bypassed.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable if filed prior to the mandatory expiry of the 10-day statutory notice period required under Section 8(1) read with Section 9(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The expiry of the mandatory ten-day period from the delivery of the demand notice under Section 8(1) is an absolute condition precedent for filing an operational debt insolvency application under Section 9 of the IBC; simultaneous issuance of demand notice and petition filing renders the proceedings incurably void and non-maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(1) explicitly mandates that an application can be filed only 'after the expiry of the period of ten days from the date of delivery of the notice or invoice'. An application presented before the lapse of ten days cannot be entertained or admitted by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 9(5), and transferred winding-up petitions failing compliance stand abated under Rule 5. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparing the date of dispatch/service of the Section 8(1) demand notice with the date of presentation of the Form-5 petition under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was filed on the same day the Section 8(1) notice was issued, violating the statutory waiting period and rendering the admission order illegal.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 17.05.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is set aside; the transferred winding-up petition stands abated under Rule 5[cite: 20]. The appointment of the IRP, declaration of moratorium, freezing of accounts, and all actions taken by the IRP are declared illegal and set aside[cite: 20]. The Corporate Debtor is released from the rigors of the IBC to function independently through its Board of Directors[cite: 20]. Adjudicating Authority to determine and Corporate Debtor to pay IRP fees[cite: 20]. Creditor granted liberty to file a fresh Section 9 application after complying with Section 8(1)[cite: 20]. Appeal disposed of without costs[cite: 20].
summary: A director of Vama Apparels India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Gas Jeans Pvt. Ltd. in a transferred winding-up petition[cite: 20]. The Appellant demonstrated that the operational creditor issued the Section 8(1) demand notice on the exact same date it filed Form-5 under Section 9[cite: 20]. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT held that the ten-day waiting period following delivery of the demand notice under Section 8(1) is a mandatory condition precedent under Section 9(1) of the IBC[cite: 20]. An application filed before the completion of ten days is non-maintainable and void ab initio, resulting in the quashing of the admission order and abatement of the petition[cite: 20].

case_title: Parmod Yadav & Anr. vs. Divine Infracon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Parmod Yadav & Sneha Yadav (mother and daughter, lessors) are the Appellants/Operational Creditors; Divine Infracon Pvt. Ltd. (lessee/hotel developer) is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Hotelier-Buyer Agreement dated 10.01.2012 and Lease Agreement dated 16.08.2014 (effective retrospectively from 10.01.2012) for a 15-year commercial lease of Service Apartment No. 915-A (super built-up area 68 sq. meters), Soul City Service Apartment Complex, Dwarka, New Delhi, at a monthly rent of Rs. 1,37,250/- plus service tax, with a 15-year lock-in period. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed totaled Rs. 2,74,63,957.77, comprising unpaid accrued rent of Rs. 12,62,700/-, interest of Rs. 1,95,718.03 @ 12% p.a., and unexpired lock-in period monthly rentals from 10.04.2016 to 09.01.2027 amounting to Rs. 2,60,05,539.74. Corporate Debtor counterclaimed unpaid maintenance charges of Rs. 3,60,841/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease terminated by Corporate Debtor on 04.04.2016. Corporate Debtor issued an arbitration invocation notice under Section 21 of the Arbitration Act on 17.01.2017 suggesting three sole arbitrator names. Appellants issued Section 8(1) demand notice on 22.04.2017 (served on 24.04.2017); Section 9 petition filed in 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Notice dated 17.01.2017 invoking Clause 32 of the Hotelier-Buyer Agreement dated 10.01.2012 for the appointment of a sole arbitrator to adjudicate disputes arising out of the agreement, sale deed, and lease; termination notice dated 04.04.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. IB/209/ND/2017 under Section 9 of the IBC. NCLT New Delhi rejected the petition on 28.09.2017 on the ground of a pre-existing dispute evidenced by the prior arbitration invocation notice. The lessors appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the issuance of a notice requesting the appointment of a sole arbitrator under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 prior to the service of a Section 8(1) demand notice constitutes an 'existence of a dispute' barring a Section 9 application under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, arbitral proceedings commence on the date when a request for the dispute to be referred to arbitration is received by the respondent; the commencement of arbitral proceedings prior to the issuance of a statutory demand notice constitutes an irrefutable pre-existing dispute under the IBC, rendering a Section 9 application non-maintainable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC requires the absence of any pre-existing dispute or pending arbitral proceedings at the time the demand notice is served. By operation of Section 21 of the Arbitration Act, 1996, arbitral proceedings are legally seized and commenced upon dispatch/receipt of the arbitration invocation notice, thereby excluding the matter from insolvency resolution without needing to decide whether commercial leasing falls within 'services' under Section 5(21). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the date of receipt of the Section 21 arbitration notice relative to the date of delivery of the Section 8(1) demand notice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because arbitral proceedings had commenced on 17.01.2017—months before the demand notice was issued on 22.04.2017—a bona fide pre-existing dispute existed, rendering the Section 9 petition barred.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. The order dated 28.09.2017 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, NCLT New Delhi, rejecting the Section 9 application, is affirmed. No order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: Appellants leased a service apartment to Divine Infracon Pvt. Ltd. under a 15-year lease with a lock-in period[cite: 21]. Following premature lease termination by the debtor, the Appellants filed a Section 9 application claiming Rs. 2.74 Crores in rent arrears and unexpired lock-in rent[cite: 21]. NCLT New Delhi dismissed the petition due to a pre-existing dispute[cite: 21]. Affirming the dismissal, NCLAT held that because the Corporate Debtor had issued an arbitration notice proposing a sole arbitrator under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 prior to the Section 8 demand notice, arbitral proceedings had legally commenced[cite: 21]. This established a valid pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 proceedings[cite: 21].

case_title: Mr. Rajendra K. Bhuta, Resolution Professional vs. Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Rajendra K. Bhuta is the Appellant/Resolution Professional of Guruashish Construction Private Limited (Corporate Debtor); Maharashtra Housing and Area Development Authority (MHADA) is the Respondent/Statutory Land Owning Authority; Union Bank of India is the Financial Creditor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Land measuring 40 acres originally belonging to Bombay Housing & Area Development Board (vested in MHADA in 1966) was allotted to a society in 1988. On 10.04.2008, a Joint Development Agreement (JDA) was executed between the Society, the Corporate Debtor, and MHADA for constructing buildings to rehouse 672 tenants, hand over earmarked area to MHADA, and construct a free-sale component. The Corporate Debtor took a Rs. 200 Crore term loan from Union Bank of India on 25.03.2011. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Corporate Debtor defaulted on the term loan facility provided by Union Bank of India, with total default amounting to Rs. 254,53,85,278/- as on 30.04.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Flat purchasers filed Bombay High Court Suit No. 40 of 2017 on 20.03.2017. MHADA issued a revocation letter on 24.04.2017 following a stop-work notice issued in 2015. Section 7 petition was filed on 15.05.2017 and admitted on 24.07.2017. MHADA demanded land handover on 12.01.2018 under clause 6.1 of the JDA. RP responded on 15.01.2018 claiming moratorium protection. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint Development Agreement dated 10.04.2008; tripartite agreement dated 09.11.2011; MHADA's stop-work notices and contract termination letters establishing development rights without formal conveyance or transfer of title to the land. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed MA 137 of 2018 before NCLT Mumbai seeking an amendment in MA 96 of 2018 to apply Section 14(1)(d) moratorium against MHADA to restrain land recovery. NCLT Mumbai rejected the application on 02.04.2018. The RP appealed before NCLAT; during appeal pendency, the 270-day CIRP period expired on 19.04.2018.
legal_issues: 1. Whether development rights over third-party/statutory authority land held under a Joint Development Agreement constitute an asset of the Corporate Debtor attracting statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC. 2. Whether an appeal challenging the non-application of Section 14(1)(d) moratorium survives once the maximum statutory CIRP period of 270 days has lapsed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Land handed over to a developer solely for execution of a joint development project without formal transfer or conveyance of proprietary title does not constitute an asset or property of the corporate debtor; hence, the statutory moratorium under Section 14(1)(d) cannot be invoked to prevent the landowning statutory authority from taking back possession upon lawful termination of the development contract. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(d) of the IBC protects properties occupied by or in the possession of the Corporate Debtor, but where contractual rights are purely developmental and not proprietary assets of the Corporate Debtor, third-party statutory landowners cannot be injuncted. Furthermore, once the maximum 270-day CIRP duration expires, the statutory moratorium period ceases to operate, rendering challenges to moratorium application purely academic. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the terms of the Joint Development Agreement to establish whether title and ownership were ever conveyed to the developer or remained vested in the statutory body. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor possessed mere development rights without ownership over MHADA's land, and because the 270-day CIRP period had already lapsed on 19.04.2018, the appeal is devoid of merit and academic.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs. The order dated 02.04.2018 passed by the Adjudicating Authority, NCLT Mumbai Bench, is sustained.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Guruashish Construction Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order refusing to enforce a Section 14(1)(d) moratorium over 40 acres of land belonging to MHADA, which had revoked a 2008 Joint Development Agreement due to project default. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under the Joint Development Agreement, the land was handed over strictly for development without transferring proprietary title or ownership, meaning it did not constitute an asset of the Corporate Debtor under Section 14(1)(d). The Tribunal further noted that since the statutory 270-day CIRP period had already expired, the moratorium had lapsed, making the appeal academic.

case_title: Prowess International Private Limited vs. Action Ispat & Power Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prowess International Private Limited is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; Action Ispat & Power Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying operational transactions involving supply of goods/services for which operational debt was claimed under Section 9 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose out of unpaid operational debt leading to the filing of a Section 9 application before NCLT Principal Bench; specific default amount is not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The impugned judgment was pronounced in open court on 15.03.2017 in the presence of Appellant's counsel. The Appellant applied for a certified copy on 18.08.2017 (after a 5-month gap), which was prepared on 21.08.2017. The appeal was filed on 22.09.2017 after a delay of more than six months without an initial application for condonation of delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Court appearance records of 15.03.2017 establishing presence of Appellant's counsel; filing timeline records and lack of any documented steps or explanation for inaction between 15.03.2017 and 18.08.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, rejected Appellant's Section 9 petition on 15.03.2017. The Appellant filed an appeal before NCLAT on 22.09.2017, later submitting IA No. 292 of 2018 seeking condonation of delay by pleading that limitation should run only from the supply of the certified copy.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the limitation period for filing an appeal before NCLAT under Section 61 of the IBC commences from the date of pronouncement/knowledge of the order or from the date a certified copy is obtained under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. Whether NCLAT has the statutory power to condone a delay beyond 15 days past the initial 30-day period prescribed under the proviso to Section 61(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Limitation for preferring an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is strictly thirty days from the date of knowledge or pronouncement of the order; NCLAT's condonation jurisdiction is strictly capped at an additional fifteen days under the proviso to Section 61(2), and the wider limitation mechanism under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 has no application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(1) operates with a non-obstante clause over the Companies Act, 2013. Unlike Section 421(3) of the Companies Act—where limitation is computed from when a copy is made available—Section 61(2) mandates filing within thirty days of the order/knowledge. Under the proviso to Section 61(2), the Tribunal cannot condone delay beyond fifteen days, making any appeal filed after forty-five days absolute and jurisdictional bar. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of whether the appellant or its counsel had knowledge on the date of open-court pronouncement and computing the total calendar days elapsed up to the date of appeal presentation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had open-court knowledge on 15.03.2017 and failed to provide any reasonable explanation for the five-month delay in applying for a copy; the appeal filed over six months later is barred by limitation.
operative_order: The application for condonation of delay (I.A. No. 292 of 2018) is rejected, and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 223 of 2017 is dismissed as barred by limitation. No costs.
summary: Prowess International Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi rejecting its Section 9 application under the IBC. The impugned judgment was pronounced in open court in the presence of Appellant's counsel on 15.03.2017, but the Appellant applied for a certified copy five months later and filed the appeal on 22.09.2017. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the 30-day limitation runs from the date of knowledge/pronouncement, overriding Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. As the Tribunal's power to condone delay is strictly limited to 15 days, an appeal filed after six months is jurisdictionally barred.

case_title: Mr. Chetan Sharma vs. Rungta Industries (P) Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 66 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 67, 68, 69 & 70 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Chetan Sharma (Director/Shareholder of Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd.) is the Appellant; Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; J.R. Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd., Abhi Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd., Jai Lakshmi Solvents Pvt. Ltd., Arohul Foods Pvt. Ltd., and Rungta Industries Pvt. Ltd. are the Respondents/Operational Creditors; Dinesh Arora is the former Managing Director. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase orders placed by Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd. for supply and delivery of crude rice bran oil, followed by raised commercial invoices. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of operational debts across five creditors: J.R. Agro (Rs. 5,08,43,252/-), Abhi Agro (Rs. 28,59,514/-), Jai Lakshmi Solvents (Rs. 26,40,525/-), Arohul Foods (Rs. 24,75,178/-), and Rungta Industries (Rs. 14,97,879/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In J.R. Agro's case, Section 8(1) demand notice was issued on 18.01.2017 and served on the Corporate Debtor on 23.01.2017. Section 9 petition was filed on 20.02.2017. No reply was sent within ten days; notice of dispute was issued belatedly on 02.03.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance confirmation letter dated 30.11.2015 confirming credit balance of Rs. 5,08,43,252/- in J.R. Agro's ledger; Commercial Tax (Sales Tax) monthly returns filed with the Commercial Tax Department Kanpur showing input tax credit availed on purchases from the operational creditors; internal MoU dated 19.05.2016 between Dinesh Arora and the Sharma group transferring personal liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditors filed CP Nos. 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17/ALD/2017 under Section 9. NCLT Allahabad Bench admitted the petition against Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd. on 30.05.2017/01.06.2017, declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP. Director Chetan Sharma appealed against the admission orders.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an internal Memorandum of Understanding between shareholders/directors transferring debt liabilities to an outgoing Managing Director constitutes a valid novation under Section 62 of the Contract Act binding on third-party operational creditors. 2. Whether an internal dispute among shareholders/directors constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC to warrant dismissal of a Section 9 application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An outstanding trade liability of an incorporated company is an asset in the hands of the creditor that cannot be unilaterally transferred to a third party by the debtor without the creditor's express consent; private inter-se shareholder agreements or internal managerial fraud disputes do not constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC vis-à-vis third-party creditors. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: 'Dispute' under Section 5(6) must strictly exist between the Corporate Debtor and the Operational Creditor prior to the delivery of the Section 8 demand notice. Under Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, novation requires consensus ad idem involving the creditor; an inter-se shareholder agreement cannot absolve the distinct corporate entity from its debt under Section 9 of the Companies Act, 2013, particularly when the company affirmed the transactions by claiming input tax credit in its sales tax filings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of contractual privity, debtor ledger confirmations, and statutory sales tax returns demonstrating receipt of goods and availing of fiscal credits versus belated notices of dispute issued beyond the statutory ten-day window under Section 8(2). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor acknowledged supplies in its tax filings and ledger confirmations; internal fraud allegations against the ex-MD lacked privity with the creditors, and the belated Section 8(2) response did not establish a genuine pre-existing dispute.
operative_order: All connected appeals (Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 66, 67, 68, 69, and 70 of 2017) are dismissed. The NCLT admission and moratorium order is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: Mr. Chetan Sharma, director of Swadisht Oils Pvt. Ltd., appealed the admission of Section 9 CIRP applications filed by five operational creditors who supplied crude rice bran oil. The Appellant argued that the supplies were fraudulently received by an ex-Managing Director who assumed all liabilities via an internal MoU dated 19.05.2016, constituting contract novation and a pre-existing dispute. Dismissing the appeals, NCLAT held that debt liabilities cannot be unilaterally transferred to a third party without the creditor's consent, and internal shareholder disputes do not qualify as a pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) IBC. As the company acknowledged purchases in its tax returns to claim input tax credits, the Section 9 admission was upheld.

case_title: Dr. M.A.S Subramanian & Ors. vs. Mr. T.S. Sivakumar & Ors. (In re Indian Overseas Bank)
appeal_number: Review Application No. 2 of 2018 in Company Appeal (AT) No. 12 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Overseas Bank (Orleanpet Branch, Puducherry) is the Review Applicant/Non-party Secured Lender; Dr. M.A.S. Subramanian & family are Appellants/Original Respondents; T.S. Sivakumar & group are Respondents/Original Petitioners; Hotel Mass Private Limited is the Subject Company; Vee Pee Estate and Hotels Pvt. Ltd. is the Purchaser. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Indian Overseas Bank granted a term loan facility to Vee Pee Estate and Hotels Pvt. Ltd. in 2011 to purchase the property and assets of Hotel Mass Pvt. Ltd., which was secured by creating and perfecting an equitable mortgage over the hotel's property in 2011/2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement action involving fraudulent transfer of 3,15,860 equity shares and sale of prime hotel real estate and assets for Rs. 3,93,80,706/- (with prayer to deposit Rs. 58.50 Crores); mortgage debt extended by the bank was collateral to this transaction. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hotel Mass incorporated in 1982; disputed capital hikes occurred 1998-2003; sale deed executed on 31.10.2011 (registered as Doc No. 1844 of 2013); equitable mortgage created on 06.03.2013; company petition filed in 2014; NCLAT final appeal judgment delivered on 12.07.2018; review application decided on 24.09.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale deed dated 31.10.2011 executed by the Subramanian group in favor of Vee Pee Estate; Board minutes of Vee Pee Estate dated 06.03.2013 creating equitable mortgage in favor of the Bank; absence of any pleadings or records before NCLT or NCLAT regarding the bank loan and mortgage. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In an oppression and mismanagement company petition, NCLAT delivered a final judgment on 12.07.2018 setting aside share transfers and declaring that the sale deed dated 31.10.2011 executed in favor of Vee Pee Estate was not binding on Hotel Mass Pvt. Ltd. Indian Overseas Bank, a non-party secured creditor, filed Review Application No. 2 of 2018 under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking review of the judgment on the ground that it held an equitable mortgage over the property.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a third-party non-party financial institution can maintain an application for 'review' of a final appellate judgment under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 or Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016. 2. Whether facts that were never part of the original record can be introduced to establish an 'error apparent from the record' to review an appellate judgment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of review is not an inherent judicial power and must be expressly conferred by statute; the rectification power under Section 420(2) can be invoked strictly by existing parties to rectify a patent, self-evident error apparent on the face of the record without travelling beyond it, and cannot be invoked by a non-party seeking adjudication of extraneous third-party rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 applies exclusively to 'parties' to the proceeding and is restricted to correcting manifest errors on record; it cannot be converted into an independent review power. Inherent powers under Rule 11 of NCLAT Rules cannot create a substantive right of review that the legislature omitted to provide. An order in an inter-se oppression proceeding declaring an alienation non-binding on the company does not cancel the title deed per se and cannot be reopened on external evidence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of whether the alleged factual error appears on the face of the record without requiring inquiry into extrinsic documents or new claims not originally litigated. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bank was neither a shareholder nor a party to the proceedings, and its mortgage documents were never part of the record; hence, no mistake apparent from the record existed, making the review application non-maintainable.
operative_order: Review Application No. 2 of 2018 is rejected. No order as to costs.
summary: Indian Overseas Bank filed a review application under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 11 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 seeking recall of NCLAT's final judgment in an oppression appeal involving Hotel Mass Pvt. Ltd. The judgment had set aside share transfers and declared a 2011 property sale deed non-binding on the company, impacting the Bank's equitable mortgage over the property. Rejecting the application, NCLAT held that review is not an inherent power and Section 420(2) is available only to existing parties to rectify manifest errors on the record. Since the mortgage claims were never part of the record, a third party cannot seek review on extrinsic facts.

case_title: Sudhir Sales & Services Ltd. vs. D-Art Furniture Systems Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sudhir Sales & Services Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor; D-Art Furniture Systems Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor; ESAJV D-Art India Pvt. Ltd. and Commonwealth Games Organising Committee are third parties. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Turnkey rental contract for diesel generator (DG) sets, including supply, installation, maintenance, and removal for the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi, initially valued at Rs. 1,62,49,360/- and later enhanced on 02.09.2010 to Rs. 1,93,20,620/- for 58 DG sets. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total invoices raised were Rs. 2,89,41,684/-, adjusted by credit notes of Rs. 28,65,776/- to a net invoice amount of Rs. 2,60,75,908/-. The Corporate Debtor paid Rs. 1,99,05,742/-, leaving an unpaid principal default of Rs. 56,37,899/- (plus Rs. 5,32,262/- TDS deposited later). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Letter acknowledging debt sent by Corporate Debtor on 13.11.2013. Statutory winding-up notice under Companies Act, 1956 sent on 13.04.2016. High Court winding-up petition transferred to NCLT on 15.02.2017 and withdrawn on 27.11.2017 with liberty to file under IBC. Section 8 demand notice issued on 20.12.2017; Section 9 petition filed on 24.01.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's letter dated 13.11.2013 admitting the claim of Rs. 56,37,899/- subject only to back-to-back receipt of funds from its client/arbitration with the Games Organising Committee; Section 8(2) reply dated 09.09.2017 alleging defective DG sets and unauthorized diesel invoices for the first time. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed CP No. (IB) 94 (PB)/2018 under Section 9. NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench dismissed the petition on 24.04.2018, holding that the letter dated 13.11.2013 and reply dated 09.09.2017 disclosed a pre-existing dispute. The Operational Creditor appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a debtor's letter acknowledging liability while conditioning payment on back-to-back realization of funds from a third party or pending third-party arbitration constitutes a 'pre-existing dispute' under Section 5(6) of the IBC. 2. Whether quality and invoicing disputes raised for the first time in response to a Section 8(1) demand notice can be treated as a valid pre-existing dispute.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pre-existing dispute under Section 5(6) of the IBC must genuinely exist between the operational creditor and the corporate debtor prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice; disputes raised as an afterthought for the very first time in reply to a statutory demand notice or reliance on third-party arbitration do not constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 8(2) and Section 9 in terms of the tests in *Mobilox* and *Innoventive*, the dispute must be pre-existing, non-illusory, and supported by tangible evidence. An admission of liability where payment is deferred solely due to a pay-when-paid arrangement involving a third-party arbitration does not negate the existence of a due and payable operational debt between the contracting parties. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of chronological communications between the parties to verify whether objections regarding defective equipment or invoices were recorded prior to the Section 8 notice or raised subsequently as an afterthought. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor's 2013 letter admitted debt without complaining of quality or pricing, and the dispute raised in the Section 8 reply dated 09.09.2017 was an afterthought; no valid pre-existing dispute existed.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 24.04.2018 passed by NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi in CP No. (IB) 94 (PB)/2018 is set aside. The matter is remitted to the Adjudicating Authority with directions to admit the Section 9 application in the absence of any defect, with liberty to the parties to settle the claim prior to formal admission. No order as to costs.
summary: Sudhir Sales & Services Ltd. appealed an order of NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi rejecting its Section 9 IBC application against D-Art Furniture Systems Pvt. Ltd. for an unpaid balance of Rs. 56,37,899/- arising from rental of generator sets for the 2010 Commonwealth Games. NCLT held the debt was subject to a pre-existing dispute based on a 2013 letter citing pending third-party arbitration and the Corporate Debtor's reply to the Section 8 notice. Allowing the appeal, the NCLAT ruled that deferring payment due to third-party claims is not an operational dispute, and defenses regarding equipment quality raised for the first time in reply to a Section 8 notice are spurious afterthoughts. The case was remitted for admission under Section 9.

case_title: Gaja Trustee Company Private Limited & Ors. vs. Haldia Coke and Chemicals Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gaja Trustee Company Private Limited and others are the Appellants/Shareholders (holding a 32% equity stake); Haldia Coke and Chemicals Private Limited is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor; Sh. M. Natarajan, CEO, was the authorized person on behalf of the Board of Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Share Subscription and Shareholders' Agreement dated 31.05.2010 executed between the Appellants and the Respondent Company, pursuant to which Appellants invested Rs. 125 Crores, and the Articles of Association (AoA) were amended to embed Affirmative Vote Matters. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under commercial and financial debt obligations under Section 3(12) of the IBC; specific numerical debt figures are not itemized in the appellate judgment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Board of Directors passed a resolution on 13.05.2017 authorizing the CEO to initiate CIRP. The Section 10 application was subsequently admitted by NCLT Chennai Bench on 11.07.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles of Association, particularly Article 1.1.3 (specifying liquidation, dissolution, or winding up as Affirmative Vote Matters), Article 9.1 (requiring prior written consent of investors), and Article 9.2 (requiring decisions to be taken exclusively in a general meeting). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Corporate Debtor filed CP No. 509/(IB)/CB/2017 under Section 10 based solely on the Board resolution without obtaining approval of shareholders in an Extraordinary General Meeting (EoGM). NCLT Chennai Bench admitted the application on 11.07.2017 and appointed an IRP. Aggrieved minority shareholders appealed before NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Board of Directors has the independent power under Section 179 of the Companies Act, 2013 to file an application under Section 10 of the IBC without placing the proposal before the shareholders in an Extraordinary General Meeting (EoGM). 2. Whether a Section 10 filing initiated by the Board of Directors in contravention of affirmative voting and general meeting covenants of the Articles of Association is valid and maintainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Board of Directors of a corporate entity is not competent to voluntarily initiate corporate insolvency resolution proceedings against the company under Section 10 of the IBC without prior authorization or approval from shareholders in a general meeting, especially where the company's Articles of Association place explicit internal governance fetters on corporate dissolution and winding up. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 179(1) and (4) of the Companies Act, 2013 subjects the Board's powers to restrictions contained in the Articles of Association and decisions reserved for general meetings; Section 179(3) does not grant the Board unilateral authority to file for insolvency that could potentially terminate the company's existence via liquidation, distinguishing Section 10 from creditor-led actions under Section 7 or 9. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of corporate constitutional documents (Articles of Association) and corporate governance agreements to assess contractual limitations, negative covenants, and voting requirements restricting managerial authority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 10 petition filed pursuant to a mere Board resolution without EoGM shareholder approval was ultra vires the Articles of Association and not maintainable.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 11.07.2017 passed by NCLT Chennai Bench in CP No. 509/(IB)/CB/2017 is set aside[cite: 6]. The appointment of the IRP, order of moratorium, account freezing, and all consequential actions taken by the IRP are declared illegal and set aside[cite: 6]. The Section 10 application is dismissed, the Corporate Debtor is released from all rigors of the IBC to function independently through its Board of Directors, and NCLT is directed to determine the IRP's fee payable by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. No costs[cite: 6].
summary: Shareholders holding a 32% equity stake appealed an NCLT Chennai order admitting a voluntary Section 10 CIRP application filed by the Board of Directors of Haldia Coke and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 6] Appellants contended that under the company's Articles of Association, winding-up or insolvency required prior investor consent and approval in an Extraordinary General Meeting[cite: 6]. Allowing the appeal, NCLAT held that Section 179 of the Companies Act limits Board powers to provisions in the Articles of Association[cite: 6]. The Board cannot unilaterally trigger Section 10 IBC without shareholder approval in an EoGM, rendering the admission order, moratorium, and appointment of the IRP illegal and non-est[cite: 6].

case_title: Peoples General Hospital Pvt. Ltd. vs. Alliance Industries Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 105 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 107, 108, 110, 111 & 112 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Peoples General Hospital Pvt. Ltd. and Suresh Narayan Vijay are Appellants; Alliance Industries Limited and Ashok Kumar Khosla are Respondents/Original Petitioners. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate equity holdings, fund diversion to trusts, and failed share buy-back arrangements within Peoples Group companies leading to an oppression and mismanagement company petition. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement dispute regarding alleged illegal diversion of investments and buyback of shares occurring between 2001 and 2006, continuing through failed settlement negotiations up to 2014-2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Diversion and share events arose 2001-2006; settlement talks occurred on 10.10.2013, 26.03.2014, 23.06.2014, and 05.04.2016. The original company petition under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956 was filed on 08.01.2015. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Chronology of inter-party correspondence, settlement meeting minutes, and requisition notice for EoGM in 2014 relied upon by the petitioners to plead continuous oppression and refute claims of laches. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Transferred petition TP 120/2016 pending before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. Appellants filed IA 16/2016 seeking dismissal of the petition on grounds of delay, laches, and limitation. By order dated 29.05.2017, NCLT dismissed IA 16/2016, holding limitation to be a mixed question of fact and law reserved for final hearing. Appellants did not appeal that order, but filed IA 259/2017 under Section 420(2) seeking review/recall of the 29.05.2017 order. On 16.02.2018, NCLT dismissed the application for lack of review jurisdiction, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the National Company Law Tribunal has the statutory or inherent power to review or recall its own substantive orders under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 or Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016. 2. Whether the omission to discuss specific precedents cited in written submissions concerning limitation and laches constitutes a 'mistake apparent from the record' rectifiable under Section 420(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of judicial review is not an inherent power and must be expressly conferred by statute; the rectification jurisdiction of a tribunal under Section 420(2) is strictly confined to patent, manifest, and self-evident errors apparent on the face of the record without requiring elaborate arguments, and does not permit a rehearing or reconsideration of substantive determinations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 empowers the Tribunal only to rectify a 'mistake apparent from the record' within two years; it does not confer a power of review. Non-consideration or non-discussion of judicial authorities cited by a party on an issue involving mixed questions of law and fact (such as limitation and delay/laches) cannot be equated with an error apparent on the face of the record. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Distinction between patent, clerical, or self-evident errors striking on mere inspection versus complex points requiring a long-drawn process of reasoning where two opinions are conceivably possible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application was an impermissible review petition in the garb of rectification; NCLT rightly declined to review its order dated 29.05.2017.
operative_order: All connected Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 105, 107, 108, 110, 111, and 112 of 2018 are dismissed[cite: 7]. Each appeal is dismissed with costs quantified at Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh only) to be paid by the respective Appellants to the State through the Ministry of Corporate Affairs[cite: 7].
summary: Appellants challenged an order of the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissing their applications under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which sought the recall/review of an earlier order refusing to dismiss an oppression petition on grounds of limitation and laches[cite: 7]. The Appellants contended that failure by the Tribunal to discuss their cited precedents constituted an error apparent on the face of the record[cite: 7]. Dismissing the appeals with costs of Rs. 1 lakh per appeal, the NCLAT held that the power of review is not an inherent power and is absent under Section 420(2)[cite: 7]. Non-discussion of fact-dependent case law does not amount to a manifest error rectifiable under the statute[cite: 7].

case_title: Thota Gurunath Reddy & Ors. vs. Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Thota Gurunath Reddy, an individual promoter-shareholder, along with Paradigm Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (holding 47.88% total equity) are Appellants/Petitioners; Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1; Gleneagles Development Pte. Ltd. (Singapore company holding 51% majority equity) is Respondent No. 2. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Share Purchase Agreement, Share Subscription Agreement, and Shareholders' Agreement all dated 18.02.2015, under which Respondent No. 2 acquired 51% control of Respondent No. 1 for an aggregate consideration of Rs. 293 Crores (Rs. 170 Crores for secondary purchase and Rs. 123 Crores subscription). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Oppression and mismanagement action alleging fund diversion, excessive commissions to overseas associates (Parkway Group), suppression of hospital operations, and attempting to force share dilution via a Rs. 29 Crore working capital call. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Agreements executed on 18.02.2015; board meeting proposing Rs. 29 Crore capital call held on 26.08.2016; company petition filed in 2016; reference order passed by NCLT on 20.04.2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Share Purchase and Shareholders' Agreements containing international arbitration dispute resolution clauses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 19/241/HDB/2016 before NCLT Hyderabad Bench under Sections 241-244 of the Companies Act, 2013. Respondent No. 2 filed CA No. 51 of 2016 under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to refer parties to international arbitration. By order dated 20.04.2017, NCLT, sitting as a judicial authority, referred the parties to arbitration. Appellants challenged this reference by preferring an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 before NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. Whether an appeal lies before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 against an order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal acting as a 'judicial authority' referring parties to arbitration under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 2. Whether statutory appeals under Section 421 of the Companies Act are barred when an order is governed by the exhaustive, self-contained provisions of Section 50 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an adjudicatory forum exercises jurisdiction as a 'judicial authority' under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the right and forum of appeal must be traced solely from within the Arbitration Act itself; general appellate provisions in the statute constituting the tribunal cannot be invoked to bypass the statutory bar against appeals under Section 50 of the Arbitration Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 50 of the Arbitration Act is exhaustive and forms a self-contained code allowing appeals only against orders *refusing* to refer parties to arbitration under Section 45; an order that *refers* parties to arbitration is non-appealable. Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 applies exclusively to orders passed by the NCLT in its capacity as a 'Tribunal' under the Companies Act, not when functioning as a judicial authority under the Arbitration Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Determination of the source of adjudicatory power under which the impugned order was passed to establish subject-matter appellate maintainability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order referring the dispute to arbitration was made under Section 45 of the Arbitration Act, 1996; hence, the appeal filed under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 is fundamentally not maintainable.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Appellants filed an oppression and mismanagement petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 against Continental Hospitals Pvt. Ltd. and its majority Singapore shareholder, Gleneagles Development Pte. Ltd.[cite: 8] The NCLT Hyderabad Bench, acting on an application under Section 45 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, referred the parties to international arbitration pursuant to agreements[cite: 8]. Appellants challenged this order before NCLAT under Section 421 of the Companies Act[cite: 8]. Dismissing the appeal as not maintainable, NCLAT held that an order passed by the Tribunal acting as a 'judicial authority' under Section 45 is governed exclusively by Section 50 of the Arbitration Act, which bars appeals against orders referring parties to arbitration[cite: 8].

case_title: GMB Ceramics Ltd. vs. Spartek Ceramics India Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 258 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 160 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pr. Director General of Income Tax and GMB Ceramics Ltd. are Appellants/Creditors; Spartek Ceramics India Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Sick Company/Demerged Company; Neycer is a connected entity. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Modified Rehabilitation Scheme and demerger scheme formulated under SICA restructuring Neycer and Spartek Ceramics, involving unsecured loan funding to clear creditor liabilities. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in respect of unabsorbed income tax losses to the extent of Rs. 77.12 Crores, anticipated capital gains tax revenue loss, and unpaid commercial creditor dues owed to GMB Ceramics Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demerger scheme sanctioned by BIFR on 20.10.2016. SICA was repealed and SICA Repeal Act, 2003 was notified w.e.f. 01.12.2016. Central Government issued Notification S.O. 1683(E) (Removal of Difficulties Order, 2017) on 24.05.2017 providing a 90-day window to appeal deemed resolution plans before NCLAT. Appeals lodged in 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanctioned demerger scheme dated 20.10.2016 passed in BIFR Case No. 63/2006, granting tax exemptions and restructuring liabilities without consent of the Income Tax department. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Aggrieved by the BIFR scheme dated 20.10.2016, appeals pending before AAIFR abated upon SICA repeal on 01.12.2016. Relying on the Central Government Removal of Difficulties Order dated 24.05.2017 (treating sanctioned BIFR schemes as approved resolution plans under Section 31(1) of the IBC), Appellants directly approached NCLAT under Section 61 read with Section 32 of the IBC.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Central Government, via an executive order under Section 242 of the IBC, can confer appellate jurisdiction upon the NCLAT to hear appeals against BIFR orders by amending the Eighth Schedule to the IBC. 2. Whether an executive notification granting 90 days to appeal can override the mandatory limitation period of 30 days (plus 15 days condonable) prescribed under Section 61(2) of the IBC. 3. Whether a BIFR demerger scheme sanctioned prior to the enactment of the IBC can be legally treated as an approved Resolution Plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory appellate jurisdiction and periods of limitation cannot be created, expanded, or altered by executive orders under a 'removal of difficulties' clause; an executive order that introduces provisions in conflict with substantive legislative enactments is ultra vires and invalid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 of the IBC restricts the Central Government to removing difficulties in giving effect to the provisions of the IBC itself; it does not authorize the executive to revive abated SICA proceedings, amend the substantive terms of the Eighth Schedule, or alter Section 61(2) limitation limits. Section 61(2) provides a strict 30-day period extendable by at most 15 days, leaving NCLAT without jurisdiction to entertain appeals beyond 45 days. Furthermore, a BIFR scheme never approved by a Committee of Creditors under Section 30(4) cannot be deemed an approved resolution plan under Section 31(1). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison between statutory limitation mandates and executive modifications, and examination of whether the scheme complied with mandatory CIRP approval procedures under Section 30 of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals against the BIFR scheme are barred by limitation and not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC.
operative_order: Both appeals are dismissed as barred by limitation and not maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 9]. The impugned scheme dated 20.10.2016 is noted to be illegal as it contravened the law and lacked CoC approval under Section 30(4), but cannot be formally set aside for want of jurisdiction[cite: 9]. Parties are left to raise objections before any court where implementation may be sought[cite: 9]. No order as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: The Income Tax Department and GMB Ceramics appealed to NCLAT against a BIFR demerger scheme dated 20.10.2016 sanctioned under SICA, invoking Central Government Notification S.O. 1683(E) dated 24.05.2017 (issued under Section 242 IBC), which treated BIFR schemes as approved resolution plans under Section 31(1) IBC and allowed 90 days to appeal[cite: 9]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that executive removal-of-difficulty orders cannot alter substantive law or override the mandatory 30+15 day limitation limit under Section 61(2) IBC[cite: 9]. The Tribunal declared that it lacked jurisdiction to entertain the time-barred appeals, observing additionally that BIFR schemes lacking CoC approval cannot constitute valid resolution plans[cite: 9].

case_title: Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs vs. Gitanjali Gems Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 103 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 119 & 124 to 133 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Union of India (Ministry of Corporate Affairs) is the Petitioner/Appellant; Gitanjali Gems Ltd. (promoted by Mehul Choksi), Firestar International Ltd., Firestar Diamond International Pvt. Ltd., Diamond R US, Solar Exports, Stellar Diamonds (promoted by Nirav Modi), along with their partners, directors, key managerial personnel, and connected family trusts are Respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore diamond export and trading operations underpinned by fraudulent LoUs (Letters of Undertaking) and Foreign Letters of Credit (FLCs) obtained from Punjab National Bank without credit limits. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive bank fraud exceeding Rs. 11,400 Crores (escalating beyond Rs. 14,000 Crores), causing wrongful loss to Punjab National Bank through unauthorized overseas SWIFT transactions and Buyer's Credit disbursements. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: PNB registered CBI FIRs on 31.01.2018 and 15.02.2018. MCA directed SFIO investigation on 17.02.2018 under Section 212. MCA filed CP No. 277/2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench; ex-parte asset restraint order passed on 23.02.2018; modification order vacating restraints on certain independent directors passed on 02.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CBI FIRs detailing fraudulent bypassing of PNB's Core Banking System (CBS) using manipulated SWIFT messages, property schedules showing extensive corporate/personal assets, and SFIO ongoing probe records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: MCA filed CP 277/2018 under Sections 221, 222, 241, 242, 246 r/w 339 alleging prejudice to public interest. NCLT Mumbai Bench granted an interim order on 23.02.2018 freezing assets of all respondent entities, LLPs, trusts, and directors/individuals. On 02.04.2018, NCLT vacated the restraint entirely against five directors/professionals (Sujal Shah, Gopal Krishnan Nair, Suresh Senapathy, Gautam Mukkavilli, and Sanjay Rishi) and partially modified it for others. MCA appealed the exoneration, while individual directors appealed the freeze orders.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 241(2), 246, 339, and 340 of the Companies Act, 2013 to freeze personal assets of directors, partners, trusts, and individuals during an ongoing SFIO investigation into corporate fraud prejudicial to public interest. 2. Whether the Tribunal can exonerate or vacate interim restraint orders against individual directors prior to the conclusion and submission of the SFIO investigation report.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In proceedings initiated in public interest concerning systemic corporate fraud, the Tribunal possesses plenary interim powers under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 246, 339, and 340 to freeze the assets of companies, LLPs, and associated individuals/directors to prevent alienation of assets, and cannot grant premature exonerations while statutory investigations are actively underway. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 241(2) read with Section 242 empowers the Tribunal to pass comprehensive orders to protect the public interest; incorporating Sections 339, 340, and 341 mutatis mutandis through Section 246 extends liability and interim injunctive power across individuals, officers, and connected firms. Section 221 read with Section 242(4) cannot be restricted merely to corporate assets when fraudulent diversion of public money to individual accounts/trusts is prima facie evident. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of a prima facie case of large-scale financial fraud, public interest endangerment, and the necessity to preserve assets pending a comprehensive forensic investigation report by the SFIO. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The complete vacation of the freeze against five directors was premature and impermissible before receipt of the SFIO report; however, reasonable monthly allowances for personal subsistence should be permitted to all affected individuals.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 103 and 119 of 2018 are allowed; Company Appeals (AT) Nos. 124 to 133 of 2018 are disposed of[cite: 10]. The NCLT order dated 02.04.2018 exonerating and vacating restraint on Respondents 43, 44, 51, 52, and 53 is set aside[cite: 10]. All named Appellants and Respondents are permitted to withdraw a subsistence allowance of Rs. 1,00,000/- per month from their bank accounts (Rs. 2,00,000/- for Respondent No. 35)[cite: 10]. The blanket restraint order dated 23.02.2018 against removal, transfer, or disposal of funds, assets, and properties shall continue until further orders[cite: 10]. No costs[cite: 10].
summary: The Ministry of Corporate Affairs filed a petition under Sections 241-242 read with Section 221 and 339 of the Companies Act, 2013, concerning the Rs. 11,400+ Crore PNB fraud orchestrated via Nirav Modi and Mehul Choksi entities[cite: 10]. NCLT Mumbai initially froze the personal and corporate assets of all involved companies, trusts, and directors[cite: 10], but subsequently vacated the freeze for five professional/independent directors[cite: 10]. Setting aside the vacation order, the NCLAT ruled that under Section 242(4) read with Sections 221, 339, and 340, the Tribunal has ample jurisdiction to freeze individual assets in public-interest fraud cases and cannot exonerate respondents prior to the submission of the SFIO investigation report[cite: 10]. The freeze was reinstated with a Rs. 1,00,000 monthly subsistence allowance[cite: 10].

case_title: Export Import Bank of India vs. Resolution Professional, JEKPL Private Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 304 of 2017 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 16 of 2018 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 302 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: In CA 304/2017 & 16/2018, Export Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank) is the Claimant/Financial Creditor; JEKPL Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Counter Corporate Guarantor; Jubilant Enpro Private Limited (JEPL) is the Corporate Guarantor; and Jubilant Energy N.V. (JENV, Netherlands) is the Principal Borrower. In CA 302/2017, Axis Bank Limited is the Claimant/Financial Creditor, Edu Smart Services Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor, and Educomp Solutions Limited is the Principal Borrower. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: EXIM Bank disbursed a Dollar Loan facility of USD 50 Million to JENV sanctioned on 13.04.2011/18.05.2011, secured by a Corporate Guarantee from JEPL and a Counter Corporate Guarantee/Supplementary Guarantee executed by JEKPL on 01.08.2011. In Axis Bank's case, a Master Restructuring Agreement dated 25.03.2014 and Corporate Guarantee dated 03.06.2015 were executed by Edu Smart in favor of SBICAP Trustee for consortium lenders. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JENV's loan account was classified as NPA on 17.05.2016 (JEHNV on 01.05.2016). For Axis Bank, default arose from credit facilities aggregating to a verified/claimed default amount of Rs. 396,76,07,676.68. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: EXIM Bank recalled JENV's loan facilities on 30.03.2017 and invoked both the Corporate Guarantee and Counter Corporate Guarantee via letters dated 30.03.2017. In Axis Bank's case, public announcements inviting claims were issued on 27.06.2017; claims were lodged in Form C on 22.07.2017 and updated on 11.08.2017 without formal prior guarantee invocation. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deeds of Guarantee and Counter Guarantee dated 01.08.2011 stipulating joint and several liability as principal debtors; JEKPL's Annual Report for FY 2016-17 admitting corporate guarantee liabilities; and the Master Restructuring Agreement and Corporate Guarantee dated 03.06.2015 treating the guarantor as principal debtor under Clause 12. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: JEKPL initiated voluntary CIRP under Section 10 (CP No. 24/ALD/2017). The RP rejected EXIM Bank's claim on 04.08.2017, and NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed EXIM's Section 60(5) application on 27.11.2017 (CA 159/2017) and approved the resolution plan on 15.12.2017 (CA 223/2017). In Edu Smart's Section 7 CIRP (CP IB-102(PB)/2017 initiated by DBS Bank), NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi dismissed Axis Bank's Section 60(5) application on 27.10.2017, holding the claim contingent since the guarantee was not invoked prior to CIRP commencement.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a creditor holding a Counter Corporate Guarantee or uninvoked Corporate Guarantee qualifies as a Financial Creditor under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8)(h) of the IBC. 2. Whether the invocation or maturity of a corporate guarantee is a mandatory prerequisite for a creditor to lodge a claim or be inducted into the Committee of Creditors.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor holding a guarantee or counter-guarantee obligation backed by underlying financial debt disbursed for the time value of money is a financial creditor; the right to file and collate a claim under the IBC encompasses matured, unmatured, or contingent claims, meaning formal pre-CIRP invocation of a guarantee is not a condition precedent for participating as a financial creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(h) read with Section 5(7) includes counter-indemnity and guarantee obligations arising from borrowings where money is disbursed against consideration for the time value of money, and does not restrict counter-indemnity instruments solely to those issued by banks. Further, 'claim' under Section 3(6) encompasses rights to payment whether matured, unmatured, fixed, or contingent, which does not require an existing 'default' under Section 3(12) as a threshold for claim collation under Section 18(1)(b) or 25(2)(e). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the underlying contracts (Guarantee Deeds, Counter Corporate Guarantee Deeds, and Loan Restructuring Agreements) to verify whether terms bind the guarantor jointly and severally as a principal debtor and whether the debt arose from financial disbursements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: EXIM Bank and Axis Bank are Financial Creditors under Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8); their exclusion from the Committee of Creditors was illegal, invalidating any resolution plan approved in their absence without fresh CoC consideration.
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 27.11.2017 and 15.12.2017 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench, and the order dated 27.10.2017 passed by NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench are set aside.
