Resolution Professionals and Adjudicating Authorities are directed to treat EXIM Bank and Axis Bank as Financial Creditors and members of their respective Committees of Creditors, convene fresh meetings of the CoC to reconsider compliant resolution plans under Section 30(2) without rebidding, with no order as to costs.
summary: Export Import Bank of India and Axis Bank challenged NCLT orders upholding the rejection of their claims as financial debts and their exclusion from Committees of Creditors. EXIM Bank held a Counter Corporate Guarantee from JEKPL Pvt. Ltd., while Axis Bank held an uninvoked Corporate Guarantee from Edu Smart Services Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT allowed the appeals, establishing that counter-guarantees fall within financial debt under Section 5(8)(h) and that claim submission under Section 3(6) encompasses unmatured and contingent debts. The Appellate Tribunal ruled that pre-CIRP invocation of a guarantee is unnecessary for CoC inclusion and directed both banks to be inducted into their respective CoCs to reconsider resolution plans.

case_title: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Financial Creditor; Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. is Respondent No. 1/Corporate Debtor; Mohd. Sabir Parvez (Director of Corporate Debtor) is Respondent No. 2; and Mr. M.L. Jain is Respondent No. 3/Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying financial debt obligations leading to initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under Section 7 insolvency proceedings in CP (IB) No. 97/7/HDB/2017; exact quantified sum of default is not detailed in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition was admitted on 11.08.2017, with certified order copy made available on 21.08.2017; IRP took charge and CoC was constituted by 15.09.2017. Litigation intervened between 15.09.2017 and 28.02.2018. The statutory 180-day and 270-day CIRP timelines were imminent when CA 93/2018 was filed. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Interlocutory timeline records establishing that out of the initial 270 days, approximately 166 days were lost solely due to interim stay orders of NCLT in CA No. 197/2017 (challenging CoC constitution) and the replacement of the Resolution Professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CIRP was initiated on 11.08.2017 by NCLT Hyderabad Bench. NCLT granted an interim stay on CoC proceedings on 15.09.2017, which was vacated on 28.02.2018. Upon an application for extension (CA No. 93 of 2018), NCLT Hyderabad passed an interim order on 27.04.2018 merely extending CIRP till 15.05.2018 instead of excluding the litigated stay period, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: 1. Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal has the statutory power to exclude the period lost during judicial stays or unforeseen procedural impediments when calculating the 180/270-day CIRP timeline under Section 12 of the IBC. 2. Whether the 166-day period during which CoC meetings were stayed by the NCLT should be excluded from the corporate insolvency resolution process timeline.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal possesses equitable authority to exclude time lost due to unforeseen litigation hurdles, judicial stays, or vacancy in the office of the Resolution Professional from the statutory CIRP period under Section 12, ensuring the corporate debtor is afforded a viable resolution opportunity before resorting to liquidation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 must be construed purposively to prevent premature liquidation; periods during which CIRP is effectively rendered inoperative through court-mandated injunctions or administrative paralysis do not count toward the substantive 180/270-day statutory duration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the chronological case record and court orders demonstrating an absolute freeze or total impossibility of proceeding with CIRP activities, such as an interim judicial stay restraining CoC meetings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 166 days consumed between 15.09.2017 and 28.02.2018 due to the NCLT's interim stay order must be excluded from the computation of the 270 days, and the CIRP timeline is extended accordingly.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 27.04.2018 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench in CA No. 93/2018 is modified. The period of 166 days is excluded from the CIRP timeline, and the Resolution Professional and Committee of Creditors are granted 166 additional days effective immediately from 08.05.2018 to conclude the CIRP. Appeal disposed of.
summary: Quinn Logistics India Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an interim order of the NCLT Hyderabad Bench that merely granted a brief extension of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Mack Soft Tech Pvt. Ltd. instead of excluding the period during which proceedings were judicially stalled. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and formulated the definitive rule that judicial stay periods, RP vacancy, or litigation delays beyond parties' control can be excluded from calculating the 180/270 days under Section 12 of the IBC. The Tribunal directed the exclusion of 166 days and granted an equivalent period from the date of the order to complete the CIRP.

case_title: Numetal Limited vs. Satish Kumar Gupta & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 169 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 207, 171, 172 & 173 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Standard Chartered Bank and State Bank of India are Financial Creditors; Essar Steel India Limited (ESIL) is the Corporate Debtor (promoted by Mr. Ravi Ruia); Satish Kumar Gupta is the Resolution Professional; Numetal Limited and ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. (AM India) are competing Resolution Applicants. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-crore consortium banking credit facilities extended to ESIL, which defaulted, leading to Section 7 insolvency admission. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amounted to tens of thousands of crores of NPA debt owed by ESIL. Connected NPAs included Uttam Galva and KSS Petron, having aggregate NPA debts of approximately Rs. 7,000 Crores as on 31.03.2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 02.08.2017. EOI invited on 06.10.2017; AM India submitted EOI on 11.10.2017 and Numetal on 20.10.2017. Section 29A was inserted via Ordinance on 23.11.2017. First resolution plans were submitted on 12.02.2018; fresh/second round plans submitted on 29.03.2018 / 02.04.2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: On 12.02.2018, Numetal held 25% shares via Aurora Enterprises Ltd. (AEL), 100% owned by Mr. Rewant Ruia (son of promoter Ravi Ruia). AEL divested its 25% shareholding completely on 29.03.2018 to Crinium Bay (VTB), INDO, and TPE. AM India's connected entity, AM Netherlands, held 29.05% shares and co-promoter status in Uttam Galva (NPA > 1 year) and Fraseli/Mittal Investments held management/affirmative control in KSS Global/KSS Petron (NPA). AM Netherlands and Fraseli divested shareholdings in Uttam Galva and KSS Global on 07.02.2018 and 09.02.2018 without paying overdue amounts, placing Rs. 7,000 Crores conditionally in an escrow account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP disqualified both applicants on 12.02.2018 under Section 29A(c) and (h). In Section 60(5) applications, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 19.04.2018 confirmed ineligibility of both under Section 29A but remanded to CoC under the second proviso to Section 30(4) to permit AM India 30 days to pay overdue NPA amounts. Both parties appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: 1. How is the expression 'person acting in concert' under Section 29A of the IBC to be defined, and was Numetal ineligible as of 12.02.2018 and 29.03.2018? 2. Can a resolution applicant cure disqualification under Section 29A(c) by merely divesting shareholding/control in an NPA company prior to plan submission without clearing all overdue amounts under the proviso to Section 29A(c)?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of an explicit definition in the IBC or statutes listed in Section 3(37), Regulation 2(1)(q) of SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011 applies to define 'person acting in concert'; ineligibility under Section 29A(c) attaches as a statutory stigma once an account is classified as NPA for over a year, which can be cured exclusively by paying all overdue amounts and charges under its proviso, and not through eleventh-hour divestment of shares. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A is remedial to purge corporate defaults. Regulation 2(1)(q) has statutory force under SEBI Act Section 30/31. Under Section 29A(c) read with the second proviso to Section 30(4), an applicant who submitted an EOI (first stage of a plan) prior to the 23.11.2017 amendment must be given an opportunity to clear overdues; divestment alone does not wash away the statutory disability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Piercing corporate holding structures and examining shareholding records, voting arrangements, and familial links to determine beneficial ownership, joint action, and exercise of control over NPA companies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Numetal was ineligible on 12.02.2018 due to AEL's shareholding, but became eligible on 29.03.2018 upon complete exit of AEL. AM India was ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to promoter/control status in Uttam Galva and KSS Petron, which could only be purged by direct payment of overdue amounts, not conditional escrow deposits.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19.04.2018 regarding Numetal's ineligibility as of 29.03.2018 is set aside; Numetal's plan dated 29.03.2018 is declared eligible for CoC consideration. AM India is granted three days (until 11.09.2018) to unconditionally pay all overdue amounts with interest in the accounts of Uttam Galva and KSS Petron. If paid, the CoC shall consider AM India's plan alongside Numetal's. The period from 26.04.2018 to 07.09.2018 spent in appeal is excluded from the 270-day CIRP period. Appeals disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: In the corporate insolvency of Essar Steel India Ltd., the Resolution Professional disqualified Numetal Ltd. and ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the IBC. NCLAT held that 'persons acting in concert' under Section 29A is governed by Regulation 2(1)(q) of SEBI SAST Regulations, 2011. Numetal was ineligible during the first bid due to shareholding by the promoter's son's firm (AEL), but became eligible for its second bid on 29.03.2018 after AEL's exit. ArcelorMittal was held ineligible under Section 29A(c) due to promoter and controlling stakes in NPA entities (Uttam Galva and KSS Petron), ruling that share divestment without paying overdue amounts does not cure Section 29A(c) disqualification, granting three days to clear all overdue debts.

case_title: Binani Industries Limited vs. Bank of Baroda & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 82 of 2018 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 123, 188, 216 & 234 of 2018
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of Baroda is the Financial Creditor; Binani Cement Limited (BCL) is the Corporate Debtor; Binani Industries Limited (BIL) is the promoter/holding company of BCL; Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL, an UltraTech competitor) and UltraTech Cement Limited are Resolution Applicants; Vijay Kumar Iyer is the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multi-bank credit facilities and corporate guarantees extended to Binani Cement Limited, which experienced systemic debt servicing failure. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Aggregate verified claims totaled Rs. 7,289.05 Crores, comprising direct financial debts, corporate guarantee exposures, and operational debts. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated in 2017 (CP (IB) No. 359/KB/2017). Resolution plans submitted on 12.02.2018. RPPL submitted a revised offer on 07.03.2018; UltraTech submitted a revised offer on 08.03.2018. CoC approved RPPL's plan on 14.03.2018. On 28.05.2018, in its 17th meeting following NCLT directions, CoC unanimously approved UltraTech's plan with 100% voting share. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RPPL's plan offered Rs. 6,932.46 Crores total, providing 100% payment to direct financial creditors, but discriminating against corporate guarantee financial creditors (EXIM Bank given 72.59%, SBI Hong Kong 10%) and allocating only 35% (Rs. 151 Crores out of Rs. 443.23 Crores) to unrelated operational creditors and 0% to related operational creditors. UltraTech's plan offered Rs. 7,950.34 Crores (including Rs. 2,427 Crores offer, Rs. 350 Crores working capital, and 100% payment to all financial creditors and unrelated operational creditors plus 10% interest). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC initially approved RPPL's plan on 14.03.2018. Objections were filed by BIL, UltraTech, and operational creditors. By order dated 02.05.2018, NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected RPPL's plan as discriminatory and directed CoC to consider UltraTech's plan. BIL sought termination of CIRP by offering to settle under Section 12A, which NCLT rejected. RPPL and BIL appealed to NCLAT; RP appealed against adverse remarks.
legal_issues: 1. Whether a resolution plan that discriminates between financial creditors similarly situated (direct exposure vs. corporate guarantee beneficiaries) and discriminates against operational creditors by paying them mere liquidation value violates the IBC. 2. Whether the Committee of Creditors is empowered under the Process Document and CIRP regulations to consider and negotiate a revised, higher resolution plan submitted prior to final plan approval to ensure value maximization. 3. Whether a corporate debtor's promoter can unilaterally terminate an ongoing CIRP by offering full settlement without following the mandate of Section 12A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency resolution plan cannot discriminate between similarly situated financial creditors or treat operational creditors inequitably by relegating them to nominal liquidation value; value maximization of the corporate debtor's assets for all stakeholders is the primary objective of the IBC, and the process is not a recovery mechanism or an auction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) and the IBC scheme mandate a level playing field for operational and financial credit. Regulation 38 cannot override the Code to legitimize discrimination or impose liquidation value on operational or dissenting financial creditors. The CoC's duty under Section 25(2)(h) and Regulation 36B permits flexibility to negotiate and entertain revised offers before final approval to achieve maximization of asset value. Furthermore, Section 12A is non-retroactive and strictly conditional upon 90% CoC voting approval, barring unilateral promoter settlements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparative analysis of the financial distribution matrix across creditor classes to detect unjustifiable disparity and evaluation of the CoC's compliance with procedural rules regarding timeline modifications and plan evaluations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: RPPL's plan was discriminatory and invalid; UltraTech's revised plan offered full value maximization to all stakeholders without discrimination and complied fully with Section 30(2), warranting approval under Section 31.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 123 & 188 of 2018 (preferred by Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd.) and Nos. 82 & 216 of 2018 (preferred by Binani Industries Ltd.) are dismissed. Company Appeal No. 234 of 2018 is allowed, expunging all adverse observations against Resolution Professional Vijay Kumar Iyer. UltraTech Cement Limited's revised resolution plan approved by 100% CoC vote is approved under Section 31 of the IBC. Records of CP (IB) No. 359/KB/2017 are remitted to NCLT Kolkata Bench to constitute a monitoring committee and oversee plan implementation. No costs.
summary: In the CIRP of Binani Cement Limited, the NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected the resolution plan of Rajputana Properties Pvt. Ltd. (RPPL) for discriminating between financial creditors and paying operational creditors mere liquidation value, directing consideration of UltraTech Cement Ltd.'s higher offer. Affirming the NCLT, the NCLAT held that the IBC's primary object is asset value maximization and balanced treatment of all stakeholders, prohibiting discrimination against operational creditors or similarly placed guarantee beneficiaries. Dismissing RPPL's and promoter Binani Industries' appeals while setting aside adverse remarks against the RP, the Appellate Tribunal approved UltraTech's revised plan providing 100% payment to all creditors.

case_title: Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta & Anr. vs Meridian Construction Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta & Anr. are the Appellants/Petitioners, and Meridian Construction Pvt. Ltd. and Harresh N. Mehta are the Respondents[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying dispute concerning the alteration, renovation, and development of an immovable property known as 'Hendre House, Girgaon', Mumbai[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; matter pertains to oppression, mismanagement, and unauthorized alteration of immovable corporate property[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Mumbai passed interim orders on 13 January 2017 (IA No. 03/2016 in TCP No. 31/(MAH)/2015) and an injunction order on 8 February 2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT had issued an interim restraint on 23 February 2017 prohibiting construction/alteration; Respondent No. 2 filed an affidavit on 20 March 2017 justifying actions, which was rejected[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Dissatisfied with NCLT's interim orders, Appellants moved NCLAT; during appeal, repeated adjournments were sought for settlement, which failed to culminate in final terms[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal should keep interlocutory appeals pending indefinitely for settlement discussions, or remit the matter to the lower tribunal with directions to maintain status quo and decide the main company petition on merits[cite: 19].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Prolonged interim proceedings should not delay the final adjudication of a company petition; where interim protections adequately balance party interests, the appellate court should remand the matter for expeditious final determination[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The tribunal must balance equity by safeguarding the subject property while ensuring the primary company petition and pending contempt proceedings are adjudicated without undue delay[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where parties repeatedly seek extensions without finalizing settlement terms, further adjournments must be refused to avoid procedural abuse[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that its interim protective order should remain operative until the NCLT finally disposes of the company petition, remitting the matter accordingly[cite: 19].
operative_order: Both appeals stand disposed of; interim order of 23 February 2017 to continue until the NCLT finally decides the company petition; NCLT directed to adjudicate the petition on merits or record settlement if filed, and dispose of contempt proceedings if an unconditional apology is tendered[cite: 19].
summary: Appellants Dharamdas Nandlal Mehta and another appealed against interim orders of NCLT Mumbai concerning alterations to 'Hendre House, Girgaon' in an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 19]. While the NCLAT had earlier restrained construction, the parties repeatedly sought adjournments to negotiate a settlement[cite: 19]. Refusing further delay, the NCLAT ruled that protracted settlement talks should not stall justice[cite: 19]. It ordered its interim restraint to remain in effect until NCLT Mumbai finally disposes of the company petition on merits, and remitted the matter while granting liberty to file settlement terms if finalized[cite: 19].

case_title: M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs Devinder Singh Shant & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. and its co-promoters are Appellants, and Devinder Singh Shant & Ors. are Respondents[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Commercial real estate operations regarding the sale and leasing of shops, cinema hall, multiplexes, and restaurants in 'Globe Shopping Centertainment'[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute concerns management, property disposition, and signing authorities of company bank accounts[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal arose from an NCLT order passed in January 2017 in Company Petition No. 49 of 2016[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties executed and submitted agreed terms for property monetization, joint bank account operations, advertisement in three newspapers, and revenue-sharing mechanisms[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT passed an order in CP No. 49 of 2016, which was appealed in Company Appeal (AT) No. 32 of 2017; the parties formulated a mutual interim working arrangement before NCLAT[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can formalize a consent arrangement governing company asset management and bank account operations to maintain corporate functioning pending the final adjudication of an oppression petition[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To prevent the stalling of commercial enterprises during shareholder litigation, the tribunal may adopt consensual operational frameworks that balance control, preserve assets, and protect business continuity[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying Section 422 of the Companies Act 2013, company petitions must be prosecuted and determined expeditiously, and interim asset management mechanisms should facilitate, rather than obstruct, the main trial[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on mutual consent of all contesting factions to establish transparency through joint bank operations and public advertisements[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the appeal should be disposed of by substituting the impugned order with the agreed interim arrangement, directing expeditious trial of the company petition[cite: 20].
operative_order: Order of January 2017 modified in terms of the agreed 11-point interim framework; parties directed to cooperate with the NCLT for early disposal under Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013; appeal stands disposed of with no costs[cite: 20].
summary: In a shareholder dispute regarding M/s Goldstar Enclave Pvt. Ltd. and its commercial complex 'Globe Shopping Centertainment', the parties appealed an NCLT interim order in CP No. 49 of 2016[cite: 20]. Before the NCLAT, the parties reached an agreed interim framework governing the leasing/sale of units, public advertisements, escrow arrangements, and joint operation of bank accounts[cite: 20]. The NCLAT disposed of the appeal by substituting the impugned order with these agreed terms and directing the NCLT to expedite the final hearing of the petition in accordance with Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 20].

case_title: Siddharth Nahata vs Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Siddharth Nahata, Director of Tryst Industries Pvt. Ltd., is the Appellant/Corporate Debtor; Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent/Operational Creditor[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A principal-dealer arrangement where the Appellant was to sell articles received from the Respondent and make payments upon execution of purchase orders[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Operational Creditor claimed an outstanding debt of Rs. 33.78 lakhs, inclusive of overdue interest[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: A Section 8 demand notice was sent on 22 May 2017, to which the Appellant replied on 7 June 2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant produced prior correspondence from 20 July 2016 and 3 August 2016, alongside a criminal complaint, demonstrating a pre-existing dispute regarding the Respondent violating dealership terms by selling directly in the Appellant's territory[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 9 application on 8 September 2017[cite: 21]. The Appellant challenged this, arguing that a valid dispute existed prior to the demand notice[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 insolvency application can be admitted when correspondence and admissions establish a genuine, pre-existing dispute over business conduct prior to the issuance of the statutory demand notice[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority must reject an insolvency application under Section 9 if there is substantive evidence of a real, pre-existing dispute between the parties before the issuance of the demand notice[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8 and 9 of the IBC mandate that operational creditors cannot initiate CIRP if the corporate debtor raises a plausible dispute supported by historical correspondence[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on pre-notice letters from July and August 2016 and the Respondent's own admission in their counter-affidavit confirming the principal-dealer relationship to validate the dispute's existence[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that a valid prior dispute existed, meaning the Section 9 application should not have been admitted[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. The impugned order admitting the Insolvency Resolution Process is quashed and set aside. Further proceedings are stopped. No orders as to costs[cite: 21].
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT's admission of a Section 9 insolvency petition filed by Billets Elektro Werke Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 21]. Although the parties reached a compromise during the appeal, the NCLAT evaluated the case on merits[cite: 21]. Finding clear evidence of a pre-existing dispute regarding their dealership agreement prior to the Section 8 notice, the NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the insolvency proceedings[cite: 21].

case_title: Design Worx Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. vs Premier Restaurants Private Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Design Worx Infrastructure India Pvt. Ltd. is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and Premier Restaurants Private Ltd. is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Operational Creditor was assigned a job work contract initially valued at Rs. 95 lakhs[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid amounts with the Corporate Debtor alleging unilateral escalations without approval and claiming liquidated damages for delays capped at 10% of the contract[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Execution was originally slated for 31 July 2015, extended to January 2016, and eventually handed over in March 2016[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor produced emails dated 4 May 2016 and 17 May 2017 showing dissatisfaction with the work (unresolved snags), proof of engaging a third party to finish the job, and rent liabilities of Rs. 11 lakhs incurred due to the handover delay[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench rejected the Section 9 application on 8 May 2017 in C.P. No. (IB)-76 (ND)/2017, determining that a dispute existed between the parties[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether documented dissatisfaction regarding job execution, unresolved snags, and financial losses due to project delays constitute a valid 'existence of dispute' barring a Section 9 application[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor's insolvency petition is not maintainable if the corporate debtor establishes a pre-existing dispute regarding service quality or execution delays[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(6) defining 'dispute' includes contestations over the quality of goods or services, making claims of unresolved snags and resultant damages sufficient to reject a Section 9 petition[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal found that pre-notice emails demanding snag rectification, engagement of third-party contractors, and documented rent liabilities adequately proved the existence of a dispute[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's specific finding that a dispute existed prior to the demand notice, rendering the appeal meritless[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit[cite: 23].
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the NCLT's rejection of its Section 9 insolvency application against Premier Restaurants Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 23]. The Corporate Debtor provided emails demonstrating dissatisfaction with the job work, project delays causing rent liabilities, and the necessity of hiring third parties to rectify unremoved snags[cite: 23]. The NCLAT upheld the rejection, confirming that these elements clearly established a pre-existing dispute under the IBC[cite: 23].

case_title: Mitcon Consultancy & Engineering Services Ltd. vs Al-Ameen Green Energy Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mitcon Consultancy & Engineering Services Ltd. is the Appellant; Al-Ameen Green Energy Pvt. Ltd. is the Respondent[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debt arising from a work order issued by the Respondent[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant claimed outstanding dues that were liable to be paid prior to filing the Section 9 application[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The underlying work order was dated 18 May 2015. The NCLT rejected the Section 9 application on 23 October 2017[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Paragraph 7 of the work order dated 18 May 2015 clearly outlined the payment terms demonstrating maturity[cite: 24]. Furthermore, no dispute existed prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai rejected the Section 9 application, classifying the claim as premature[cite: 24]. The Operational Creditor appealed, and the Respondent failed to appear[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether an Adjudicating Authority can dismiss a Section 9 application as premature when documentary evidence confirms the debt payment had matured, and whether a dispute raised for the first time in reply to a Section 8 notice prevents CIRP initiation[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application cannot be dismissed as premature if the underlying contract or work order explicitly establishes that the payment date had passed before the application's filing[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A valid 'dispute' under the IBC must exist prior to the receipt of the Section 8 demand notice; raising a dispute merely in response to the notice is insufficient[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied heavily on the written 'Terms of payment' in the work order, determining that the NCLT had ignored plain documentary evidence in favor of baseless statements by the corporate debtor[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that the debt had matured and the Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate the factual record, necessitating reversal[cite: 24].
operative_order: The NCLT order dated 23 October 2017 is set aside[cite: 24]. The case is remitted to NCLT Chennai to admit the application if complete after notice, or to grant the Appellant time to cure defects[cite: 24]. No costs[cite: 24].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Chennai order that rejected its Section 9 IBC application as premature[cite: 24]. The NCLAT found that the Adjudicating Authority failed to examine the payment terms in the May 2015 work order, which clearly proved the debt had matured[cite: 24]. Furthermore, the Corporate Debtor raised a dispute only after receiving the Section 8 notice[cite: 24]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and remitted the matter for admission[cite: 24].

case_title: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd & Ors vs Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd & Ors are the Appellants. Malaxmi Infra Ventures (India) Ltd is the 1st Respondent, and Mr. Y. Harish Chandra Prasad is the 2nd Respondent[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Disputes involving corporate directorship and allegations of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; pertains to maintainability of an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The NCLT passed the impugned order in CP No. 42/2011 on 31 January 2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLAT had already affirmed in a prior order (dated 23 March 2017 in AT No. 78 of 2017) that the company petition was unmaintainable with respect to the 2nd Respondent[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad ruled the company petition was only maintainable for the 1st Respondent and that the 2nd Respondent lacked locus standi[cite: 25]. Incongruously, the NCLT ordered the Appellant company to appoint the 2nd Respondent as a Director[cite: 25]. The Appellants appealed this specific direction[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal can validly grant substantive affirmative relief (such as directing appointment as a Director) to a petitioner whom it concurrently found lacked locus standi to maintain the petition[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicating authority cannot grant substantive relief to a party within a proceeding if it has explicitly determined that the party lacks the locus standi to maintain the petition[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relief under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act is strictly contingent upon the maintainability of the petition; non-maintainability strips the tribunal of jurisdiction to issue directions favoring the unqualified party[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied on the logical contradiction in the NCLT's own order and its prior appellate validation of the non-maintainability finding to strike down the relief[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that directing the company to appoint a party found to lack standing was legally unjustified[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is allowed. Clause (iv) of the impugned judgment directing the appointment of the second petitioner as a Director is set aside. Interim orders vacated. No order as to costs[cite: 25].
summary: Brahmani Infratech Pvt Ltd appealed a contradictory NCLT Hyderabad order regarding an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 25]. The NCLT had ruled the petition was only maintainable for the 1st Respondent and that the 2nd Respondent lacked locus standi, yet it inexplicably ordered the company to appoint the 2nd Respondent as a Director[cite: 25]. The NCLAT set aside this specific direction, reasoning that substantive relief cannot be granted to a party whose petition was held unmaintainable[cite: 25].

case_title: Bhikhunhai J. Patel & Anr vs Hetshri Dairy Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhikhunhai J. Patel and another are the Appellants/Petitioners, and Hetshri Dairy Pvt. Ltd. and others are the Respondents[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The matter pertains to a dispute over shareholding and membership within the Respondent company[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is an oppression and mismanagement case. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Specific timeline dates of earlier notices are not detailed in the text. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The NCLT evaluated the Annual Return and Form No. 2, which demonstrated the Appellants did not possess the requisite 1/10th shares or 1/10th membership[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed the original petition (TP No. 74/397-398/NCLT/AHM/2016) on 5th April 2017 on the ground that the Appellants lacked the eligibility criteria to file under Sections 397 and 398[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellants held the requisite 1/10th shareholding to maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement under the Companies Act, 1956.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition for oppression and mismanagement is not maintainable if the petitioners fail to establish the threshold requirement of holding one-tenth of the issued share capital or representing one-tenth of the total members[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act require strict compliance with the numerical threshold for eligibility[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Bald allegations of fabricated annual returns cannot be accepted without a substantive documentary record proving the requisite shareholding on the date of filing[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Tribunal held that the Appellants lacked the statutory minimum 1/10th shares to sustain the petition, warranting dismissal[cite: 1].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, and there shall be no order as to cost[cite: 1].
summary: In this company appeal, the Appellants challenged an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing their petition for oppression and mismanagement[cite: 1]. The core issue was whether the Appellants held the mandatory 1/10th shareholding required under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 1]. The NCLAT upheld the lower tribunal's finding, noting that the company's Annual Return and Form No. 2 indicated the Appellants did not meet the required membership threshold[cite: 1]. Rejecting the Appellants' unsupported claims that the returns were fabricated, the NCLAT concluded that disputed questions of fact regarding eligibility without corroborating records could not yield relief, ultimately dismissing the appeal for lack of merit[cite: 1].

case_title: Sudha Commercial Company Ltd vs Milkfood Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sudha Commercial Company Ltd is the Appellant/Petitioner, and Milkfood Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 2]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The dispute involves internal corporate amendments concerning shareholding changes and a specific land transaction[cite: 2]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial debt default metric is applicable in this limitation dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The contested land transaction occurred in the year 2007, making it a subject of limitation scrutiny during the 2016-2017 proceedings[cite: 2]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal reviewed the amendment applications (Nos. 21 and 9 of 2016) against the historical timeline of the 2007 land transaction[cite: 2]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh partly allowed an amendment petition (Company Petition No. 28/Chd/PB./2016) on 27th June 2017, but rejected the portion concerning the 2007 land transaction[cite: 2].
legal_issues: Whether the amendment prayer regarding a land transaction from 2007 is barred by the laws of limitation under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Claims relating to transactions that fall outside the statutory limitation period cannot be introduced via an amendment to a company petition[cite: 2]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs limitation periods for proceedings before the Tribunal, thereby barring stale claims[cite: 2]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal calculated the time elapsed since the 2007 transaction to determine if the claim survived the limitation period[cite: 2]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that the part of the amendment seeking relief for a 2007 land transaction was rightly rejected as time-barred, affirming the lower tribunal's selective allowance of the amendment[cite: 2].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, with liberty open to the appellant to raise validly pleaded issues regarding shareholding changes during the final hearing. There shall be no order as to costs[cite: 2].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT Chandigarh order that partially allowed their amendment petition against Milkfood Ltd[cite: 2]. The core issue focused on the NCLT's refusal to permit amendments concerning a land transaction from 2007[cite: 2]. The NCLAT evaluated this under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013, which governs limitation[cite: 2]. It determined that introducing a decade-old transaction was fundamentally barred by limitation[cite: 2]. Consequently, the NCLAT affirmed the lower tribunal's decision to reject that specific part of the amendment, dismissing the appeal while clarifying that validly pleaded shareholding issues could still be pursued during the final hearing[cite: 2].

case_title: Yogendra Yasupal vs M/S. Jigsaw Solutions & Anr
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Jigsaw Solutions is the Operational Creditor, the 2nd Respondent is the Corporate Debtor, and Yogendra Yasupal is the Appellant/Director[cite: 3]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of services by the Operational Creditor to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 3]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default triggered a Section 9 application; exact financial metrics are not detailed in the text. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor failed to raise a dispute regarding service quality upon receiving the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 3]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant relied on an anticipatory bail order from the Madras High Court to allege a pre-existing dispute, while the Operational Creditor's application was deemed complete[cite: 3]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai admitted the Section 9 application (Company Petition No. 559/(IB)/CB/2017) and declared a moratorium on 15th September 2017, which the Appellant challenged[cite: 3].
legal_issues: Whether observations against individual officers in a court order or internal communications constitute an 'existence of dispute' to bar the admission of a Section 9 petition under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General observations against individual officers in unrelated court orders do not constitute a pre-existing dispute regarding a corporate debt[cite: 3]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 8(2) of the IBC mandates that a dispute must be explicitly raised regarding the quality of goods or services prior to the demand notice[cite: 3]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The tribunal evaluates whether a specific, written objection about service quality was raised directly by the Corporate Debtor in response to the Section 8 notice[cite: 3]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench concluded that since no written objection regarding service quality was made at the Section 8(2) stage, the anticipatory bail order did not demonstrate a valid statutory dispute, justifying admission of the petition[cite: 3].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost[cite: 3].
summary: This insolvency appeal involves a Corporate Debtor's director challenging the admission of a Section 9 IBC petition filed by Operational Creditor M/s. Jigsaw Solutions[cite: 3]. NCLT Chennai had previously admitted the petition and initiated a moratorium[cite: 3]. The Appellant argued that a pre-existing dispute existed, citing an anticipatory bail order from the Madras High Court[cite: 3]. The NCLAT rejected this argument, ruling that isolated court observations against individuals do not amount to a valid dispute under the Code[cite: 3]. Relying on the Supreme Court's Mobilox Innovations ruling, the NCLAT noted the Corporate Debtor failed to raise specific written objections regarding service quality during the Section 8 notice stage, thereby dismissing the appeal[cite: 3].

case_title: Sak Industries Pvt Ltd vs Fenance Auto Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: SAK Industries Pvt Ltd is the Appellant/Operational Creditor, and Fenance Auto Ltd is the Respondent/Corporate Debtor[cite: 4]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational debt underlying a Section 9 insolvency application[cite: 4]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The specific default amount and date are not detailed. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The core timeline issue was the statutory 7-day period mandated to remove defects in an IBC application[cite: 4]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The primary evidentiary document relied upon was the Supreme Court judgment in M/s Surendra Trading Company, which interpreted the defect-removal timeline[cite: 4]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi rejected the Section 9 application on 19th July 2017 specifically because the Appellant failed to remove application defects within the mandated 7-day window[cite: 4].
legal_issues: Whether the 7-day timeline prescribed under the IBC for removing defects in an insolvency application is mandatory or directory.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory time limit of seven days granted to an applicant to rectify defects in an insolvency petition is directory, not mandatory[cite: 4]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisos to Sections 7(5), 9(5), and 10(4) of the IBC regarding the 7-day period for curing defects do not act as strict bars that automatically invalidate a petition if breached[cite: 4]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal relied entirely on the binding precedent established by the Supreme Court in 'M/s Surendra Trading Company', overturning earlier rigid interpretations[cite: 4]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The bench ruled that the lower tribunal erred in rejecting the petition solely for missing the 7-day defect removal window, and that the applicant must be granted an opportunity to cure defects[cite: 4].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 19th July 2017 is set aside, and the case is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to allow the appellant time to remove defects. There shall be no order as to cost[cite: 4].
summary: The Operational Creditor appealed the rejection of its Section 9 insolvency petition by NCLT New Delhi[cite: 4]. The lower tribunal had dismissed the petition because the Creditor failed to cure application defects within the 7-day statutory period, treating the deadline as mandatory[cite: 4]. The NCLAT examined the appeal in light of a recent Supreme Court judgment in M/s Surendra Trading Company, which clarified that the 7-day timeline under IBC Sections 7, 9, and 10 is directory, not mandatory[cite: 4]. Applying this binding ruling, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's dismissal, allowed the appeal, and remanded the matter, directing the Adjudicating Authority to grant the Appellant time to rectify the defects[cite: 4].

case_title: Anand Kumar & Ors vs Usha Kumar & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anand Kumar and others are the Appellants, and Usha Kumar and others are the Respondents[cite: 5]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An internal corporate dispute concerning a poorly functioning company leading to an interim NCLT order[cite: 5]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial default metrics apply to this procedural dispute. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The original interim order was passed on 6th March 2017; the amendment application was filed more than 90 days later, exceeding the 30-day limit[cite: 5]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal evaluated the chronology of the filings and determined there was no substantive error in the original March 6 order warranting correction[cite: 5]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed Interlocutory Application No. 236 of 2017, refusing to amend the interim order originally passed in IA No. 72 of 2015[cite: 5].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses the jurisdiction to review or recall its interim orders beyond the 30-day statutory limit in the absence of a patent error.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The National Company Law Tribunal lacks the inherent jurisdiction to review or recall its own orders, except to correct apparent errors within a strict 30-day window[cite: 5]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 155 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 strictly confines the power to rectify errors to a 30-day limitation period from the date of the original order[cite: 5]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The bench assessed the timing of the application (filed after 90 days) and the absence of any visible illegality or perversity in the original interim order[cite: 5]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appellate tribunal concluded that since the application was filed well beyond the 30-day limit and there was no factual error in the original order, no interference was justified[cite: 5].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed. Parties are directed to co-operate with the Tribunal for the expeditious disposal of the Company Petition, preferably within three months. No order as to cost[cite: 5].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT Kolkata order that refused to amend an interim order passed three months prior[cite: 5]. The dispute centered on whether the tribunal could review its earlier decision based on an alleged error[cite: 5]. The NCLAT noted that the NCLT lacks general powers to review or recall its orders, except via inherent powers under Rule 11 or 155 of the NCLT Rules to correct errors within 30 days[cite: 5]. Because the Appellants filed their interlocutory application after 90 days, and the NCLAT found no actual error or perversity in the original interim order, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 5]. The NCLAT directed expedited disposal of the main pending petition[cite: 5].

case_title: Pallavi Gems Pvt Ltd & Anr vs M/S Haresh N Mataliya & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Pallavi Gems Pvt Ltd & Anr are the Appellants, and M/S Haresh N Mataliya & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding a company petition initially filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 came into force on June 1, 2016, after the original petition was filed[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The maintainability of the Company Petition was challenged on the grounds of limitation under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT rejected the interlocutory application challenging the petition's maintainability on limitation grounds, which prompted this appeal[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether the period of limitation prescribed under Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 is applicable retroactively to a company petition filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board before the section came into force[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provisions regarding limitation do not apply retroactively to petitions already pending before the implementation of those provisions[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013, establishing limitation periods, was not applicable to petitions filed before the Company Law Board prior to June 1, 2016[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal verified the date of filing against the effective date of the statute[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellate Tribunal held that the petition was maintainable and could not be dismissed on limitation grounds, thereby upholding the NCLT's order[cite: 6].
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal declined to interfere with the impugned order, effectively dismissing the appeal[cite: 6].
summary: The Appellants challenged an NCLT order that rejected their application to dismiss a pending company petition on the grounds of limitation[cite: 6]. The NCLAT observed that the original petition was filed before the erstwhile Company Law Board prior to Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013 coming into force on June 1, 2016[cite: 6]. Consequently, the limitation rules of Section 433 did not apply retroactively to the case[cite: 6]. Finding no error in the lower tribunal's decision that the petition was maintainable, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 6].

case_title: K Ishwara Bhatt vs M/S Sun Pharmaceutical Ltd & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: K. Ishwara Bhatt is the Appellant, and M/s Sun Pharmaceutical Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed; dispute pertains to territorial jurisdiction for a company petition[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The registered office of the respondent company is located in the State of Gujarat (Ahmedabad)[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, passed an order on January 25, 2017, transferring C.P.No. 61/59/2015 to the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench for lack of territorial jurisdiction in Delhi[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT Principal Bench has territorial jurisdiction to hear a company petition when the respondent company's registered office is located in the State of Gujarat[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Territorial jurisdiction over a company rests exclusively with the NCLT Bench that governs the state where the company's registered office is located[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 434(1)(a) read with Section 419(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, and Rule 64 of the NCLT Rules establish that jurisdiction is determined solely by the location of the registered office[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the undisputed fact that the registered office of the respondent is in Ahmedabad[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the company is registered in Gujarat, the NCLAT affirmed that only the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench possesses territorial jurisdiction over the matter[cite: 7].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no order as to cost, and the parties are directed to cooperate with NCLT Ahmedabad for the early disposal of the Company Petition[cite: 7].
summary: The Appellant challenged an order by the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, which transferred their company petition to the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench[cite: 7]. The core issue was territorial jurisdiction, as the respondent company's registered office is in Gujarat[cite: 7]. Relying on statutory provisions and the precedent set in '63 Moons Technology Limited', the NCLAT held that Benches, including the Principal Bench, have territorial jurisdiction exclusively based on the location of a company's registered office[cite: 7]. Finding no ground to interfere with the transfer, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal and directed cooperation for early disposal[cite: 7].

case_title: Prabir Mukherjee vs M/s. Jatia Cotton Mills Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prabir Mukherjee is the Appellant (a respondent in the original CP), and M/s. Jatia Cotton Mills Limited & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not applicable; dispute centers on procedural clubbing of multiple company petitions[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant requested three company petitions be heard together because the parties were common, but the reliefs sought in the petitions were not identical[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Kolkata Bench rejected C.A. No. 87 of 2017 on July 11, 2017, refusing to tie the cases together due to non-identical reliefs[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal is obligated to club and hear multiple company petitions together solely because the parties are common, despite differing reliefs[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The decision to consolidate and hear multiple petitions together is a discretionary power of the Tribunal, dependent on the nature of the cases and identicality of reliefs[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not mandate appellate interference in a Tribunal's procedural discretion regarding case management unless there is an apparent illegality[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal examined whether the reliefs sought across the three petitions were identical to warrant a joint hearing[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since deciding whether to hear petitions together or separately falls within the Tribunal's discretion and there was no illegality, interference was unwarranted[cite: 8].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no costs[cite: 8].
summary: The Appellant challenged a procedural order by the NCLT Kolkata Bench that refused to club three company petitions together for a joint hearing[cite: 8]. Although the parties in the petitions were common, the NCLT noted that the reliefs sought were not identical[cite: 8]. The NCLAT upheld this decision, stating that the choice to hear cases together or separately is inherently up to the Tribunal's discretion, based on the nature of the case and the specific reliefs[cite: 8]. Finding no illegality in the lower tribunal's exercise of its discretion, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 8].

case_title: Abro Technologies (P) Ltd vs Delhi Warehousing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s. Abro Technologies (P) Ltd. is the Appellant, and M/s. Delhi Warehousing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate dispute regarding the reduction of the Appellant's shareholding[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant's shareholding was reduced below 10% in the year 2008, yet the petition was filed approximately eight years later[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Tribunal observed that there was an unexplained delay of eight years before the Appellant approached the judicial authority[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi, dismissed the Company Petition under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 on December 22, 2016, citing delay and laches[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether a petition for oppression and mismanagement is maintainable when filed after an unexplained delay of eight years from the cause of action[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A petition alleging oppression and mismanagement must be filed within a reasonable period; significant, unexplained delays will result in dismissal due to laches[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Equitable remedies under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956 are barred if the petitioner sleeps on their rights for an unreasonable timeframe[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal assessed the timeline from the 2008 share reduction to the filing date, noting the complete lack of explanation for the eight-year gap[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT held that the Appellant's failure to move the erstwhile Company Law Board within a reasonable time constituted laches, thereby justifying the petition's rejection[cite: 9].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit[cite: 9].
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Principal Bench's dismissal of their company petition filed under Sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 9]. The dispute arose from the Appellant's shareholding being reduced below 10% in 2008[cite: 9]. However, the Appellant waited approximately eight years before initiating legal action, without providing any grounds to explain this significant delay[cite: 9]. The NCLAT affirmed the lower tribunal's decision, ruling that the equitable relief sought was barred by severe delay and laches[cite: 9]. Consequently, finding no merit in the case, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 9].

case_title: Sri Haridas Pottath vs Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sri Haridas Pottath is the Appellant, and Peerless Engineering Products Pvt. Ltd. alongside Dr. Sabhapathi Dorai Raju are the Respondents[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate governance dispute concerning the convening of an Extraordinary General Body Meeting (EOGM)[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Respondent filed an application for the Tribunal to direct the convening of an EOGM, which the Tribunal allowed the respondents to proceed with independently[cite: 10]. The Appellant was not the original petitioner in the matter[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT passed an order on August 29, 2017, dismissing the application for directions but giving liberty to proceed with the EOGM. The Appellant challenged this, but subsequently sought to withdraw the appeal[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether an appellant who is not the original petitioner has standing or is prejudiced by an order allowing an EOGM to proceed, such that they may challenge the order[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal may be permitted to be withdrawn if the appellant is not adversely affected by the impugned order and retains the right to raise substantive issues in the appropriate corporate forum[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 1956, parties can raise their grievances within the convened EOGM itself rather than preemptively litigating the procedural order to convene it[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the Appellant's non-petitioner status and confirmed that the Appellant's rights would not be compromised by attending the EOGM[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT granted the Appellant's request to withdraw the appeal, concluding that the Appellant could raise all relevant questions during the EOGM itself[cite: 10].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, without any liberty to challenge the same impugned order dated August 29, 2017 before the Appellate Tribunal again. No cost[cite: 10].
summary: The Appellant filed an appeal against an NCLT order that allowed the Respondents to proceed with convening an Extraordinary General Body Meeting (EOGM) under Section 186 of the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 10]. During the hearing, the NCLAT observed that the Appellant, who was not the original petitioner, would not be adversely affected by the order because he retained the right to raise all his questions and objections at the EOGM itself[cite: 10]. Acknowledging this, the Appellant sought permission to withdraw the appeal[cite: 10]. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal but explicitly denied liberty to challenge the same NCLT order again, thereby dismissing the appeal without costs[cite: 10].

case_title: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah vs Mis. Gujrat Gas Company Ltd. & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Kamlesh Kalidas Shah is the Appellant, and Mis. Gujrat Gas Company Ltd. & Ors are the Respondents[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Not explicitly detailed in the brief order[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Appellant had been pursuing the matter since 2013 before the incorrect forum[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant recognized they had been litigating in the wrong forums (erstwhile Company Law Board and then NCLT) and needed to file a civil suit for declaration[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order but subsequently requested to withdraw the appeal to file a suit for declaration accompanied by a Section 14 Limitation Act petition[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellant should be granted liberty to withdraw the appeal and pursue a suit for declaration before the appropriate forum due to prosecuting the matter before the wrong forum[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal can permit an appellant to withdraw an appeal and grant liberty to pursue remedies in the correct forum if they were previously litigating in an incorrect forum[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the Limitation Act is invoked to seek exclusion of time spent litigating bona fide in a court lacking jurisdiction[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal accepted the Appellant's submission regarding their erroneous choice of forum[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT granted liberty to file the appropriate petition, subject to limitation bars, and disposed of the appeal as withdrawn[cite: 11].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of as withdrawn, granting liberty to the Appellant to file a suit for declaration if otherwise not barred by limitation[cite: 11].
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order but subsequently requested permission to withdraw the appeal[cite: 11]. case_title: Sri Trivikram & Ors vs The Mysore Stoneware Pipes & Potteries Ltd & Ors

case_title: Prem Sarup Narula vs Bycell Telecommunications India Pvt. Ltd.

FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Corporate Debtor replied to the demand notice asserting that the dues were fully settled, indicating a pre-existing dispute[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed the Section 9 application on 28th September, 2017, due to the existence of a dispute[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 9 of the IBC is maintainable when the corporate debtor raises a dispute regarding full and final settlement of dues[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An insolvency application by an operational creditor cannot be admitted if there is a pre-existing dispute regarding the settlement of dues[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 'existence of dispute' under Section 9 of the IBC is satisfied when the corporate debtor provides evidence or a plausible defense of having settled the claim[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the corporate debtor's reply to the demand notice asserting full payment of USD 33,000[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that since a dispute existed regarding the payment, the issue should be decided by a competent civil court and not via the corporate insolvency resolution process[cite: 16].

summary: The Appellant, an Operational Creditor, challenged the NCLT's dismissal of a Section 9 IBC application against Bycell Telecommunications India Pvt. Ltd[cite: 16]. case_title: P.B. Amolik & Ors vs The Bombay Diocesan Trust Association

summary: In this matter, the Appellants' counsel approached the NCLAT to rectify typographical errors present in a prior judgment dated May 1, 2017[cite: 18]. case_title: Shaw Traders vs Balaji Paper & Newsprint Pvt. Ltd

FACTUAL EVIDENCE: A notice of dispute was sent by the Corporate Debtor to the Operational Creditor prior to the proceedings[cite: 20]. legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when it is both barred by limitation and unprosecuted due to the appellant's repeated failure to appear[cite: 20].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is liable to be dismissed for default if the appellant repeatedly fails to appear, especially when the appeal is also time-barred[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9 of the IBC prohibits the initiation of insolvency proceedings when the corporate debtor has issued a valid notice of dispute, as interpreted by the Supreme Court in Mobilox Innovations[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal noted the physical absence of the Appellant's counsel across multiple called dates and the Registry's note regarding the expiration of limitation[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLAT concluded that due to the persistent non-appearance and the appeal being time-barred, it warranted outright dismissal[cite: 20].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for being barred by limitation and for default of appearance[cite: 20].
summary: The Appellant, an Operational Creditor, had filed a Section 9 application under the IBC which was rejected by the lower Adjudicating Authority[cite: 20]. When the matter reached the NCLAT, the Registry flagged the appeal as time-barred[cite: 20]. Despite being granted an adjournment on December 13 to allow for appearance, the Appellant repeatedly failed to attend the hearings[cite: 20]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal for default and for being barred by limitation[cite: 20].

case_title: Anil Gupta & Ors vs Yogesh Mahajan & Ors

case_title: Dentsu Media And Holdings India P Ltd. & Ors vs Roc Nct Of Delhi & Haryana
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dentsu Media and Holdings India P Ltd. & Ors are the Appellants, and the ROC NCT of Delhi & Haryana is the Respondent[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Regulatory matters involving the Registrar of Companies; details are not specified[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appeal was filed with a delay of 52 days[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The delay in filing the appeal exceeded the maximum permissible condonation period[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Appellants filed an appeal alongside a petition for condonation of delay, which was heard by the NCLAT on February 7, 2017[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal possesses the statutory authority to condone a delay in filing an appeal that exceeds the maximum limit prescribed by the Companies Act[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal lacks the jurisdiction to condone a delay in filing an appeal if the delay period exceeds the strict statutory maximum cap[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 restricts the Appellate Tribunal's power to condone delays to a maximum period of 45 days[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Tribunal calculated the delay to be 52 days, objectively exceeding the 45-day statutory limit[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the 52-day delay surpassed the statutory maximum of 45 days, the NCLAT concluded it lacked the power to condone it, rendering the appeal barred by limitation[cite: 22].
operative_order: The petition for condonation of delay is dismissed. The appeal stands dismissed being barred by limitation[cite: 22].
summary: The Appellants, Dentsu Media and Holdings India P Ltd., filed an appeal before the NCLAT challenging an unspecified order, but the filing was delayed by 52 days[cite: 22]. The NCLAT noted that under Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, the tribunal is statutely capped at condoning delays up to a maximum of 45 days[cite: 22]. Because the Appellants' delay of 52 days exceeded this strict statutory limit, the NCLAT held that it had no authority to condone it[cite: 22]. Consequently, the petition for condonation was rejected, and the appeal was dismissed as barred by limitation[cite: 22].

case_title: M/s Bengal Chemicals & Druggists Association vs Kalyan Choudhury

summary: The Appellant, M/s Bengal Chemicals & Druggists Association, filed an appeal accompanied by an application to condone a delay of 99 days[cite: 23]. case_title: Devraj Vasant Immanual & Ors vs Ysp Balraj & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Devraj Vasant Immanual & Ors are the Appellants, and Ysp Balraj & Ors (including the 1st respondent company) are the Respondents[cite: 24]. 2. operative_order: The Tribunal is directed to hear the parties on merit and dispose of the company petition preferably by May 15, 2017, without waiting for the investigation report. If submitted within ten days, it may be considered; otherwise, the matter proceeds on record. The appeal is disposed of[cite: 24].
summary: The Appellants appealed an order from NCLT Chennai that directed a Chartered Accountant to investigate allegations of financial siphoning by the respondents[cite: 24]. Emphasizing the need for expeditious resolution, the NCLAT declined to interfere with the probe order itself but directed the NCLT to finalize the petition based on the existing record preferably by May 15, 2017, without indefinitely awaiting the investigation report[cite: 24].

case_title: Sysco Industries Ltd vs Ecoplast Ltd

FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The parties reached a mutual settlement during the pendency of the appeal, which included the provision of a cheque by the Appellant[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Supreme Court, exercising its powers under Article 142, accepted the settlement in Civil Appeal No. 10581 of 2017, thereby closing the proceedings before the NCLT and NCLAT[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal before the NCLAT should be closed when the Supreme Court has already exercised its powers under Article 142 to accept a settlement between the parties[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the Supreme Court exercises its plenary powers to accept a settlement and dispose of underlying proceedings, pending appeals before lower tribunals are rendered infructuous and must be closed[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 142 of the Constitution of India grants the Supreme Court the authority to pass decrees necessary for doing complete justice, including validating settlements that override pending insolvency proceedings[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The NCLAT solely relied on the documented order of the Supreme Court dated 28th August 2017[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Supreme Court's order explicitly disposed of the pending proceedings based on the accepted settlement, the NCLAT formally closed the appeal before it[cite: 25].
operative_order: In view of the order passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the appeal is closed and stands disposed of[cite: 25].
summary: In this insolvency appeal between Sysco Industries Ltd and Ecoplast Ltd, the NCLAT was informed that the parties had reached a mutual settlement[cite: 25]. The Supreme Court of India had already reviewed this matter in Civil Appeal No. 10581 of 2017[cite: 25]. Exercising its extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 142 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court accepted the settlement on August 28, 2017, directing that the provided cheque must be honored to avoid contempt, and subsequently disposed of the pending NCLT proceedings[cite: 25]. Bound by the Supreme Court's order disposing of the underlying matter, the NCLAT officially closed and disposed of the present appeal[cite: 25].

case_title: Srei Infrastructure Finance Ltd vs Naveen Bansal & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Respondent No. 1 (Naveen Bansal) is the Petitioner; Appellant (SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd) is the Financier (5th Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: The Appellant financed approximately Rs. 50 crores to the company. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable; dispute centers on corporate oppression. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Not applicable as it is governed by Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act 1956. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Appellant filed an interim application stating there was a privity of contract between the parties, which it later alleged was a typographical error. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Company Petition No.99/2014 was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement. The Appellant sought dismissal of the petition against it, which the NCLT rejected on May 17, 2017. The Appellant subsequently sought to withdraw its appeal to rectify the typographical error before the NCLT.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant should be permitted to withdraw its appeal to rectify an alleged typographical error in its pleadings before the lower Tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal to allow a party to rectify erroneous pleadings before the lower adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: N/A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal allowed the withdrawal without determining the merit of whether the pleading was genuinely a typographical error, leaving it to the lower tribunal.
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with no order as to cost. The Tribunal may consider the application uninfluenced by the Appellate Tribunal's observations if the issue is raised again.
summary: The respondent filed a petition alleging oppression and mismanagement against the company, impleading the appellant financier[cite: 2]. The appellant sought dismissal of the petition against it, which the NCLT rejected based on the appellant's own pleading of a privity of contract[cite: 2]. Claiming this was a typographical error, the appellant sought to withdraw its appeal to correct the error before the NCLT[cite: 2]. The NCLAT allowed the withdrawal without ruling on the merits[cite: 2].

case_title: Axis Nirman And Industries Limited & Anr vs M/S. Hotel Birsa (P) Limited & Ors
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/S. Hotel Birsa (P) Limited & Ors are the Petitioners; Axis Nirman and Industries Limited is Appellant 1 (Respondent No. 7 below). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding internal shareholding, unauthorized increase in share capital, and a Memorandum of Understanding to sell shares to an external entity, Libra Retailer Private Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: N/A. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: N/A. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Disputed share allotments of 1,20,000 and 90,000 shares to Respondents 7 and 4 respectively. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A petition was filed alleging oppression and mismanagement. On April 7, 2017, the NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed the petition, cancelled specific share allotments, and directed the petitioners to execute share transfers to an outsider (Libra). The Appellants challenged this common order.
legal_issues: Whether a Tribunal adjudicating an oppression and mismanagement petition has the jurisdiction to direct the sale of shares to an outsider when other existing shareholders are present.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Company Law Tribunal lacks the jurisdiction to compel the sale of a party's shares to an outsider, particularly when existing shareholders might be willing to purchase them. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Remedial directives under the Companies Act cannot mandatorily enforce an MoU favoring a non-member outsider against internal shareholder rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: N/A. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: While affirming the finding of oppression and mismanagement, the NCLAT concluded that directing the sale of shares to an external party exceeded the Tribunal's jurisdiction.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed in part, setting aside the NCLT's direction that compelled the sale of shares to the outsider entity, in alignment with a parallel judgment (C.A (AT) No. 162 of 2017). No order as to cost.
summary: In an oppression and mismanagement petition, the NCLT Kolkata allowed the petition, cancelled various share allotments, and uniquely directed the petitioners to sell their shares to an outsider entity under a Memorandum of Understanding[cite: 3]. The appellants challenged this order[cite: 3]. Relying on its precedent in a connected appeal, the NCLAT ruled that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction to mandate the sale of shares to an outsider when existing shareholders were available[cite: 3]. It set aside that specific direction while upholding the core finding of oppression and mismanagement[cite: 3].

case_title: Vimal Organics Limited vs Anya Polytech & Fertilizers Pvt. Ltd
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vimal Organics Limited is the Operational Creditor; Anya Polytech & Fertilizers Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A May 3, 2014 agreement for the supply, engineering, erection, and commissioning of a 50MTPD Zinc Sulphate Manufacturing Plant. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid invoices related to the supply of goods and services (amount unstated). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 8 demand notice was issued; Corporate Debtor replied on July 20, 2017. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails dated February 25, May 31, and June 18, 2016, wherein the Corporate Debtor raised prior complaints regarding improper commissioning, failure to achieve the 40.0 MT/day production target, and 15 undelivered items. 6.
