summary: Mr. Manan Chandraprakash Bhavsar appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's order dated February 27, 2017, passed in C.P. No. 01/58-59/CLB/AHM/2015[cite: 14]. The NCLAT declined to interfere with the lower tribunal's decision to hear pending applications together with the main petition, noting that the NCLT was expected to dispose of the matter expeditiously pursuant to Section 422 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 14]. The appellate tribunal clarified that it did not decide whether the appellant was a necessary party, leaving that question for the NCLT's final determination[cite: 14].

case_title: M/s. Madhur Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. M/s. Facor Steels Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are M/s. Madhur Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (claiming as a financial creditor), and the Respondent is M/s. Facor Steels Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution application filed by the corporate debtor under Section 10 of the IBC, 2016, alongside a separate pending winding-up petition before the High Court involving a claim of Rs. 5.81 crores with interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed debt amount of Rs. 5.81 crores plus interest payable by the corporate debtor to the appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority passed the admission order on March 8, 2017; appeal heard and decided on May 9, 2017[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records showing the appellant filed a claim of Rs. 5.81 crores with interest before the Insolvency Resolution Professional, and a pending winding-up petition before the High Court affected by the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against the Mumbai Bench Adjudicating Authority's order admitting a Section 10 application under the I&B Code, 2016[cite: 15].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with the admission of a Section 10 IBC application when the application is complete under sub-section (4) of Section 10 and whether claims can be pursued before the IRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with an order admitting a corporate applicant's insolvency petition under Section 10 of the IBC if the petition is complete under Section 10(4) and free from legal illegality. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict adherence to the completion criteria of Section 10(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, and the impact of the Section 14 moratorium on pending winding-up proceedings[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the completeness of the statutory application and the availability of alternative remedies through claims filed with the Insolvency Resolution Professional[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The prayer to set aside the admission order is rejected because the Section 10 application was complete, while protecting the appellant's liberty to pursue its financial claims before the IRP[cite: 15].
operative_order: The prayer to interfere with the impugned order is rejected, but it is clarified that this order will not come in the way of the Appellant's claim as raised before the Insolvency Resolution Professional. The appeal stands disposed of with no order as to costs[cite: 15].
summary: M/s. Madhur Engineers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 36 of 2017 challenging the Mumbai Bench Adjudicating Authority's order dated March 8, 2017, which admitted a corporate insolvency petition under Section 10 of the IBC[cite: 15]. The appellant argued that it was a financial creditor owed Rs. 5.81 crores with interest and that a pending High Court winding-up petition would be affected by the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 15]. The NCLAT found that the Section 10 petition was complete under Section 10(4) and declined to interfere, while noting that the appellant was free to pursue its claim before the Insolvency Resolution Professional[cite: 15].

case_title: Sree Metaliks Ltd. vs. M/s. Srei Equipment Finance Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sree Metaliks Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and the Respondent is M/s. Srei Equipment Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Equipment finance facility resulting in an insolvency petition under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in terms of exact monetary figures in the short order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench on January 30, 2017; appellate hearing held on February 21, 2017[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions made by counsel indicating the appellant had no objection to the insolvency proceedings under the Code[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dated January 30, 2017, where the respondent agreed to replace the Interim Resolution Professional via Committee of Creditors consultation[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an insolvency admission order can be disposed of when the corporate debtor expresses no objection and the financial creditor agrees to substitute the Interim Resolution Professional.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will dispose of an insolvency appeal without interference when the corporate debtor consents to the proceedings and the creditor agrees to a substitution of the Interim Resolution Professional through proper committee channels. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Implementation of resolution professional replacement mechanisms under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent and instructions provided by counsel on behalf of the financial creditor[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of based on joint submissions and undertakings regarding the replacement of the IRP[cite: 16].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of in view of the submissions made by the respondent's counsel that the IRP will step down and a new IRP's name will be proposed by the Committee of Creditors for NCLT Kolkata Bench consideration[cite: 16].
summary: Sree Metaliks Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 3 of 2017 challenging the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order dated January 30, 2017[cite: 16]. During the hearing, the appellant submitted that it had no objection to the initiation of proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 16]. Furthermore, the respondent's counsel stated that the existing Interim Resolution Professional would step down without prejudice and that a new IRP would be chosen through the Committee of Creditors to be placed before the NCLT[cite: 16]. Consequently, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal[cite: 16].

case_title: Purshottam Vishandas Raheja & Ors. vs. M/s. Courchevel Trading Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Purshottam Vishandas Raheja & Ors. and the Respondent is M/s. Courchevel Trading Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leave and license agreement concerning company property under corporate disputes. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned order passed on February 20, 2017; appeal decided on April 6, 2017; license extension granted up to June 30, 2017[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Practical difficulties in leasing out property and the need for uninterrupted revenue inflow for the company[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal challenging the NCLT Mumbai Bench order in I.A. No. 04/2017 in TCP No. 88/597/398/NCLT/MB/MAH/2014, which allowed the extension of a leave and license agreement[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal should interfere with an NCLT order extending a leave and license agreement to protect company revenue and address leasing difficulties.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with interlocutory management orders that extend lease terms to secure uninterrupted revenue and mitigate practical leasing difficulties without causing prejudice to petitioners[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Balance of convenience and preservation of company assets during pending company petitions[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of practical property management needs and consistency with coordinate bench orders[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of with directions for the primary tribunal to expedite the final hearing of the main company petitions[cite: 17].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of with observations confirming the 4-month lease extension up to June 30, 2017, and directing parties to commence immediate arguments for the disposal of the main Company Petitions preferably by May 15, 2017[cite: 17]. No costs[cite: 17].
summary: Purshottam Vishandas Raheja & Ors. filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 83 of 2017 challenging the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order dated February 20, 2017, which permitted the renewal of a leave and license agreement for four months until June 30, 2017[cite: 17]. The NCLAT declined to interfere, noting that the extension prevented prejudice by securing an uninterrupted inflow of revenue and addressing leasing difficulties[cite: 17]. Citing consistency with related appeals, the tribunal disposed of the appeal while directing parties to conclude arguments on the main company petitions by May 15, 2017[cite: 17].

case_title: Hounslow Builders Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Lakshmi Steels
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Hounslow Builders Pvt. Ltd. and the Respondent is M/s. Lakshmi Steels. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency and debt recovery dispute. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal listed and disposed of on December 14, 2017[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Instructions received by the appellant's counsel to withdraw the appeal[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant sought permission to withdraw the insolvency appeal during the hearing[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an insolvency appeal and whether liberty should be granted to challenge the same impugned order again.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant is entitled to withdraw an appeal upon request, but the appellate tribunal may bar future challenges against the same impugned order[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of procedural withdrawal discretion in insolvency appellate proceedings[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of counsel's instructions and voluntary withdrawal request[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn without liberty to re-litigate the same order[cite: 18].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, without any liberty to challenge the same very impugned order before the Appellate Tribunal[cite: 18].
summary: Hounslow Builders Pvt. Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 287 of 2017 against M/s. Lakshmi Steels before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal[cite: 18]. During the hearing on December 14, 2017, the appellant's counsel stated that she had received instructions to withdraw the appeal[cite: 18]. The NCLAT granted the request, dismissing the appeal as withdrawn while expressly denying any liberty to challenge the same impugned order before the appellate tribunal again[cite: 18].

case_title: Ghanshyam Sarda vs. The Agarpara Company Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Ghanshyam Sarda and the Respondents are The Agarpara Company Ltd. & Ors. (including Respondent Nos. 1, 18, and 30 represented by senior advocates). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate management dispute and company petition proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned procedural order passed on July 4, 2017; appellate disposal on August 16, 2017[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Directions by the lower authority requiring parties to file replies and rejoinders[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against an NCLT procedural order directing pleadings, disposed of in terms of a parallel order passed on the same day in Company Appeal (AT) No. 264 of 2017[cite: 19].
legal_issues: Whether a procedural order directing the filing of replies and rejoinders should be modified in light of concurrent appellate rulings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Procedural orders directing pleadings in company law disputes can be modified or disposed of in alignment with parallel appellate decisions delivered on the same date[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Harmonization of procedural directions across connected company appeals[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of concurrent appellate proceedings and filings[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of and the impugned procedural order stands modified in terms of the companion appeal[cite: 19].
operative_order: The appeal stands disposed of following the order passed in Company Appeal (AT) No. 264 of 2017, and the impugned order dated July 4, 2017, stands modified accordingly, with no order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary: Ghanshyam Sarda filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 265 of 2017 against The Agarpara Company Ltd. & Ors. challenging an NCLT order dated July 4, 2017, which directed parties to file replies and rejoinders[cite: 19]. Noting a concurrent decision rendered on August 16, 2017, in Company Appeal (AT) No. 264 of 2017, the NCLAT disposed of the appeal and modified the impugned procedural order accordingly, with no order as to costs[cite: 19].

case_title: M/s. Della Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s. Rei Agro Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Della Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (acting as a third party/creditor) and the Respondents are M/s. Rei Agro Ltd. & Anr. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution application filed under Section 9 of the IBC, 2016, leading to admission, a moratorium order, and appointment of an Interim Resolution Professional. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in the short order, but involved debt recovery claims by a third party. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority Kolkata Bench admission order passed on February 27, 2017; appellate decision rendered on May 9, 2017[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Moratorium order staying recovery proceedings, coupled with statutory public notice requirements under Section 15 of the IBC[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A third party filed an appeal challenging the admission order because the moratorium stayed its recovery proceedings, which the NCLAT rejected while preserving claim rights before the IRP[cite: 20].
legal_issues: Whether a third party or creditor can challenge an order admitting a Section 9 insolvency application and imposing a moratorium solely because recovery proceedings are stayed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with a valid Section 9 insolvency admission order and statutory moratorium at the instance of a third-party creditor whose recovery proceedings are incidentally stayed, provided alternative statutory remedies exist[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Scope of Section 14 moratorium and Section 15 public notice claim procedures under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Satisfaction of Section 9(5) requirements by the adjudicating authority and availability of claims via IRP public announcements[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal lacks merit and the challenge is rejected, while affirming the appellant's liberty to submit claims before the Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 20].
operative_order: The prayer to interfere with the impugned order is rejected for lack of merit, but it remains open to the appellant to apply and raise its claim pursuant to the advertisement published by the IRP. The appeal stands disposed of[cite: 20].
summary: M/s. Della Constructions Pvt. Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 35 of 2017 as a third party challenging the Kolkata Bench Adjudicating Authority's order dated February 27, 2017, which admitted a Section 9 insolvency application against M/s. Rei Agro Ltd., declared a moratorium, and appointed an IRP[cite: 20]. The appellant's main grievance was that its debt recovery proceedings were stayed by the moratorium[cite: 20]. The NCLAT held that there was no ground to interfere with the admission order and noted that all creditors could raise their claims before the IRP pursuant to public notices issued under Section 15 of the Code, thereby dismissing the appeal while preserving claim rights[cite: 20].

case_title: Kanak Resources Management Limited & Anr. vs. Mr. Vivek Agarwal & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Kanak Resources Management Limited & Anr., and the Respondents are Mr. Vivek Agarwal & Anr. (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of services under an operational arrangement, culminating in an application under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in monetary terms within the short order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Adjudicating Authority order passed on September 25, 2017; appellate decision rendered on October 5, 2017[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Absence of any document or evidence demonstrating the pre-existence of a dispute relating to the 'quality of service' raised by the appellants prior to the issuance of the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi order admitting the Section 9 application, which the appellate tribunal found was correctly decided[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted a Section 9 application under the IBC, 2016, in the absence of any pre-existing dispute regarding service quality prior to a Section 8 notice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC is rightly admitted by the Adjudicating Authority if the application is complete and there is no documentary proof showing an existing dispute raised prior to the Section 8 notice[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Interpretation of pre-existing dispute thresholds under Sections 8 and 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of records to verify whether any dispute concerning service quality was formally raised prior to the statutory demand notice[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal lacks merit because the Section application was complete and no prior dispute existed, leading to the dismissal of the appeal[cite: 21].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for lack of merit. No costs[cite: 21].
summary: Kanak Resources Management Limited & Anr. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 203 of 2017 challenging the NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi order dated September 25, 2017, which admitted an operational insolvency application under Section 9 of the IBC[cite: 21]. The NCLAT observed that the application was complete and that no documents showed any pre-existing dispute regarding the quality of service raised prior to the Section 8 demand notice[cite: 21]. Consequently, the appellate tribunal held that the Adjudicating Authority rightly admitted the application and dismissed the appeal with no costs[cite: 21].

case_title: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust, the Respondent is the Competition Commission of India (CCI), and Respondent Nos. 2 to 5 are contesting parties. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Competition law proceedings and regulatory determinations before the CCI. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Parallel appeal decided on December 5, 2017; current appeal disposed of on December 7, 2017[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Prior appellate adjudication upholding the impugned judgment in Competition Appeal (AT) No. 04 of 2017, rendering the matter a judgment in rem[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant sought to withdraw the appeal with liberty to file a fresh one, which was contested on the grounds that a coordinate bench had already dismissed a parallel challenge as a judgment in rem[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw a competition appeal with liberty to file a fresh petition when the underlying judgment has already been upheld as a judgment in rem in a parallel appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal against a judgment that operates as a judgment in rem and has been conclusively upheld by the appellate tribunal cannot be re-litigated, and liberty to file a fresh appeal on the same cause of action must be denied[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of the doctrine of judgment in rem in competition law appellate proceedings[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of prior appellate rulings delivered on December 5, 2017, in connected matters[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn, and the request for liberty to file a fresh appeal on the same cause of action is explicitly declined[cite: 22].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as withdrawn. Liberty to file a fresh appeal founded on the same cause of action is declined[cite: 22].
summary: Jawaharlal Nehru Port Trust filed Competition Appeal (AT) No. 15 of 2017 against the Competition Commission of India & Ors.[cite: 22]. During the hearing, the appellant sought to withdraw the appeal with liberty to file a fresh one for the same cause of action[cite: 22]. Opposing respondents pointed out that the impugned judgment had already been upheld by the appellate tribunal on December 5, 2017, in Competition Appeal (AT) No. 04 of 2017, constituting a judgment in rem that could not be questioned even by a non-party[cite: 22]. Keeping this in view, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal as withdrawn while declining any liberty to file a fresh appeal[cite: 22].

case_title: Doloo Tea Co. (India) Ltd. vs. Kanubhai C. Patel & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Doloo Tea Co. (India) Ltd. and the Respondents are Kanubhai C. Patel & Ors. (represented by senior advocates and counsel). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition and corporate shareholding disputes before the NCLT Guwahati Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and disposed of on April 20, 2017[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions made by counsel seeking voluntary withdrawal to pursue contentions before the primary tribunal[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following initial arguments, the appellants sought permission to withdraw the appeal, which the tribunal granted while clarifying that except for the substitution question, no other issues (including the 1/10th share capital threshold) were decided[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw a company appeal with liberty to raise all contentions before the NCLT while preserving specific interim determinations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellant may withdraw an appeal to raise all contentions before the primary adjudicating authority, provided the appellate court clarifies which specific interlocutory questions (such as substitution) stand concluded[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Preservation of statutory thresholds and primary forum jurisdiction in company law disputes[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of counsel's submissions and limitation of appellate findings to resolved issues like substitution[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with liberty to agitate all remaining issues before the Guwahati Bench of the NCLT[cite: 23].
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of as withdrawn with liberty to the appellants to raise all contentions before the National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench, clarifying that no issues other than substitution are decided[cite: 23].
summary: Doloo Tea Co. (India) Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 49 of 2017 against Kanubhai C. Patel & Ors[cite: 23]. After some arguments on April 20, 2017, the appellants' counsel sought and was granted permission to withdraw the appeal with liberty to raise all contentions before the National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench[cite: 23]. The NCLAT explicitly clarified that it did not decide any issues—including whether the petitioners held one-tenth of the company's total share capital—except for the question of substitution, which stood decided[cite: 23].

case_title: M/s. Lease Pal India Pvt. Ltd. vs. ACPL HR Services Pvt. Ltd.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 969 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 312 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Lease Pal India Pvt. Ltd. and the Respondent is ACPL HR Services Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency dispute arising from an order passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT), New Delhi in IB-208/ND/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the interlocutory order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on October 17, 2017; application filed seeking condonation of a 14-day delay in filing the appeal[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Grounds presented in the application explaining the cause of delay in preferring the appeal[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An interlocutory application (I.A. No. 969 of 2017) was filed to condone a 14-day delay in filing Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 312 of 2017[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a 14-day delay in filing an insolvency appeal can be condoned when sufficient grounds are shown by the appellant.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will condone a minor statutory delay in filing an appeal if the appellant demonstrates satisfactory and sufficient grounds[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Condonation of delay principles under insolvency appellate frameworks[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluation of the explanation and grounds provided in the delay condonation application[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay of 14 days is successfully explained and condoned, allowing the interlocutory application[cite: 24].
operative_order: The delay of 14 days in preferring the appeal is condoned, and I.A. No. 969 of 2017 stands disposed of[cite: 24].
summary: M/s. Lease Pal India Pvt. Ltd. filed an interlocutory application (I.A. No. 969 of 2017) seeking the condonation of a 14-day delay in filing Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 312 of 2017 against the NCLT New Delhi order dated October 17, 2017[cite: 24]. The NCLAT reviewed the submissions, expressed satisfaction with the grounds shown in the appeal, and condoned the 14-day delay, disposing of the interlocutory application accordingly[cite: 24].

case_title: Vikas Promoters Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Abinash Chander Mahajan & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Vikas Promoters Pvt. Ltd. & Ors., and the Respondents are Abinash Chander Mahajan & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition proceedings (C.P. No. 110(ND)2009) involving financial deposits and adjustments. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed deposit of Rs. 3.5 crores subsequent to an attempted adjustment of Rs. 50 lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned orders pronounced on March 22, 2017, and August 4, 2017; appeals decided on September 12, 2017[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records showing failure to satisfy limitation requirements for the March 22, 2017 order, alongside subsequent deposits totaling Rs. 3.5 crores[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appeals filed against two orders where the challenge to the first order was not pressed due to limitation bars, and the challenge to the second order (refusing to modify the first order) was rejected as the primary order had reached finality[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an appellate tribunal can interfere with a subsequent order refusing to modify a primary tribunal order that has already attained finality due to limitation bars.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not interfere with an order declining to modify a prior ruling that has already reached finality, though parties may bring subsequent factual compliance (such as monetary deposits) to the primary tribunal's notice without implying judicial approval of specific debt adjustments[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Finality of unappealed or time-barred tribunal orders under company law[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of limitation compliance and the legal effect of finality on interlocutory modification requests[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals are dismissed because the primary order attained finality and was barred by limitation, though the appellants retain the liberty to inform the tribunal of subsequent deposits[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal against the order dated March 22, 2017, is dismissed as not pressed and barred by limitation. The appeal against the order dated August 4, 2017, is dismissed with observations that this order does not bar the appellants from bringing subsequent deposits of Rs. 3.5 crores to the Tribunal's notice, without permitting the adjustment of Rs. 50 lakhs[cite: 25].
summary: Vikas Promoters Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. filed Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 299-300 of 2017 challenging orders dated March 22, 2017, and August 4, 2017, passed in Company Petition No. 110(ND)2009[cite: 25]. Because the appellants could not satisfy the delay condonation requirements for the March 22 order, they did not press that challenge, leading to its dismissal as time-barred[cite: 25]. Regarding the August 4 order—where the NCLT refused to modify the earlier ruling despite a subsequent deposit of Rs. 3.5 crores—the NCLAT declined to interfere since the primary order had reached finality, though it clarified that the appellants could still apprise the tribunal of their deposit without endorsing any specific Rs. 50 lakh adjustment[cite: 25]. Both appeals were accordingly dismissed[cite: 25].

case_title: Ellora Paper Mills Limited & Anr. vs. Ajithnath Steels Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Ellora Paper Mills Limited & Anr., and the Respondent is Ajithnath Steels Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution process arising from C.P. No. 716/I&BP/2017 before the NCLT Mumbai Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT order passed on August 21, 2017; appellate decision rendered on November 15, 2017[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Expiry of the original Interim Resolution Professional's license and subsequent appointment of an eligible regular Resolution Professional after 30 days[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against the NCLT Mumbai Bench order changing the IRP after 30 days, which became infructuous upon the regular RP taking charge[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal challenging the replacement of an Interim Resolution Professional becomes infructuous once a regular Resolution Professional is appointed after 30 days.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal challenging interlocutory administrative arrangements regarding resolution professionals becomes infructuous and is liable to be dismissed when the underlying event (appointment of a regular Resolution Professional) has taken place[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Transition from Interim Resolution Professional to regular Resolution Professional under corporate insolvency rules[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acceptance by appellant counsel that the regular RP has taken over after 30 days[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal has become infructuous and is dismissed with no costs[cite: 26].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed being infructuous. No cost[cite: 26].
summary: Ellora Paper Mills Limited & Anr. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 153 of 2017 challenging the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated August 21, 2017, which changed the Interim Resolution Professional after 30 days[cite: 26]. During the hearing, the respondent noted that the original IRP's license had expired and another eligible person had been appointed[cite: 26]. Because the appellants accepted that a regular Resolution Professional had taken over after 30 days, rendering the appeal infructuous, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal accordingly[cite: 26].

case_title: M/s. Zapp India Limited vs. M/s. Maheshwar Textile & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is M/s. Zapp India Limited and the Respondents are M/s. Maheshwar Textile & Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution proceedings bearing Appeal No. IB No. (IB)-170(ND) of 2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior order passed on September 22, 2017; clarification application (I.A. No. 856 of 2017) decided on November 16, 2017[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clear statutory framework specifying that the Interim Resolution Professional functions for 30 days, followed by the regular Resolution Professional[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An interlocutory application seeking clarification of an earlier order was filed, which the appellate tribunal dismissed as the statutory position was already unambiguous[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether a clarification application regarding the tenure and functioning of an Interim Resolution Professional should be entertained when the statutory mandate is clear.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications seeking clarification of unambiguous tribunal orders and statutory timelines—where an Interim Resolution Professional functions for 30 days before a Resolution Professional takes over—are unwarranted and liable to be dismissed[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Statutory tenure limits of Interim Resolution Professionals under insolvency law[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Review of prior order dated September 22, 2017, and lack of valid grounds for ambiguity[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No grounds are made out for clarification, leading to the dismissal of the interlocutory application[cite: 27].
operative_order: I.A. No. 856 of 2017 is dismissed, and no further order is required to be passed[cite: 27].
summary: M/s. Zapp India Limited filed I.A. No. 856 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 157 of 2017 seeking clarification of the tribunal's order dated September 22, 2017[cite: 27]. The NCLAT held that no grounds were made out for clarification because the previous order was specific, emphasizing that an Interim Resolution Professional functions for 30 days before a Resolution Professional takes over the remainder of the resolution process[cite: 27]. Consequently, the interlocutory application was dismissed[cite: 27].

case_title: VA Tech Wabag Ltd. & Anr. vs. Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are VA Tech Wabag Ltd. & Anr., and the Respondents are Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. & Anr. (including 1st Respondent represented by counsel). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Insolvency resolution and debt dispute proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the withdrawal order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeals heard and disposed of on November 2, 2017[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voluntary submission by appellant counsel seeking withdrawal with no objection raised by the opposing respondent[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellants sought permission to withdraw the insolvency appeals during the hearing, which was granted upon receiving no objection from the respondents[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether appellants can withdraw insolvency appeals when the contesting respondents express no objection.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal when the appellant voluntarily seeks to withdraw and the opposing party raises no objection[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of procedural withdrawal discretion in insolvency appellate proceedings[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consent and lack of objection from counsel for the 1st respondent[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeals are dismissed as withdrawn based on the joint stance of the parties[cite: 28].
operative_order: The appeals are accordingly dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 28].
summary: VA Tech Wabag Ltd. & Anr. filed Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 216-217 of 2017 before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal against Consolidated Construction Consortium Ltd. & Anr[cite: 28]. During the hearing on November 2, 2017, the appellants' counsel sought permission to withdraw the appeals[cite: 28]. As the counsel for the 1st respondent stated there was no objection to this course of action, the NCLAT dismissed the appeals as withdrawn[cite: 28].

case_title: K. Kishan vs. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is K. Kishan and the Respondent is Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency application arising from CP(IB) No. 100/9/HDB/2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in the short order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Impugned Adjudicating Authority order passed on August 29, 2017; appellate decision rendered on November 20, 2017[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Binding precedent established on the same day in a connected case involving the same impugned order[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed against an NCLT order where the core issues were directly governed by the appellate tribunal's judgment delivered on the same date in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2017[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when the underlying issues and impugned order have already been adjudicated and dismissed in a connected coordinate appeal on the same day.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is dismissed on the same grounds as a companion judgment delivered on the same date when the subject matter and impugned order are identical[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Application of judicial consistency across connected insolvency appeals[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that the case is covered by the ruling in 'Ksheerabad Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.' (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2017)[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is dismissed for the same reasons set forth in the connected judgment with no order as to costs[cite: 29].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed for the same ground as shown in 'Ksheerabad Construction Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.' (Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2017) decided on November 20, 2017. There shall be no order as to cost[cite: 29].
summary: K. Kishan filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 211 of 2017 challenging the Adjudicating Authority's order dated August 29, 2017, passed in CP(IB) No. 100/9/HDB/2017[cite: 29]. The NCLAT noted that the exact same impugned order had been challenged in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 167 of 2017 ('Ksheerabad Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt. Ltd.'), which was dismissed by the tribunal via a judgment delivered on November 20, 2017[cite: 29]. Holding that the appellant's case was fully covered by that decision, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal on the same grounds with no order as to costs[cite: 29].

case_title: Mrs. Tripat Kaur vs. M/s. Kaliber Associates Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Contempt Petition No. 09 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 52 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Petitioner is Mrs. Tripat Kaur and the Respondents/Contemnors are M/s. Kaliber Associates Private Limited & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate financial compliance and settlement arising from prior insolvency appellate proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Payment of Rs. 1.12 crores made by contemnors through a third party, with a disputed remaining claim of Rs. 14 lakhs[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contempt proceedings heard and closed on December 5, 2017[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Acceptance by the petitioner's counsel that a substantial sum of Rs. 1.12 crores has been paid, leaving only a disputed balance of Rs. 14 lakhs[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: A contempt petition was initiated for non-compliance, which the tribunal closed upon noting that substantial payment had been made and remaining disputes fell outside contempt jurisdiction[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether contempt proceedings should be continued when a substantial part of the decretal or settled amount has been paid and the remainder is a disputed monetary claim.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt proceedings will not be pursued or continued when a substantial portion of the financial obligation has been satisfied and the remaining amount involves a genuine monetary dispute[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Scope and limits of contempt jurisdiction in enforcing appellate financial settlements[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Acknowledgment of receipt of substantial payments (Rs. 1.12 crores) alongside unresolved minor claims[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tribunal declines to proceed further in the matter since substantial compliance has occurred, leading to the closure of the contempt petition[cite: 30].
operative_order: The contempt proceeding is closed. No cost[cite: 30].
summary: Mrs. Tripat Kaur filed Contempt Petition No. 09 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 52 of 2017 against M/s. Kaliber Associates Private Limited & Ors[cite: 30]. During the hearing on December 5, 2017, the petitioner's counsel accepted that the contemnors had paid a sum of Rs. 1.12 crores through a third party, though a further claim of Rs. 14 lakhs was asserted[cite: 30]. Because a substantial part of the amount had been paid and the rest was disputed, the NCLAT ruled that it would not proceed further with the contempt action, closing the proceedings with no order as to costs[cite: 30].

case_title: K.N. Pillai & Anr. vs. R. Prasanth & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are K.N. Pillai & Anr., and the Respondents are R. Prasanth & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company law dispute. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Defective appeal filed in March 2017; defects notified on March 6, 2017; more than 7 weeks passed without taking steps[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Defects included an improper Vakalatnama, unfiled memo of parties, lack of appellants' signatures, and other formatting flaws[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal filed with multiple incurable defects where no steps were taken to remove them despite a lapse of over 7 weeks, leading to listing and dismissal[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal should be dismissed when the appellant fails to remove notified procedural defects over a period exceeding seven weeks.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal is liable to be dismissed if the appellant fails to rectify fundamental procedural defects (such as improper Vakalatnama and lack of signatures) within a reasonable time window[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Strict enforcement of appellate filing compliance rules. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification that over 7 weeks elapsed without any steps taken to cure the notified defects[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is dismissed due to uncorrected procedural defects and inaction[cite: 31].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 31].
summary: K.N. Pillai & Anr. filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 128 of 2017 against R. Prasanth & Ors[cite: 31]. Although the appeal was filed in March 2017, the appellants failed to remove notified defects—such as an improper Vakalatnama, missing memo of parties, and lack of signatures—for more than seven weeks[cite: 31]. Consequently, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 31].

case_title: Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav vs. M/s. Steel India Corporation & Anr.
appeal_number: I.A. No. 858 of 2017 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 212 of 2017
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The applicant is Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav (Director of the Corporate Debtor M/s. Shree Radha Raman Packaging Pvt. Ltd.), the original appellant is the Corporate Debtor, and the 1st Respondent is M/s. Steel India Corporation. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate insolvency resolution proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not specified in the interlocutory application order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Interlocutory application for substitution heard and decided on November 21, 2017[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Authorization and Vakalatnama previously filed by Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav on behalf of the corporate debtor[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An interlocutory application was filed to substitute a company director as the appellant and transpose the original corporate debtor as the second respondent[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether a director of a corporate debtor can be substituted as the appellant in place of the corporate debtor in an insolvency appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A director of a corporate debtor is permitted to be substituted as the appellant in an insolvency appeal, with the original corporate debtor transposed as a respondent through its Interim Resolution Professional[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Representation and standing of corporate directors in insolvency appeals[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Existence of prior authorization and independent Vakalatnama filed by the director[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The substitution application is allowed, replacing the corporate debtor appellant with its director[cite: 32].
operative_order: I.A. No. 858 of 2017 is allowed. Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav is substituted as Appellant, and Shree Radha Raman Packaging Pvt. Ltd. is transposed as Second Respondent through the Interim Resolution Professional, with necessary cause title corrections made[cite: 32].
summary: Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav, Director of the Corporate Debtor M/s. Shree Radha Raman Packaging Pvt. Ltd., filed I.A. No. 858 of 2017 seeking substitution as the appellant in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 212 of 2017 against M/s. Steel India Corporation & Anr[cite: 32]. The NCLAT heard the parties and allowed the application, substituting Shri Shyam Sunder Yadav as the appellant and transposing the original corporate debtor as the second respondent through its Interim Resolution Professional, while clarifying that his previously filed Vakalatnama would serve as an independent Vakalatnama[cite: 32].

case_title: Mrs. Sonia Khosla vs. Vikram Bakshi
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Applicant is Mrs. Sonia Khosla and the Respondent is Vikram Bakshi. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Contempt proceedings arising from corporate litigation and pending company petitions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contempt case heard and disposed of on November 17, 2017[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Request by the appellant's counsel to withdraw the contempt case coupled with a plea for an early hearing before the NCLT[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant sought permission to withdraw the contempt case to pursue expedited hearings in the main company petition before the National Company Law Tribunal[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether a contempt case can be withdrawn upon request while granting a request to direct the NCLT to expedite the main company petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant may withdraw a contempt case, and the appellate tribunal may request the primary tribunal to expedite pending proceedings (excluding matters where appeals are active)[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Exercise of administrative expedition powers over subordinate tribunals[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment of counsel's withdrawal request and judicial management of pending company petitions[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The contempt case is disposed of as withdrawn alongside an administrative request for early disposal by the NCLT[cite: 33].
operative_order: The contempt case is disposed of as withdrawn with observations requesting the National Company Law Tribunal to decide the matter pending before it at an early date, except in relation to matters where an appeal is pending[cite: 33].
summary: Mrs. Sonia Khosla filed Contempt Case (AT) No. 1 of 2017 against Vikram Bakshi[cite: 33]. During the hearing on November 17, 2017, the appellant's counsel sought permission to withdraw the case while requesting the appellate tribunal to direct the NCLT to decide the main company petition early[cite: 33]. The NCLAT permitted the withdrawal and requested the NCLT to expedite the pending proceedings, except for matters subject to active appeals[cite: 33].

case_title: Omniactive Health Technologies Ltd. vs. Indus Finance Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Omniactive Health Technologies Ltd., the Respondents include Indus Finance Limited, and Respondent No. 3 is represented by counsel. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial dispute and refund agreement involving corporate transactions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not explicitly quantified in terms of total monetary figures in the short order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal heard and disposed of on December 18, 2017[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement by the 3rd Respondent to refund the disputed amount, prompting instructions to withdraw the appeal[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The appellant sought permission to withdraw the insolvency appeal during the hearing based on an out-of-court refund settlement[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether an appellant can withdraw an insolvency appeal when a respondent agrees to refund the subject amount.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will permit the withdrawal of an appeal when the underlying dispute is resolved through an agreement by a respondent to refund the disputed funds[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Facilitating amicable settlements and withdrawals in insolvency appeals[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Confirmation of instructions given by counsel to withdraw following refund commitments[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Permission is granted and the appeal stands dismissed as withdrawn[cite: 34].
operative_order: Permission is granted, and the appeal is disposed of as withdrawn[cite: 34].
summary: Omniactive Health Technologies Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 257 of 2017 against Indus Finance Limited & Ors[cite: 34]. During the hearing on December 18, 2017, the appellant's counsel stated that she had been instructed by counsel Mr. Rishi Agarwal to withdraw the appeal because the 3rd Respondent had agreed to refund the amount[cite: 34]. The NCLAT granted permission and disposed of the appeal as withdrawn[cite: 34].

case_title: Innoventive Industries Ltd. vs. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Innoventive Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor through IRP) and the Respondent is Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Utility service contract for electricity supply subject to an insolvency moratorium. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Consumption charges due from the date of moratorium (January 17, 2017) until September 2017. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Moratorium imposed on January 17, 2017; prior order passed on September 21, 2017; appellate order issued on October 6, 2017[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submissions showing the respondent's willingness to restore electricity connections if post-moratorium consumption charges are cleared[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: An appeal arising from utility disconnections where the respondent agreed to restore power upon payment of post-moratorium dues, protecting the corporate debtor's ongoing status[cite: 35].
legal_issues: Whether an Interim Resolution Professional can be directed to pay post-moratorium utility consumption charges to secure the restoration of essential electrical services for an ongoing corporate debtor.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional is liable to pay utility consumption charges incurred strictly from the date of the moratorium onward, and upon such payment, utility providers must restore essential services within 48 hours to keep the corporate debtor a going concern, while pre-moratorium dues must be handled through the resolution plan[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Scope of moratorium protections under Section 14 of the IBC, 2016, regarding pre-moratorium versus post-moratorium operational dues[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of post-moratorium consumption periods (January 17, 2017, to September 2017) and utility restoration timelines[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal is disposed of by allowing the IRP to pay post-moratorium electricity charges, mandating the restoration of power within 48 hours, and exempting the debtor from pre-moratorium dues at this stage[cite: 35].
operative_order: The IRP is allowed to pay charges due to the respondent for electricity consumption from the date of moratorium (January 17, 2017) until September 2017. Upon deposit, the respondent shall restore the electrical connection within 48 hours, and the IRP shall pay ongoing monthly consumption charges thereafter. Pre-moratorium dues are excluded from immediate payment and deferred for consideration under the resolution plan. The appeal stands disposed of[cite: 35].
summary: Innoventive Industries Ltd. filed Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 156 of 2017 against Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Ltd[cite: 35]. During the hearing on October 6, 2017, the respondent stated it would restore the corporate debtor's electrical connection if consumption dues since the moratorium date (January 17, 2017) were paid[cite: 35]. The NCLAT permitted the IRP to pay electricity consumption charges from January 17, 2017, to September 2017, directing the respondent to restore power within 48 hours to ensure the company remained a going concern while making ongoing monthly payments mandatory[cite: 35]. The tribunal clarified that the corporate debtor was not liable to pay pre-moratorium dues at this stage, leaving those to be addressed under the resolution plan[cite: 35].

summary.case_title: Babulal Vardhaji Gurjar vs. Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Babulal Vardhaji Gurjar is the Suspended Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 1); JM Financial Assets Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Assignee of Corporation Bank (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities sanctioned and disbursed on 22.12.2007 by Corporation Bank along with consortium member Indian Overseas Bank against equitable mortgage of 9 industrial plots/buildings and hypothecation of current and movable assets[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default committed on 08.07.2011; total claimed default arising out of bank loan facilities[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Consortium lender Indian Overseas Bank issued recall notice on 15.11.2011, followed by SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice published on 28.12.2011; debt assigned to JM Financial on 30.03.2013; Section 7 petition filed on 21.03.2018[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered Assignment Agreement dated 30.03.2013; Corporate Debtor's Annual Reports dated 13.09.2012, 15.09.2013, 01.09.2014, and 10.09.2016 continuously acknowledging the loan; OA No. 172/2013 pending under Section 19 of RDDBFI Act before DRT Aurangabad; One Time Settlement proposal letter dated 31.07.2018 sent by Corporate Debtor[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted JM Financial's Section 7 petition on 09.08.2018 in CP (IB) 488/I&BP/MB/2018; NCLAT initially dismissed the appeal on 17.09.2018, but the Supreme Court remitted the matter on 26.02.2019 in Civil Appeal No. 10710 of 2018 to examine the root issue of statutory limitation[cite: 10].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an application under Section 7 of the IBC filed in March 2018 for a default occurring on 08.07.2011 is barred by limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and whether continuing balance sheet acknowledgments, pending DRT recovery proceedings, and mortgage security enforceability extend or protect the debt from being time-barred[cite: 10].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the IBC, an application under Section 7 is not time-barred where the debt is continuously acknowledged in balance sheets, pending recovery proceedings under special debt recovery statutes maintain a continuous cause of action, and the underlying debt is secured by a mortgage attracting a 12-year period of limitation under property laws[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A applies the Limitation Act, 1963 to IBC proceedings; under Article 137, the right to apply under the Code accrued upon the enforcement of the IBC on 01.12.2016; furthermore, Section 5(7) read with Section 5(8) covers secured debts backed by mortgages, where Article 61(b) grants 12 years for enforceability against mortgaged assets, preventing the debt from becoming legally unpayable[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the debt was payable in fact and law under Innoventive Industries, relying on statutory balance sheet disclosures from 2012 to 2016, DRT recovery proceedings, and a written OTS offer dated 31.07.2018 as conclusive evidence of subsisting liability[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt was neither barred by limitation nor extinguished, and the Section 7 petition was filed well within the statutory period under Article 137 read with Section 238A[cite: 10].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is found devoid of merit and is dismissed[cite: 10]. The order of admission dated 9th August, 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP (IB) 488/I&BP/MB/2018 is upheld[cite: 10]. No order as to costs[cite: 10].
summary.summary: Babulal Vardhaji Gurjar, suspended director of Veer Gurjar Aluminium Industries Pvt. Ltd., appealed the admission of a Section 7 IBC petition filed by JM Financial Assets Reconstruction Company Pvt. Ltd., contending that default occurred on 8th July 2011 and the 2018 petition was time-barred[cite: 10]. Upon remand from the Supreme Court, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the right to apply under the Code accrued upon its inception on 1st December 2016[cite: 10]. Moreover, the debt was continuously acknowledged in corporate annual reports, recovery remained pending before the DRT, and the claim was secured by registered mortgages attracting a twelve-year limitation period, establishing that the financial debt remained fully payable in law[cite: 10].

summary.case_title: Standard Chartered Bank & Ors. vs. Satish Kumar Gupta, R.P. of Essar Steel Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Essar Steel India Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Satish Kumar Gupta is the Resolution Professional; ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Standard Chartered Bank (SCB), State Bank of India (SBI), and consortium lenders are Financial Creditors; various entities (MSTC, BPCL, IOCL, Sakar, DGVC, State Tax Officer) are Operational Creditors; Prashant Ruia is the Suspended Promoter[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Heavy industrial debt facilities, working capital, trade supplies, and a USD 500 Million loan extended by SCB to Essar Steel Offshore Limited backed by Corporate Debtor's corporate guarantee and share pledge[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claims filed reached Rs. 82,541 Crores; RP admitted Rs. 49,473 Crores for Financial Creditors and initially Rs. 5,074 Crores for Operational Creditors, with resolution package offering upfront payment of Rs. 42,000 Crores[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 02.08.2017; CoC approved resolution plan on 25.10.2018; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench conditionally approved plan on 08.03.2019[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved plan proposed 91.99% payout to secured lenders with project asset charge but only 1.74% (Rs. 60.71 Cr out of Rs. 3,487.10 Cr) to SCB, and 0% to operational creditors with claims of Rs. 1 Crore or more; EBIDTA generated during CIRP stood at approx. Rs. 3,495 Crores[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench approved ArcelorMittal's plan with non-binding recommendations on 08.03.2019; multiple appeals filed challenging commercial discrimination in distribution, CoC delegation of power to a core committee, and promoter ineligibility[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors has the jurisdiction to delegate distribution powers to a core sub-committee and discriminate between secured financial creditors based on project asset charge, whether financial creditors and operational creditors can be treated disparately with operational creditors receiving nil payment, and who is entitled to profits earned during the CIRP[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Committee of Creditors possesses no statutory power to determine or alter the inter se distribution of resolution proceeds or delegate negotiations to an unauthorized core committee; a resolution plan must ensure non-discriminatory and equitable treatment between secured financial creditors and operational creditors without creating artificial sub-classes based on the nature of charge[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Regulation 38(1A) mandate that the manner of distribution among all stakeholders is exclusively the prerogative of the Resolution Applicant, not the CoC; Section 53 liquidation waterfall applies strictly upon asset liquidation and cannot be imported into Section 31 resolution distributions to reduce operational creditors to nil[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied the principles of equitable treatment enunciated in Swiss Ribbons, examining whether the distribution demonstrated rational parity between financial and operational creditors and protected operational debts incurred to maintain the debtor as a going concern[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC's distribution assigning 90-92% to select lenders and 0% to large operational creditors was arbitrary and invalid; the plan is modified to distribute the Rs. 42,000 Crores upfront consideration to provide an equitable pro-rata distribution of approx. 60.7% across both financial and operational creditors[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: The appeal of Standard Chartered Bank and operational creditors is allowed, and the NCLT approval order dated 8th March, 2019 is modified[cite: 11]. The resolution plan consideration of Rs. 42,000 Crores is re-apportioned to pay 60.7% pro-rata to both Financial Creditors (Rs. 3,00,30.44 Cr) and Operational Creditors (Rs. 1,19,69.55 Cr), retaining 100% payout for employees and claims under Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 11]. CIRP operational profits of Rs. 3,495 Crores ordered to be distributed pro-rata among creditors[cite: 11]. Ruia's appeal challenging eligibility is dismissed[cite: 11].
summary.summary: Multiple stakeholders appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 8th March 2019 approving ArcelorMittal's resolution plan for Essar Steel India Limited, which allocated 91.99% of claims to secured financial creditors with project asset charges while offering Standard Chartered Bank 1.74% and large operational creditors 0%[cite: 11]. The NCLAT held that the Committee of Creditors has no jurisdiction to decide inter se distribution or delegate powers to a core sub-committee[cite: 11]. Reaffirming Swiss Ribbons, the Appellate Tribunal held that Section 53 cannot justify discriminatory zero-payouts to operational creditors[cite: 11]. The NCLAT modified the plan to distribute the Rs. 42,000 Crore consideration equally on a 60.7% pro-rata basis across financial and operational debts[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: Sesh Nath Singh & Anr. vs. Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Co-Operative Bank Ltd. & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sesh Nath Singh and Akshay Kumar Singh are Directors of the Corporate Debtor (Appellants); Debi Fabtech Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor; Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Co-operative Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Animesh Mukhopadhyay is the Interim Resolution Professional (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Grant of cash credit facility of Rs. 1 Crore by Financial Creditor to Corporate Debtor pursuant to sanction letter dated 12.02.2012 secured by hypothecation of book debts[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt servicing led to classification of Corporate Debtor's loan account as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.03.2013 for outstanding cash credit dues[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI Act issued on 18.01.2014; Section 13(4) possession notice issued on 13.02.2014; Corporate Debtor filed Writ Petition WP No. 33799(W) of 2014 before Calcutta High Court on 19.12.2014; High Court stayed SARFAESI actions on 24.07.2017; Section 7 IBC application filed on 27.08.2018[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letter dated 12.02.2012, hypothecation agreement, SARFAESI notices, District Magistrate Hooghly possession order dated 11.05.2017, and interim stay order of the Calcutta High Court dated 24.07.2017[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed CP (IB) No. 1202/KB/2018 under Section 7 of IBC before NCLT Kolkata Bench; NCLT admitted the petition and initiated CIRP on 25.04.2019 holding debt and default were undisputed; Appellants appealed on grounds of limitation[cite: 12].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the period during which a financial creditor was bona fide prosecuting recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, 2002 can be excluded under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 to save an application under Section 7 of the IBC from being barred by limitation under Article 137[cite: 12].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a creditor has been bona fide prosecuting recovery proceedings with due diligence before another forum or under a statutory recovery enactment against the corporate debtor, the time consumed in such proceedings is excludable under Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 while computing the three-year period under Article 137 for initiating insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 137 prescribes a three-year limitation period commencing from default; however, Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act applies to exclude periods of diligent civil prosecution in computing limitation, ensuring that bona fide litigating creditors are not time-barred when statutory recovery steps were stayed by high court orders[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examined the chronology of continuous litigation from the issuance of Section 13(2) notice on 18.01.2014 until the Calcutta High Court's restraining order dated 24.07.2017 to verify whether the financial creditor acted with due diligence and absence of negligence[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding the period of 3 years and 6 months spent prosecuting SARFAESI remedies, the Section 7 petition filed on 27.08.2018 was well within limitation[cite: 12].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed[cite: 12]. The impugned order of NCLT Kolkata Bench dated 25th April, 2019 initiating Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process is upheld[cite: 12]. No order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary.summary: Sesh Nath Singh and another, directors of Debi Fabtech Private Limited, challenged the NCLT Kolkata order dated 25th April 2019 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Baidyabati Sheoraphuli Co-operative Bank Ltd., arguing that the loan account was declared an NPA on 31st March 2013 and the 2018 petition was time-barred under Article 137 of the Limitation Act[cite: 12]. The NCLAT held that the financial creditor had diligently and bona fide pursued recovery under the SARFAESI Act from 18th January 2014 until the Calcutta High Court stayed the proceedings on 24th July 2017[cite: 12]. Applying Section 14(2) of the Limitation Act, this three-and-a-half-year period was excluded, rendering the Section 7 petition within limitation[cite: 12].

summary.case_title: Y. Shivram Prasad vs. S. Dhanapal & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Y. Shivram Prasad is the Promoter, Director, and Shareholder of Servalakshmi Papers Ltd. (Appellant); Servalakshmi Papers Ltd. (SPL) is the Corporate Debtor; S. Dhanapal is the Liquidator/IRP; Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. (ARCIL) and Sripathi Papers and Boards (P) Ltd. are Resolution Applicants/Financial Creditors[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Establishment and operation of a paper manufacturing plant with a capacity of 300 TPD (90,000 MTPA) and a 15 MW captive power plant funded by consortium loans[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under loan facilities triggered CIRP; in the absence of an approved resolution plan upon expiry of 270 days, the company faced liquidation[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Statutory CIRP period of 270 days expired without CoC securing a 66% majority vote for any modified resolution plan; NCLT Chennai Division Bench passed the liquidation order on 21.06.2017[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor operated a state-of-the-art facility employing over 300 direct and 200 indirect workers with 120 dependent ancillary units; 'Modified ARCIL Resolution Plan' and 'Modified Sripathi Resolution Plan' were submitted but failed to secure the requisite majority of the CoC[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following the lapse of the 270-day CIRP period, NCLT Chennai ordered SPL into liquidation on 21.06.2017; the Promoter and ARCIL appealed, praying for an opportunity to revive the company and avoid corporate death[cite: 13].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Liquidator appointed under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is mandated to explore revival of the Corporate Debtor by taking recourse to a Scheme of Compromise or Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 and selling the enterprise as a going concern prior to resorting to piecemeal asset liquidation[cite: 13].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liquidation under the IBC is an absolute measure of last resort; during liquidation, the Liquidator and Adjudicating Authority must first take active steps to revive the corporate debtor as a going concern through a compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, or through a going-concern sale, before liquidating individual assets[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Harmoniously reading Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 with Sections 33, 35, and 230(1) of the IBC and Regulation 32 of the Liquidation Regulations, the liquidator appointed under the IBC is empowered to sponsor a Section 230 scheme; the NCLT acts dual-fold as the IBC Adjudicating Authority and Company Court to ensure revival and asset maximization[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Followed the Supreme Court's decisions in Swiss Ribbons and Meghal Homes, establishing that preserving business undertakings, sustaining worker employment, and exploring commercial revival take statutory precedence over corporate death[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator must invite and place schemes under Section 230 before a reconstituted committee of creditors, and only upon total failure of compromise and going-concern sale may asset liquidation proceed[cite: 13].
summary.operative_order: Both appeals are disposed of with mandatory directions[cite: 13]. The Liquidator is directed to take steps under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 for compromise or arrangement, moving the NCLT Chennai Bench accordingly, and consulting the creditors on feasibility[cite: 13]. If revival through compromise fails, the Liquidator must sell the Corporate Debtor in its totality as a going concern to protect employment[cite: 13]. Outright asset sale permitted only upon failure of these revival measures[cite: 13]. No costs[cite: 13].
summary.summary: Y. Shivram Prasad, promoter of Servalakshmi Papers Ltd., and ARCIL appealed the NCLT Chennai liquidation order dated 21st June 2017 after the 270-day CIRP elapsed without an approved resolution plan[cite: 13]. Reversing the automatic course toward piecemeal asset distribution, the NCLAT held that liquidation is a last resort and corporate death must be averted[cite: 13]. Relying on the Supreme Court's rulings in Swiss Ribbons and Meghal Homes, the Tribunal directed the Liquidator to first explore revival by inviting and submitting a Scheme of Compromise or Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013, or selling the debtor as a going concern before commencing asset sales[cite: 13].

summary.case_title: Committee of Creditors of Amtek Auto Ltd. vs. Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors of Amtek Auto Ltd. through Corporation Bank is the Appellant; Dinkar T. Venkatasubramanian is the Resolution Professional; Liberty House Group Pte Ltd. (LHG) is the Successful Resolution Applicant; Deccan Value Investors LP (DVI) is the withdrew bidder; Amtek Auto Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Amtek Auto Ltd., wherein LHG's resolution plan was approved by the CoC with 94.20% voting share and subsequently approved by the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: LHG failed to implement the approved plan, defaulting on furnishing a Performance Guarantee and failing to deposit 15% upfront cash consideration amounting to Rs. 528.75 Crores into an escrow account[cite: 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP initiated on 24.07.2017; LHG plan approved by CoC on 02.04.2018; plan sanctioned by NCLT on 25.07.2018; LHG defaulted in September 2018; NCLT passed the impugned order on 13.02.2019[cite: 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bid bond guarantee invocation of Rs. 50 Crores rejected by Barclays Bank on 27.11.2018; LHG's correspondence alleging inflated valuation of plant and machinery (valued by RBSA at Rs. 1,284 Crores vs. vendor quotes of Rs. 400-500 Crores) and misrepresentations in the Information Memorandum regarding 66% inter-dependency on group companies[cite: 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CoC filed CA No. 567/2018 under Section 60(5) read with Section 74(3) seeking 90 days fresh CIRP period and prosecution of LHG; NCLT Chandigarh rejected the prayer for restarting CIRP on 13.02.2019 but gave liberty to lodge complaints with IBBI/Central Government[cite: 15].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can exclude time or extend the CIRP beyond the statutory 270 days to invite fresh resolution plans upon the failure of a successful resolution applicant to implement an approved plan, and whether the NCLT can directly refer a defaulting resolution applicant for prosecution under Section 74(3) without following natural justice under Section 424 and investigation procedures under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Non-implementation or willful default of an approved resolution plan after the expiry of the mandatory maximum 270-day CIRP period cannot serve as a ground to restart the resolution process or grant time extensions to invite fresh plans, leaving liquidation under Section 33 as the only permissible statutory recourse[cite: 15]; furthermore, referrals for criminal prosecution under Section 74(3) require adherence to principles of natural justice and procedural investigation under company law[cite: 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12 mandates strict adherence to the CIRP timeframe; upon default in implementing an approved resolution plan where 270 days have elapsed, Section 33(3) and (4) mandates liquidation; Section 236(2) bars courts from taking cognizance under Section 74(3) except upon a complaint by IBBI or Central Government, requiring the Tribunal under Section 424 to afford a hearing and utilize the investigative framework of Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 before prosecution is initiated[cite: 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applied statutory deadline verification confirming the lapse of 270 days without exceptional grounds for tolling, and evaluated whether alleged Information Memorandum discrepancies could legally excuse non-compliance under Section 31[cite: 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Re-tendering of the corporate debtor is impermissible post-270 days, directing the Adjudicating Authority to order liquidation while reserving investigation under Section 213 read with Section 74(3)[cite: 15].
summary.operative_order: All appeals are disposed of. The prayer of the CoC to exclude time and invite fresh resolution plans is rejected, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to pass an order of liquidation in accordance with law and Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15]. The blanket liberty granted by the NCLT to move IBBI/Central Government is set aside, granting liberty instead to apply under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Section 74(3) of the IBC before NCLT after notice and hearing[cite: 15]. No costs[cite: 15].
summary.summary: The Committee of Creditors of Amtek Auto Ltd. and Liberty House Group Pte Ltd. (LHG) cross-appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 13th February 2019[cite: 15]. LHG failed to implement the approved resolution plan, citing inflated asset valuations and flawed disclosures in the Information Memorandum[cite: 15]. The CoC sought a 90-day extension beyond the 270-day CIRP period to invite fresh plans[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that the statutory 270-day ceiling under Section 12 cannot be extended due to a resolution applicant's default, mandating that the NCLT initiate liquidation under Section 33[cite: 15]. The Tribunal also held that actions under Section 74(3) require compliance with natural justice under Section 424 and the investigative procedure under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 15].

summary.case_title: Oswal Greentech Ltd. & Ors. vs. Pankaj Oswal & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Oswal Greentech Ltd., Oswal Agro Mills Ltd., and Mrs. Aruna Oswal (widow) are Appellants; Mr. Pankaj Oswal (eldest son) is Respondent No. 1/Petitioner[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transmission and succession of 5,35,30,960 equity shares (approximately 40% equity stake) in Oswal Agro Mills Ltd. registered in the name of Late Mr. Abhey Kumar Oswal[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under IBC are inapplicable as the proceedings arise out of a company petition under Sections 241 and 242 alleging corporate oppression and mismanagement[cite: 16]. 4.
