STATUTORY TIMELINES: Nomination in Form SH-13 executed on 18.06.2015; shareholder expired intestate on 29.03.2016; shares transmitted to Mrs. Aruna Oswal on 16.04.2016; partition suit CS No. 53 of 2017 filed in Delhi High Court in February 2017 with status quo order on 08.02.2017; company petition filed on 16.03.2018[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered nomination under Section 72 favoring Mrs. Aruna Oswal; civil suit pleadings demonstrating Respondent No. 1 is one of four Class I legal heirs claiming 1/4th of the estate (13,382,740 shares / 9.97%), alongside his direct registered holding of 42,900 shares (0.03%), totaling over 10%[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 56/CHD/PB/2018 before NCLT Chandigarh; Appellants raised a preliminary objection on maintainability under Section 244 arguing Respondent No. 1 held only 0.03% registered shares; NCLT dismissed objections on 13.11.2018 holding the petition maintainable[cite: 16].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a nomination executed under Section 72 of the Companies Act, 2013 vests absolute beneficially indefeasible ownership of shares in the nominee to the complete exclusion of legal heirs under succession law, and whether a legal heir entitled on intestacy can maintain a petition for oppression and mismanagement under Section 241 read with Section 244 prior to formal entry in the register of members[cite: 16].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Nomination under company law is merely a mechanism for temporary fiduciary holding and does not create absolute beneficially indefeasible title in the nominee or override general succession laws; legal heirs inheriting shares by operation of law are entitled to maintain an action against oppression and mismanagement even prior to formal registration on the register of members[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 72 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Rule 19(8) allow the company to treat the nominee as holder for transmission and operational convenience, but the beneficial estate vests in the legal heirs under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956; applying the principle in World Wide Agencies, legal representatives representing the estate of a deceased member stand in the shoes of the member for the purposes of Sections 241 and 242, and qualify for waiver under Section 244(4) where estate division is sub judice[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether prima facie status as a Class I legal heir claiming a 1/4th undivided intestate interest, combined with registered shareholding, satisfied the proprietary threshold under Section 244[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The nominee holds shares in a fiduciary capacity for the legal heirs; Respondent No. 1 possesses requisite locus standi under Section 244 to maintain the petition, which is also a fit case for waiver under Section 244(4)[cite: 16].
summary.operative_order: The appeals are dismissed as devoid of merit. The order dated 13th November 2018 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench holding the petition maintainable is upheld. No order as to costs[cite: 16].
summary.summary: Oswal Greentech Ltd., Oswal Agro Mills Ltd., and Mrs. Aruna Oswal appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 13th November 2018 holding a petition under Sections 241 and 242 filed by Pankaj Oswal maintainable[cite: 16]. Appellants argued that Late Abhey Kumar Oswal had nominated Aruna Oswal under Section 72 of the Companies Act, 2013, making her the exclusive owner of his 5.35 crore shares, thereby reducing Pankaj Oswal's direct holding to 0.03%, well below the 10% threshold under Section 244[cite: 16]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, ruling that nomination does not confer beneficial title or abrogate succession laws[cite: 16]. Relying on World Wide Agencies, the Appellate Tribunal held that legal heirs represent the estate and can maintain oppression proceedings, also holding the case fit for waiver under Section 244(4)[cite: 16].

summary.case_title: Amritsar Swadeshi Woollen Mills Private Limited vs. Vinod Krishan Khanna & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amritsar Swadeshi Woollen Mills Private Limited is the Appellant (Company); Vinod Krishan Khanna, Vimal Krishan Khanna, Asha Khanna, Rahul Khanna, and Chandrakanta Khanna are Respondents/Original Petitioners; original Respondents Nos. 2 to 9 are majority shareholders[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Buy-out of minority shareholding to resolve a deadlock and terminate an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under IBC are inapplicable; the financial issue pertains to the determination of the fair valuation of shares at Rs. 10.35 per share as of 31.03.2007, with 9% simple interest awarded from 01.04.2007 until payment[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition filed on 14.03.2007; CLB order recording petitioners' willingness to exit on fair valuation passed on 01.04.2011; valuer substituted on 11.08.2011; valuation report submitted on 20.07.2012; CA No. 405/2012 filed on 09.08.2012; NCLT passed final impugned order on 08.06.2018[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation Report dated 20.07.2012 fixing fair value at Rs. 10.35 per share; company audited financial accounts showing accumulated post-tax profits of Rs. 2.15 Crores between 2012 and 2017 while respondents were excluded from dividends and management[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Petitioners filed CP No. 25/2007 before CLB alleging oppression; upon transfer, NCLT New Delhi Bench-3 disposed of the petition on 08.06.2018, directing Petitioners to sell their shares to the Respondents at Rs. 10.35 per share along with 9% simple interest per annum from 01.04.2007 until payment; the Company appealed against the interest award and clerical ambiguity regarding the purchasing parties[cite: 17].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT, while directing a minority buy-out under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, possesses the equitable jurisdiction to award interest on the fair valuation of shares from the valuation date when the preliminary exit order did not mention interest, and whether an appeal filed solely by the company enures to the benefit of non-appealing purchasing shareholders to correct clerical errors in the operative order[cite: 17].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In oppression and mismanagement proceedings under company law, the Tribunal exercises equitable jurisdiction under Section 242 and has inherent power to award reasonable interest on the share value from the valuation date to prevent unjust enrichment by the majority who utilized the company's funds; furthermore, the court has full authority to correct clerical drafting omissions to identify the actual individual purchasing shareholders[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242 confers wide powers to provide for any matter that is just and equitable; an interlocutory order directing valuation is not a final decree that extinguishes the court's equitable jurisdiction to grant restitutionary interest under the principles of Renuka Datla; Section 242(2)(b) and (c) distinguishes between share purchases by members and share buy-backs by the company, requiring explicit directions on capital reduction if the company itself were the purchaser[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the minority's valuation objections were bona fide and balanced commercial retention of funds against the financial return of the company, holding that 9% interest was excessive and adjusting it to 6%[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Grant of interest from the valuation date is legally justified, but to balance equities the interest rate is modified from 9% to 6% per annum, with the purchasing parties clarified as Respondents 2 to 9[cite: 17].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is partly allowed. The impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 8th June 2018 is modified: (i) Petitioners are directed to sell their shares to Respondents 2 to 9 (not the company) at the fair value of Rs. 10.35 per share; (ii) the interest rate awarded on the consideration from 01.04.2007 till payment is reduced from 9% to 6% per annum (simple interest); (iii) compliances to be carried out within 2 months before the Bench Officer. No costs[cite: 17].
summary.summary: Amritsar Swadeshi Woollen Mills Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 8th June 2018, which directed minority shareholders (the Khanna family) to exit the company by selling their shares at Rs. 10.35 per share along with 9% simple interest per annum from 1st April 2007[cite: 17]. The Appellant argued that the 2011 CLB order directing valuation was a consent order that did not provide for interest[cite: 17]. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Renuka Datla, the NCLAT held that the Tribunal has broad equitable powers under Section 242 to award interest on retained share value[cite: 17]. However, to balance equity, the NCLAT reduced the interest rate from 9% to 6% per annum and clarified that the purchasing parties were the individual majority shareholders (Respondents 2 to 9) rather than the company itself[cite: 17].

summary.case_title: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Tata Sons Ltd. & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd. and Sterling Investment Corp. Pvt. Ltd. (SP Group holding 18.37% equity) are Appellants; Tata Sons Ltd. is Respondent No. 1 Company; Ratan N. Tata is Respondent No. 2; Cyrus Pallonji Mistry is Respondent No. 11 (Appellant in companion appeal); Sir Dorabji Tata Trust and Sir Ratan Tata Trust (Tata Trusts holding 66% equity) and their nominee directors are Respondents[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Longstanding corporate governance, joint participation, and holding company structure governing Tata Sons Ltd. and operating subsidiaries across diverse global sectors[cite: 18]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under IBC are inapplicable; the matter concerns corporate oppression, directorial removal, and misuse of affirmative voting powers under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cyrus Mistry appointed Executive Chairman on 18.12.2012 (effective 29.12.2012); NRC unanimously praised his performance on 28.06.2016; suddenly removed without notice on 24.10.2016; subsequently removed as director from TCS, Tata Industries, and TTSL in December 2016; Tata Sons altered status to private company pendente lite via RoC letter[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of Board meeting dated 24.10.2016 showing non-agenda introduction of removal motion based on pre-decided Trust instructions without circulating legal opinions; statutory NRC report dated 28.06.2016 commending Mistry's performance; over 550 emails demonstrating interference by Ratan Tata and N.A. Soonawala in commercial transactions (Welspun acquisition, spectrum bidding, Docomo settlement); RoC endorsement converting company to private without NCLT sanction[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 82/2016 before NCLT Mumbai; following a waiver granted under Section 244 by NCLAT on 21.09.2017, NCLT dismissed the company petition on merits on 09.07.2018 with disparaging remarks; Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 18].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the sudden, unnotified removal of the Executive Chairman at the dictate of majority trust shareholders, pervasive interference in board affairs through affirmative voting clauses (Articles 121 and 121A), threatened abuse of Article 75 squeeze-out powers, and the conversion of a major public holding company into a private company without Tribunal approval constitute acts of oppression and mismanagement justifying relief under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 18].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The exercise of majority voting power and affirmative governance vetoes to operate as a 'super board', dictating executive dismissals without notice, undermining independent fiduciary duties, and converting public company status without statutory judicial sanction, constitutes conduct lacking probity that is prejudicial and oppressive under company law[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 encompass continuous prejudicial conduct affecting minority proprietary rights and company interests; winding up on just and equitable grounds was established, but since winding up would unfairly prejudice members, Section 242 remedies apply; Section 14 mandates that conversion of a public company into a private company requires an order of approval from the Tribunal, rendering administrative conversion by the Registrar of Companies illegal[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the chain of events established a consecutive pattern of oppressive interference, relying on the contemporaneous favorable NRC appraisal, board minutes showing pre-orchestrated ouster without notice, and email communications showing pervasive interference by non-board trustees[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The removal of Cyrus Mistry was illegal and oppressive, the conversion to a private company was void for lack of NCLT approval under Section 14, and the company's affairs were conducted in a manner prejudicial to minority shareholders, necessitating reinstatement and protective restrictions against Article 75[cite: 18].
summary.operative_order: Both appeals are allowed. The NCLT Mumbai judgment dated 9th July 2018 is set aside, and all disparaging remarks against Appellants are expunged[cite: 18]. Cyrus Pallonji Mistry is restored to his original position as Executive Chairman of Tata Sons Ltd. and as Director of group companies for the remainder of his tenure (reinstatement as Executive Chairman suspended for 4 weeks)[cite: 18]. The appointment of the replacement Executive Chairman is declared illegal[cite: 18]. Ratan N. Tata and the nominee directors of Tata Trusts are directed to desist from taking advance decisions requiring board approval[cite: 18]. Article 75 squeeze-out powers shall not be exercised against the minority shareholders except under exceptional, recorded circumstances[cite: 18]. The conversion of Tata Sons Ltd. into a private company by the Registrar of Companies is declared illegal and set aside, restoring its status as a Public Company[cite: 18]. No costs[cite: 18].
summary.summary: Cyrus Investments Pvt. Ltd., Sterling Investment Corp., and Cyrus Pallonji Mistry appealed against the NCLT Mumbai judgment dated 9th July 2018 dismissing their petition under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 against Tata Sons Ltd. and its majority trustees[cite: 18]. The Appellants challenged Mistry's abrupt removal as Executive Chairman on 24th October 2016, pervasive interference in board affairs through affirmative voting clauses (Articles 121 and 121A), threatened squeeze-outs under Article 75, and the company's conversion into a private entity[cite: 18]. Setting aside the NCLT judgment, the NCLAT held that the actions of the majority and trust nominees were oppressive and prejudicial to corporate governance[cite: 18]. The Appellate Tribunal declared Mistry's removal illegal, restored him as Executive Chairman and Director, restrained the misuse of Article 75, and quashed the conversion to a private company for non-compliance with Section 14[cite: 18].

summary.case_title: Shailesh Sangani vs. Joel Cardoso & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shailesh Sangani is the Promoter, Shareholder, and Director of the Corporate Debtor (Appellant); Joel Cardoso is the Shareholder and Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Priority Marketing Private Limited is the Corporate Debtor (Respondent No. 2)[cite: 19]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Advancement of interest-free unsecured loans repayable on demand by Respondent No. 1 to the Corporate Debtor between 01.04.2002 and 29.11.2007 to fund company operations and meet working capital requirements[cite: 19]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total unsecured loan advanced was Rs. 3,23,46,475/-; part repayments of Rs. 1,78,10,100/- were made between 2008 and 2010, leaving an outstanding balance of Rs. 1,45,36,475/-; default occurred upon failure to comply with the demand notice[cite: 19]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Unsecured loans advanced between 01.04.2002 and 29.11.2007; balance confirmed on 01.04.2016; auditor confirmation emailed on 05.12.2017; demand notice served; Section 7 petition admitted on 31.08.2018[cite: 19]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's Balance Sheet for 2009 recording the loan under 'unsecured loans'; balance confirmation of accounts dated 01.04.2016 for Rs. 1,45,36,475/-; Balance Sheet as of 31.03.2017 recording non-current liability of Rs. 4,72,76,182/- under 'long term borrowings'; confirmation letter dated 05.12.2017 issued by Statutory Auditor Ganesh Mehta[cite: 19]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP No. 1732/I&BP/2018 under Section 7 of the IBC before NCLT Mumbai Bench; NCLT admitted the petition on 31.08.2018, holding the debt fell within 'long term borrowings'; Appellant appealed arguing an interest-free loan lacks the 'time value of money'[cite: 19].
summary.legal_issues: Whether an interest-free unsecured loan advanced by a shareholder or promoter to a corporate debtor to sustain business operations constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the 'time value of money' under Section 5(8)(f) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016[cite: 19].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The payment of interest is not an indispensable prerequisite for a debt to constitute a 'financial debt' under the IBC; funds infused by a stakeholder to protect and enhance the corporate debtor's business prospects constitute a transaction having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f), where the time value of money is reflected in business survival and asset growth[cite: 19]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The suffix 'if any' to the term 'interest' in Section 5(8) establishes that financial debt encompasses both interest-bearing and interest-free disbursements; under Section 5(8)(f), funds raised by an enterprise to overcome liquidity crises have the commercial effect of a borrowing, and the resulting economic enhancement, production increase, and share value growth accrue to the stakeholder as the consideration for the time value of money[cite: 19]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examined company financial statements, auditor balance confirmations, and general ledger records to determine whether the transaction was treated as long-term borrowings rather than equity capital or a non-refundable gift[cite: 19]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The interest-free unsecured loan was classified as a long-term borrowing in the debtor's books and satisfies Section 5(8)(f), rendering Respondent No. 1 a Financial Creditor entitled to initiate CIRP under Section 7[cite: 19].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit. The order dated 31st August 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP against Priority Marketing Private Limited is affirmed. No order as to costs[cite: 19].
summary.summary: Shailesh Sangani, director of Priority Marketing Private Limited, appealed against an order of NCLT Mumbai dated 31st August 2018 admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by Joel Cardoso[cite: 19]. Cardoso had extended interest-free unsecured loans amounting to Rs. 3.23 Crores, of which Rs. 1.45 Crores remained unpaid[cite: 19]. The Appellant contended that an interest-free loan lacked consideration for the time value of money and could not be classified as a financial debt under Section 5(8)[cite: 19]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that interest is not mandatory for a financial debt[cite: 19]. When a stakeholder infuses funds to support the company, the transaction has the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f), and the preservation and growth of company value satisfy the requirement of time value of money[cite: 19].

summary.case_title: Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal vs. M/s. Piramal Enterprises Ltd.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal is the Appellant Shareholder of the Corporate Guarantors; All India Society for Advance Education and Research is the Principal Borrower; M/s. Piramal Enterprises Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Sunrise Naturopathy and Resorts Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Guarantor No. 1; Sunsystem Institute of Information Technology Pvt. Ltd. is Corporate Guarantor No. 2[cite: 20]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 38,00,00,000/- sanctioned and disbursed in two tranches (28.10.2013 and 01.11.2013) by the Financial Creditor to the Principal Borrower, guaranteed by both Corporate Guarantors[cite: 20]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed default amount was Rs. 40,28,76,461/- with the date of default identified as 11.11.2017, after the Principal Borrower had repaid over Rs. 22 Crores[cite: 20]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Civil Suit filed on 15.09.2017; simultaneous demand notices issued to both Corporate Guarantors on 24.10.2017 and 26.10.2017 calling for repayment within 15 days; Section 7 applications filed thereafter[cite: 20]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Agreement dated 18.10.2013, guarantee documents, identical Form-1 filings against both corporate guarantors, and demand notices[cite: 20]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi admitted CP No. (IB)-65(PB)/2018 against Corporate Guarantor No. 2 on 24.05.2018 and subsequently admitted CP No. (IB)-66(PB)/2018 against Corporate Guarantor No. 1 on 31.05.2018[cite: 20].
summary.legal_issues: Whether Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the IBC can be initiated against a Corporate Guarantor without proceeding against the Principal Borrower, and whether simultaneous or consecutive Section 7 applications can be admitted against two Corporate Guarantors for the exact same underlying financial debt and default[cite: 20].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a financial creditor may proceed against a corporate guarantor without initiating insolvency against the principal debtor, once a Section 7 petition is admitted against one corporate guarantor for a specific financial debt, a second insolvency petition cannot be admitted against another corporate guarantor for the identical debt and default[cite: 20]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Counter-indemnity obligations under Section 5(8)(h) constitute financial debts, entitling the creditor to invoke Section 7 against a guarantor without first proceeding against the principal borrower; however, because the same claim cannot be lodged simultaneously before multiple resolution professionals in separate CIRPs, consecutive admission of petitions for the identical debt against co-guarantors is legally impermissible[cite: 20]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the claim metrics in Form-1 against both entities were identical in respect of debt amount, date of default, and underlying loan agreements, establishing duplicate initiation for the identical liability[cite: 20]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The admission of CIRP against the first Corporate Guarantor exhausted the right to trigger CIRP for the same debt, rendering the subsequent admission against the second Corporate Guarantor invalid[cite: 20].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 346 of 2018 is dismissed, upholding the CIRP initiation against Sunsystem Institute of Information Technology Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 20]. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 347 of 2018 is allowed, setting aside the admission order dated 31.05.2018 against Sunrise Naturopathy and Resorts Pvt. Ltd., releasing it from the rigors of moratorium and CIRP[cite: 20]. No costs[cite: 20].
summary.summary: Dr. Vishnu Kumar Agarwal, shareholder of two corporate guarantors, challenged separate NCLT orders admitting Section 7 applications filed by Piramal Enterprises Ltd. for the same loan default[cite: 20]. The loan of Rs. 38 Crores disbursed to the principal borrower had been guaranteed by two corporate entities[cite: 20]. The NCLAT held that although a financial creditor may initiate CIRP against a corporate guarantor without proceeding against the principal debtor, it cannot maintain two separate CIRP applications for the same debt and default[cite: 20]. Having admitted CIRP against the first guarantor on 24th May 2018, the subsequent admission against the second guarantor on 31st May 2018 was impermissible and set aside[cite: 20].

summary.case_title: Gouri Prasad Goenka vs. Punjab National Bank & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gouri Prasad Goenka is the Appellant and Ex-Chairman of the Corporate Debtor; Punjab National Bank is the Financial Creditor (Respondent No. 1); Vikas Prakash Gupta is the Interim Resolution Professional; NRC Limited is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Working capital fund-based, non-fund-based, and term loan facilities extended by PNB to NRC Limited beginning 23.02.2005, enhanced on 02.05.2006, and restructured on 10.03.2008 and 30.12.2008[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed as of 31.03.2018 was Rs. 273,09,68,793/- after SARFAESI notice under Section 13(2) demanded Rs. 78,31,57,403/- as of 11.02.2010[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor declared a Sick Industrial Unit by BIFR on 16.07.2009; SICA repealed and Section 7 of IBC enforced on 01.12.2016; OTS proposal letter sent on 04.08.2018; Section 7 petition filed in May 2018[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: BIFR order dated 16.07.2009 granting Section 22(1) protection, loan agreements, banker's book certificates, and written OTS proposal letter dated 04.08.2018 offering settlement[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: PNB filed CP (IB) No. 1886/MB/2018 before NCLT Mumbai; NCLT admitted the petition on 27.11.2018, holding the authority of the signatory valid and debt defaulted; Appellant appealed on the ground of statutory limitation[cite: 21].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the period during which an inquiry or scheme was pending under the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985 is excluded under Section 22(5) of SICA for computing limitation under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for a Section 7 IBC petition, and whether a written OTS proposal constitutes a fresh acknowledgment under Section 18[cite: 21].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory suspension of legal remedies during the pendency of proceedings before the BIFR under Section 22(1) of SICA must be excluded under Section 22(5) when computing the three-year limitation period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act for filing an insolvency application; further, an unexpired written acknowledgment under Section 18 renews limitation[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 22(5) of SICA expressly excludes the duration when the creditor's right of enforcement remained suspended, running from the BIFR declaration (16.07.2009) until the enforcement of Section 7 of the IBC on 01.12.2016; an application filed within three years of that date is timely, supported additionally by written acknowledgments under Section 18(1)[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examined the BIFR register of proceedings, the date of IBC notification, and the Corporate Debtor's written settlement letters to determine the continuity of an enforceable financial liability[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding the SICA period from 16.07.2009 to 01.12.2016, and considering the debtor's written acknowledgment on 04.08.2018, the Section 7 application filed in May 2018 was well within the statutory limitation period[cite: 21].
summary.operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as devoid of merit. The order of admission dated 27th November, 2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in CP (IB) No. 1886/MB/2018 is upheld. No order as to costs[cite: 21].
summary.summary: Gouri Prasad Goenka, ex-chairman of NRC Limited, appealed the NCLT Mumbai order dated 27th November 2018 admitting Punjab National Bank's Section 7 IBC application for outstanding dues of Rs. 273 Crores, asserting that the debt was time-barred[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the period between 16th July 2009 and 1st December 2016 stood excluded under Section 22(5) of SICA due to the statutory suspension of legal proceedings while the company was before the BIFR[cite: 21]. Additionally, the Corporate Debtor's written OTS proposal dated 4th August 2018 operated as a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, keeping the petition within limitation[cite: 21].

summary.case_title: Padmanabhan Venkatesh vs. Shri V. Venkatachalam & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Padmanabhan Venkatesh is the Promoter of the Corporate Debtor; Indian Bank is the Dissenting Financial Creditor; Maharashtra Seamless Ltd. (MSL) is the Resolution Applicant; V. Venkatachalam is the Resolution Professional; United Seamless Tubulaar Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Manufacturing plant for seamless pipes financed by term loans of Rs. 1652 Crores from Deutsche Bank and working capital borrowings of Rs. 245 Crores from Indian Bank[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total admitted financial debt was over Rs. 1897 Crores (acknowledged claims over Rs. 2060 Crores); liquidation value was determined by CoC at an average of Rs. 597.54 Crores; MSL offered an upfront payout of Rs. 477 Crores[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved MSL's plan on 20.04.2018 with 87.10% voting share; revised liquidation value recorded on 16.10.2018; NCLT approved plan on 21.01.2019; implementation order passed on 28.02.2019[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports of K. Vijay Bhaskar Reddy (Rs. 681 Cr), P. Madhu (Rs. 513 Cr), and third valuer Duff & Phelps (Rs. 352 Cr); CoC 9th meeting minutes adopting average liquidation value of Rs. 597.54 Crores; resolution plan proposing 25% payout to financial creditors and lower/nil allocation to operational creditors[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad approved MSL's plan on 21.01.2019; Promoter and Indian Bank appealed against the undervaluation and operational creditor discrimination; MSL appealed against NCLT's refusal to direct police assistance for plant possession[cite: 22].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan offering an upfront payment lower than the liquidation value and providing discriminatory treatment to operational creditors can be approved under Section 30(2) and Section 31 of the IBC, and whether the appellate authority can direct modification of the upfront amount to match the liquidation value[cite: 22].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A resolution plan must aim at asset maximization and cannot offer an upfront payout below the established liquidation value of the corporate debtor to acquire assets at a discount; operational creditors must be accorded fair and equitable treatment on par with financial creditors[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) read with amended Regulation 38 requires that operational creditors be protected and given priority, ensuring they receive not less than their proportionate liquidation share and roughly equitable parity with financial creditors; Section 31 requires adherence to statutory objects, empowering the Tribunal to condition approval upon augmenting upfront consideration to the liquidation value[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contrasted the resolution applicant's proposed upfront consideration of Rs. 477 Crores against the CoC-accepted average liquidation value of Rs. 597.54 Crores, determining an impermissible deficit of Rs. 120.54 Crores[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan was discriminatory and below liquidation value; MSL was required to enhance its upfront consideration to Rs. 597.54 Crores and provide 25% to operational creditors, failing which the approval would be vacated[cite: 22].
summary.operative_order: Appeals are disposed of with directions: MSL is directed to increase its upfront payment from Rs. 477 Crores to Rs. 597.54 Crores (an additional Rs. 120.54 Crores) within 30 days into escrow, distributing it proportionately between Financial and Operational Creditors at an equal 25% ratio[cite: 22]. Upon deposit, MSL shall receive possession; on failure to deposit, the approval order shall stand set aside for NCLT to pass consequential orders[cite: 22]. Resolution Professional directed to take interim physical custody with police assistance[cite: 22]. No costs[cite: 22].
summary.summary: Padmanabhan Venkatesh (promoter) and Indian Bank appealed the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 21st January 2019 approving Maharashtra Seamless Ltd.'s (MSL) resolution plan for United Seamless Tubulaar Pvt. Ltd., while MSL appealed seeking plant possession[cite: 22]. Appellants argued that the upfront bid of Rs. 477 Crores was substantially lower than the CoC's liquidation valuation of Rs. 597.54 Crores and discriminated against operational creditors[cite: 22]. The NCLAT held that a resolution applicant cannot acquire the corporate debtor below its liquidation value and must treat operational creditors equitably[cite: 22]. The Tribunal directed MSL to deposit an additional Rs. 120.54 Crores within 30 days to match the Rs. 597.54 Crore liquidation value, failing which the plan would stand set aside[cite: 22].

summary.case_title: S.C. Sekaran vs. Amit Gupta & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: S.C. Sekaran is the Appellant representing the management of the Corporate Debtors; Amit Gupta is the Liquidator/Resolution Professional; Hindustan Dorr-Oliver Limited and HDO Technologies Limited are the Corporate Debtors[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Industrial equipment engineering, manufacturing, and technology enterprises undergoing CIRP where submitted resolution plans were withdrawn[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics under banking and credit facilities initiated CIRP; with no viable plan approved at the end of the CIRP timeline, liquidation was ordered under Section 33(1)[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plans originally submitted by Eight Finance Pvt. Ltd. and Pennar Industries Ltd. were withdrawn; NCLT Mumbai Bench passed liquidation orders on 25.06.2018; appeal filed immediately thereafter[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Withdrawal statements of prospective bidders Eight Finance and Pennar Industries, combined with substantial ongoing manufacturing infrastructure and employment rolls requiring preservation as a going concern[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai ordered liquidation of both companies under Section 33(1) on 25.06.2018; management appealed praying that the liquidator be directed to preserve the companies as going concerns and explore a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 24].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a Liquidator appointed under Section 33 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is mandated to explore revival of the Corporate Debtor by taking recourse to a Scheme of Compromise or Arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 before proceeding to dismantle and sell off company assets[cite: 24].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Liquidation under the IBC is an absolute measure of last resort; during the liquidation stage, the liquidator must take steps to keep the corporate debtor a going concern and explore compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 before proceeding with piecemeal sale of assets[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 applies to companies in liquidation under the IBC pursuant to Section 230(1); relying on Meghal Homes and Swiss Ribbons, preserving the enterprise and averting corporate death takes statutory priority over immediate dissolution[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Evaluated whether the operational assets and ongoing structure permitted revival, balancing the failure of CIRP against the opportunity for stakeholders to present a Section 230 compromise within a strict time limit[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator must pursue compromise or arrangement under Section 230 within a 90-day window, followed by a going-concern sale of the enterprise, resorting to asset sales only upon total failure of revival[cite: 24].
summary.operative_order: Appeals are disposed of with directions: While declining to interfere with the liquidation orders dated 25.06.2018, the Liquidator is directed to first take steps under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 to effect a compromise or arrangement within 90 days[cite: 24]. Pendency of prior appeals (12.07.2018 to date) excluded from the liquidation period[cite: 24]. Only upon failure of compromise and going-concern sale may asset liquidation proceed[cite: 24]. No costs[cite: 24].
summary.summary: The management of Hindustan Dorr-Oliver Limited and HDO Technologies Limited appealed against the NCLT Mumbai liquidation orders dated 25th June 2018 passed after resolution applicants withdrew their bids[cite: 24]. The Appellants requested directions for the liquidator to maintain the companies as going concerns and explore a scheme under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 24]. Reaffirming the principle from Swiss Ribbons and Meghal Homes that liquidation is a last resort, the NCLAT directed the liquidator to complete a Section 230 compromise or arrangement process within 90 days[cite: 24]. Piecemeal sale of company assets was permitted only upon failure to achieve revival or a sale as a going concern[cite: 24].

summary.case_title: Jindal Steel and Power Limited vs. Arun Kumar Jagatramka & Anr.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jindal Steel and Power Limited, an unsecured creditor of the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 is Arun Kumar Jagatramka, erstwhile promoter and shareholder of Corporate Debtor Gujarat NRE Coke Limited; Respondent No. 2 is Gujarat NRE Coke Limited represented through Liquidator Sumit Binani[cite: 11]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) was initiated under Section 7 of the IBC on 07.04.2017 upon the Corporate Debtor's own application due to severe default in honoring debt obligations[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics were not specified, but the corporate debtor defaulted extensively on dues owed to secured and unsecured lenders, culminating in failure to obtain an acceptable resolution plan within the 270-day CIRP period[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 07.04.2017; order of liquidation passed under Section 33 on 11.01.2018 upon expiry of 270 days; Promoter's appeal against liquidation [Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 55-56 of 2018] was dismissed allowing liquidation to continue; Promoter filed C.A. (CAA) No. 198/KB/2018 under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Respondent No. 1, an erstwhile promoter ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC to submit a resolution plan during CIRP, proposed a financial scheme of compromise and arrangement with creditors and members under Section 230 of the Companies Act during the liquidation phase[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench, by order dated 15.05.2018 in C.A. (CAA) No. 198/KB/2018, entertained the promoter's application and ordered steps to convene meetings and formulate a scheme of compromise and arrangement between the promoter, corporate debtor, and creditors[cite: 11]; Appellant appealed under Section 421 of the Companies Act[cite: 11].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a scheme of compromise and arrangement under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable during a liquidation proceeding under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; and whether an erstwhile promoter who is barred under Section 29A of the IBC from submitting a resolution plan is legally eligible to propose a compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 to regain control of the corporate debtor[cite: 11].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While a scheme of compromise and arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 is legally permissible during liquidation under the IBC to facilitate revival as a going concern, a promoter or person who suffers from statutory ineligibility under Section 29A of the IBC is disqualified from proposing such a scheme[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 harmoniously with the objects of the IBC and the proviso to Section 35(1)(f) of the IBC—which strictly prohibits the liquidator from selling debtor assets to anyone ineligible to be a resolution applicant—the disqualifications enumerated under Section 29A apply to schemes of compromise and arrangement during liquidation[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: In accordance with the Supreme Court's ruling in Swiss Ribbons, the primary legislative objective is to protect the corporate debtor from corporate death and from its own erstwhile management; therefore, an applicant ineligible under Section 29A cannot utilize Section 230 to achieve indirectly what is expressly barred under the Code[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Respondent No. 1 was disqualified under Section 29A of the IBC, his application under Sections 230 to 232 of the Companies Act was non-maintainable and should have been rejected at the threshold[cite: 11].
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 15.05.2018 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in C.A. (CAA) No. 198/KB/2018 is set aside; the matter is remitted to the Liquidator and the Adjudicating Authority to proceed with liquidation in accordance with the law and the principles enunciated in Y. Shivram Prasad; no order as to costs[cite: 11].
summary.summary: Jindal Steel and Power Limited appealed against an order of NCLT Kolkata Bench that entertained an application under Sections 230–232 of the Companies Act, 2013 filed by Arun Kumar Jagatramka, erstwhile promoter of Gujarat NRE Coke Limited (in liquidation), proposing a scheme of compromise and arrangement[cite: 11]. The Appellant contended that the promoter was ineligible under Section 29A of the IBC[cite: 11]. NCLAT held that while Section 230 schemes are permissible during liquidation, the statutory bar under Section 29A read with the proviso to Section 35(1)(f) applies equally to prevent ineligible promoters from regaining company assets through schemes of arrangement[cite: 11]. Consequently, NCLAT allowed the appeal and quashed the NCLT's order[cite: 11].

summary.case_title: V Hotels Limited vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is V Hotels Limited (Corporate Debtor), with co-appellant Tulip Star Hotels Ltd.; Respondent is Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Limited (ARCIL, Financial Creditor/Assignee of Bank of India)[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 129 Crores originally sanctioned under Loan Agreement dated 08.03.2002 by a consortium led by Bank of India, subsequently restructured via ECB arrangement and converted into a non-fund bank guarantee facility under Deed of Variation dated 15.09.2003[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Bank guarantee was invoked on 02.09.2008 where Bank of India disbursed Rs. 24,49,59,208/-; persistent defaults led to the Corporate Debtor's account being declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 01.12.2008; debt was assigned to ARCIL on 31.12.2008; claimed default escalated to Rs. 235,46,34,381/- (principal plus interest at 22%)[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified NPA on 01.12.2008; settlement talks failed and ARCIL issued Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 10.07.2013; Corporate Debtor made various court-ordered deposits in DRT/DRAT/Bombay High Court proceedings totaling over Rs. 72 Crores up to 21.07.2017; Section 7 IBC application was filed on 03.04.2018[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ARCIL relied on Section 18 of the Limitation Act, citing letters such as one dated 17.03.2012 acknowledging outstanding settlement liability, entries in books of accounts, and Article 62 of the Limitation Act claiming a 12-year period for mortgage enforcement; Corporate Debtor proved that the NPA occurred on 01.12.2008 and that no valid written acknowledgment of liability occurred before the 3-year limitation period expired in December 2011[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench rejected the Corporate Debtor's maintainability objections (MA 693/2018) on 01.05.2019 and admitted the Section 7 application on 31.05.2019, holding that the application was within the 12-year limitation period under Article 62; Corporate Debtor and its shareholder appealed[cite: 12].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the period of limitation for filing an application under Section 7 of the IBC is governed by Article 137 (three years from date of default/NPA) or Article 62 (twelve years for mortgage enforcement) of the Limitation Act, 1963; and whether an acknowledgment of liability under Section 18 made after the initial 3-year limitation period had already expired can revive a time-barred debt for IBC initiation[cite: 12].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications under Section 7 of the IBC are governed exclusively by Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requiring the application to be filed within three years from the date default occurred (date of NPA); Article 62 applies solely to suits for enforcing mortgaged property and has no application to Section 7 petitions[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 238A of the IBC read with Supreme Court rulings in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave and B.K. Educational Services, the IBC is not a money recovery suit, and time begins to run from the date of default/NPA[cite: 12]. Parallel recovery proceedings under SARFAESI or before DRT do not extend limitation under the IBC[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, an acknowledgment in writing must be made before the expiration of the prescribed period of limitation; any acknowledgment made after the three-year period has lapsed is ineffective to revive the debt[cite: 12]. Furthermore, mere entries in books of accounts without specific signed acknowledgment do not extend limitation[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Default occurred when the account was declared NPA on 01.12.2008, causing limitation to expire in December 2011; because the Section 7 petition was filed only on 03.04.2018 without any valid acknowledgment prior to December 2011, the claim was barred by limitation[cite: 12].
summary.operative_order: The impugned orders dated 01.05.2019 and 31.05.2019 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting the Section 7 petition are set aside; V Hotels Limited is released from the rigours of CIRP to function under its Board of Directors; the IRP/RP shall handover management and assets, with CIRP fees and costs to be determined by NCLT and borne by ARCIL; both appeals are allowed with no order as to costs[cite: 12].
summary.summary: V Hotels Limited and shareholder Tulip Star Hotels Ltd. challenged orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench admitting a Section 7 IBC application filed by ARCIL on 03.04.2018 for recovery of debts assigned by Bank of India[cite: 12]. The loan had been declared an NPA on 01.12.2008[cite: 12]. NCLT admitted the petition holding that a 12-year limitation period under Article 62 applied to mortgaged debts[cite: 12]. Relying on Supreme Court precedents in Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave and Jignesh Shah, NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that Article 137 governs Section 7 applications, prescribing a strict 3-year limitation from the date of NPA[cite: 12]. Holding that acknowledgments after December 2011 could not revive an expired debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, NCLAT quashed the CIRP[cite: 12].

summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Amit Gupta, Promoter and 93.30% Shareholder of Corporate Debtor M/s Varanasi Auto Sales Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent is Yogesh Gupta, Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was an automobile dealership entity whose commercial agency agreement with Tata Motors was terminated in August 2017[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Commercial defaults prompted the Corporate Debtor to voluntarily initiate insolvency resolution[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 10 application was admitted on 26.04.2018; RP published Invitation for Expression of Interest (EOI) fixing deadline as 12:00 Noon on 18.08.2018; Appellant sent an informal email bidding for resolution at 12:07 PM on 18.08.2018; CoC reviewed and rejected the submission on 21.08.2018; RP formally notified deficiency on 27.08.2018; Appellant filed CA No. 259/2018 before NCLT on 19.10.2018[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant's submission comprised an email merely attaching PAN card and three years of ITRs, omitting mandatory undertakings under Regulation 36A (including criteria compliance and Section 29A eligibility); Appellant belatedly produced an unverified MSME acknowledgement form dated 30.03.2009 containing express disclaimers that it conferred no legal rights, while failing to provide any statutory MSME Memorandum Certificate[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench, by order dated 09.08.2019 in CA No. 259/2018, dismissed Appellant's application seeking cancellation of EOI and issuance of a revised EOI, holding that Corporate Debtor failed to establish MSME status and non-compliant bids submitted past deadline could not be entertained[cite: 13].
summary.legal_issues: Whether a promoter disqualified under Section 29A can claim statutory exemption under Section 240A without proving MSME registration by producing a valid Memorandum Certificate; whether an informal email submitted after the deadline without mandatory undertakings qualifies as a valid EOI under Regulation 36A; and whether admission of a Section 10 petition prior to the June 2018 amendment is invalid for want of an AGM/EGM special resolution[cite: 13].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under the summary, time-bound framework of the IBC, a Resolution Applicant claiming exemption under Section 240A from Section 29A disqualifications must affirmatively furnish an official MSME Memorandum Certificate; neither the RP nor the Adjudicating Authority is required to conduct factual investigations into accounts to assess MSME status under Section 7 of the MSMED Act, 2006[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36A(6) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations mandates rejection of any EOI received after the specified deadline; furthermore, under Regulation 36A(7), an EOI must be unconditional and accompanied by explicit undertakings of eligibility and criteria compliance[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unverified submission form or acknowledgement bearing express caveats cannot substantiate MSME classification[cite: 13]. Similarly, Section 10(3)(c) requiring shareholder approval introduced by amendment on 06.06.2018 does not apply retrospectively to Section 10 applications admitted prior to that date[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Appellant failed to submit a compliant EOI within the prescribed deadline, failed to establish MSME status to claim Section 240A relief, and abused IBC proceedings, justifying dismissal of the appeal[cite: 13].
summary.operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 903 of 2019 is rejected and dismissed, affirming the order dated 09.08.2019 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench in CA No. 259/2018; no order as to costs[cite: 13].
summary.summary: Amit Gupta, promoter and majority shareholder of Varanasi Auto Sales Pvt. Ltd., appealed an order of NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissing his application to direct the RP to issue a revised Expression of Interest (EOI)[cite: 13]. The Appellant had sent an email after the 12:00 Noon deadline on 18.08.2018 attaching only ITRs and PAN, subsequently claiming MSME exemption under Section 240A from Section 29A disqualification[cite: 13]. NCLAT held that EOI submissions must strictly adhere to Regulation 36A timelines and mandatory undertakings[cite: 13]. It ruled that a party claiming Section 240A benefits must provide a formal MSME Memorandum Certificate, as RPs cannot conduct detailed accounting inquiries[cite: 13]. Finding no procedural flaw or retrospective application of amended Section 10, NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 13].

summary.case_title: Lagadapati Ramesh vs. Mrs. Ramanathan Bhuvaneshwari & Ors.
summary.material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Lagadapati Ramesh (Promoter of Corporate Debtor) in Appeal No. 574/2019, alongside Commune Properties India Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. (Group Companies) in Appeal No. 592/2019; Respondent is Mrs. Ramanathan Bhuvaneshwari, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Bhuvana Infra Projects Private Limited[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was incorporated in 2011 as an exclusive subcontracting construction arm for its group companies (Golden Gate Properties Ltd., Prisha Properties India Pvt. Ltd., and Commune Properties India Pvt. Ltd.)[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Forensic audit and audited financial statements for FY 2017-18 revealed fraudulent siphoning and diversion totaling Rs. 46,11,63,402/- comprising overdue net receivables of Rs. 32,20,64,568/-, diverted company assets worth Rs. 1,51,76,560/-, unverified missing assets of Rs. 74,41,849/-, siphoned scrap sales of Rs. 2,23,57,233/-, and un-invoiced consumed inventory written off amounting to Rs. 9,41,23,192/-[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 CIRP admitted on 17.01.2018 in C.P. (IB) No. 122/BB/2017; RP filed I.A. No. 446/2018 under Section 66 read with Sections 25(2), 69, and 70 of the IBC to attach personal assets of promoters and recover dues; NCLT passed impugned order on 16.04.2019[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP submitted forensic audit report dated 14.12.2018 demonstrating that the debtor had been turned into an asset-less shell company with zero employees and diverted capital, while promoters refused to surrender records and assets under Section 25(2); Appellants countered that outstanding amounts represented retention moneys undergoing reconciliation[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench, by order dated 16.04.2019 in I.A. No. 446/2018, invoked Sections 212 and 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 and directly ordered the Central Government to refer the investigation of the Corporate Debtor, group entities, Bank of Maharashtra officials, and promoters straight to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO)[cite: 14].
summary.legal_issues: Whether the NCLT sitting as the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC possesses statutory power under Section 212 of the Companies Act, 2013 to directly mandate an investigation by the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO); and what constitutes the correct legal procedure when an Adjudicating Authority discovers fraudulent transactions under Section 66 and penal offences under Sections 68 to 73 of the IBC[cite: 14].
summary.ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority/NCLT lacks jurisdiction under Section 212 of the Companies Act, 2013 to directly refer a matter to the SFIO; its investigative power is restricted to Section 213, where it may recommend an investigation by an Inspector appointed by the Central Government[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 212 reserves the power to initiate an SFIO probe exclusively to the Central Government upon satisfaction of specified statutory conditions; the Tribunal may only trigger an investigation under Section 213(b) by requesting the Central Government to appoint Inspectors[cite: 14]. Only if the Inspector's report uncovers serious fraud may the Central Government refer the case to the SFIO, which may ultimately culminate in prosecution before a Special Court under Section 236 of the IBC or Section 435 of the Companies Act[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: While the Adjudicating Authority can order contribution to debtor assets under Section 66, it cannot directly impose penal sanctions or prison sentences under Sections 68-73, as criminal prosecution requires complaint filing under Section 236(2) and trial by a Special Court[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in directly assigning an investigation to the SFIO under Section 212; the order must be modified to direct the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, to appoint Inspectors under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 14].
summary.operative_order: The impugned order dated 16.04.2019 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench is modified; the direction mandating an immediate SFIO investigation is set aside, and the matter is referred to the Secretary, Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India, to cause an investigation through an Inspector or Inspectors under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 to determine whether offences under Sections 68 to 73 of the IBC have occurred, with liberty to the Central Government to entrust the case subsequently to SFIO if warranted; both appeals stand disposed of with no costs[cite: 14].
summary.summary: Promoters and group entities of Corporate Debtor Bhuvana Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an order of NCLT Bengaluru Bench in an application under Section 66 of the IBC directly ordering the Central Government to refer the Corporate Debtor, its promoters, and bank officials to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) for fraud exceeding Rs. 46 Crores[cite: 14]. NCLAT held that the NCLT has no jurisdiction under Section 212 of the Companies Act to directly order an SFIO investigation[cite: 14]. The Tribunal's authority is limited to Section 213, whereby it may refer suspected fraud to the Central Government to appoint Inspectors, and only the Central Government can subsequently decide whether to assign the case to SFIO or pursue prosecution before a Special Court under Section 236 of the IBC[cite: 14]. NCLAT accordingly modified the order[cite: 14].
